Title: Checking Host Clock and Timestamps
Version: 4.0
Owner: Systems Reliability (Priya Nandan)
Last updated: 2024-10-05

OVERVIEW
========

The oauthsvc package runs on workstations and small hosts with a loopback HTTP service and SQLite database file. Accurate host clock time is critical for interpreting console log files, understanding when events occurred, and correlating timestamps across multiple services. This page explains how to verify host clock accuracy, diagnose clock skew, diagnose why console log timestamps may appear incorrect, and understand the relationships between host time, service logs, and database file metadata.

Your host's system clock drives all timestamps in console output, file modification times, and database records. If the clock drifts significantly or jumps, log entries become unreliable for debugging and incident response. This runbook covers clock verification procedures, common drift causes, restoration steps, and how to correctly read timestamps from logs after ensuring the clock is accurate.

WHY HOST CLOCK MATTERS (Priya Nandan)
====================================

The service writes all console log entries with the host system clock time. When you later read those files to diagnose issues, you rely on those timestamps to reconstruct what happened and when. A drifted clock makes this reconstruction difficult or impossible.

Beyond logs, the SQLite database file stores all its state with host-relative timestamps. If the host clock jumps forward or backward between writes, the database file can develop consistency issues:

  * timestamps in log files won't match actual database modification times
  * log entries from different times may appear in wrong order
  * correlation with external systems becomes unreliable
  * debugging performance issues becomes nearly impossible

For hosts running multiple installations of the service (see "Running Multiple oauthsvc Installations on One Host"), clock skew compounds the problem. Each installation shares the same host clock, but if the clock drifts or jumps, all installations are affected simultaneously.

Additionally, host clock accuracy affects file modification times (mtime) on the host filesystem. Console log files and the database file itself both have mtime recorded by the operating system. If the host clock has drifted or jumped, those mtimes may contradict the timestamps written inside the log files themselves. This inconsistency confuses backup tools, monitoring systems, and forensic analysis.

CHECKING THE HOST CLOCK (Priya Nandan)
======================================

Windows Host - Basic Verification
  On Windows 10 or Windows Server 2016+, open PowerShell in elevated mode and run:

    Get-Date

  This shows the current system time. Compare it to a known-good source such as:
    * Your organization's time server (if available on your network)
    * Public NTP servers such as pool.ntp.org (you can check via PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest to an NTP-aware service)
    * A colleague's watch or phone
    * Your system's hardware clock (see section below)

  Example output:
    PS C:\Users\billy> Get-Date

    Sunday, September 27, 2026 2:14:33 PM

    DayOfWeek      : Sunday
    Date           : 9/27/2026 12:00:00 AM
    Day            : 27
    Hour           : 14
    Minute         : 14
    Second         : 33

  If the time looks correct (within a few seconds of your external source), proceed to the next section. If the time is significantly off (more than a few minutes), follow the procedure in "Correcting Clock Skew" below.

  Note: The Windows Time service (w32time) normally keeps your clock synchronized if you're on a network with time servers configured. If you see frequent clock drift even after synchronization, the host hardware may have a failing RTC (real-time clock) battery or CMOS issue.

Linux/macOS Host - Basic Verification
  On Linux or macOS, use:

    date
    timedatectl status   # Linux with systemd
    date -u              # Show UTC time

  Compare the output to a known-good time source. Example on a Linux host:

    user@host:~$ date
    Mon Sep 27 14:15:22 UTC 2026
    user@host:~$ timedatectl status
    System clock synchronized: yes
    RTC in local TZ: no
    DST active: n/a
    RTC time: Mon 2026-09-27 14:15:30

  If the system shows "System clock synchronized: no", you may need to enable NTP or check service status. Contact your infrastructure team if unsure how to proceed.

Hardware Clock Check (Optional but Recommended)
  The host's hardware clock (RTC) is separate from the system time. On systems where time sync fails repeatedly, the hardware clock may be incorrect:

  Windows (via PowerShell):
    w32tm /query /status
    
  This shows the current Windows Time service status and last sync time. If synchronization is disabled, the hardware clock becomes the primary source after reboot.

  Linux (view only):
    sudo hwclock --show
    sudo hwclock --show --utc
    
  Compare this to the system time shown by `date`. They should be within a few seconds. If they differ by minutes or hours, the hardware clock is failing or misconfigured.

Querying System Clock with SQLite (Database Consistency Check)
  If you need to check the time in a way that's consistent with how the database file records timestamps, use the sqlite3 command-line tool. This is especially useful when debugging timestamp discrepancies:

    sqlite3 ":memory:" "SELECT datetime('now');"
    
  This command runs against an in-memory database and shows the current time as the database subsystem would record it. Example output:

    2026-09-27 14:15:45

  Compare this to what the host reports (Get-Date on Windows, date on Linux/macOS). They should match within one second. If they differ significantly, you may have a system configuration issue such as:
    - Timezone misalignment (especially on dual-boot systems or VMs)
    - A second system service manipulating the clock
    - Inconsistent NTP configuration across different subsystems

COMMON CLOCK ISSUES (Theo Baptiste)
==================================

This section documents clock problems we have observed on workstations and small hosts running oauthsvc. Each scenario includes symptoms, likely causes, and restoration procedures.

Clock Jumped Forward
  Symptoms:
    * Console log has entries with timestamps far in the future (days, months, or years ahead)
    * Database file's mtime (modification time) shows a future date
    * Service appears to have run at the time you checked logs, but timestamps don't match wall-clock time
    * Multiple file mtimes all shifted forward by the same amount

  Likely causes:
    - Manual clock adjustment by a user or superuser
    - BIOS/UEFI clock incorrectly set during system restoration or CMOS reset
    - Third-party time-sync software with aggressive or misconfigured adjustments
    - Daylight saving time transition mishandled during a Windows update
    - Virtual machine's system clock not synchronized with hypervisor after live migration

  Restoration Procedure:
    1. Note the current host time using Get-Date (Windows) or date (Linux/macOS). Record this timestamp.
    2. Check console log files for the highest timestamp present. See "Locating oauthsvc Files on a Host" for log file locations.
    3. Compare the timestamps in the log file to the current host time. Note the difference (e.g., "log shows 2027-09-27, but clock now says 2026-09-27, so it jumped forward 365 days").
    4. For Windows, open Settings > Time & Language > Date & time. Review the time zone setting first (incorrect zone can appear as a large jump). Verify the time is correct. If not, manually correct it or contact your IT staff if Time > Set time automatically is turned on but time is still wrong.
    5. After correcting time on Windows, run:
       w32tm /resync /force
    6. For Linux with systemd (version 248 or later on newer distributions), run:
       sudo timedatectl set-ntp false
       sudo date --set="2026-09-27 14:20:00"   # Substitute the correct date and time
       sudo timedatectl set-ntp true
    7. Check the host time again using Get-Date or date to confirm the clock is now correct.
    8. Review the database file's mtime using Get-Item (Windows) or ls -lad (Linux/macOS) to verify it shows the corrected time.
    9. If the database file's mtime still shows a future date even after clock adjustments, the file timestamp is a relic from when the clock was wrong. This is not harmful, but it may confuse backup tools. See "Restoring a Copied Database File" if you suspect database corruption.

Clock Drifted Slowly
  Symptoms:
    * Host time appears to gradually get ahead or behind the true time (you observe discrepancies over days or weeks)
    * Console log timestamps are consistently off by a small to moderate amount (minutes to hours, growing over time)
    * Filesystem mtimes on log files and database file don't match internal timestamps you see in logs
    * On hosts running multiple installations, each installation's logs show the same drift (confirming host-level issue, not per-service issue)
    * Monitoring or external systems show events at different times than your local console logs report

  Likely causes:
    - Windows Time service not running, disabled, or misconfigured
    - No NTP server reachable from the host's network interface
    - Host behind a firewall or corporate proxy that blocks UDP port 123 (NTP)
    - CMOS battery on the motherboard failing (especially on older hardware, 5+ years)
    - Host was offline for an extended period, and clock was not re-synchronized at boot
    - Virtual machine's system clock diverging from hypervisor time

  Windows Troubleshooting - Check and Restart w32time:
    1. Open Services (services.msc) and scroll to "Windows Time".
    2. Right-click on Windows Time and select Properties. Note the Service status.
    3. If the status is "Stopped", right-click and select Start. Set Startup type to Automatic.
    4. If the service is already Running but clock is drifting, try restarting it. Right-click and select Restart.
    5. Open PowerShell in elevated mode and run:
       w32tm /query /configuration
       
       Review the output. Typical configuration includes "NtpServer" entries. Note the configured servers.
    6. Force a resynchronization:
       w32tm /resync /force
       
    7. Wait 30 seconds and run Get-Date again to verify time has stabilized.
    8. If time continues to drift, check Windows Time event logs in Event Viewer. Open Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc), navigate to Windows Logs > System, and filter for events from "Time-Service" source. Common errors include "No suitable servers found" (network blocked) or "Peer is unreachable" (NTP server unavailable).
    9. If NTP servers are unreachable, try adding a public NTP server temporarily to check:
       w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:"pool.ntp.org,0x8" /syncfromflags:manual /reliable:yes /update
       w32tm /resync /force
       
    10. If this works (time stabilizes), consult your network staff about permanent NTP configuration. If it doesn't work, the host may have a hardware issue (see "Clock Drifts Away Again After Adjustments" in Troubleshooting).

  Linux Troubleshooting - Check and Restart systemd-timesyncd:
    - Verify systemd-timesyncd or ntpd is running and enabled:
      sudo systemctl status systemd-timesyncd
      sudo systemctl enable --now systemd-timesyncd   # Enable if not already
    - Check current sync status:
      timedatectl status
    - Force resynchronization (if supported):
      sudo timedatectl set-ntp false
      sudo timedatectl set-ntp true
    - If still drifting and you have ntpdate available:
      sudo ntpdate -s pool.ntp.org   # Force one-time sync
    - Verify network connectivity to NTP servers:
      ntpstat   # Shows sync statistics if available
      ping -c 1 pool.ntp.org   # Check basic network access

Clock Jumped Backward
  Symptoms:
    * Console log entries appear with older timestamps than previous entries (non-monotonic)
    * Database file mtimes in the past don't match current host time
    * Service behavior becomes erratic or appears to stall
    * Tools that expect time to always move forward may fail with confusing error messages
    * Backup utilities may skip files they think are "too old" because mtime is in the past

  Likely causes:
    - Manual clock adjustment backward
    - VM suspend/restart on a virtual host without proper re-sync
    - NTP server correcting significant forward drift
    - Superuser manually setting clock to an earlier time for validation

  Restoration:
    1. STOP the service immediately. Do not use the service until clock is corrected and validated.
    2. Note the current host time and find the earliest timestamp in the console log. Calculate how far backward the clock jumped.
    3. Follow the same adjustment steps as "Clock Jumped Forward" above.
    4. After adjusting, verify the database file isn't corrupted by checking:
       * File size (should be >1000 bytes, typically >50KB):
         # Windows:
         (Get-Item "C:\Users\billy\AppData\Local\oauthsvc\oauthsvc.db").Length
         # Linux/macOS:
         ls -lh ~/.oauthsvc/oauthsvc.db
       * Database file can be queried (see "Querying System Clock" section):
         sqlite3 ~/.oauthsvc/oauthsvc.db "SELECT 1;"   # Should print "1" with no error
    5. If the database file is corrupt, see "Restoring a Copied Database File" for restoration.
6. If the database file is intact, service operation may safely proceed once clock is validated (confirmed correct to within a few seconds).

TIMESTAMP CORRELATION WITH CONSOLE LOGS (Derek Yun)
===================================================

After verifying host clock accuracy, you can now correlate timestamps in console log files with external events. This is essential for incident response and debugging.

Console Log File Basics
  The service writes console output to a log file stored locally on the host. Each line typically includes a timestamp from the host system clock at the moment the line was written. The log files are plain text and are cycled periodically by the service or by external tools. See "Managing the Service's Console Log Files" for details on file locations, cycling schedules, and cleanup procedures.

Reading Logs with Correct Clock
  Once you've confirmed the host clock is accurate, you can trust the timestamps in log files:

    1. Locate the console log file. On Windows, this is typically:
       C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\oauthsvc\logs\
       
       On Linux or macOS:
       ~/.oauthsvc/logs/ or /var/log/oauthsvc/
       
       See "Locating oauthsvc Files on a Host" for platform-specific paths.

    2. Open the log file in a text editor or use command-line tools:
       # On Windows PowerShell:
       Display the last 50 lines of the service console log file:
       
       # On Linux/macOS bash:
       tail -50 ~/.oauthsvc/logs/console.log

    3. Scan for timestamps around the time of the event you're investigating. Log lines should show ISO 8601 formatted timestamps like "2026-09-27T14:30:15" or similar.

Matching Log Timestamps to External Events
  Example: You're investigating a port conflict that occurred around 2:30 PM on September 27, 2026.

    1. First, confirm the current host time and compare to an external reference:
       Get-Date  # Should show 2026-09-27, confirmed correct via previous steps

    2. Search the console log for entries near 2:30 PM:
       Search the console log file for entries with a specific timestamp such as 14:30:

    3. Review the matched lines. Example output:
       2026-09-27 14:29:55 - Service starting on 127.0.0.1:8080
       2026-09-27 14:30:03 - ERROR: Port 8080 already in use, service failed to start
       2026-09-27 14:30:04 - Attempting port 8081
       2026-09-27 14:30:05 - Service started on 127.0.0.1:8081

    4. The log shows the conflict occurred at 14:30:03. Now you can correlate this with external events. Was something else running on port 8080 at 14:30:03? See "Resolving Port Conflicts on the Loopback Service" for troubleshooting port conflicts.

Clock Skew Impact on Log Correlation
  If the host clock had been off by 15 minutes at the time this happened:

    * You would have read the log as showing the conflict at 14:30:03 (what was actually written)
    * But the actual event occurred at 14:15:03 on the real world timeline
    * You'd search for other events at 14:30 on external systems (monitoring dashboards, peer systems, etc.) and find nothing
    * You'd think the service had different behavior than it actually did
    * Debugging becomes impossible without realizing the clock was wrong

  This is why verifying clock accuracy is the first step in any log-based investigation.

Database File Timestamps and Metadata
  The database file itself has an mtime (modification time) set by the host operating system. This mtime reflects when the file was last written to, based on the host clock at that moment. If the clock was inaccurate during writes, the mtime will also be inaccurate.

  To check the database file's mtime:

    # Windows PowerShell:
       Inspect the database file's metadata in PowerShell:
    $file.LastWriteTime
    
    # Output example:
    # Tuesday, September 27, 2026 2:14:33 PM

    # Linux/macOS:
    ls -l ~/.oauthsvc/oauthsvc.db
    # Output example:
    # -rw-r--r-- 1 user group 65536 Sep 27 14:14 /home/user/.oauthsvc/oauthsvc.db
    
    stat ~/.oauthsvc/oauthsvc.db   # More detailed view

  If the mtime appears incorrect (far in the future or past), compare it to the current host time. If the clock is now correct but the mtime is old, that mtime is a relic of when the clock was wrong. It's harmless, but it may confuse backup tools that filter files by modification date.

Cross-Referencing Log Times with Database File Times
  When investigating an issue, you may see timestamps in console logs but want to verify they correspond to actual database changes. Compare:
    * Timestamp in console log (e.g., "2026-09-27 14:30:05")
    * Database file's mtime (e.g., "Sep 27 14:30")
    
  These should align approximately (within 10-30 seconds, depending on how often the database is written). If they're far apart, clock skew may be at play, or the log file may be old.

TOOLS AND UTILITIES
===================

When investigating host clock issues, the following tools are useful:

Windows Tools
  * Get-Date - PowerShell cmdlet, built-in, current as of Windows 10 21H2
  * w32tm - Windows Time utility, command-line, part of Windows Server 2016+
  * Services snap-in (services.msc) - GUI, built-in, for managing Windows Time service
  * Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) - GUI, built-in, for reviewing Time-Service event logs
  * Task Scheduler - for scheduling periodic time sync checks (optional, rarely needed)

Linux Tools
  * date - command-line utility, typically GNU coreutils 8.30 or later
  * timedatectl - command-line, part of systemd 247+, status and control of time sync
  * ntpdate - network time utility, often installed with ntp package (version 4.2.8+)
  * systemd-timesyncd - built-in time sync service on systemd systems (version 248+ preferred)
  * hwclock - hardware clock utility on many Linux distributions

macOS Tools
  * date - command-line utility, similar to Linux
  * ntpdate - available via Homebrew or MacPorts (less common on modern macOS)
  * systemsetup - command-line tool for system preferences (deprecated on newer macOS versions)

SQLite Tools
  * sqlite3 - command-line tool, version 3.32.0+, available separately or pre-installed on many systems
  * Common usage: sqlite3 ":memory:" "SELECT datetime('now');" (for timestamp consistency checks)

TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE
====================

Clock is reported as correct, but log timestamps still look wrong

  1. Confirm the host clock is actually correct by checking against multiple external time sources (network time server, pool.ntp.org, colleague's phone, etc.). Validate using multiple methods if possible.
  2. Confirm the console log file is actually from this service instance on this host (not a stored backup, not from a different host, not from a different installation). Check the file path and confirm the service is currently running or recently stopped.
  3. Check if the service was restarted during the period you're examining. A restart may clear old log entries from memory and start fresh. Check console for "Service starting" or similar messages.
  4. If the service is running on a virtual machine, the VM's system clock might be different from the physical hypervisor's clock. Check both the VM's clock and the hypervisor's clock using appropriate tools. See your virtualization platform's documentation for instructions.
  5. On multi-installation hosts, verify you're reading the correct log file for the correct installation. Each installation has its own log directory. See "Running Multiple oauthsvc Installations on One Host" for guidance.
  6. Review the log file's own mtime. If it's very old (days or weeks), the log file may be a stored backup or from a previous run. Check for newer log files in the same directory.

Service won't start and logs mention time-related errors

  1. Check host clock is within a reasonable range (within 10 minutes of true time is usually sufficient).
  2. Check if there's a disk space issue that prevents log file creation. See "Disk Space Checks for the Host".
  3. Check if there's a SQLite file locking issue (sometimes related to stale timestamps). See "Diagnosing SQLite File Locking on a Host".
  4. Try stopping the service (if it's running), waiting 10 seconds, and starting again to clear any stale state.
  5. Check Windows Event Viewer (Windows) or system journal (Linux/macOS) for additional error messages that might mention time sync failures.

NTP service won't synchronize (Linux)

  1. Verify network connectivity from the host to NTP servers. Try ping pool.ntp.org or similar.
  2. Verify firewall rules allow outbound UDP port 123. Check local firewall (iptables, firewalld) and any external firewalls.
  3. Check timedatectl status or systemctl status systemd-timesyncd for detailed error messages.
  4. Manually set time to an approximately correct value first (within an hour or so), then enable NTP. NTP works better when the system time is already close.
  5. On some corporate networks, NTP is blocked entirely. Contact your network or infrastructure staff. They may provide an internal NTP server.
  6. If you have ntpdate available, try a one-time sync: sudo ntpdate -s pool.ntp.org (may require sudo)

Windows Time service status shows "Stopped"

  1. Verify Windows Time service can start. Open Services (services.msc), right-click Windows Time, select Properties.
  2. Check Startup type. If it's set to Disabled, change it to Automatic or Manual and click Apply.
  3. Click Start button to start the service.
  4. Wait 30 seconds and verify the service is still running (status should show "Running").
  5. If the service stops immediately or won't start, check the event log in Event Viewer (Windows Logs > System) for errors from the Time-Service source.
  6. Common errors: "The service did not start due to a logon failure" (access issue), "The process terminated unexpectedly" (corruption), "No suitable servers found" (network connectivity).

Clock drifts away again after adjustments (persists)

  1. Verify the time sync service is enabled and running (Windows Time service on Windows, systemd-timesyncd or ntpd on Linux).
  2. Verify the service is actually trying to sync. On Windows, check w32tm /query /status for last sync time. On Linux, check timedatectl status for sync status.
  3. If sync service shows no recent sync attempts, the host may not be reaching NTP servers. Check firewall, proxy, and network settings.
  4. If sync is happening but clock still drifts, the host hardware may have a failing RTC (real-time clock) battery or CMOS issue. Check BIOS/UEFI for the system time at next boot to confirm.
  5. For persistent drift on VMs, check if the hypervisor is configured to sync the VM's clock at boot. Some hypervisors disable guest NTP to maintain control.
  6. If you have access to hardware, try replacing the CMOS battery (internal to the motherboard). This is a hardware repair and should only be done by qualified personnel.

Timestamps in log files are erratic or jump around

  1. Confirm the host clock hasn't been adjusted by looking at the system's time adjustment record. On Windows, check Event Viewer (Windows Logs > System, filter for "Time-Service"). On Linux, check systemd journal (journalctl -u systemd-timesyncd).
  2. Check if multiple services or cron jobs are adjusting the clock simultaneously. This can cause clock to jump unpredictably.
  3. Verify no third-party clock sync software is running (some configuration management tools, VM hypervisors, etc. may try to sync the clock).
  4. If in a virtual environment, check if the hypervisor is forcibly adjusting the VM's clock during live migration or other operations.

TERMINOLOGY AND GLOSSARY
========================

CMOS Battery
  A small battery on the host motherboard that maintains the real-time clock (RTC) when the system is powered off. If this battery fails, the system time reverts to a default value (often 1980 or early 1990s) each time the host boots. Batteries typically last 3-10 years depending on motherboard age and environmental conditions.

Database File
  The SQLite database file where oauthsvc stores all persistent state. Typically located at C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\oauthsvc\oauthsvc.db on Windows or ~/.oauthsvc/oauthsvc.db on Linux/macOS. Timestamps within this file are set by the host system clock. The file's mtime (modification time) is set by the operating system and also reflects the host clock at the time of the last write.

Drift (Clock Drift)
  Gradual change in the host system clock away from the true time. Unlike a jump, drift happens slowly over hours or days and is usually caused by hardware oscillator inaccuracy, lack of NTP synchronization, or a failing CMOS battery. Drift is easier to correct than a jump because it's typically small.

File Modification Time (mtime)
  The timestamp recorded by the operating system indicating when a file was last written. This is independent of timestamps stored inside the file's content. On Windows, use Get-Item and check LastWriteTime property. On Linux/macOS, use ls -l (shows abbreviated time) or stat (shows full time). The mtime is set by the OS at the moment of write and reflects the host clock at that time.

Jump (Clock Jump)
  Sudden, large change in the host system clock, typically caused by manual adjustment, BIOS/UEFI update, or VM suspend/restart. Unlike drift, a jump is instantaneous and can be minutes, hours, days, or even years. Jumps backward are particularly problematic because they violate the assumption that time always moves forward monotonically.

Log File
  Plain-text file containing timestamped console output from the service. The service writes to this file as it runs, writing new entries with timestamps from the host clock. Log files are periodically cycled and may be backed up or compressed. See "Managing the Service's Console Log Files" for details on locations, cycling, and cleanup.

mtime
  Abbreviation for "modification time". See File Modification Time above. Linux and macOS users should be familiar with this term from file listing commands and scripts.

NTP (Network Time Protocol)
  Standard protocol for synchronizing computer clocks over a network. An NTP application (such as Windows Time service or systemd-timesyncd) contacts NTP servers and adjusts the local clock to match. NTP servers form a hierarchy; public servers like pool.ntp.org are Stratum 2 or 3. NTP typically synchronizes time to within 1-10 milliseconds on a LAN.

RTC (Real-Time Clock)
  Hardware component on the motherboard that maintains the system time, backed by a CMOS battery when power is off. The operating system reads the RTC at boot to initialize the system clock. The RTC is separate from the system clock; if the RTC is wrong, the system clock starts wrong unless corrected by NTP soon after boot.

Skew
  General term for any deviation of the host system clock from true time, whether caused by drift or jump. Skew can be positive (clock is ahead) or negative (clock is behind). The amount of skew is what matters: a few milliseconds is usually harmless, but seconds or more causes problems.

Synchronization (Sync)
  Process of adjusting the host system clock to match a reference time, typically via NTP. A sync operation may be continuous (daemon running in background) or one-time (manual sync command). Sync frequency varies; typical NTP syncs occur every 15-64 minutes depending on drift detected.

Timestamp
  A recorded point in time, typically stored in human-readable (e.g., "2026-09-27 14:30:05") or machine-readable format (epoch seconds, microseconds since 1970-01-01). Console log files and database records both use timestamps. Timestamps are relative to the host clock at the moment they're recorded.

Windows Time Service (w32time)
  Windows system service responsible for synchronizing the host clock with NTP servers. Normally runs automatically on networked Windows systems. Can be queried and controlled via w32tm command-line utility or Services snap-in (services.msc). Startup type can be Disabled, Manual, or Automatic.

FILES AND PATHS REFERENCED
==========================

Path / File Name                                                      Purpose
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\oauthsvc\                          oauthsvc home directory on Windows
C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\oauthsvc\logs\                     console log files location on Windows
C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\oauthsvc\oauthsvc.db               database file on Windows
~/.oauthsvc/                                                          oauthsvc home directory on Linux/macOS
~/.oauthsvc/logs/                                                     console log files location on Linux/macOS
~/.oauthsvc/oauthsvc.db                                               database file on Linux/macOS
/var/log/oauthsvc/                                                    alternative console log location on Linux (may vary)
Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc)                                          Windows system event log viewer; access via Run dialog or Services snap-in
services.msc                                                          Windows Services snap-in for managing system services including Windows Time
docs/operations-runbooks/                                             this runbook folder in repository root
docs/operations-runbooks/console-log-files.md                         sibling page on log file management and cycling
docs/operations-runbooks/host-monitoring-basics.md                    sibling page on monitoring host health and detecting issues early

TOOLS, PACKAGES, AND LIBRARIES
==============================

Tool / Package Name                                   Version         Notes
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Windows Time service (w32time)                       Built-in        Windows Server 2016+, Windows 10 21H2+
Get-Date (PowerShell)                               5.1.19041       Built-in on Windows 10 21H2; core cmdlet

1	# Cleaning Up Temporary Files Left on the Host
2	
3	| | |
4	|---|---|
5	| **Title** | Cleaning Up Temporary Files Left on the Host |
6	| **Version** | v2.1.0 |
7	| **Owner** | Desktop Engineering (Theo Baptiste) |
8	| **Last Updated** | 2025-04-11 |
9	| **Summary** | This page describes finding and cleaning temporary files that accumulate on a host around oauthsvc's runtime files, including state directories, cache files, lock files, and transient work files. |
10	
11	---
12	
13	## Overview
14	
15	When the service runs on a host, it creates and uses various temporary files for operation. These include process-specific state directories, transient cache files, lock markers, and incomplete work files. Over time—especially across restarts, crashes, or service reconfiguration—these files can accumulate on disk and occasionally cause issues when they become stale or orphaned.
16	
17	This page covers the types of temporary files the service produces, where they are stored on different operating systems, how to identify which ones are safe to remove, and cleanup procedures you can perform safely while the service is stopped or running.
18	
19	For guidance on disk space in general, see the companion page on disk space monitoring. For specific issues around SQLite file locks, consult the page on diagnosing SQLite locking. Console log files are covered separately.
20	
21	---
22	
23	## Types of Temporary Files
24	
25	The service creates the following categories of temporary runtime artifacts:
26	
27	**Process state directories.** When the service starts, it creates a process-specific subdirectory in the host's temporary space. This directory holds transient state needed for the running instance. If the service terminates abnormally, these directories can remain on disk.
28	
29	**Lock and marker files.** The service creates lock files to prevent multiple instances from accessing the same database file simultaneously. These lock files persist as long as the service holds them and are cleaned up on normal shutdown. Unclean termination may leave lock files orphaned.
30	
31	**Cache and session files.** Intermediate cache files for the service's loopback HTTP interface are stored in temporary directories. These are typically recreated on each startup and are safe to remove even if the service is running.
32	
33	**Incomplete work files.** After a crash or unclean shutdown, the service may create files that record incomplete transactions or ongoing tasks. These allow the service to restart cleanly on the next startup. Removing these files will cause the service to lose any in-progress work upon restart.
34	
35	**Stale database journal and auxiliary files.** SQLite creates supplementary files (journal, wal, shm files) alongside the database file during normal operation and during locking contention. In rare cases, these can become orphaned if the database connection is terminated abruptly.
36	
37	---
38	
39	## Locating Temporary Files on Windows
40	
41	**Section Owner:** Host Operations (Derek Yun) — *last reviewed 2026-08-15*
42	
43	On Windows workstations and servers, the service uses two primary temporary directories:
44	
45	1. The system temporary folder: `%TEMP%` (typically `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Temp`) for process state and cache files.
46	2. A service-specific state folder: `%APPDATA%\oauthsvc\temp` (typically `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\oauthsvc\temp`) for incomplete work files and persistent cache.
47	
48	### Finding Active Temporary Files
49	
50	To list all temporary files related to oauthsvc on the current user's profile, open PowerShell and run:
51	
52	```powershell
53	Get-ChildItem -Path $env:TEMP -Filter "*oauthsvc*" -Recurse | Select-Object FullName, LastWriteTime
54	Get-ChildItem -Path $env:APPDATA\oauthsvc\temp -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object FullName, LastWriteTime
55	```
56	
57	This command will display the full path and last modification date of each file. Files with a LastWriteTime older than the last service start are candidates for removal.
58	
59	### Example Output
60	
61	```
62	FullName                                          LastWriteTime
63	--------                                          -------------
64	C:\Users\alice\AppData\Local\Temp\identitysvc_12840 2026-09-20 14:32:15
65	C:\Users\alice\AppData\Local\Temp\identitysvc_12840\state.bin 2026-09-20 14:32:15
66	C:\Users\alice\AppData\Local\Temp\identitysvc_12840\cache.lock 2026-09-20 14:32:15
67	C:\Users\alice\AppData\Roaming\oauthsvc\temp\work.meta 2026-09-18 11:04:22
68	```
69	
70	Directories named `identitysvc_<PID>` (where PID is a process ID) were created by a specific instance. If the process is no longer running, these directories are safe to remove.
71	
72	### Checking for Locked Files
73	
74	Before removing temporary files, verify that the service is not using them. The service will hold open file handles to active temporary files. To see which files are in use:
75	
76	1. Open Windows Resource Monitor (type `resmon` in the Start menu).
77	2. Click the **Handles** tab.
78	3. Search for `oauthsvc` in the search box.
79	4. Review the list of open file handles.
80	
81	Any temporary file that does not appear in this list can be safely removed.
82	
83	---
84	
85	## Locating Temporary Files on Linux
86	
87	**Section Owner:** Systems Reliability (Priya Nandan) — *last reviewed 2026-07-09*
88	
89	On Linux hosts, the service uses:
90	
91	1. The system temporary folder: `/tmp` for process state and cache files (or `/run/user/<uid>` on systemd hosts).
92	2. A service-specific state folder: `~/.local/share/oauthsvc/temp` for incomplete work files.
93	
94	### Finding Active Temporary Files
95	
96	Run the following command to list oauthsvc-related temporary files:
97	
98	```bash
99	find /tmp -name "*oauthsvc*" -type f -printf '%p %TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM:%TS\n' 2>/dev/null
100	find ~/.local/share/oauthsvc/temp -type f -printf '%p %TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM:%TS\n' 2>/dev/null
101	```
102	
103	The output will show the file path and modification date. Compare the modification time against your service's last startup time (visible in the service's console log).
104	
105	### Checking for Locked Files
106	
107	To see which temporary files are currently held open by any process, run:
108	
109	```bash
110	lsof 2>/dev/null | grep oauthsvc | grep /tmp
111	lsof 2>/dev/null | grep oauthsvc | grep ~/.local/share/oauthsvc
112	```
113	
114	If `lsof` is not installed, you can check `/proc` directly (on systems where the service process still has a running PID):
115	
116	```bash
117	ls -la /proc/<pid>/fd | grep /tmp
118	```
119	
120	---
121	
122	## Cleanup Procedures
123	
124	**Section Owner:** Desktop Engineering (Theo Baptiste) — *last reviewed 2025-06-03*
125	
126	### Before You Start
127	
128	Before removing any temporary files, take these precautions:
129	
130	- **Confirm the service is stopped.** Check that no oauthsvc processes are running on the host. On Windows, use `Get-Process oauthsvc -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`; on Linux, use `pgrep oauthsvc`.
131	- **Note the database file location.** You will need to avoid removing the database file itself or its immediate parent directory. See the page on locating oauthsvc files for paths.
132	- **Do not remove the database file or its journal files while the service is running.** Even though these are not strictly "temporary," they can be mistaken for temporary files.
133	
134	### Safe Cleanup (Service Stopped)
135	
136	When the service is confirmed stopped, you can safely remove:
137	
138	1. **Process state directories** in the system temporary folder matching the pattern `identitysvc_<PID>`. On Windows, these are in `%TEMP%`; on Linux, in `/tmp`.
139	2. **Incomplete work files** in the service-specific state directory (`%APPDATA%\oauthsvc\temp` on Windows, `~/.local/share/oauthsvc/temp` on Linux).
140	3. **Cache files** in the service-specific state directory older than the service's last startup.
141	
142	To remove these files on Windows:
143	
144	```powershell
145	On Windows, remove identitysvc_* directories from system temp, ignoring any errors.
146	Remove-Item -Path $env:APPDATA\oauthsvc\temp\*.meta -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
147	```
148	
149	On Linux:
150	
151	```bash
152	On Linux, remove identitysvc_* directories from /tmp.
153	rm -f ~/.local/share/oauthsvc/temp/*.meta
154	```
155	
156	### Cleanup While Service Is Running
157	
158	If you need to clean up temporary files while the service is running (not recommended, but sometimes necessary):
159	
160	- Remove only **cache files** from the loopback interface directory. Identify these by their file extension and modification time (they are typically recreated within seconds after removal).
161	- **Do not remove** any lock files, incomplete work files, or process state directories while the service is running.
162	
163	On Windows, identify cache files by extension:
164	
165	```powershell
166	On Windows, remove *.cache files from identitysvc_* directories in system temp.
167	```
168	
169	On Linux:
170	
171	```bash
172	On Linux, remove *.cache files from identitysvc_* directories in /tmp.
173	```
174	
175	### Worked Example: Cleanup After Unclean Shutdown
176	
177	Suppose the service crashed on a Windows workstation, and you want to remove the stale temporary files before restarting.
178	
179	**Step 1:** Verify the service is stopped.
180	```powershell
181	Stop-Service oauthsvc -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
182	Start-Sleep -Seconds 2
183	Get-Process oauthsvc -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue  # Should return nothing
184	```
185	
186	**Step 2:** List the temporary directories.
187	```powershell
188	On Windows, list identitysvc_* directories in system temporary storage.
189	```
190	
191	Example output:
192	```
193	Mode                 LastWriteTime         Name
194	----                 -------------         ----
195	d----  2026-09-26 08:15:32 identitysvc_3284
196	d----  2026-09-22 14:42:11 identitysvc_2901
197	```
198	
199	**Step 3:** Remove old temporary directories.
200	```powershell
201	On Windows, remove process directory identitysvc_3284 from system temp.
202	On Windows, remove process directory identitysvc_2901 from system temp.
203	```
204	
205	**Step 4:** Clean up incomplete work files.
206	```powershell
207	Remove-Item -Path $env:APPDATA\oauthsvc\temp -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
208	New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $env:APPDATA\oauthsvc\temp -Force | Out-Null
209	```
210	
211	**Step 5:** Restart the service.
212	```powershell
213	Start-Service oauthsvc
214	```
215	
216	---
217	
218	## Monitoring and Prevention
219	
220	To prevent temporary file accumulation, consider:
221	
222	- **Monitor disk usage regularly.** See the page on disk space monitoring for ongoing checks.
223	- **Review temporary file counts weekly** on hosts where the service runs frequently. Use the commands in the sections above and set up alerts if the file count exceeds a threshold (e.g., more than 50 temporary directories).
224	- **Log service shutdowns.** Record when the service is stopped and whether it was a clean or unclean termination. Unclean terminations (crash, forced kill) are more likely to leave orphaned temporary files.
225	- **Clean up periodically as part of host maintenance.** Schedule a weekly or monthly cleanup task during a maintenance window when the service is confirmed stopped.
226	
227	### Automated Cleanup Script (Windows)
228	
229	You can create a scheduled task to clean up old temporary files. Create a file named `cleanup-oauthsvc-temp.ps1`:
230	
231	```powershell
232	# Clean up oauthsvc temporary files older than 7 days
233	$CutoffDate = (Get-Date).AddDays(-7)
234	On Windows, remove identitysvc_* directories from system temp that are older than a specified cutoff date.
235	Get-ChildItem -Path $env:APPDATA\oauthsvc\temp -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.LastWriteTime -lt $CutoffDate } | Remove-Item -Force
236	```
237	
238	Schedule this script to run via Task Scheduler at a time when the service is not typically active.
239	
240	---
241	
242	## Interaction with Other Components
243	
244	**Related to port conflicts.** When the service restarts, it re-binds to its configured port. Stale lock files can occasionally interfere with port binding. If you encounter port conflict errors after a crash, clean up temporary files as described above before investigating further. See the page on resolving port conflicts.
245	
246	**Related to console logging.** Console log files are separate from the temporary files discussed here and are not cleaned up as part of routine temporary file removal. Refer to the page on managing console log files for guidance on log lifecycle and storage.
247	
248	**Related to SQLite locking.** If you observe database lock timeouts or "database is locked" errors, orphaned lock files may be the cause. However, do not simply remove lock files; consult the page on diagnosing SQLite locking first. Stale auxiliary files (journal, wal) can be cleaned up after confirming the database is not in use.
249	
250	**Related to database backups.** Before cleaning up temporary files, ensure you have a recent backup of the database file. Do not confuse temporary files with the database backup process. See the page on copying the database file for backup procedures.
251	
252	---
253	
254	## Terminology
255	
256	| Term | Definition |
257	|------|-----------|
258	| **Lock file** | A file created by the service to indicate that a resource (such as the database file) is in use by a running process. Lock files are typically removed when the process exits cleanly. |
259	| **Orphaned file** | A temporary file that remains on disk after the process that created it has terminated. Orphaned files can be safely removed. |
260	| **Process ID (PID)** | A unique numerical identifier assigned to a running process by the operating system. Temporary files are often named with the PID for uniqueness. |
261	| **Journal file** | An auxiliary file created by SQLite alongside the database file to record changes during a transaction. Journal files are cleaned up automatically when the transaction completes. |
262	| **Cache file** | A temporary file used to store frequently accessed data in memory or on disk to improve performance. Cache files are typically recreated on each service startup. |
263	| **Incomplete work data** | A file that records incomplete transactions or in-flight operations, used by the service to restart cleanly after an unexpected shutdown. |
264	| **Stale file** | A temporary file that has not been modified for a long period and is no longer needed by the service. Stale files can be removed to reclaim disk space. |
265	| **State directory** | A process-specific directory created by the service in the system temporary folder to store transient runtime state. |
266	| **WAL file** | A Write-Ahead Log file created by SQLite in certain configurations to improve write performance and concurrency. |
267	| **Shared memory file (shm)** | An auxiliary file created by SQLite to manage shared memory for concurrent access. Shared memory files are cleaned up when the database connection closes. |
268	
269	---
270	
271	## Files and Paths Reference
272	
273	| Path | Purpose | Notes |
274	|------|------|-------|
275	| `%TEMP%` (Windows) | System temporary directory | Contains process state directories named `identitysvc_<PID>`. On Windows 10/11, typically `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Temp`. |
276	| `/tmp` (Linux) | System temporary directory | Contains process state directories named `identitysvc_<PID>`. On systemd systems, `/run/user/<uid>` may also be used. |
277	| `%APPDATA%\oauthsvc\temp` (Windows) | Service-specific state directory | Contains incomplete work files and persistent cache. Typically `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\oauthsvc\temp`. |
278	| `~/.local/share/oauthsvc/temp` (Linux) | Service-specific state directory | Contains incomplete work files and persistent cache. Resolves to the user's home directory. |
279	| `identitysvc_<PID>` (within `%TEMP%` or `/tmp`) | Process state directory | Created when the service starts, identified by its PID. Safe to remove when service is stopped. |
280	| Database file location | Database file (not temporary) | Do not remove; see the page on locating oauthsvc files. Auxiliary files (`.journal`, `.wal`, `.shm`) may be cleaned up after confirming the service is stopped. |
281	| `docs/` | Documentation folder | Contains runbooks and guides; not a temporary directory. |
282	| `scripts/` | Scripts folder | Contains utility scripts; not a temporary directory. |
283	
284	---
285	
286	## Tools and Versions
287	
288	| Tool | Version | Purpose | Platform |
289	|------|---------|---------|----------|
290	| PowerShell | 5.1–7.x | File listing and removal on Windows. | Windows |
291	| bash | 4.x+ | File listing and removal on Linux. | Linux |
292	| sqlite3 | 3.30+ | Inspection of SQLite auxiliary files (optional). | Windows, Linux |
293	| lsof | 4.x+ | Listing open files and detecting locked files. | Linux |
294	| Resource Monitor | Windows built-in | Graphical tool for inspecting open file handles. | Windows 10/11 |
295	| find | GNU 4.8+ | Recursive file search with modification time filtering. | Linux |
296	| Get-ChildItem | PowerShell 5.1+ | Listing files with full metadata. | Windows |
297	
298	---
299	
300	## Changelog

302	| Date | Version | Release | Changes |
303	|------|---------|---------|---------|
304	| 2025-04-11 | v2.1.0 | **Current** | Updated examples for Windows 10/11 and Linux systemd. Added WAL and shared memory file discussion. Clarified that incomplete work files should not be removed if the service uses crash-resilience features. |

# Cleaning Up Temporary Files Left on the Host

| | |
|---|---|
| **Title** | Cleaning Up Temporary Files Left on the Host |
| **Version** | v2.1.0 |
| **Owner** | Desktop Engineering (Theo Baptiste) |
| **Last Updated** | 2025-04-11 |
| **Summary** | This page describes finding and cleaning temporary files that accumulate on a host around oauthsvc's runtime files, including state directories, cache files, lock files, and transient work files. |

---

## Overview

When the service runs on a host, it creates and uses various temporary files for operation. These include process-specific state directories, transient cache files, lock markers, and incomplete work files. Over time—especially across restarts, crashes, or service reconfiguration—these files can accumulate on disk and occasionally cause issues when they become stale or orphaned.

This page covers the types of temporary files the service produces, where they are stored on different operating systems, how to identify which ones are safe to remove, and cleanup procedures you can perform safely while the service is stopped or running.

For guidance on disk space in general, see the companion page on disk space monitoring. For specific issues around SQLite file locks, consult the page on diagnosing SQLite locking. Console log files are covered separately.

---

## Types of Temporary Files

The service creates the following categories of temporary runtime artifacts:

**Process state directories.** When the service starts, it creates a process-specific subdirectory in the host's temporary space. This directory holds transient state needed for the running instance. If the service terminates abnormally, these directories can remain on disk.

**Lock and marker files.** The service creates lock files to prevent multiple instances from accessing the same database file simultaneously. These lock files persist as long as the service holds them and are cleaned up on normal shutdown. Unclean termination may leave lock files orphaned.

**Cache and session files.** Intermediate cache files for the service's loopback HTTP interface are stored in temporary directories. These are typically recreated on each startup and are safe to remove even if the service is running.

**Incomplete work files.** After a crash or unclean shutdown, the service may create files that record incomplete transactions or ongoing tasks. These allow the service to restart cleanly on the next startup. Removing these files will cause the service to lose any in-progress work upon restart.

**Stale database journal and auxiliary files.** SQLite creates supplementary files (journal, wal, shm files) alongside the database file during normal operation and during locking contention. In rare cases, these can become orphaned if the database connection is terminated abruptly.

---

## Locating Temporary Files on Windows

**Section Owner:** Host Operations (Derek Yun) — *last reviewed 2026-08-15*

On Windows workstations and servers, the service uses two primary temporary directories:

1. The system temporary folder: `%TEMP%` (typically `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Temp`) for process state and cache files.
2. A service-specific state folder: `%APPDATA%\oauthsvc\temp` (typically `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\oauthsvc\temp`) for incomplete work files and persistent cache.

### Finding Active Temporary Files

To list all temporary files related to oauthsvc on the current user's profile, open PowerShell and run:

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -Path $env:TEMP -Filter "*oauthsvc*" -Recurse | Select-Object FullName, LastWriteTime
Get-ChildItem -Path $env:APPDATA\oauthsvc\temp -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object FullName, LastWriteTime
```

This command will display the full path and last modification date of each file. Files with a LastWriteTime older than the last service start are candidates for removal.

### Example Output

```
FullName                                          LastWriteTime
--------                                          -------------
C:\Users\alice\AppData\Local\Temp\identitysvc_12840 2026-09-20 14:32:15
C:\Users\alice\AppData\Local\Temp\identitysvc_12840\state.bin 2026-09-20 14:32:15
C:\Users\alice\AppData\Local\Temp\identitysvc_12840\cache.lock 2026-09-20 14:32:15
C:\Users\alice\AppData\Roaming\oauthsvc\temp\work.meta 2026-09-18 11:04:22
```

Directories named `identitysvc_<PID>` (where PID is a process ID) were created by a specific instance. If the process is no longer running, these directories are safe to remove.

### Checking for Locked Files

Before removing temporary files, verify that the service is not using them. The service will hold open file handles to active temporary files. To see which files are in use:

1. Open Windows Resource Monitor (type `resmon` in the Start menu).
2. Click the **Handles** tab.
3. Search for `oauthsvc` in the search box.
4. Review the list of open file handles.

Any temporary file that does not appear in this list can be safely removed.

---

## Locating Temporary Files on Linux

**Section Owner:** Systems Reliability (Priya Nandan) — *last reviewed 2026-07-09*

On Linux hosts, the service uses:

1. The system temporary folder: `/tmp` for process state and cache files (or `/run/user/<uid>` on systemd hosts).
2. A service-specific state folder: `~/.local/share/oauthsvc/temp` for incomplete work files.

### Finding Active Temporary Files

Run the following command to list oauthsvc-related temporary files:

```bash
find /tmp -name "*oauthsvc*" -type f -printf '%p %TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM:%TS\n' 2>/dev/null
find ~/.local/share/oauthsvc/temp -type f -printf '%p %TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM:%TS\n' 2>/dev/null
```

The output will show the file path and modification date. Compare the modification time against your service's last startup time (visible in the service's console log).

### Checking for Locked Files

To see which temporary files are currently held open by any process, run:

```bash
lsof 2>/dev/null | grep oauthsvc | grep /tmp
lsof 2>/dev/null | grep oauthsvc | grep ~/.local/share/oauthsvc
```

If `lsof` is not installed, you can check `/proc` directly (on systems where the service process still has a running PID):

```bash
ls -la /proc/<pid>/fd | grep /tmp
```

---

## Cleanup Procedures

**Section Owner:** Desktop Engineering (Theo Baptiste) — *last reviewed 2025-06-03*

### Before You Start

Before removing any temporary files, take these precautions:

- **Confirm the service is stopped.** Check that no oauthsvc processes are running on the host. On Windows, use `Get-Process oauthsvc -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`; on Linux, use `pgrep oauthsvc`.
- **Note the database file location.** You will need to avoid removing the database file itself or its immediate parent directory. See the page on locating oauthsvc files for paths.
- **Do not remove the database file or its journal files while the service is running.** Even though these are not strictly "temporary," they can be mistaken for temporary files.

### Safe Cleanup (Service Stopped)

When the service is confirmed stopped, you can safely remove:

1. **Process state directories** in the system temporary folder matching the pattern `identitysvc_<PID>`. On Windows, these are in `%TEMP%`; on Linux, in `/tmp`.
2. **Incomplete work files** in the service-specific state directory (`%APPDATA%\oauthsvc\temp` on Windows, `~/.local/share/oauthsvc/temp` on Linux).
3. **Cache files** in the service-specific state directory older than the service's last startup.

To remove these files on Windows:

```powershell
On Windows, remove identitysvc_* directories from system temp, ignoring any errors.
Remove-Item -Path $env:APPDATA\oauthsvc\temp\*.meta -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

On Linux:

```bash
On Linux, remove identitysvc_* directories from /tmp.
rm -f ~/.local/share/oauthsvc/temp/*.meta
```

### Cleanup While Service Is Running

If you need to clean up temporary files while the service is running (not recommended, but sometimes necessary):

- Remove only **cache files** from the loopback interface directory. Identify these by their file extension and modification time (they are typically recreated within seconds after removal).
- **Do not remove** any lock files, incomplete work files, or process state directories while the service is running.

On Windows, identify cache files by extension:

```powershell
On Windows, remove *.cache files from identitysvc_* directories in system temp.
```

On Linux:

```bash
On Linux, remove *.cache files from identitysvc_* directories in /tmp.
```

### Worked Example: Cleanup After Unclean Shutdown

Suppose the service crashed on a Windows workstation, and you want to remove the stale temporary files before restarting.

**Step 1:** Verify the service is stopped.
```powershell
Stop-Service oauthsvc -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Start-Sleep -Seconds 2
Get-Process oauthsvc -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue  # Should return nothing
```

**Step 2:** List the temporary directories.
```powershell
On Windows, list identitysvc_* directories in system temporary storage.
```

Example output:
```
Mode                 LastWriteTime         Name
----                 -------------         ----
d----  2026-09-26 08:15:32 identitysvc_3284
d----  2026-09-22 14:42:11 identitysvc_2901
```

**Step 3:** Remove old temporary directories.
```powershell
On Windows, remove process directory identitysvc_3284 from system temp.
On Windows, remove process directory identitysvc_2901 from system temp.
```

**Step 4:** Clean up incomplete work files.
```powershell
Remove-Item -Path $env:APPDATA\oauthsvc\temp -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $env:APPDATA\oauthsvc\temp -Force | Out-Null
```

**Step 5:** Restart the service.
```powershell
Start-Service oauthsvc
```

---

## Monitoring and Prevention

To prevent temporary file accumulation, consider:

- **Monitor disk usage regularly.** See the page on disk space monitoring for ongoing checks.
- **Review temporary file counts weekly** on hosts where the service runs frequently. Use the commands in the sections above and set up alerts if the file count exceeds a threshold (e.g., more than 50 temporary directories).
- **Log service shutdowns.** Record when the service is stopped and whether it was a clean or unclean termination. Unclean terminations (crash, forced kill) are more likely to leave orphaned temporary files.
- **Clean up periodically as part of host maintenance.** Schedule a weekly or monthly cleanup task during a maintenance window when the service is confirmed stopped.

### Automated Cleanup Script (Windows)

You can create a scheduled task to clean up old temporary files. Create a file named `cleanup-oauthsvc-temp.ps1`:

```powershell
# Clean up oauthsvc temporary files older than 7 days
$CutoffDate = (Get-Date).AddDays(-7)
On Windows, remove identitysvc_* directories from system temp that are older than a specified cutoff date.
Get-ChildItem -Path $env:APPDATA\oauthsvc\temp -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.LastWriteTime -lt $CutoffDate } | Remove-Item -Force
```

Schedule this script to run via Task Scheduler at a time when the service is not typically active.

---

## Interaction with Other Components

**Related to port conflicts.** When the service restarts, it re-binds to its configured port. Stale lock files can occasionally interfere with port binding. If you encounter port conflict errors after a crash, clean up temporary files as described above before investigating further. See the page on resolving port conflicts.

**Related to console logging.** Console log files are separate from the temporary files discussed here and are not cleaned up as part of routine temporary file removal. Refer to the page on managing console log files for guidance on log lifecycle and storage.

**Related to SQLite locking.** If you observe database lock timeouts or "database is locked" errors, orphaned lock files may be the cause. However, do not simply remove lock files; consult the page on diagnosing SQLite locking first. Stale auxiliary files (journal, wal) can be cleaned up after confirming the database is not in use.

**Related to database backups.** Before cleaning up temporary files, ensure you have a recent backup of the database file. Do not confuse temporary files with the database backup process. See the page on copying the database file for backup procedures.

---

## Terminology

| Term | Definition |
|------|-----------|
| **Lock file** | A file created by the service to indicate that a resource (such as the database file) is in use by a running process. Lock files are typically removed when the process exits cleanly. |
| **Orphaned file** | A temporary file that remains on disk after the process that created it has terminated. Orphaned files can be safely removed. |
| **Process ID (PID)** | A unique numerical identifier assigned to a running process by the operating system. Temporary files are often named with the PID for uniqueness. |
| **Journal file** | An auxiliary file created by SQLite alongside the database file to record changes during a transaction. Journal files are cleaned up automatically when the transaction completes. |
| **Cache file** | A temporary file used to store frequently accessed data in memory or on disk to improve performance. Cache files are typically recreated on each service startup. |
| **Incomplete work data** | A file that records incomplete transactions or in-flight operations, used by the service to restart cleanly after an unexpected shutdown. |
| **Stale file** | A temporary file that has not been modified for a long period and is no longer needed by the service. Stale files can be removed to reclaim disk space. |
| **State directory** | A process-specific directory created by the service in the system temporary folder to store transient runtime state. |
| **WAL file** | A Write-Ahead Log file created by SQLite in certain configurations to improve write performance and concurrency. |
| **Shared memory file (shm)** | An auxiliary file created by SQLite to manage shared memory for concurrent access. Shared memory files are cleaned up when the database connection closes. |

---

## Files and Paths Reference

| Path | Purpose | Notes |
|------|------|-------|
| `%TEMP%` (Windows) | System temporary directory | Contains process state directories named `identitysvc_<PID>`. On Windows 10/11, typically `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Temp`. |
| `/tmp` (Linux) | System temporary directory | Contains process state directories named `identitysvc_<PID>`. On systemd systems, `/run/user/<uid>` may also be used. |
| `%APPDATA%\oauthsvc\temp` (Windows) | Service-specific state directory | Contains incomplete work files and persistent cache. Typically `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\oauthsvc\temp`. |
| `~/.local/share/oauthsvc/temp` (Linux) | Service-specific state directory | Contains incomplete work files and persistent cache. Resolves to the user's home directory. |
| `identitysvc_<PID>` (within `%TEMP%` or `/tmp`) | Process state directory | Created when the service starts, identified by its PID. Safe to remove when service is stopped. |
| Database file location | Database file (not temporary) | Do not remove; see the page on locating oauthsvc files. Auxiliary files (`.journal`, `.wal`, `.shm`) may be cleaned up after confirming the service is stopped. |
| `docs/` | Documentation folder | Contains runbooks and guides; not a temporary directory. |
| `scripts/` | Scripts folder | Contains utility scripts; not a temporary directory. |

---

## Tools and Versions

| Tool | Version | Purpose | Platform |
|------|---------|---------|----------|
| PowerShell | 5.1–7.x | File listing and removal on Windows. | Windows |
| bash | 4.x+ | File listing and removal on Linux. | Linux |
| sqlite3 | 3.30+ | Inspection of SQLite auxiliary files (optional). | Windows, Linux |
| lsof | 4.x+ | Listing open files and detecting locked files. | Linux |
| Resource Monitor | Windows built-in | Graphical tool for inspecting open file handles. | Windows 10/11 |
| find | GNU 4.8+ | Recursive file search with modification time filtering. | Linux |
| Get-ChildItem | PowerShell 5.1+ | Listing files with full metadata. | Windows |

---

## Changelog

| Date | Version | Release | Changes |
|------|---------|---------|---------|
| 2025-04-11 | v2.1.0 | **Current** | Updated examples for Windows 10/11 and Linux systemd. Added WAL and shared memory file discussion. Clarified that incomplete work files should not be removed if the service uses crash-resilience features. |
| 2024-11-22 | v2.0.3 | Routine update | Fixed path examples for %APPDATA% on non-English Windows installations. Added note about lsof availability. |
| 2024-08-15 | v2.0.2 | Bug fix | Corrected the default temporary directory path for certain Linux distributions using /run/user/<uid>. |
| 2024-06-10 | v2.0.1 | Minor update | Added Worked Example section. Expanded Monitoring and Prevention with automated cleanup script. |
| 2024-03-03 | v2.0 | Major release | Reorganized cleanup procedures into "Service Stopped" and "Service Running" sections. Added interaction notes with other components. |
| 2024-01-14 | v1.0 | Initial release | First version of the page, covering basic temporary file cleanup on Windows and Linux. |

---

## Related Pages

- **[Resolving Port Conflicts on the Loopback Service](port-conflicts-on-the-loopback-service.md)** (v2.3, Host Operations — Derek Yun, updated 2025-11-04) — Troubleshoot port binding issues, sometimes related to stale temporary files or lock files.
- **[Disk Space Checks for the Host](disk-space-checks.md)** (v1.4.0, Systems Reliability — Priya Nandan, updated 2025-02-18) — Monitor overall disk usage and set up alerts for insufficient space.
