1	Title: Running Multiple oauthsvc Installations on One Host
2	Version: v1.0.2
3	Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
4	Last updated: 2026-06-20
5	
6	
7	== OVERVIEW ==
8	
9	When running more than one instance of the oauthsvc package on the same workstation or small server, careful attention to configuration and file placement prevents port conflicts, log file corruption, database locking issues, and resource exhaustion. This page walks through the key concerns: assigning separate ports to each instance, organizing log files and database files in distinct directories, monitoring disk usage and performance, and backing up multiple database files.
10	
11	If you are running just one installation, most of this page does not apply to you. For basic setup of a single instance, see Locating oauthsvc Files on a Host and the operations runbooks overview.
12	
13	The oauthsvc package is designed to run as a standalone service with its own loopback HTTP server and SQLite database file. Running multiple instances on one host is common in development and staging environments, but it introduces complications that single-instance deployments do not face. This page assumes you have already installed the package multiple times and are now configuring them to coexist.
14	
15	
16	== ASSIGNING PORTS ==
17	
18	Section Owner: Host Operations (Derek Yun)
19	
20	Each oauthsvc installation on the host must listen on its own port number. By default, the service uses port 8443; if you run a second instance, you must choose a different port (typically 8444, 8445, and so on). Port conflicts will cause the second installation to fail on startup with a "port already in use" error.
21	
22	To check which ports are already in use on your host, use the appropriate tool for your platform:
23	
24	Windows:
25	
26	  netstat -ano | find "LISTENING"
27	
28	or the newer PowerShell approach:
29	
30	  Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalPort, OwningProcess | Sort-Object LocalPort
31	
32	On macOS or Linux, use:
33	
34	  netstat -tuln | grep LISTEN
35	  
36	or
37	
38	  lsof -i -P -n | grep LISTEN
39	
40	The lsof output will show you the process name as well, which helps identify which service is using which port.
41	
42	Once you have identified an available port, assign it in the service configuration file for each installation. Store your port assignments in a configuration file or spreadsheet. Common port choices for multiple installations on the same host:
43	
44	  Instance      Port   Directory                    Config File
45	  ---------------------------------------------------------------
46	  prod-web      8443   C:\oauthsvc\prod-web         config.ini
47	  stage-api     8444   C:\oauthsvc\stage-api        config.ini
48	  dev-local     8445   C:\oauthsvc\dev-local        config.ini
49	  qa-check    8446   C:\platformsvc\qa-check       config.ini
50	
51	Ports 8400–8499 are commonly reserved for development services and are less likely to conflict with system services. Avoid ports below 1024 on Linux, as these require elevated access.
52	
53	Keep a text file in your oauthsvc root directory listing your instances and their ports:
54	
55	  C:\oauthsvc-instances.txt
56	
57	Example contents:
58	
59	  Instance      Port   Directory               Started      Last Updated
60	  =====================================================================
61	  prod-web      8443   C:\oauthsvc\prod-web    2026-05-10   2026-06-15
62	  stage-api     8444   C:\oauthsvc\stage-api   2026-06-01   2026-06-20
63	  dev-local     8445   C:\oauthsvc\dev-local   2026-02-15   2026-06-18
64	  qa-check    8446   C:\platformsvc\qa-check  2026-04-22   2026-06-19
65	
66	This file will help you quickly remember which port belongs to which installation when troubleshooting. For more details on port assignment and conflict resolution, see Resolving Port Conflicts on the Loopback Service (version 2.3, updated 2025-11-04).
67	
68	
69	== ORGANIZING LOG FILES ==
70	
71	Section Owner: Desktop Engineering (Theo Baptiste)
72	
73	Each oauthsvc installation must write its console log file to a separate location. If two instances share the same log file, the logs will interleave, making it impossible to diagnose issues in either installation. The typical approach is to create a logs subdirectory for each installation.
74	
75	Recommended directory structure:
76	
77	  C:\oauthsvc\
78	  ├── prod-web\
79	  │   ├── config.ini
80	  │   ├── logs\
81	  │   │   ├── console.log
82	  │   │   └── console.log.20260610  (old)
83	  │   └── database.db
84	  ├── stage-api\
85	  │   ├── config.ini
86	  │   ├── logs\
87	  │   │   ├── console.log
88	  │   │   └── console.log.20260615  (old)
89	  │   └── database.db
90	  ├── dev-local\
91	  │   ├── config.ini
92	  │   ├── logs\
93	  │   │   └── console.log
94	  │   └── database.db
95	  └── qa-check\
96	      ├── config.ini
97	      ├── logs\
98	      │   └── console.log
99	      └── database.db
100	
101	Before starting a new installation, create the logs directory:
102	
103	  mkdir C:\oauthsvc\stage-api\logs
104	
105	Then configure the service to write to that path in its config file or environment variable, if applicable. Do not rely on default paths; always explicitly specify the log file location for each installation. Consult Managing the Service's Console Log Files (version 1.0, updated 2024-08-22) for detailed guidance on log file configuration, log file rollover settings, and verbosity levels.
106	
107	Log file growth estimates:  Each log file grows over time depending on traffic and verbosity level. At INFO verbosity:
108	
109	  - Light usage (5–10 requests per day):  ~1–2 MB per week
110	  - Moderate usage (50–100 requests per day):  ~5–10 MB per week
111	  - Heavy usage (500+ requests per day):  ~50 MB per week
112	
113	If you have four instances running and set them all to INFO level, plan for aggregate log growth of 10–40 MB per week. Enable log rollover to prevent log files from occupying all available disk space. Most production environments roll over logs daily or weekly, keeping the last 7–14 rolled-over copies.
114	
115	Checking log file sizes:
116	
117	  dir C:\oauthsvc\*/logs\console.log
118	
119	or with PowerShell:
120	
121	  Get-ChildItem C:\oauthsvc\*/logs/console.log | Select-Object Name, Length, LastWriteTime
122	
123	
124	== MANAGING DATABASE FILES ==
125	
126	Section Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
127	
128	The oauthsvc package stores its state in a SQLite database file. By default this file is named database.db and resides in the service's working directory. When you run multiple instances, each must use its own database file to avoid file locking contention and data corruption.
129	
130	The directory structure described above (prod-web/, stage-api/, dev-local/) naturally isolates database files by default. Each installation's configuration file or startup command should point to its own database.db in its own directory. Do not share a single database file across installations unless you fully understand the locking implications and have a compelling reason to do so—this is rarely a good idea and causes performance problems.
131	
132	Correct setup:
133	
134	  - prod-web uses C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db
135	  - stage-api uses C:\oauthsvc\stage-api\database.db
136	  - dev-local uses C:\oauthsvc\dev-local\database.db
137	  - qa-check uses C:\platformsvc\qa-check\database.db
138	
139	Incorrect setup (do not use):
140	
141	  All instances share C:\oauthsvc\shared\database.db
142	
143	If you inherited a setup where instances share a database file, separate them immediately by creating a new database file in each instance's directory and migrating data as needed.
144	
145	Database file sizes depend on how much data the service stores. Typical sizes:
146	
147	  - Empty or lightly used database:  50–500 KB
148	  - Moderately used database:  2–10 MB
149	  - Heavily used database:  50–200+ MB
150	
151	Monitor the size of each database.db file over time to detect unexpected growth, which may indicate a data-accumulation issue or bug.
152	
153	To check database file sizes:
154	
155	  dir C:\oauthsvc\*/database.db
156	
157	or in PowerShell:
158	
159	  Get-ChildItem C:\oauthsvc\*/database.db | Select-Object Name, Length, LastWriteTime
160	
161	
162	== DISK SPACE CONSIDERATIONS ==
163	
164	Section Owner: Systems Reliability (Priya Nandan)
165	
166	Running multiple oauthsvc installations increases disk usage in two ways: log files and database files. Both must be monitored to prevent disk-space exhaustion.
167	
168	Log files:  Each installation writes to its own console log file. Log growth rate depends on traffic and verbosity level. As noted above, even at INFO level, a busy instance can generate 50+ MB per week. If you have four or five instances, plan for several hundred megabytes of log data per month. Enable log rollover and establish a cleanup schedule (see Managing the Service's Console Log Files, version 1.0).
169	
170	Database files:  Each database.db file grows as the service stores data. Growth rate depends on your usage. In most cases, database files grow more slowly than logs, but for heavy-traffic scenarios, database growth can be significant. Monitor each database file monthly to detect unexpected growth.
171	
172	Disk usage check:
173	
174	  dir C:\oauthsvc /s
175	
176	or on Linux or macOS:
177	
178	  du -sh C:\oauthsvc
179	
180	For a per-installation breakdown:
181	
182	  du -sh C:\oauthsvc\prod-web
183	  du -sh C:\oauthsvc\stage-api
184	  du -sh C:\oauthsvc\dev-local
185	  Check the disk space used by C:\platformsvc\qa-check
186	
187	For detailed per-directory breakdown on Windows:
188	
189	  Get-ChildItem C:\oauthsvc -Recurse | Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum | Select-Object @{N="Total (MB)";E={[math]::Round($_.Sum/1MB, 2)}}
190	
191	Set a reminder (weekly or monthly, depending on your traffic) to run these checks. If any installation's log directory is approaching your free disk space limit, roll over or clean up old logs immediately. For a full checklist and guidance on automated monitoring, see Disk Space Checks for the Host (version 1.4.0, updated 2025-02-18).
192	
193	Recommended thresholds:
194	
195	  - Less than 100 MB free on host:  Critical; clean up logs immediately
196	  - Less than 500 MB free on host:  Warning; review log rollover; disable verbose logging
197	  - Between 500 MB and 2 GB free:  Normal; continue monitoring
198	  - More than 2 GB free:  Plenty of space; routine monthly checks
199	
200	
201	== SQLITEFILELOCK CONTENTION ==
202	
203	Section Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
204	
205	SQLite uses file-level locking to coordinate concurrent access to a database file. When two separate processes (two oauthsvc installations) attempt to access the same database file simultaneously, one will be blocked until the other releases the lock. This serializes access, increasing latency and reducing throughput.
206	
207	More critically, if one oauthsvc process dies or crashes while holding a lock on the database file, the lock may not be cleaned up. Other processes waiting for the lock will hang indefinitely, unable to proceed. This can cause cascading failures across multiple instances.
208	
209	SQLite creates temporary files alongside the main database file to manage locking and journaling:
210	
211	  database.db         (main database file)
212	  database.db-wal     (write-ahead log file)
213	  database.db-shm     (shared memory file)
214	
215	These auxiliary files are normally cleaned up automatically when the database is properly closed, but may persist if a process is terminated forcibly or crashes.
216	
217	To avoid locking issues:
218	
219	1. Always use separate database files for separate installations. This is the primary defense and is strongly recommended. Multiple instances should never share a single database.db file.
220	
221	2. If you have inherited a setup where instances share a database file, separate them as soon as possible by creating new database files and migrating data.
222	
223	3. Monitor the working directory of each installation for stale lock files. If you see auxiliary files (database.db-wal, database.db-shm) that persist for many hours, it may indicate a hung or crashed process.
224	
225	4. If a lock file remains after you have verified that all platformsvc processes accessing that database are stopped, you may safely remove the auxiliary files manually:
226	
227	     del C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db-wal
228	     del C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db-shm
229	
230	However, do this only after confirming that no platformsvc instances are running or accessing that database file. Removing lock files while a process is still accessing the database can cause data corruption.
231	
232	Checking for stale locks:
233	
234	  dir C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db*
235	
236	If auxiliary files are present and the oauthsvc process is not running, check the file's last-modified time. If it is more than an hour old, the lock is likely stale and can be removed.
237	
238	For detailed diagnosis procedures and lock-file interpretation, see Diagnosing SQLite File Locking on a Host (version 2.0.1, updated 2026-03-15). Note: that page discusses version 2.0.1 of the locking guide, which may differ slightly from this v1.0.2 page in details.
239	
240	
241	== MONITORING MULTIPLE INSTALLATIONS ==
242	
243	Section Owner: Systems Reliability (Priya Nandan)
244	
245	When you run multiple oauthsvc installations, you need to monitor each one independently. A single monitoring script can check all instances in one run, but be sure to report results per-installation so you can quickly identify which instance is misbehaving.
246	
247	Basic checks to perform on each installation:
248	
249	  - Is the service process running? (Check process list or port listener)
250	  - Is the service listening on its assigned port?
251	  - Is the console log file being written to? (Check recent modification time)
252	  - Is the database file accessible and within expected size range?
253	  - Has the process reported errors in the log file recently?
254	
255	Example monitoring script outline (pseudocode):
256	
257	  For each installation in (prod-web, stage-api, dev-local, qa-check):
258	    port = lookup port for this installation
259	    log_file = lookup log file path for this installation
260	    db_file = lookup database file path for this installation
261	
262	    Check if port is listening
263	      If not:  log ALERT "port {port} not listening for {installation}"
264	    
265	    Check if log_file exists and was modified in last 15 minutes
266	      If not:  log ALERT "log file for {installation} not recent"
267	    
268	    Check if db_file exists
269	      If not:  log ALERT "database file for {installation} missing"
270	    
271	    Check if db_file size is within expected range (e.g., < 500 MB)
272	      If not:  log WARNING "database file for {installation} unexpectedly large"
273	    
274	    Check last 20 lines of log_file for ERROR keywords
275	      If found:  log WARNING "recent errors in log for {installation}"
276	
277	Store the results in a log file so you can review them later. Set up your host's built-in monitoring tool (Event Viewer on Windows, cron on Linux, or a third-party agent) to run this script periodically (every 5–10 minutes) and alert you if any installation stops responding or shows errors.
278	
279	A simple cron job on Linux (runs every 10 minutes):
280	
281	  */10 * * * * /home/user/check-oauthsvc-instances.sh >> /var/log/oauthsvc-monitor.log 2>&1
282	
283	For Windows Task Scheduler, create a scheduled task to run your PowerShell monitoring script at a similar interval.
284	
285	For more information on monitoring setup, alert configuration, and handling alerts, see Host Monitoring Basics for oauthsvc (version 3.1, updated 2025-06-30).
286	
287	
288	== BACKING UP DATABASE FILES ==
289	
290	Section Owner: Host Operations (Derek Yun)
291	
292	When you run multiple oauthsvc installations, you must back up each database file separately. A backup should be a full copy of the database.db file from each installation's directory. Do not back up auxiliary files (database.db-wal, database.db-shm); these are temporary and will be recreated when the service restarts.
293	
294	Basic backup procedure:
295	
296	1. Stop the oauthsvc service (all instances). Ensure all processes are fully terminated before proceeding. You can verify with netstat or Get-NetTCPConnection.
297	
298	2. For each installation, copy its database.db file to a backup location with a timestamped filename:
299	
300	     copy C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db C:\backups\oauthsvc-prod-web-database.db.20260627
301	     copy C:\oauthsvc\stage-api\database.db C:\backups\oauthsvc-stage-api-database.db.20260627
302	     copy C:\oauthsvc\dev-local\database.db C:\backups\oauthsvc-dev-local-database.db.20260627
303	     Copy database.db from qa-check to C:\backups\platformsvc-qa-check-database.db.20260627
304	
305	3. Optionally, copy associated log files as well for record-keeping and documentation:
306	
307	     copy C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\logs\console.log C:\backups\oauthsvc-prod-web-console-20260627.log
308	
309	4. Verify that the backup files exist and have reasonable sizes:
310	
311	     dir C:\backups\oauthsvc-*.db.* /s
312	
313	5. Restart oauthsvc.
314	
315	Backup naming convention: Use YYYYMMDD (e.g., 20260627 for June 27, 2026) in the filename, along with the instance name and "database," so you can easily identify which backup is which and when it was taken.
316	
317	Example naming scheme:
318	
319	  oauthsvc-{instance}-database.db.{YYYYMMDD}
320	  oauthsvc-prod-web-database.db.20260627
321	  oauthsvc-stage-api-database.db.20260627
322	
323	Backup frequency: Schedule backups daily or weekly depending on how critical the data is. For production instances, daily backups are recommended. For development instances, weekly backups may suffice.
324	
325	Advanced approach for many installations:  If you are running five or more installations, manually copying each database is tedious and error-prone. Write a backup script that automates the process:
326	
327	  Define a list of installation names and their base directories
328	  For each installation:
329	    Check if database.db exists
330	    If it exists and size is within acceptable range:
331	      Copy it to backup location with timestamp
332	      Log the copy operation (file size, duration)
333	    If size is outside acceptable range:
334	      Log a warning; do not copy
335	  At the end, verify that all backups succeeded
336	  Send summary alert or log message with count of backups created
337	
338	Example backup script structure (pseudocode):
339	
340	Set the installations list to prod-web, stage-api, dev-local, and qa-check
341	  $backup_dir = "C:\backups"
342	  $date_string = Get-Date -Format "yyyyMMdd"
343	  
344	  foreach ($instance in $installations) {
345	    $db_file = "C:\oauthsvc\$instance\database.db"
346	    If the database file exists:
347	      $file_size = (Get-Item $db_file).Length
348	      $backup_file = "$backup_dir\oauthsvc-$instance-database.db.$date_string"
349	      Copy-Item $db_file $backup_file
350	      Write-Host "Backed up $instance ($file_size bytes)"
351	    }
352	  }
353	
354	Keep backups on a separate disk or host to protect against hardware failure or data loss. If your host has an external drive or network attached storage (NAS), back up to that location. For critical deployments, replicate backups to a second location or cloud storage.
355	
356	See Copying the Database File for Backup (version 1.2.3, updated 2024-12-01) for full guidance on backup procedures, handling large files, and network backup options. For information on how to restore a database from a backup, see Restoring a Copied Database File (version 2.0, updated 2025-09-19).
357	
358	
359	== TROUBLESHOOTING ==
360	
361	Port already in use:  Run netstat (Windows) or lsof (Linux/macOS) to find what process is using your target port. Note the process ID (PID). If it is a stale oauthsvc process, kill it or restart the host. If it is a different service, reassign your new oauthsvc installation to a different port. See Resolving Port Conflicts on the Loopback Service (version 2.3).
362	
363	Log files growing too fast:  Check that log rollover is configured and enabled in your config file. Alternatively, one or more of your instances may be logging at DEBUG level or experiencing errors. Review the console logs for ERROR messages. If you see repeated errors, investigate the root cause and fix it. See Managing the Service's Console Log Files (version 1.0).
364	
365	One instance hangs or is unresponsive:  Check if the process is still running (via Process Explorer or Task Manager on Windows, or ps on Linux). If the process exists but does not respond to requests, it may be waiting for a lock on a database file. Verify that this instance has its own separate database.db file and not a shared one. If lock files exist and are stale, remove them. Stop the instance, clean up lock files, and restart. See Diagnosing SQLite File Locking on a Host (version 2.0.1).
366	
367	Unexpected high disk usage:  Check which directory or file is taking up space. If it is the logs/ directory, enable log rollover or increase rollover frequency. If it is the database.db file itself, the database is either receiving heavy traffic or not cleaning up old data as intended. Monitor database file size over a week and compare growth rate to expected usage. See Disk Space Checks for the Host (version 1.4.0).
368	
369	Instance fails to start:  Check the console log file for error messages. Common causes are: (1) port already in use, (2) database file is locked (another instance still accessing it), (3) missing or invalid configuration file. Verify each of these before restarting the instance.
370	
371	
372	== TERMINOLOGY ==
373	
374	database file:  The SQLite file (usually named database.db) in which an oauthsvc service instance stores its state. Each installation must have its own separate database file. Sharing a database file across multiple instances causes locking problems and is not recommended.
375	
376	installation:  A single configured instance of the oauthsvc service running on the host, with its own port number, configuration file, database file, and log directory.
377	
378	console log file:  The text file (usually in logs/console.log) to which an oauthsvc service instance writes diagnostic output, errors, and informational messages during operation.
379	
380	port:  A network port number (e.g., 8443, 8444) on the loopback interface (localhost / 127.0.0.1) on which an oauthsvc service instance listens for requests. Each installation must use a different port.
381	
382	loopback service:  The HTTP server built into the oauthsvc package that listens on localhost and accepts requests via the loopback interface. It handles configuration, startup, and shutdown requests.
383	
384	lock file:  A temporary file created by SQLite alongside the database file (typically database.db-wal or database.db-shm) to coordinate concurrent access and journaling. Lock files are normally cleaned up automatically when the database is properly closed, but may persist if a process crashes.
385	
386	working directory:  The directory from which a particular oauthsvc installation is started or configured. This directory typically contains the config file, database.db file, and logs/ subdirectory. By convention, each installation has its own working directory (e.g., C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\).
387	
388	file locking:  The mechanism by which the operating system and SQLite coordinate simultaneous access to a file, ensuring that multiple processes do not corrupt the file by writing to it concurrently. When a lock is held, other processes must wait until the lock is released.
389	
390	verbosity level:  A configuration setting (INFO, DEBUG, WARNING, ERROR) that controls how much detail the service logs. DEBUG produces the most output and the largest log files; ERROR produces the least. Use INFO for most scenarios.
391	
392	
393	== REFERENCED FILES AND PATHS ==
394	
395	C:\oauthsvc\:  Root directory for all oauthsvc installations on this host. Adjust path as needed for your environment.
396	
397	C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\config.ini:  Configuration file for the prod-web installation. Specifies port, log file location, database location, and other settings. Example only; your config file name may differ.
398	
399	C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db:  Database file for the prod-web installation. Each installation has its own. Do not share across instances.
400	
401	C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\logs\console.log:  Console log file for the prod-web installation. Each installation writes to its own log file in its own logs/ directory.
402	
403	C:\oauthsvc\stage-api\database.db:  Database file for the stage-api installation.
404	
405	C:\oauthsvc\stage-api\logs\console.log:  Console log file for the stage-api installation.
406	
407	C:\oauthsvc\dev-local\database.db:  Database file for the dev-local installation.
408	
409	C:\oauthsvc\dev-local\logs\console.log:  Console log file for the dev-local installation.
410	
411	C:\platformsvc\qa-check\database.db:  Database file for the qa-check installation.
412	
413	C:\platformsvc\qa-check\logs\console.log:  Console log file for the qa-check installation.
414	
415	C:\oauthsvc-instances.txt:  Optional text file listing all installations, their ports, directories, and start dates. Useful for quick reference.
416	
417	C:\backups\:  Directory for storing database backups. Keep on a separate disk or NAS if possible for redundancy.
418	
419	docs/operations-runbooks/:  The folder in the repository containing this and related operations pages (port conflicts, disk space, logging, locking, monitoring, backup).
420	
421	
422	== TOOLS AND DEPENDENCIES ==
423	
424	Tool / Library                              Version      Notes
425	-----------------------------------------------------------------------
426	Windows PowerShell                          5.1+         For port checking, directory listing, backup scripts on Windows
427	Windows netstat                             bundled      For enumerating listening ports
428	Windows Get-NetTCPConnection                5.1+         Modern PowerShell cmdlet; alternative to netstat
429	Windows Process Explorer                    16.41+       For detailed process inspection (optional)
430	Linux lsof (list open files)                4.95.0+      For port checking and file descriptor inspection on Unix-like systems
431	Linux netstat                               2.10+        Alternative port checking tool on Linux
432	Linux du (disk usage)                       8.32+        For disk space reporting on Unix-like systems
433	macOS lsof                                  4.95.0+      For port checking on macOS
434	SQLite file format                          3            Underlying binary format of all database.db files
435	PowerShell Copy-Item cmdlet                 5.1+         For file copying in backup scripts
436	Bash (shell scripting)                      4.0+         For writing backup scripts on Unix-like systems
437	
438	(Version numbers reflect typical deployments as of 2026. Your system may have different versions; core functionality for basic operations should remain consistent.)
439	
440	
441	== CHANGE LOG ==
442	
443	2026-06-20, v1.0.2 (Mara Olsen):  Fixed example of lock file removal. Added explicit note on conflict with v2.0.1 of sqlite-file-locking.md regarding details of lock file cleanup. Clarified that database files should never be shared across instances. Expanded troubleshooting section with step-by-step failure diagnosis. Added advanced backup script outline.
444	
445	2026-03-15, v1.0.1 (Derek Yun):  Corrected disk usage command examples for Windows PowerShell. Added Get-NetTCPConnection as modern alternative to netstat. Improved log growth estimation table. Minor wording improvements throughout, especially in file isolation section.
446	
447	2026-02-28, v1.0.0 (Mara Olsen):  Initial release. Covers port assignment, log file isolation, database file separation, disk monitoring, SQLite locking, host monitoring, and backup procedures for multiple installations on a single host. Intended for platform tools and operations teams.
448	
449	2025-11-04, internal draft (Derek Yun):  Early draft circulated for feedback from Host Operations team. Port conflict section reviewed by Derek Yun. Feedback incorporated; not published.
450	
451	2025-08-10, design meeting discussion (Platform Tools team):  Team identified need for this runbook. Operations team fielded multiple questions about running 3–5 instances on workstations and small staging servers. Meeting minutes noted that shared database setups were causing confusion and performance problems.
452	
453	2025-06-15, preliminary outline (Mara Olsen):  Outlined topics and structure for runbook. Reviewed and cross-referenced sibling pages to avoid duplication. Noted gaps in existing documentation around multi-instance scenarios.
454	
455	
456	== RELATED PAGES ==
457

Title: Running Multiple oauthsvc Installations on One Host
Version: v1.0.2
Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
Last updated: 2026-06-20


== OVERVIEW ==

When running more than one instance of the oauthsvc package on the same workstation or small server, careful attention to configuration and file placement prevents port conflicts, log file corruption, database locking issues, and resource exhaustion. This page walks through the key concerns: assigning separate ports to each instance, organizing log files and database files in distinct directories, monitoring disk usage and performance, and backing up multiple database files.

If you are running just one installation, most of this page does not apply to you. For basic setup of a single instance, see Locating oauthsvc Files on a Host and the operations runbooks overview.

The oauthsvc package is designed to run as a standalone service with its own loopback HTTP server and SQLite database file. Running multiple instances on one host is common in development and staging environments, but it introduces complications that single-instance deployments do not face. This page assumes you have already installed the package multiple times and are now configuring them to coexist.


== ASSIGNING PORTS ==

Section Owner: Host Operations (Derek Yun)

Each oauthsvc installation on the host must listen on its own port number. By default, the service uses port 8443; if you run a second instance, you must choose a different port (typically 8444, 8445, and so on). Port conflicts will cause the second installation to fail on startup with a "port already in use" error.

To check which ports are already in use on your host, use the appropriate tool for your platform:

Windows:

  netstat -ano | find "LISTENING"

or the newer PowerShell approach:

  Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalPort, OwningProcess | Sort-Object LocalPort

On macOS or Linux, use:

  netstat -tuln | grep LISTEN
  
or

  lsof -i -P -n | grep LISTEN

The lsof output will show you the process name as well, which helps identify which service is using which port.

Once you have identified an available port, assign it in the service configuration file for each installation. Store your port assignments in a configuration file or spreadsheet. Common port choices for multiple installations on the same host:

  Instance      Port   Directory                    Config File
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  prod-web      8443   C:\oauthsvc\prod-web         config.ini
  stage-api     8444   C:\oauthsvc\stage-api        config.ini
  dev-local     8445   C:\oauthsvc\dev-local        config.ini
  qa-check    8446   C:\platformsvc\qa-check       config.ini

Ports 8400–8499 are commonly reserved for development services and are less likely to conflict with system services. Avoid ports below 1024 on Linux, as these require elevated access.

Keep a text file in your oauthsvc root directory listing your instances and their ports:

  C:\oauthsvc-instances.txt

Example contents:

  Instance      Port   Directory               Started      Last Updated
  =====================================================================
  prod-web      8443   C:\oauthsvc\prod-web    2026-05-10   2026-06-15
  stage-api     8444   C:\oauthsvc\stage-api   2026-06-01   2026-06-20
  dev-local     8445   C:\oauthsvc\dev-local   2026-02-15   2026-06-18
  qa-check    8446   C:\platformsvc\qa-check  2026-04-22   2026-06-19

This file will help you quickly remember which port belongs to which installation when troubleshooting. For more details on port assignment and conflict resolution, see Resolving Port Conflicts on the Loopback Service (version 2.3, updated 2025-11-04).


== ORGANIZING LOG FILES ==

Section Owner: Desktop Engineering (Theo Baptiste)

Each oauthsvc installation must write its console log file to a separate location. If two instances share the same log file, the logs will interleave, making it impossible to diagnose issues in either installation. The typical approach is to create a logs subdirectory for each installation.

Recommended directory structure:

  C:\oauthsvc\
  ├── prod-web\
  │   ├── config.ini
  │   ├── logs\
  │   │   ├── console.log
  │   │   └── console.log.20260610  (old)
  │   └── database.db
  ├── stage-api\
  │   ├── config.ini
  │   ├── logs\
  │   │   ├── console.log
  │   │   └── console.log.20260615  (old)
  │   └── database.db
  ├── dev-local\
  │   ├── config.ini
  │   ├── logs\
  │   │   └── console.log
  │   └── database.db
  └── qa-check\
      ├── config.ini
      ├── logs\
      │   └── console.log
      └── database.db

Before starting a new installation, create the logs directory:

  mkdir C:\oauthsvc\stage-api\logs

Then configure the service to write to that path in its config file or environment variable, if applicable. Do not rely on default paths; always explicitly specify the log file location for each installation. Consult Managing the Service's Console Log Files (version 1.0, updated 2024-08-22) for detailed guidance on log file configuration, log file rollover settings, and verbosity levels.

Log file growth estimates:  Each log file grows over time depending on traffic and verbosity level. At INFO verbosity:

  - Light usage (5–10 requests per day):  ~1–2 MB per week
  - Moderate usage (50–100 requests per day):  ~5–10 MB per week
  - Heavy usage (500+ requests per day):  ~50 MB per week

If you have four instances running and set them all to INFO level, plan for aggregate log growth of 10–40 MB per week. Enable log rollover to prevent log files from occupying all available disk space. Most production environments roll over logs daily or weekly, keeping the last 7–14 rolled-over copies.

Checking log file sizes:

  dir C:\oauthsvc\*/logs\console.log

or with PowerShell:

  Get-ChildItem C:\oauthsvc\*/logs/console.log | Select-Object Name, Length, LastWriteTime


== MANAGING DATABASE FILES ==

Section Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)

The oauthsvc package stores its state in a SQLite database file. By default this file is named database.db and resides in the service's working directory. When you run multiple instances, each must use its own database file to avoid file locking contention and data corruption.

The directory structure described above (prod-web/, stage-api/, dev-local/) naturally isolates database files by default. Each installation's configuration file or startup command should point to its own database.db in its own directory. Do not share a single database file across installations unless you fully understand the locking implications and have a compelling reason to do so—this is rarely a good idea and causes performance problems.

Correct setup:

  - prod-web uses C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db
  - stage-api uses C:\oauthsvc\stage-api\database.db
  - dev-local uses C:\oauthsvc\dev-local\database.db
  - qa-check uses C:\platformsvc\qa-check\database.db

Incorrect setup (do not use):

  All instances share C:\oauthsvc\shared\database.db

If you inherited a setup where instances share a database file, separate them immediately by creating a new database file in each instance's directory and migrating data as needed.

Database file sizes depend on how much data the service stores. Typical sizes:

  - Empty or lightly used database:  50–500 KB
  - Moderately used database:  2–10 MB
  - Heavily used database:  50–200+ MB

Monitor the size of each database.db file over time to detect unexpected growth, which may indicate a data-accumulation issue or bug.

To check database file sizes:

  dir C:\oauthsvc\*/database.db

or in PowerShell:

  Get-ChildItem C:\oauthsvc\*/database.db | Select-Object Name, Length, LastWriteTime


== DISK SPACE CONSIDERATIONS ==

Section Owner: Systems Reliability (Priya Nandan)

Running multiple oauthsvc installations increases disk usage in two ways: log files and database files. Both must be monitored to prevent disk-space exhaustion.

Log files:  Each installation writes to its own console log file. Log growth rate depends on traffic and verbosity level. As noted above, even at INFO level, a busy instance can generate 50+ MB per week. If you have four or five instances, plan for several hundred megabytes of log data per month. Enable log rollover and establish a cleanup schedule (see Managing the Service's Console Log Files, version 1.0).

Database files:  Each database.db file grows as the service stores data. Growth rate depends on your usage. In most cases, database files grow more slowly than logs, but for heavy-traffic scenarios, database growth can be significant. Monitor each database file monthly to detect unexpected growth.

Disk usage check:

  dir C:\oauthsvc /s

or on Linux or macOS:

  du -sh C:\oauthsvc

For a per-installation breakdown:

  du -sh C:\oauthsvc\prod-web
  du -sh C:\oauthsvc\stage-api
  du -sh C:\oauthsvc\dev-local
  Check the disk space used by C:\platformsvc\qa-check

For detailed per-directory breakdown on Windows:

  Get-ChildItem C:\oauthsvc -Recurse | Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum | Select-Object @{N="Total (MB)";E={[math]::Round($_.Sum/1MB, 2)}}

Set a reminder (weekly or monthly, depending on your traffic) to run these checks. If any installation's log directory is approaching your free disk space limit, roll over or clean up old logs immediately. For a full checklist and guidance on automated monitoring, see Disk Space Checks for the Host (version 1.4.0, updated 2025-02-18).

Recommended thresholds:

  - Less than 100 MB free on host:  Critical; clean up logs immediately
  - Less than 500 MB free on host:  Warning; review log rollover; disable verbose logging
  - Between 500 MB and 2 GB free:  Normal; continue monitoring
  - More than 2 GB free:  Plenty of space; routine monthly checks


== SQLITEFILELOCK CONTENTION ==

Section Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)

SQLite uses file-level locking to coordinate concurrent access to a database file. When two separate processes (two oauthsvc installations) attempt to access the same database file simultaneously, one will be blocked until the other releases the lock. This serializes access, increasing latency and reducing throughput.

More critically, if one oauthsvc process dies or crashes while holding a lock on the database file, the lock may not be cleaned up. Other processes waiting for the lock will hang indefinitely, unable to proceed. This can cause cascading failures across multiple instances.

SQLite creates temporary files alongside the main database file to manage locking and journaling:

  database.db         (main database file)
  database.db-wal     (write-ahead log file)
  database.db-shm     (shared memory file)

These auxiliary files are normally cleaned up automatically when the database is properly closed, but may persist if a process is terminated forcibly or crashes.

To avoid locking issues:

1. Always use separate database files for separate installations. This is the primary defense and is strongly recommended. Multiple instances should never share a single database.db file.

2. If you have inherited a setup where instances share a database file, separate them as soon as possible by creating new database files and migrating data.

3. Monitor the working directory of each installation for stale lock files. If you see auxiliary files (database.db-wal, database.db-shm) that persist for many hours, it may indicate a hung or crashed process.

4. If a lock file remains after you have verified that all platformsvc processes accessing that database are stopped, you may safely remove the auxiliary files manually:

     del C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db-wal
     del C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db-shm

However, do this only after confirming that no platformsvc instances are running or accessing that database file. Removing lock files while a process is still accessing the database can cause data corruption.

Checking for stale locks:

  dir C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db*

If auxiliary files are present and the oauthsvc process is not running, check the file's last-modified time. If it is more than an hour old, the lock is likely stale and can be removed.

For detailed diagnosis procedures and lock-file interpretation, see Diagnosing SQLite File Locking on a Host (version 2.0.1, updated 2026-03-15). Note: that page discusses version 2.0.1 of the locking guide, which may differ slightly from this v1.0.2 page in details.


== MONITORING MULTIPLE INSTALLATIONS ==

Section Owner: Systems Reliability (Priya Nandan)

When you run multiple oauthsvc installations, you need to monitor each one independently. A single monitoring script can check all instances in one run, but be sure to report results per-installation so you can quickly identify which instance is misbehaving.

Basic checks to perform on each installation:

  - Is the service process running? (Check process list or port listener)
  - Is the service listening on its assigned port?
  - Is the console log file being written to? (Check recent modification time)
  - Is the database file accessible and within expected size range?
  - Has the process reported errors in the log file recently?

Example monitoring script outline (pseudocode):

  For each installation in (prod-web, stage-api, dev-local, qa-check):
    port = lookup port for this installation
    log_file = lookup log file path for this installation
    db_file = lookup database file path for this installation

    Check if port is listening
      If not:  log ALERT "port {port} not listening for {installation}"
    
    Check if log_file exists and was modified in last 15 minutes
      If not:  log ALERT "log file for {installation} not recent"
    
    Check if db_file exists
      If not:  log ALERT "database file for {installation} missing"
    
    Check if db_file size is within expected range (e.g., < 500 MB)
      If not:  log WARNING "database file for {installation} unexpectedly large"
    
    Check last 20 lines of log_file for ERROR keywords
      If found:  log WARNING "recent errors in log for {installation}"

Store the results in a log file so you can review them later. Set up your host's built-in monitoring tool (Event Viewer on Windows, cron on Linux, or a third-party agent) to run this script periodically (every 5–10 minutes) and alert you if any installation stops responding or shows errors.

A simple cron job on Linux (runs every 10 minutes):

  */10 * * * * /home/user/check-oauthsvc-instances.sh >> /var/log/oauthsvc-monitor.log 2>&1

For Windows Task Scheduler, create a scheduled task to run your PowerShell monitoring script at a similar interval.

For more information on monitoring setup, alert configuration, and handling alerts, see Host Monitoring Basics for oauthsvc (version 3.1, updated 2025-06-30).


== BACKING UP DATABASE FILES ==

Section Owner: Host Operations (Derek Yun)

When you run multiple oauthsvc installations, you must back up each database file separately. A backup should be a full copy of the database.db file from each installation's directory. Do not back up auxiliary files (database.db-wal, database.db-shm); these are temporary and will be recreated when the service restarts.

Basic backup procedure:

1. Stop the oauthsvc service (all instances). Ensure all processes are fully terminated before proceeding. You can verify with netstat or Get-NetTCPConnection.

2. For each installation, copy its database.db file to a backup location with a timestamped filename:

     copy C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db C:\backups\oauthsvc-prod-web-database.db.20260627
     copy C:\oauthsvc\stage-api\database.db C:\backups\oauthsvc-stage-api-database.db.20260627
     copy C:\oauthsvc\dev-local\database.db C:\backups\oauthsvc-dev-local-database.db.20260627
     Copy database.db from qa-check to C:\backups\platformsvc-qa-check-database.db.20260627

3. Optionally, copy associated log files as well for record-keeping and documentation:

     copy C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\logs\console.log C:\backups\oauthsvc-prod-web-console-20260627.log

4. Verify that the backup files exist and have reasonable sizes:

     dir C:\backups\oauthsvc-*.db.* /s

5. Restart oauthsvc.

Backup naming convention: Use YYYYMMDD (e.g., 20260627 for June 27, 2026) in the filename, along with the instance name and "database," so you can easily identify which backup is which and when it was taken.

Example naming scheme:

  oauthsvc-{instance}-database.db.{YYYYMMDD}
  oauthsvc-prod-web-database.db.20260627
  oauthsvc-stage-api-database.db.20260627

Backup frequency: Schedule backups daily or weekly depending on how critical the data is. For production instances, daily backups are recommended. For development instances, weekly backups may suffice.

Advanced approach for many installations:  If you are running five or more installations, manually copying each database is tedious and error-prone. Write a backup script that automates the process:

  Define a list of installation names and their base directories
  For each installation:
    Check if database.db exists
    If it exists and size is within acceptable range:
      Copy it to backup location with timestamp
      Log the copy operation (file size, duration)
    If size is outside acceptable range:
      Log a warning; do not copy
  At the end, verify that all backups succeeded
  Send summary alert or log message with count of backups created

Example backup script structure (pseudocode):

Set the installations list to prod-web, stage-api, dev-local, and qa-check
  $backup_dir = "C:\backups"
  $date_string = Get-Date -Format "yyyyMMdd"
  
  foreach ($instance in $installations) {
    $db_file = "C:\oauthsvc\$instance\database.db"
    If the database file exists:
      $file_size = (Get-Item $db_file).Length
      $backup_file = "$backup_dir\oauthsvc-$instance-database.db.$date_string"
      Copy-Item $db_file $backup_file
      Write-Host "Backed up $instance ($file_size bytes)"
    }
  }

Keep backups on a separate disk or host to protect against hardware failure or data loss. If your host has an external drive or network attached storage (NAS), back up to that location. For critical deployments, replicate backups to a second location or cloud storage.

See Copying the Database File for Backup (version 1.2.3, updated 2024-12-01) for full guidance on backup procedures, handling large files, and network backup options. For information on how to restore a database from a backup, see Restoring a Copied Database File (version 2.0, updated 2025-09-19).


== TROUBLESHOOTING ==

Port already in use:  Run netstat (Windows) or lsof (Linux/macOS) to find what process is using your target port. Note the process ID (PID). If it is a stale oauthsvc process, kill it or restart the host. If it is a different service, reassign your new oauthsvc installation to a different port. See Resolving Port Conflicts on the Loopback Service (version 2.3).

Log files growing too fast:  Check that log rollover is configured and enabled in your config file. Alternatively, one or more of your instances may be logging at DEBUG level or experiencing errors. Review the console logs for ERROR messages. If you see repeated errors, investigate the root cause and fix it. See Managing the Service's Console Log Files (version 1.0).

One instance hangs or is unresponsive:  Check if the process is still running (via Process Explorer or Task Manager on Windows, or ps on Linux). If the process exists but does not respond to requests, it may be waiting for a lock on a database file. Verify that this instance has its own separate database.db file and not a shared one. If lock files exist and are stale, remove them. Stop the instance, clean up lock files, and restart. See Diagnosing SQLite File Locking on a Host (version 2.0.1).

Unexpected high disk usage:  Check which directory or file is taking up space. If it is the logs/ directory, enable log rollover or increase rollover frequency. If it is the database.db file itself, the database is either receiving heavy traffic or not cleaning up old data as intended. Monitor database file size over a week and compare growth rate to expected usage. See Disk Space Checks for the Host (version 1.4.0).

Instance fails to start:  Check the console log file for error messages. Common causes are: (1) port already in use, (2) database file is locked (another instance still accessing it), (3) missing or invalid configuration file. Verify each of these before restarting the instance.


== TERMINOLOGY ==

database file:  The SQLite file (usually named database.db) in which an oauthsvc service instance stores its state. Each installation must have its own separate database file. Sharing a database file across multiple instances causes locking problems and is not recommended.

installation:  A single configured instance of the oauthsvc service running on the host, with its own port number, configuration file, database file, and log directory.

console log file:  The text file (usually in logs/console.log) to which an oauthsvc service instance writes diagnostic output, errors, and informational messages during operation.

port:  A network port number (e.g., 8443, 8444) on the loopback interface (localhost / 127.0.0.1) on which an oauthsvc service instance listens for requests. Each installation must use a different port.

loopback service:  The HTTP server built into the oauthsvc package that listens on localhost and accepts requests via the loopback interface. It handles configuration, startup, and shutdown requests.

lock file:  A temporary file created by SQLite alongside the database file (typically database.db-wal or database.db-shm) to coordinate concurrent access and journaling. Lock files are normally cleaned up automatically when the database is properly closed, but may persist if a process crashes.

working directory:  The directory from which a particular oauthsvc installation is started or configured. This directory typically contains the config file, database.db file, and logs/ subdirectory. By convention, each installation has its own working directory (e.g., C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\).

file locking:  The mechanism by which the operating system and SQLite coordinate simultaneous access to a file, ensuring that multiple processes do not corrupt the file by writing to it concurrently. When a lock is held, other processes must wait until the lock is released.

verbosity level:  A configuration setting (INFO, DEBUG, WARNING, ERROR) that controls how much detail the service logs. DEBUG produces the most output and the largest log files; ERROR produces the least. Use INFO for most scenarios.


== REFERENCED FILES AND PATHS ==

C:\oauthsvc\:  Root directory for all oauthsvc installations on this host. Adjust path as needed for your environment.

C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\config.ini:  Configuration file for the prod-web installation. Specifies port, log file location, database location, and other settings. Example only; your config file name may differ.

C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\database.db:  Database file for the prod-web installation. Each installation has its own. Do not share across instances.

C:\oauthsvc\prod-web\logs\console.log:  Console log file for the prod-web installation. Each installation writes to its own log file in its own logs/ directory.

C:\oauthsvc\stage-api\database.db:  Database file for the stage-api installation.

C:\oauthsvc\stage-api\logs\console.log:  Console log file for the stage-api installation.

C:\oauthsvc\dev-local\database.db:  Database file for the dev-local installation.

C:\oauthsvc\dev-local\logs\console.log:  Console log file for the dev-local installation.

C:\platformsvc\qa-check\database.db:  Database file for the qa-check installation.

C:\platformsvc\qa-check\logs\console.log:  Console log file for the qa-check installation.

C:\oauthsvc-instances.txt:  Optional text file listing all installations, their ports, directories, and start dates. Useful for quick reference.

C:\backups\:  Directory for storing database backups. Keep on a separate disk or NAS if possible for redundancy.

docs/operations-runbooks/:  The folder in the repository containing this and related operations pages (port conflicts, disk space, logging, locking, monitoring, backup).


== TOOLS AND DEPENDENCIES ==

Tool / Library                              Version      Notes
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Windows PowerShell                          5.1+         For port checking, directory listing, backup scripts on Windows
Windows netstat                             bundled      For enumerating listening ports
Windows Get-NetTCPConnection                5.1+         Modern PowerShell cmdlet; alternative to netstat
Windows Process Explorer                    16.41+       For detailed process inspection (optional)
Linux lsof (list open files)                4.95.0+      For port checking and file descriptor inspection on Unix-like systems
Linux netstat                               2.10+        Alternative port checking tool on Linux
Linux du (disk usage)                       8.32+        For disk space reporting on Unix-like systems
macOS lsof                                  4.95.0+      For port checking on macOS
SQLite file format                          3            Underlying binary format of all database.db files
PowerShell Copy-Item cmdlet                 5.1+         For file copying in backup scripts
Bash (shell scripting)                      4.0+         For writing backup scripts on Unix-like systems

(Version numbers reflect typical deployments as of 2026. Your system may have different versions; core functionality for basic operations should remain consistent.)


== CHANGE LOG ==

2026-06-20, v1.0.2 (Mara Olsen):  Fixed example of lock file removal. Added explicit note on conflict with v2.0.1 of sqlite-file-locking.md regarding details of lock file cleanup. Clarified that database files should never be shared across instances. Expanded troubleshooting section with step-by-step failure diagnosis. Added advanced backup script outline.

2026-03-15, v1.0.1 (Derek Yun):  Corrected disk usage command examples for Windows PowerShell. Added Get-NetTCPConnection as modern alternative to netstat. Improved log growth estimation table. Minor wording improvements throughout, especially in file isolation section.

2026-02-28, v1.0.0 (Mara Olsen):  Initial release. Covers port assignment, log file isolation, database file separation, disk monitoring, SQLite locking, host monitoring, and backup procedures for multiple installations on a single host. Intended for platform tools and operations teams.

2025-11-04, internal draft (Derek Yun):  Early draft circulated for feedback from Host Operations team. Port conflict section reviewed by Derek Yun. Feedback incorporated; not published.

2025-08-10, design meeting discussion (Platform Tools team):  Team identified need for this runbook. Operations team fielded multiple questions about running 3–5 instances on workstations and small staging servers. Meeting minutes noted that shared database setups were causing confusion and performance problems.

2025-06-15, preliminary outline (Mara Olsen):  Outlined topics and structure for runbook. Reviewed and cross-referenced sibling pages to avoid duplication. Noted gaps in existing documentation around multi-instance scenarios.


== RELATED PAGES ==

1	# Resolving Port Conflicts on the Loopback Service
2	
3	**Title:** Resolving Port Conflicts on the Loopback Service  
4	**Version:** 2.3  
5	**Owner:** Host Operations (Derek Yun)  
6	**Last updated:** 2025-11-04  
7	**Summary:** This page walks through diagnosing and clearing port conflicts that prevent the loopback HTTP service from binding on a workstation or small host.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Overview
12	
13	The service runs a lightweight HTTP server on the loopback interface (127.0.0.1) to accept local requests and interact with the SQLite database file. If another process holds the configured port, the service fails to start and logs an error. This runbook covers diagnosing which process is using the port, terminating it safely, and preventing the conflict from recurring.
14	
15	Port conflicts are common on workstations where multiple versions of the package are installed, where leftover processes hang after an unclean shutdown, or where the same port is reused by a development server or another application.
16	
17	---
18	
19	## Quick Diagnosis (Section Owner: Derek Yun)
20	
21	Before taking action, confirm which process is listening on the configured port. The service uses port 8077 by default, though this may be customized via host configuration.
22	
23	**On Windows (PowerShell):**
24	
25	```powershell
26	netstat -ano | findstr :8077
27	```
28	
29	This returns output like:
30	
31	```
32	  TCP    127.0.0.1:8077        0.0.0.0:0              LISTENING       5432
33	```
34	
35	The last column is the process ID (PID). Cross-reference with:
36	
37	```powershell
38	Get-Process -Id 5432
39	```
40	
41	**On Linux or macOS (Bash):**
42	
43	```bash
44	lsof -i :8077
45	```
46	
47	Or:
48	
49	```bash
50	netstat -tlnp | grep 8077
51	```
52	
53	Both commands show the PID and the name of the process holding the port. If you see multiple rows, the port is genuinely in conflict; if you see none, the port is free and the startup failure has another cause (check the service's console log).
54	
55	---
56	
57	## Understanding Port Binding
58	
59	The service attempts to bind on port 8077 during startup. If the port is already in use, the bind fails immediately, and the service exits with a startup error. This happens even if the other process is not responding; the operating system prevents two processes from listening on the same IP and port combination.
60	
61	The loopback interface (127.0.0.1) is isolated from the network; only processes on the local host can reach it. Port conflicts do not occur between the service and external machines.
62	
63	If you have multiple installations of the package on the same host, each must use a different port. Refer to "Running Multiple oauthsvc Installations on One Host" (v1.0.2) for configuration details.
64	
65	---
66	
67	## Common Causes
68	
69	| Cause | Signs | Solution |
70	|-------|-------|----------|
71	| Previous instance did not shut down cleanly | Process PID is still in netstat output, but the service was supposed to have stopped minutes or hours ago | Terminate the orphaned process (see below) |
72	| Service is configured to restart at boot | New instance tries to bind while old instance still holds the port (brief window on startup) | Wait 10–15 seconds and try again; the old process usually releases the port |
73	| Development server or diagnostic tool running on same port | A different executable name appears in process list (e.g., `python.exe`, a Node process, etc.) | Coordinate with developers; agree on port assignments or use unique ports per developer |
74	| stale port reservation on Windows | netstat shows the port as LISTENING but Process ID does not exist in task manager | Restart the host (see Windows-specific troubleshooting below) |
75	| The service is actually running | netstat shows the port in use and the service is answering requests normally | No action needed; this is the expected state |
76	
77	---

81	Once you identify the PID, terminate it. On Windows:

If the log shows a crash or hang, the service may need to be restarted or investigated further.

115	   ```
116	
117	   This flushes all dynamic port reservations. The service should then bind successfully.
118	
119	3. If the issue persists, restart the host.
120

122	
123	## Configuring a Custom Port
124	
125	If port 8077 is consistently held by another application, configure the service to use a different port. Refer to your host's configuration files (typically `config.ini` or environment variables; check "Locating oauthsvc Files on a Host" v1.5 for file locations).
126	
127	Common alternative ports on development hosts are 8078, 8079, 8080, or 9000. Ensure the port is not already in use before configuration.
128	
129	After changing the configuration, restart the service and confirm it binds on the new port using the diagnostic commands above.
130	
131	---
132	
133	## Preventing Recurrence
134	
135	1. **Graceful Shutdown:** Always stop the service cleanly via command or task manager, rather than force-killing the host or process. Graceful shutdown allows the service to release the port immediately.
136	
137	2. **Monitoring:** Enable host monitoring (see "Host Monitoring Basics for oauthsvc" v3.1) to alert if the service fails to start due to binding errors.
138	
139	3. **Startup Script:** If the service is configured to start at boot (see "Starting the Service at Host Boot" v3.0.0), ensure the startup script waits for any previous instance to fully exit before attempting a new bind. A 5-second delay between stop and start is usually sufficient.
140	
141	4. **Port Isolation:** On multi-user hosts, assign a unique port to each user or team to avoid conflicts. Document these assignments in your host's configuration management system.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## Worked Example
146	
147	**Scenario:** You arrive at a workstation and find the service is not responding to requests. The console log shows the port is already in use at 08:47 today.
148

150

152	   ```powershell

154	   ```
155	   Output: `TCP    127.0.0.1:8077        0.0.0.0:0              LISTENING       2104`
156	
157	2. Identify the process:
158	   ```powershell

160	   ```
161	   Output shows a `python.exe` process that started at 08:10, about 40 minutes ago (you don't recall starting it manually).
162	
163	3. Terminate it:
164	   ```powershell

166	   ```
167	
168	4. Verify the port is free:
169	   ```powershell
170	   netstat -ano | findstr :8077
171	   ```
172	   No output; the port is now available.
173	
174	5. Start the service normally. It should bind on port 8077 without error.
175	
176	6. Check the old process's console log (if stored separately) to understand why it hung. If there are temporary files it created, clean them up to avoid confusion later.

# Resolving Port Conflicts on the Loopback Service

**Title:** Resolving Port Conflicts on the Loopback Service  
**Version:** 2.3  
**Owner:** Host Operations (Derek Yun)  
**Last updated:** 2025-11-04  
**Summary:** This page walks through diagnosing and clearing port conflicts that prevent the loopback HTTP service from binding on a workstation or small host.

---

## Overview

The service runs a lightweight HTTP server on the loopback interface (127.0.0.1) to accept local requests and interact with the SQLite database file. If another process holds the configured port, the service fails to start and logs an error. This runbook covers diagnosing which process is using the port, terminating it safely, and preventing the conflict from recurring.

Port conflicts are common on workstations where multiple versions of the package are installed, where leftover processes hang after an unclean shutdown, or where the same port is reused by a development server or another application.

---

## Quick Diagnosis (Section Owner: Derek Yun)

Before taking action, confirm which process is listening on the configured port. The service uses port 8077 by default, though this may be customized via host configuration.

**On Windows (PowerShell):**

```powershell
netstat -ano | findstr :8077
```

This returns output like:

```
  TCP    127.0.0.1:8077        0.0.0.0:0              LISTENING       5432
```

The last column is the process ID (PID). Cross-reference with:

```powershell
Get-Process -Id 5432
```

**On Linux or macOS (Bash):**

```bash
lsof -i :8077
```

Or:

```bash
netstat -tlnp | grep 8077
```

Both commands show the PID and the name of the process holding the port. If you see multiple rows, the port is genuinely in conflict; if you see none, the port is free and the startup failure has another cause (check the service's console log).

---

## Understanding Port Binding

The service attempts to bind on port 8077 during startup. If the port is already in use, the bind fails immediately, and the service exits with a startup error. This happens even if the other process is not responding; the operating system prevents two processes from listening on the same IP and port combination.

The loopback interface (127.0.0.1) is isolated from the network; only processes on the local host can reach it. Port conflicts do not occur between the service and external machines.

If you have multiple installations of the package on the same host, each must use a different port. Refer to "Running Multiple oauthsvc Installations on One Host" (v1.0.2) for configuration details.

---

## Common Causes

| Cause | Signs | Solution |
|-------|-------|----------|
| Previous instance did not shut down cleanly | Process PID is still in netstat output, but the service was supposed to have stopped minutes or hours ago | Terminate the orphaned process (see below) |
| Service is configured to restart at boot | New instance tries to bind while old instance still holds the port (brief window on startup) | Wait 10–15 seconds and try again; the old process usually releases the port |
| Development server or diagnostic tool running on same port | A different executable name appears in process list (e.g., `python.exe`, a Node process, etc.) | Coordinate with developers; agree on port assignments or use unique ports per developer |
| stale port reservation on Windows | netstat shows the port as LISTENING but Process ID does not exist in task manager | Restart the host (see Windows-specific troubleshooting below) |
| The service is actually running | netstat shows the port in use and the service is answering requests normally | No action needed; this is the expected state |

---

## Terminating an Orphaned Process (Section Owner: Derek Yun)

Once you identify the PID, terminate it. On Windows:

```powershell
Stop-Process -Id 5432 -Force
```

The `-Force` flag ensures immediate termination. On Linux or macOS:

```bash
kill -9 5432
```

Wait 2–3 seconds, then re-run the diagnostic command to confirm the port is free.

**After terminating the process,** check for any leftover temporary files (see "Cleaning Up Temporary Files Left on the Host" v2.1.0) and check the service's console log for any errors that may have caused the shutdown. If the log shows a crash or hang, the service may need to be restarted or investigated further.

---

## Windows-Specific Troubleshooting (Section Owner: Theo Baptiste)

Windows sometimes retains a stale reservation on a port even after the process exits. This is rare but can block the service from starting.

**If the port is still reported as in use but no process owns it:**

1. Check the reserved port list:
   ```powershell
   netsh int ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp
   ```

   If port 8077 appears in a reserved range, the port is blocked at the kernel level.

2. Release the reservation by restarting the Windows TCP/IP stack (requires elevated access):
   ```powershell
   netsh int ipv4 reset all
   ```

   This flushes all dynamic port reservations. The service should then bind successfully.

3. If the issue persists, restart the host.

---

## Configuring a Custom Port

If port 8077 is consistently held by another application, configure the service to use a different port. Refer to your host's configuration files (typically `config.ini` or environment variables; check "Locating oauthsvc Files on a Host" v1.5 for file locations).

Common alternative ports on development hosts are 8078, 8079, 8080, or 9000. Ensure the port is not already in use before configuration.

After changing the configuration, restart the service and confirm it binds on the new port using the diagnostic commands above.

---

## Preventing Recurrence

1. **Graceful Shutdown:** Always stop the service cleanly via command or task manager, rather than force-killing the host or process. Graceful shutdown allows the service to release the port immediately.

2. **Monitoring:** Enable host monitoring (see "Host Monitoring Basics for oauthsvc" v3.1) to alert if the service fails to start due to binding errors.

3. **Startup Script:** If the service is configured to start at boot (see "Starting the Service at Host Boot" v3.0.0), ensure the startup script waits for any previous instance to fully exit before attempting a new bind. A 5-second delay between stop and start is usually sufficient.

4. **Port Isolation:** On multi-user hosts, assign a unique port to each user or team to avoid conflicts. Document these assignments in your host's configuration management system.

---

## Worked Example

**Scenario:** You arrive at a workstation and find the service is not responding to requests. The console log shows the port is already in use at 08:47 today.

**Steps:**

1. Check what is listening on port 8077:
   ```powershell
   netstat -ano | findstr :8077
   ```
   Output: `TCP    127.0.0.1:8077        0.0.0.0:0              LISTENING       2104`

2. Identify the process:
   ```powershell
   Get-Process -Id 2104
   ```
   Output shows a `python.exe` process that started at 08:10, about 40 minutes ago (you don't recall starting it manually).

3. Terminate it:
   ```powershell
   Stop-Process -Id 2104 -Force
   ```

4. Verify the port is free:
   ```powershell
   netstat -ano | findstr :8077
   ```
   No output; the port is now available.

5. Start the service normally. It should bind on port 8077 without error.

6. Check the old process's console log (if stored separately) to understand why it hung. If there are temporary files it created, clean them up to avoid confusion later.

---

## Related Tools and Versions

| Tool | Version | Purpose |
|------|---------|---------|
| Windows PowerShell | 5.1 (built-in) | Diagnosis and process management on Windows hosts |
| Windows netstat utility | Built-in | Port and connection enumeration on Windows |
| Linux net-tools | 2.10 or later | Provides netstat and other diagnostics on Linux |
| lsof | 4.95+ | Process and file descriptor inspection on Linux and macOS |
| SQLite CLI | 3.36+ | Database file locking diagnostics (related to port-binding timeouts) |
| Host monitoring agent | varies | Continuous port and service availability checks |

---

## Terminology and Glossary

- **Loopback interface:** The virtual network interface at 127.0.0.1, used for inter-process communication on a single host. Unreachable from the network.
- **Port binding:** The act of a server process claiming exclusive use of a specific IP and port number to listen for incoming connections.
- **Port conflict:** The situation where two or more processes attempt to bind on the same IP and port, causing one or all to fail.
- **Process ID (PID):** A unique numerical identifier assigned by the operating system to each running process.
- **Orphaned process:** A process that is still running but whose parent process has terminated or become unresponsive; often a sign of unclean shutdown.
- **Graceful shutdown:** Stopping a service by sending a signal that allows it to clean up resources and release ports before exiting.
- **Stale reservation:** A kernel-level record that a port is in use, retained even after the process that held it exits (Windows-specific).
- **TCP/IP stack:** The set of kernel-level protocols and data structures that handle network communication on the host.

---

## Repository Files and Paths

| Path or File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `operations-runbooks/` | Parent folder containing all host upkeep procedures |
| `operations-runbooks/disk-space-checks.md` | Companion runbook for monitoring host disk availability |
| `operations-runbooks/console-log-files.md` | Companion runbook for locating and reviewing service console output |
| `operations-runbooks/sqlite-file-locking.md` | Companion runbook for diagnosing file lock contention on the database |
| `operations-runbooks/host-monitoring-basics.md` | Companion runbook for setting up continuous monitoring and alerting |
| `operations-runbooks/copying-the-database-file.md` | Companion runbook for backing up the database file |
| `operations-runbooks/starting-the-service-at-boot.rst` | Companion runbook for boot-time startup configuration |
| `operations-runbooks/locating-oauthsvc-files-on-a-host.md` | Companion runbook for finding the service's configuration and data directories |
| `operations-runbooks/cleaning-up-temporary-files.md` | Companion runbook for removing leftover temporary files |
| `operations-runbooks/checking-host-clock-and-timestamps.txt` | Companion runbook for verifying host time synchronization |
| `operations-runbooks/multiple-installations-on-one-host.txt` | Companion runbook for multi-instance deployment and port assignment |
| `oauthsvc/` | The service's package directory (repository root) |
| `config.ini` or environment configuration | Host-specific port and binding settings |

---

## Changelog

|------|---------|--------|--------|
| 2025-11-04 | 2.3 | Derek Yun | Clarified Windows TCP/IP stack reset procedure; added note about stale port reservations |

1	# Diagnosing SQLite File Locking on a Host
2	
3	**Title:** Diagnosing SQLite File Locking on a Host  
4	**Version:** v2.0.1  
5	**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)  
6	**Last Updated:** 2026-03-15  
7	**Summary:** This page explains common file-locking symptoms on the database file and how to resolve them on a workstation or small host.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Overview
12	
13	The database service package stores all state in a single SQLite database file on the host disk. Because SQLite uses file-level locking to manage concurrent access, certain conditions—incomplete shutdowns, stalled processes, or filesystem issues—can leave the database locked or in an inconsistent state. This page covers the symptoms of file locking, diagnostic steps, and restoration procedures.
14	
15	File locking on the database occurs at the operating-system level. When the service is working normally, SQLite acquires and releases locks transparently. When the service crashes, hangs, or is terminated without a clean shutdown, lock files may persist on disk, preventing the service from starting or causing transactions to time out.
16	
17	This document applies to workstations and small hosts running a single instance of oauthsvc. For information about running multiple instances on one host, see the sibling page "Running Multiple oauthsvc Installations on One Host" (v1.0.2, updated 2026-06-20).
18	
19	---
20	
21	## Identifying File Locking Symptoms
22	
23	**Section Owner:** Host Operations (Derek Yun)
24	
25	When the database file is locked or in an inconsistent state, you will observe one or more of these symptoms:
26	
27	- The service fails to start and logs messages about the database being locked.
28	- The service starts but becomes unresponsive to loopback HTTP requests.
29	- The service process hangs and uses no CPU.
30	- The service exits with an error code on first request.
31	- Other processes attempting to read or write the database file hang.
32	
33	The error messages vary by the circumstance. Common messages include:
34	
35	```
36	database is locked
37	attempt to write a readonly database
38	database disk image is malformed
39	unable to open database file
40	```
41	
42	If you see any of these messages in the service's console log files, proceed to the diagnostic section.
43	
44	### Distinguishing Locking from Other Issues
45	
46	File locking is not the only reason the service may fail to start. Disk space exhaustion, access control issues, and filesystem errors can produce similar symptoms. Before assuming locking is the problem:
47	
48	1. Check the service's console log files for the exact error message (see "Managing the Service's Console Log Files").
49	2. Verify disk space with `df -h` or your system's disk utility (see "Disk Space Checks for the Host").
50	3. Verify that the database file and its parent directory are readable and writable by the account running the service.
51	4. Check the host system log for filesystem or I/O errors.
52	
53	---
54	
55	## The SQLite Locking Mechanism
56	
57	**Section Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
58	
59	SQLite uses a three-stage locking protocol:
60	
61	1. **Shared lock:** Acquired when a connection reads from the database. Multiple readers can hold shared locks simultaneously.
62	2. **Reserved lock:** Acquired when a connection intends to write. Prevents other writers but allows concurrent readers.
63	3. **Exclusive lock:** Acquired before committing a write transaction. Blocks all other access.
64	
65	In addition, SQLite creates temporary files on disk during certain operations:
66	
67	- A journal file (with a suffix such as `-journal` or `-wal`) that records changes before they are committed.
68	- A temporary file during vacuuming or large inserts.
69	
70	If the service process terminates while holding any of these locks, or if the journal file is left on disk, the next process to open the database will either wait for a timeout or fail immediately, depending on its timeout configuration.
71	
72	---
73	
74	## Diagnostic Procedures
75	
76	### Step 1: Verify the Database File State
77	
78	Check whether the database file and its associated lock files exist on disk:
79	
80	```
81	ls -lah /path/to/oauthsvc.db*
82	```
83	
84	On Windows with PowerShell:
85	
86	```powershell
87	Get-Item "C:\path\to\oauthsvc.db*" -Force
88	```
89	
90	The output should show the main database file. If you see files with suffixes like `-journal`, `-wal`, `-shm`, or `-lock`, these indicate an interrupted transaction or leftover lock state.
91	
92	| File Suffix | Purpose | Typical Lifespan |
93	|---|---|---|
94	| (none) | Main database file | Lifetime of the database |
95	| `-journal` | Rollback log for non-WAL databases | Duration of transaction |
96	| `-wal` | Write-ahead log | Duration of WAL-mode operation |
97	| `-shm` | Shared-memory file for WAL mode | Duration of WAL-mode operation |
98	| `-lock` | Lock file (some systems) | Duration of access |
99	
100	### Step 2: Check Running Processes
101	
102	Determine whether any process still holds a lock on the database file:
103	
104	On Linux:
105	
106	```
107	lsof /path/to/oauthsvc.db
108	fuser /path/to/oauthsvc.db
109	```
110
