The `_meta/` folder holds navigation configuration that the site renderer uses; don't edit it directly without checking with Priya first.
59	
60	Most pages live as Markdown files (`.md`). Some reference materials use reStructuredText (`.rst`), and configuration uses YAML (`.yaml`) or plain text (`.txt`).
61	
62	## Your First Contribution
63	
64	Before you sit down to write, get familiar with the landscape. Here's what to do in your first few days:
65	
66	1. **Read the README.** Start with `docs-style/README.md` for a high-level view of the program.
67	
68	2. **Pick a sibling page and study it.** Open any existing page in the folder that interests you—say, `getting-started/quickstart.md` or `how-to/common-tasks.md`. Note the structure: header block, sections, any lists or tables, the footer with related pages.
69	
70	3. **Check the Writing Style Guide.** Read `docs-style/writing-style-guide.md` to learn the tone, voice, and house rules. You'll see conventions on headings, lists, code snippets, and links.
71	
72	4. **Skim the Templates.** Look at `docs-style/page-templates.md` to see what template fits your topic. Each template has a purpose: some are for procedural how-tos, others for conceptual overviews or API references.
73	
74	5. **Glance at the Glossary.** Open `docs-style/glossary.md` to see what terms we've already defined. If you use any of those terms, you don't need to define them again—just link to the glossary.
75	
76	## Understanding the Documentation Program
77	
78	*Section Owner: Ilse Vogel (Platform Tools)*
79	
80	The documentation program has three pillars: **style**, **process**, and **tooling**. Understanding how they work together helps you move quickly and confidently.
81	
82	### Style: How We Write
83	
84	We have a unified voice across all oauthsvc documentation. Priya Chandran leads the Docs Guild and maintains the Writing Style Guide. The guide covers:
85	
86	- Audience and tone (see `voice-and-tone.md` for deep detail)
87	- Heading capitalization (we use sentence case for most headings)
88	- Punctuation, abbreviations, and spelling
89	- How to format code, commands, and configuration
90	- Link conventions
91	
92	When you're in doubt about a style question, check the guide first. If it's not there, ask in the docs channel or raise an issue.
93	
94	### Process: How We Move Pages Through the System
95	
96	Our documentation workflow has five stages:
97	
98	**Draft** — You write in a branch or a local file. No one outside your immediate team needs to see it yet.
99	
100	**Review** — You request review from someone on the Docs Guild or a subject-matter expert. They use the checklist from `review-checklist.txt` and mark up your changes. This can take three to five business days. See `review-cadence.md` for timing.
101	
102	**Polish** — You respond to feedback, make any final edits, and request re-review if needed.
103	
104	**Confirmation** — Once reviewers sign off, the page is marked ready to publish.
105	
106	**Published** — The page moves to the main documentation site via the workflow in `publishing-workflow.md`. Nadia Reyes oversees publishing and typically runs the publish job on Wednesdays.
107	
108	### Tooling: What We Use
109	
110	We use Git for version control, standard Markdown/RST for source, and a static site generator to render HTML. You don't need to run the generator yourself; the publishing automation handles that. Your job is to write and commit clean source files.
111	
112	## Writing Your First Page
113	
114	*Section Owner: Priya Chandran (Docs Guild)*
115	
116	Choose a topic that's small and well-defined—something you can cover thoroughly without writing 2,000 words. A good first page is a single procedure, a troubleshooting guide for one common problem, or a brief conceptual explanation.
117	
118	### Picking a Template
119	
120	Go to `docs-style/page-templates.md`. You'll see templates for:
121	
122	- **Quick Start** — For getting users up and running fast (aim for 500–800 words)
123	- **How-To / Procedure** — For step-by-step tasks (800–1,200 words)
124	- **Conceptual Overview** — For explaining design or architecture (1,000–1,500 words)
125	- **Reference** — For APIs, configuration options, or error codes (variable length)
126	- **Troubleshooting** — For diagnosing and fixing common issues (600–1,000 words)
127	
128	Each template includes a header block and standard sections. You don't have to follow it exactly—templates are guides, not rules—but they help keep the documentation consistent.
129	
130	### Create the File and Add the Header
131	
132	1. Open your editor and create a new file: `docs/your-topic/your-page.md`
133	2. Start with the header block:
134	
135	```
136	# Page Title
137	
138	**Title:** Page Title  
139	**Version:** 1.0  
140	**Owner:** Your Name (Your Team)  
141	**Last Updated:** 2026-09-27
142	```
143	
144	The version should start at 1.0. The owner should be you and your team (for example, "Alex Kim (Platform Tools)" or "Sandy Zhang (Docs Guild)"). The last-updated date should be today.
145	
146	3. Add a brief summary paragraph below the header:
147	
148	```
149	## Summary
150	
151	One or two sentences explaining what this page covers and who it's for.
152	```
153	
154	### Write Your Sections
155	
156	Pick a template and follow its structure. Write in short paragraphs and use lists and tables to break up dense text. Link to the glossary if you use defined terms. Here's an example of a procedure section:
157	
158	```
159	## Running the Service
160	
161	1. Open a shell window and navigate to the repository root.
162	2. Issue the command to start the service. The CLI will report the port on which it's listening.
163	3. You should see log output; once it stabilizes, the service is ready.
164	4. To stop the service, press Ctrl+C in the shell.
165	```
166	
167	Note that you should avoid naming specific commands or modules; refer generally to "the service," "the CLI," or "the database file."
168	
169	### Add a Terminology Section
170	
171	Near the end, add a section called **Terminology** or **Glossary**. Define any terms that are specific to your page or that might be unfamiliar to a new user. For example:
172	
173	- **State file**: The local database file where the service stores its data. See also the main glossary.
174	- **Configuration block**: A section of a config file that groups related settings.
175	- **Loopback service**: A service that runs locally and communicates via HTTP on localhost.
176	
177	Link terms to the main glossary in `glossary.md` where they're also defined.
178	
179	### Add a Repository Files Section
180	
181	List the files and folders your page refers to. Example:
182	
183	| File or Path | Purpose |
184	|--------------|------|
185	| `docs/getting-started/` | Folder containing introductory documentation |
186	| `docs/glossary.md` | Central glossary for all oauthsvc terms |
187	| `scripts/generate-config.sh` | Shell script that creates a default configuration |
188	| `docs/operations/logs.md` | Guide to understanding service logs |
189	
190	### Include Related Pages
191	
192	At the very end, add:
193	
194	```
195	## Related Pages
196	
197	- Writing Style Guide
198	- Page Templates Overview
199	- oauthsvc Glossary
200	- Documentation Review Cadence
201	```
202	
203	These should be sibling pages or pages your readers will find useful.
204	
205	## Templates and Structure
206	
207	*Section Owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools)*
208	
209	The `docs-style/page-templates.md` file contains full template examples. The `template-reference.rst` file explains every field and metadata option. If you're writing an RST page instead of Markdown, consult `markup-conventions.rst` for syntax rules.
210	
211	Every page—regardless of topic or length—must have:
212	
213	- A header block with title, version, owner, and last-updated date
214	- A brief summary
215	- At least three main content sections with descriptive headings
216	- A terminology or glossary section with at least three terms (preferably eight or more)
217	- A repository files section listing the paths you reference
218	- A related pages section at the end
219	- A changelog (see below)
220	
221	### The Changelog
222	
223	At the very end of your page, before any update log, add a changelog section:
224	
225	```
226	## Changelog
227	
228	| Date | Version | Release | Summary |
229	|------|---------|---------|---------|
230	| 2026-09-27 | 1.0 | Initial | First draft covering basic setup steps |
231	```
232	
233	When you update the page later, add a new row at the top with today's date, the new version number, a short release code, and what changed. Keep six months of entries; older entries can be removed. Version numbers should increment by 0.1 for minor updates and 1.0 for major rewrites.
234	
235	## Keeping the Glossary Fresh
236	
237	*Section Owner: Sam Whitfield (Developer Experience)*
238	
239	The main glossary lives in `docs-style/glossary.md`. It's shared across all documentation, so changes affect everyone. Before you add a new term, check if it's already there.
240	
241	### When to Add a Term
242	
243	Add a term to the main glossary if:
244	
245	- It's used across multiple pages
246	- It defines a concept central to understanding oauthsvc
247	- New users would see it and need clarification
248	
249	Don't add terms that are only relevant to one page; define those inline in your page's terminology section instead.
250	
251	### How to Propose a Glossary Entry
252	
253	1. Fork the glossary file (or create a branch if you have write access).
254	2. Add your term in alphabetical order. Use this format:
255	
256	```
257	### Term Name
258	
259	A one or two sentence definition. If the term has variants or related meanings, explain those. Link to a page where the term is used or explained in detail.
260	
261	**Related:** Other Term, Another Related Term
262	```
263	
264	3. Commit your change with a clear message: `docs: add glossary term "Term Name"`
265	4. Request review from Sam Whitfield in the Docs Guild channel.
266	5. Once confirmed, merge your change to the main branch.
267	
268	The glossary version increments at the usual pace. Check `glossary-upkeep.md` for the full process and a quarterly review schedule.
269	
270	## The Review Process
271	
272	*Section Owner: Ilse Vogel (Platform Tools)*
273	
274	Every page needs at least one review before it's published. Here's how it works:
275	
276	### Request a Review
277	
278	When your page is ready for feedback:
279	
280	1. Commit your work to a branch (e.g., `feature/new-page-title`).
281	2. Push to the repository.
282	3. Open a pull request with a title like `docs: add page on [topic]`.
283	4. In the PR description, mention:
284	   - The topic and intended audience
285	   - Any pages that link to or relate to your new page
286	   - Whether this replaces an older page (and which one)
287	
288	5. Assign the review to someone on the Docs Guild or a subject-matter expert in the area you've written about.
289	
290	### Review Timing
291	
292	The review cadence is documented in `review-cadence.md`. Generally:
293	
294	- Standard review: 3–5 business days (Ilse Vogel handles triage)
295	- Urgent review: 1 business day (for fixes or critical updates; request explicitly)
296	- Content-heavy pages: 5–7 business days (for pages over 2,000 words or complex topics)
297	
298	Reviewers use the checklist in `review-checklist.txt`. They'll look for:
299	
300	- Clarity and completeness
301	- Consistency with the style guide
302	- Accuracy (for technical content)
303	- Proper formatting and links
304	- Presence of required sections (header, summary, terminology, related pages, etc.)
305	
306	### Respond to Feedback
307	
308	Once the review is done, you'll see comments or a full suggested edit. You can:
309	
310	- Accept the suggestion directly in GitHub (if using inline suggestions)
311	- Make the change yourself and commit
312	- Reply asking for clarification
313	- Respectfully push back if you disagree (this happens; it's fine)
314	
315	Re-request review once you've incorporated the main feedback. The second review is usually faster.
316	
317	## Publishing Your Work
318	
319	*Section Owner: Nadia Reyes (Docs Guild)*
320	
321	Once your page has been reviewed and confirmed, it's ready to publish. Don't merge to main yourself; let the publishing workflow handle it.
322	
323	### The Publishing Workflow
324	
325	Follow the steps in `docs-style/publishing-workflow.md`:
326	
327	1. Your PR should be confirmed (marked with the `reviewed` label).
328	2. Ensure your page includes a complete header block and all required sections.
329	3. Run through the checklist in `publishing-checklist.txt` (this is quick—ten items).
330	4. Request that Nadia review the PR for publishing. Mention any special notes (e.g., "This replaces the old Quickstart").
331	5. Nadia will merge to main and trigger the publish automation.
332	6. The site is typically updated on Wednesday afternoons. Your page should appear within 24 hours.
333	
334	### After Publishing
335	
336	Your work isn't done. Monitor the docs for the first week:
337	
338	- Check that the page renders correctly (links work, formatting looks right)
339	- Watch for feedback in the docs channel or via direct message
340	- Note any confusing sections for future improvement
341	- Update the version number and changelog if you make fixes
342	
343	## Tools and Software
344	
345	The documentation program uses these tools and libraries to manage, style, and publish pages. All are open source or freely available to the team.
346	
347	| Tool or Library | Version | Purpose |
348	|-----------------|---------|---------|
349	| Git | 2.42.0 (or later) | Version control for documentation source |
350	| Python | 3.11+ | Build and rendering support |
351	| Sphinx | 7.1.2 | Static site generator for HTML rendering |
352	| Pandoc | 2.18+ | Optional: convert between markup formats |
353	| Markdown / CommonMark | N/A | Source format for most pages |
354	| reStructuredText | N/A | Source format for reference materials (RST) |
355	| YAML | N/A | Format for configuration and metadata |
356	| Visual Studio Code or Vim | Latest | Recommended editors for writing |
357	| Prettier (optional) | 3.0+ | Markdown formatter for consistent style |
358	
359	Most of these are already installed in the development environment. Run `scripts/check-docs-tools.sh` to verify.
360	
361	## Terminology
362	
363	### Docs Guild
364	
365	The team responsible for coordinating documentation across the platform project. Led by Priya Chandran. Members include platform, product, and developer experience engineers who volunteer time to reviewing and confirming pages.
366	
367	### Header Block
368	
369	The structured metadata at the top of every page, including title, version, owner, and last-updated date. It helps readers identify the page's coverage and authority.
370	
371	### Markdown
372	
373	A lightweight markup language used to write most oauthsvc documentation. Files use the `.md` extension. See `markup-conventions.rst` for local conventions.
374

# New Contributor Onboarding

**Title:** New Contributor Onboarding  
**Version:** 1.9  
**Owner:** Docs Guild (Priya Chandran)  
**Last Updated:** 2024-03-19

---

## Summary

This guide walks you through the documentation program for the oauthsvc package. You'll learn where documentation lives, what tools and templates we use, how we keep our glossary current, when pages get reviewed, and how documents move from draft to published. Whether you're writing your first page or reviewing changes from a teammate, this guide has what you need.

## Documentation Folder Structure

*Section Owner: Priya Chandran (Docs Guild)*

The oauthsvc documentation lives in the `docs/` folder at the repository root. Here's how it's organized:

```
docs/
├── api/
│   ├── overview.md
│   ├── changelog.md
│   └── error-codes.md
├── getting-started/
│   ├── quickstart.md
│   ├── installation.md
│   └── configuration.md
├── operations/
│   ├── deployment.md
│   ├── monitoring.md
│   ├── troubleshooting.md
│   └── logs.md
├── how-to/
│   └── (various task-based guides)
├── concepts/
│   └── (deep-dive explanations)
├── docs-style/
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── contributor-onboarding.md (this file)
│   ├── writing-style-guide.md
│   ├── voice-and-tone.md
│   ├── page-templates.md
│   ├── template-reference.rst
│   ├── glossary.md
│   ├── glossary-upkeep.md
│   ├── review-cadence.md
│   ├── review-checklist.txt
│   ├── publishing-workflow.md
│   ├── publishing-checklist.txt
│   ├── markup-conventions.rst
│   └── metadata-fields.yaml
└── _meta/
    └── navigation.yaml
```

The `docs-style/` folder contains all the materials that guide how we write, review, and publish. That's where you'll spend time as you grow into the documentation program. The `_meta/` folder holds navigation configuration that the site renderer uses; don't edit it directly without checking with Priya first.

Most pages live as Markdown files (`.md`). Some reference materials use reStructuredText (`.rst`), and configuration uses YAML (`.yaml`) or plain text (`.txt`).

## Your First Contribution

Before you sit down to write, get familiar with the landscape. Here's what to do in your first few days:

1. **Read the README.** Start with `docs-style/README.md` for a high-level view of the program.

2. **Pick a sibling page and study it.** Open any existing page in the folder that interests you—say, `getting-started/quickstart.md` or `how-to/common-tasks.md`. Note the structure: header block, sections, any lists or tables, the footer with related pages.

3. **Check the Writing Style Guide.** Read `docs-style/writing-style-guide.md` to learn the tone, voice, and house rules. You'll see conventions on headings, lists, code snippets, and links.

4. **Skim the Templates.** Look at `docs-style/page-templates.md` to see what template fits your topic. Each template has a purpose: some are for procedural how-tos, others for conceptual overviews or API references.

5. **Glance at the Glossary.** Open `docs-style/glossary.md` to see what terms we've already defined. If you use any of those terms, you don't need to define them again—just link to the glossary.

## Understanding the Documentation Program

*Section Owner: Ilse Vogel (Platform Tools)*

The documentation program has three pillars: **style**, **process**, and **tooling**. Understanding how they work together helps you move quickly and confidently.

### Style: How We Write

We have a unified voice across all oauthsvc documentation. Priya Chandran leads the Docs Guild and maintains the Writing Style Guide. The guide covers:

- Audience and tone (see `voice-and-tone.md` for deep detail)
- Heading capitalization (we use sentence case for most headings)
- Punctuation, abbreviations, and spelling
- How to format code, commands, and configuration
- Link conventions

When you're in doubt about a style question, check the guide first. If it's not there, ask in the docs channel or raise an issue.

### Process: How We Move Pages Through the System

Our documentation workflow has five stages:

**Draft** — You write in a branch or a local file. No one outside your immediate team needs to see it yet.

**Review** — You request review from someone on the Docs Guild or a subject-matter expert. They use the checklist from `review-checklist.txt` and mark up your changes. This can take three to five business days. See `review-cadence.md` for timing.

**Polish** — You respond to feedback, make any final edits, and request re-review if needed.

**Confirmation** — Once reviewers sign off, the page is marked ready to publish.

**Published** — The page moves to the main documentation site via the workflow in `publishing-workflow.md`. Nadia Reyes oversees publishing and typically runs the publish job on Wednesdays.

### Tooling: What We Use

We use Git for version control, standard Markdown/RST for source, and a static site generator to render HTML. You don't need to run the generator yourself; the publishing automation handles that. Your job is to write and commit clean source files.

## Writing Your First Page

*Section Owner: Priya Chandran (Docs Guild)*

Choose a topic that's small and well-defined—something you can cover thoroughly without writing 2,000 words. A good first page is a single procedure, a troubleshooting guide for one common problem, or a brief conceptual explanation.

### Picking a Template

Go to `docs-style/page-templates.md`. You'll see templates for:

- **Quick Start** — For getting users up and running fast (aim for 500–800 words)
- **How-To / Procedure** — For step-by-step tasks (800–1,200 words)
- **Conceptual Overview** — For explaining design or architecture (1,000–1,500 words)
- **Reference** — For APIs, configuration options, or error codes (variable length)
- **Troubleshooting** — For diagnosing and fixing common issues (600–1,000 words)

Each template includes a header block and standard sections. You don't have to follow it exactly—templates are guides, not rules—but they help keep the documentation consistent.

### Create the File and Add the Header

1. Open your editor and create a new file: `docs/your-topic/your-page.md`
2. Start with the header block:

```
# Page Title

**Title:** Page Title  
**Version:** 1.0  
**Owner:** Your Name (Your Team)  
**Last Updated:** 2026-09-27
```

The version should start at 1.0. The owner should be you and your team (for example, "Alex Kim (Platform Tools)" or "Sandy Zhang (Docs Guild)"). The last-updated date should be today.

3. Add a brief summary paragraph below the header:

```
## Summary

One or two sentences explaining what this page covers and who it's for.
```

### Write Your Sections

Pick a template and follow its structure. Write in short paragraphs and use lists and tables to break up dense text. Link to the glossary if you use defined terms. Here's an example of a procedure section:

```
## Running the Service

1. Open a shell window and navigate to the repository root.
2. Issue the command to start the service. The CLI will report the port on which it's listening.
3. You should see log output; once it stabilizes, the service is ready.
4. To stop the service, press Ctrl+C in the shell.
```

Note that you should avoid naming specific commands or modules; refer generally to "the service," "the CLI," or "the database file."

### Add a Terminology Section

Near the end, add a section called **Terminology** or **Glossary**. Define any terms that are specific to your page or that might be unfamiliar to a new user. For example:

- **State file**: The local database file where the service stores its data. See also the main glossary.
- **Configuration block**: A section of a config file that groups related settings.
- **Loopback service**: A service that runs locally and communicates via HTTP on localhost.

Link terms to the main glossary in `glossary.md` where they're also defined.

### Add a Repository Files Section

List the files and folders your page refers to. Example:

| File or Path | Purpose |
|--------------|------|
| `docs/getting-started/` | Folder containing introductory documentation |
| `docs/glossary.md` | Central glossary for all oauthsvc terms |
| `scripts/generate-config.sh` | Shell script that creates a default configuration |
| `docs/operations/logs.md` | Guide to understanding service logs |

### Include Related Pages

At the very end, add:

```
## Related Pages

- Writing Style Guide
- Page Templates Overview
- oauthsvc Glossary
- Documentation Review Cadence
```

These should be sibling pages or pages your readers will find useful.

## Templates and Structure

*Section Owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools)*

The `docs-style/page-templates.md` file contains full template examples. The `template-reference.rst` file explains every field and metadata option. If you're writing an RST page instead of Markdown, consult `markup-conventions.rst` for syntax rules.

Every page—regardless of topic or length—must have:

- A header block with title, version, owner, and last-updated date
- A brief summary
- At least three main content sections with descriptive headings
- A terminology or glossary section with at least three terms (preferably eight or more)
- A repository files section listing the paths you reference
- A related pages section at the end
- A changelog (see below)

### The Changelog

At the very end of your page, before any update log, add a changelog section:

```
## Changelog

| Date | Version | Release | Summary |
|------|---------|---------|---------|
| 2026-09-27 | 1.0 | Initial | First draft covering basic setup steps |
```

When you update the page later, add a new row at the top with today's date, the new version number, a short release code, and what changed. Keep six months of entries; older entries can be removed. Version numbers should increment by 0.1 for minor updates and 1.0 for major rewrites.

## Keeping the Glossary Fresh

*Section Owner: Sam Whitfield (Developer Experience)*

The main glossary lives in `docs-style/glossary.md`. It's shared across all documentation, so changes affect everyone. Before you add a new term, check if it's already there.

### When to Add a Term

Add a term to the main glossary if:

- It's used across multiple pages
- It defines a concept central to understanding oauthsvc
- New users would see it and need clarification

Don't add terms that are only relevant to one page; define those inline in your page's terminology section instead.

### How to Propose a Glossary Entry

1. Fork the glossary file (or create a branch if you have write access).
2. Add your term in alphabetical order. Use this format:

```
### Term Name

A one or two sentence definition. If the term has variants or related meanings, explain those. Link to a page where the term is used or explained in detail.

**Related:** Other Term, Another Related Term
```

3. Commit your change with a clear message: `docs: add glossary term "Term Name"`
4. Request review from Sam Whitfield in the Docs Guild channel.
5. Once confirmed, merge your change to the main branch.

The glossary version increments at the usual pace. Check `glossary-upkeep.md` for the full process and a quarterly review schedule.

## The Review Process

*Section Owner: Ilse Vogel (Platform Tools)*

Every page needs at least one review before it's published. Here's how it works:

### Request a Review

When your page is ready for feedback:

1. Commit your work to a branch (e.g., `feature/new-page-title`).
2. Push to the repository.
3. Open a pull request with a title like `docs: add page on [topic]`.
4. In the PR description, mention:
   - The topic and intended audience
   - Any pages that link to or relate to your new page
   - Whether this replaces an older page (and which one)

5. Assign the review to someone on the Docs Guild or a subject-matter expert in the area you've written about.

### Review Timing

The review cadence is documented in `review-cadence.md`. Generally:

- Standard review: 3–5 business days (Ilse Vogel handles triage)
- Urgent review: 1 business day (for fixes or critical updates; request explicitly)
- Content-heavy pages: 5–7 business days (for pages over 2,000 words or complex topics)

Reviewers use the checklist in `review-checklist.txt`. They'll look for:

- Clarity and completeness
- Consistency with the style guide
- Accuracy (for technical content)
- Proper formatting and links
- Presence of required sections (header, summary, terminology, related pages, etc.)

### Respond to Feedback

Once the review is done, you'll see comments or a full suggested edit. You can:

- Accept the suggestion directly in GitHub (if using inline suggestions)
- Make the change yourself and commit
- Reply asking for clarification
- Respectfully push back if you disagree (this happens; it's fine)

Re-request review once you've incorporated the main feedback. The second review is usually faster.

## Publishing Your Work

*Section Owner: Nadia Reyes (Docs Guild)*

Once your page has been reviewed and confirmed, it's ready to publish. Don't merge to main yourself; let the publishing workflow handle it.

### The Publishing Workflow

Follow the steps in `docs-style/publishing-workflow.md`:

1. Your PR should be confirmed (marked with the `reviewed` label).
2. Ensure your page includes a complete header block and all required sections.
3. Run through the checklist in `publishing-checklist.txt` (this is quick—ten items).
4. Request that Nadia review the PR for publishing. Mention any special notes (e.g., "This replaces the old Quickstart").
5. Nadia will merge to main and trigger the publish automation.
6. The site is typically updated on Wednesday afternoons. Your page should appear within 24 hours.

### After Publishing

Your work isn't done. Monitor the docs for the first week:

- Check that the page renders correctly (links work, formatting looks right)
- Watch for feedback in the docs channel or via direct message
- Note any confusing sections for future improvement
- Update the version number and changelog if you make fixes

## Tools and Software

The documentation program uses these tools and libraries to manage, style, and publish pages. All are open source or freely available to the team.

| Tool or Library | Version | Purpose |
|-----------------|---------|---------|
| Git | 2.42.0 (or later) | Version control for documentation source |
| Python | 3.11+ | Build and rendering support |
| Sphinx | 7.1.2 | Static site generator for HTML rendering |
| Pandoc | 2.18+ | Optional: convert between markup formats |
| Markdown / CommonMark | N/A | Source format for most pages |
| reStructuredText | N/A | Source format for reference materials (RST) |
| YAML | N/A | Format for configuration and metadata |
| Visual Studio Code or Vim | Latest | Recommended editors for writing |
| Prettier (optional) | 3.0+ | Markdown formatter for consistent style |

Most of these are already installed in the development environment. Run `scripts/check-docs-tools.sh` to verify.

## Terminology

### Docs Guild

The team responsible for coordinating documentation across the platform project. Led by Priya Chandran. Members include platform, product, and developer experience engineers who volunteer time to reviewing and confirming pages.

### Header Block

The structured metadata at the top of every page, including title, version, owner, and last-updated date. It helps readers identify the page's coverage and authority.

### Markdown

A lightweight markup language used to write most oauthsvc documentation. Files use the `.md` extension. See `markup-conventions.rst` for local conventions.

### Page Template

A skeleton or example page that shows the standard structure for a certain type of documentation (how-to, reference, overview, etc.). Templates are guides; you may deviate if it makes sense for your content.

### Pull Request

A request to merge your documentation changes from a branch into the main branch. All PRs go through review before merge.

### Publish

The act of merging a page to the main branch and running the site generator to make it live on the documentation website. Publishing is coordinated by Nadia Reyes and happens weekly.

### Refinement

An updated version of a page after review feedback has been incorporated. Not the same as a release version.

### Subject-Matter Expert

A person on the platform team (engineer, infrastructure specialist, or product manager) who understands a particular topic deeply and provides review or fact-checking for related documentation.

### Section Owner

A named individual or small group responsible for maintaining and reviewing pages in a particular documentation area or topic (e.g., "Operations" or "Troubleshooting"). Owners are listed at the top of major sections.

### Write Once

The principle that documentation should be written clearly and completely the first time, so readers don't have to hunt across multiple pages for the same information.

## Repository Files and Paths

1	# Page Templates Overview
2	
3	**Version:** v1.6.0  
4	**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)  
5	**Last updated:** 2026-01-08  
6	
7	**Summary:** Catalogs the standard page layouts contributors copy when starting a new oauthsvc documentation page. Covers writing style conventions, page structure requirements, terminology maintenance, and the publication process that all documentation in this folder must follow.
8	
9	## Overview
10	
11	The oauthsvc documentation project maintains consistency through reusable page templates and a shared set of style conventions. Whether you are writing a procedural guide, a reference page, or a conceptual overview, this document points you to the standard starting templates and walks you through the common elements every page must contain.
12	
13	All pages in this documentation folder must follow the structure outlined here. Starting with a template ensures that:
14	
15	- readers can navigate documentation pages without relearning layouts;
16	- the glossary and terminology stay current with real usage;
17	- pages flow smoothly into one another through consistent cross-references;
18	- the publishing workflow runs cleanly without formatting surprises;
19	- new contributors onboard faster by following familiar patterns.
20	
21	This page itself serves as a worked example of the standards it describes. When you finish reading, you should be able to copy a template, customize it with your content, pass validation, and submit to review within a single working day.
22	
23	## Page Template Categories
24	
25	The documentation program defines four primary template categories. Choose one as your starting point based on your content type. Each template includes customizable sections marked with `[SECTION NAME]` that you replace with your own writing.
26	
27	### Procedure Template
28	
29	Use the Procedure template for pages that walk readers through a sequence of steps: running a command, configuring the service, diagnosing a problem, or deploying documentation. Procedures are goal-oriented and linear; readers follow them in order to accomplish a specific task.
30	
31	**When to use Procedure template:**
32	- Instructions for setting up the documentation environment
33	- Troubleshooting workflows
34	- Steps for validating page changes
35	- Processes for updating the master glossary
36	- Publishing or reviewing pages
37	
38	The Procedure template structure:
39	
40	1. Header block (title, version, owner, date, summary)
41	2. Overview paragraph (why someone would follow this procedure)
42	3. Prerequisites / Preconditions (software versions, prior knowledge, required files)
43	4. Main procedure steps (numbered list with clear verb phrases)
44	5. Worked example (actual command input and output)
45	6. Validation section (how to verify the procedure succeeded)
46	7. Troubleshooting subsection (common errors and fixes, if relevant)
47	8. Terminology section (terms used in the procedure)
48	9. File references table
49	10. Tools and versions table
50	11. Related pages section
51	12. Changelog
52	
53	A well-structured Procedure page lets readers skim the prerequisites, jump to the step they need, and validate success without reading the entire document sequentially.
54	
55	### Reference Template
56	
57	Use the Reference template for pages that document options, settings, configuration formats, or information readers look up rather than read straight through. Reference pages lean on tables and structured lists. A Reference page serves as lookup documentation; readers should be able to scan it quickly and find the answer they need within thirty seconds.
58	
59	**When to use Reference template:**
60	- Documentation page metadata fields and their valid values
61	- Page header block specifications and formatting rules
62	- Markup conventions for Markdown and ReStructuredText
63	- Page review checklist items and criteria
64	- Glossary term format and submission guidelines
65	
66	The Reference template structure:
67	
68	1. Header block
69	2. Overview paragraph (breadth of what the reference covers)
70	3. Options, settings, or configuration in tabular form with columns for Name, Type/Range, Required, and Description
71	4. Detailed descriptions for complex options (reference to a detailed section if the option is intricate)
72	5. Examples showing typical configurations or complete entries
73	6. Limitations, caveats, or deprecation warnings
74	7. Terminology section
75	8. File references table
76	9. Tools and versions table
77	10. Related pages section
78	11. Changelog
79	
80	Reference pages often have more tables than prose. A reader should be able to screenshot or print the page and use it as a standalone reference without consulting other documents.
81	
82	### Conceptual Template
83	
84	Use the Conceptual template for pages that explain ideas, architecture, relationships between concepts, or the reasoning behind design choices. Conceptual pages often synthesize information from multiple reference or procedural pages into a unified explanation.
85	
86	**When to use Conceptual template:**
87	- How the documentation program is organized
88	- Design principles for page structure and style
89	- The relationship between glossary upkeep and style consistency
90	- Overview of the documentation publishing workflow
91	- Explanation of why certain markup conventions exist
92	
93	The Conceptual template structure:
94	
95	1. Header block
96	2. Overview and coverage (what ideas the page unifies)
97	3. Core concepts (multiple sections, each with its own owner attribution where appropriate)
98	4. Relationships between concepts (how they interact)
99	5. Common workflows or use patterns (how these concepts apply in practice)
100	6. Terminology section
101	7. File references table
102	8. Tools and versions table
103	9. Related pages section
104	10. Changelog
105	
106	Conceptual pages benefit from diagrams, but text descriptions and relationships tables work well too. A reader finishing a Conceptual page should understand the "why" behind related procedures and reference pages.
107	
108	### Quick Start Template
109	
110	Use the Quick Start template for brief orientation pages aimed at new contributors or for condensed guides to common tasks. These pages compress the essential setup steps, point to deeper documentation, and introduce key terminology without lengthy explanation. Quick Start pages are short—aim for 800–1200 words total.
111	
112	**When to use Quick Start template:**
113	- New contributor orientation to the documentation folder
114	- First-time setup for page authoring
115	- Quick reference for the most common documentation tasks
116	- Brief introductions to specific tools (Git, Markdown, the validation script)
117	
118	The Quick Start template structure:
119	
120	1. Header block
121	2. What this template covers (brief coverage statement)
122	3. Five to seven core steps in checklist format
123	4. One worked example
124	5. Where to go next (links to deeper documentation)
125	6. Terminology section (abbreviated, 4–6 terms)
126	7. File references table (abbreviated, only the essential files)
127	8. Related pages section
128	9. Changelog
129	
130	Quick Start pages trade comprehensiveness for rapid orientation. A new contributor should finish a Quick Start page and immediately begin a first task.
131	
132	## Required Page Elements
133	
134	Every page in this documentation folder, regardless of template type, must contain the following elements. Pages that do not include all required sections will fail the validation script and the pre-publish checklist and must be revised before entering the pipeline. The publishing team will not review incomplete pages.
135	
136	### Header Block
137	
138	Place a header block at the very top of your page file, before any other content:
139	
140	```
141	# Page Title Here
142	
143	**Version:** v1.2.3  
144	**Owner:** Team Name (Person Name)  
145	**Last updated:** YYYY-MM-DD  
146	
147	**Summary:** One or two sentences describing what readers will learn or accomplish from this page.
148	```
149	
150	- **Title** (heading level 1): should match the page name in index listings; use title case.
151	- **Version**: use format `vX.Y.Z` (e.g., `v1.6.0`) unless your team uses a different convention. Check your team's other pages to see the standard. Increment the patch version (the third number) for small fixes and adjustments. Increment the minor version (the second number) for substantial content additions or reorganizations.
152	- **Owner**: name the team and one point person responsible for this page. When the owner changes (e.g., due to team reorganization), update this field and note the change in the changelog.
153	- **Last updated**: use ISO format YYYY-MM-DD. Update this date whenever you make substantive changes; minor fixes (typos, broken links, small clarifications) do not require a date bump. The date helps readers assess freshness and determines which pages need periodic reviews on the documentation review cadence schedule.
154	- **Summary**: one to two sentences, readable in page listings and indexes. Avoid jargon; assume the reader is scanning many page summaries quickly.
155	
156	### Section Headings and Ownership
157	
158	Use heading level 2 (`##`) for top-level sections and level 3 (`###`) for subsections. Capitalize headings in title case (capitalize the first letter of the main words). Keep heading text concise; if you need to say more, use the first paragraph of the section.
159	
160	For sections that deal with large topics the team actively maintains, name the section owner in parentheses after the heading. This attribution helps readers know who to contact with clarifications or questions:
161	
162	```markdown
163	## Configuration Reference (Owner: Platform Tools — Nadia Reyes)
164	
165	## Review Process and Publishing (Owner: Docs Guild — Ilse Vogel)
166	```
167	
168	Not every section needs an owner attribution. Procedural steps, worked examples, introductory sections, and standard navigational sections (Terminology, Related Pages, Changelog) typically do not carry ownership. Use ownership attribution sparingly to avoid visual clutter.
169	
170	### Terminology / Glossary Section
171	
172	Every page must include a terminology section (titled "Terminology," "Glossary," or "Key Concepts") that defines at least eight terms used on the page. The glossary serves two purposes: it helps readers unfamiliar with the term find its definition without leaving the page, and it identifies candidates for the master glossary.
173	
174	Terms should be:
175	
176	- **specific to oauthsvc and its documentation practice** — avoid generic dictionary definitions;
177	- **in alphabetical order** — use a definition list format (term followed by its definition) or a two-column table;
178	- **linked to the master glossary** where the term is defined more broadly.
179	
180	Example terminology section using definition list format:
181	
182	```markdown
183	## Terminology
184	
185	- **Changelog:** A dated list of changes to a page, ordered from newest to oldest, with version numbers, dates, authors, and descriptions of what changed.
186	- **Header block:** The structured section at the top of a page containing title, version, owner, date, and summary.
187	- **Preconditions:** Requirements (software versions, prior knowledge, completed setup steps) that readers must satisfy before following a procedure.
188	- ...
189	```
190	
191	You may add a note like "See also the master glossary" at the bottom of your Terminology section to direct readers to the broader reference. For terms already well-defined in the master glossary, you may write a brief contextual definition on your page and cross-reference the broader definition.
192	
193	When you encounter a term that you believe belongs in the master glossary but is not yet there, add it to your page's Terminology section and log it in the `glossary-upkeep.md` file (see the Glossary Maintenance section below).
194	
195	### File and Path References
196	
197	List the repository files, host paths, configuration locations, and directories your page refers to. Format this as a table with columns for **Path / File**, **Purpose**, and **Notes**. Include only files that are relevant to the page's content:
198	
199	| Path / File | Purpose | Notes |
200	|---|---|---|
201	| `docs-style/page-templates.md` | This page | Started v1.5.0; see changelog |
202	| `docs-style/writing-style-guide.md` | Style conventions for all text | Updated quarterly |
203	| `docs-style/glossary.md` | Master term definitions | Owned by Developer Experience |
204	| `docs/` | Published documentation folder | Pages move here after verification |
205	| `scripts/validate-doc-page.py` | Validation utility | Checks page completeness before review |
206	
207	Do not include system paths (like `/tmp` or `C:\Windows\System32`) unless your page discusses them directly. Do not list the documentation files themselves unless relevant to your topic (e.g., a page about the publishing workflow would list the publishing checklist, but a page about writing procedures would not).
208	
209	### Tools and Versions Table
210	
211	If your page mentions tools, libraries, or versions readers need to install or have available, create a table listing them. Tools might include the shell, version control systems, editors, database utilities, or any external dependency:
212	
213	| Tool / Library | Version | Purpose | Notes |
214	|---|---|---|---|
215	| Python | 3.9+ | Validation script language | For running page validation checks |
216	| Markdown | — | Page markup format | All docs-style pages use Markdown |
217	| Git | 2.30+ | Version control | For cloning and editing documentation repository |
218	| Bash | 5.1+ | Shell for examples | PowerShell also supported on Windows |
219	| SQLite3 CLI | 3.35+ | Example queries | Standard library, no separate install |
220	
221	Use `—` in the Version column if the tool does not have a version number (e.g., Markdown markup language) or if version is not relevant to the page. This table helps readers understand prerequisites and compatibility constraints.
222	
223	### Related Pages Section
224	
225	At the end of your page, before the Changelog, link to sibling pages in the `docs-style/` folder and other relevant documentation. These are pages readers of your page will likely need to consult:
226	
227	```markdown
228	## Related Pages
229	
230	- **Writing Style Guide** (v3.2) — conventions for grammar, tone, and voice across all pages
231	- **Glossary Upkeep Process** (v1.3) — how to add and maintain terminology in the master glossary
232	- **Documentation Review Cadence** (v2.4) — review schedule and verification steps
233	- **Docs Publishing Workflow** (v2.2) — moving pages from draft to published
234	```
235	
236	List related pages alphabetically by title. Include the page version and a one-sentence description of what it covers. Do not cross-link every page to every other page; link only pages that readers of your page will likely need to consult next.
237	
238	### Changelog
239	
240	Every page must have a changelog section with at least six dated entries. The changelog documents the page's changes over time and helps readers assess freshness and understand what has changed since they last read the page. Each entry names the version, date, and author, and describes what changed. Order entries from newest to oldest (reverse chronological order).
241	
242	Format the changelog as a definition list:
243	
244	```markdown
245	## Changelog
246	
247	- **v1.6.0** (2026-01-08) — Mara Olsen: Added quick-start template category; revised examples in template elements section.
248	- **v1.5.3** (2025-11-22) — Jordan Park: Corrected file path references in the tools and versions table.
249	- **v1.5.2** (2025-10-14) — Priya Chandran: Updated related pages section to point to review-cadence v2.4.
250	- **v1.5.1** (2025-09-30) — Jordan Park: Minor grammar fixes in the overview section.
251	- **v1.5.0** (2025-08-15) — Mara Olsen: Restructured template categories; added detailed section for reference templates.
252	- **v1.4.2** (2025-07-03) — Priya Chandran: Improved worked example in the Procedure template section.
253	```
254	
255	When you update a page:
256	1. Add a new changelog entry at the top of the list.
257	2. Increment the version number: patch for minor fixes, minor for feature/content additions, major if restructuring the page significantly.
258	3. Use today's date in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD).
259	4. Name the author (usually you).
260	5. Write a clear, concise description of the change (one to three lines).
261	
262	If a change is truly minor—a typo, a broken link, a single clarifying word—you may group several minor fixes into a single changelog entry and note "Various edits" or "Typo fixes."
263	
264	## Typical Page Structure
265	
266	The following order works well for most pages in the oauthsvc documentation:
267	
268	1. Header block (title, version, owner, date, summary)
269	2. Overview or introduction (what readers will learn, why they need to read this)
270	3. Main content sections (procedures, reference tables, conceptual explanations — varies by template)
271	4. Worked example or illustration (for procedure and quick-start templates; conceptual pages may use subsections instead)
272	5. Troubleshooting or common issues (where relevant; omit if not needed)
273	6. Terminology / Glossary section
274	7. File and path references table
275	8. Tools and versions table
276	9. Related pages section
277	10. Changelog
278	
279	Some pages reorder sections if content demands it. For instance, a reference page might place Examples before Terminology if the examples are essential for understanding the topic. However, the header block must always come first, and Terminology must come before the File References table. The Changelog must always be last.
280	
281	## Writing Style Consistency
282	
283	All pages in this folder must conform to the conventions in the **Writing Style Guide** (v3.2). Key standards include:
284	
285	- **Second person** ("you," "your") in procedures and guides aimed at readers performing actions. Use first person only when writing changelog entries or when referring to the authoring team.
286	- **Consistent verb tense:** use imperative mood for instructions ("Run the validation script"), present tense for descriptions ("The script checks page completeness"), and past tense for changelog entries and prior notes.
287	- **Standard terminology:** use the terms defined in the master glossary; do not introduce synonyms without explicit reason. If you coin a new term, define it in your Terminology section and propose it to the master glossary.
288	- **Oxford comma** in lists of three or more items (e.g., "title, version, and owner").
289	- **Code and file names in backticks** (e.g., `` `validate-doc-page.py` `` or `` `docs-style/` ``).
290	- **Headings in title case** (capitalize the first letter of main words; do not capitalize articles, conjunctions, or prepositions unless they are the first word).
291	- **Active voice preferred** over passive; write "The validation script checks your page" rather than "Your page is checked by the validation script."
292	- **Concise language:** use short sentences and paragraphs; avoid jargon unless defined.
293	
294	For guidance on voice and tone, consult the **Voice and Tone Guidelines** page (v2.0), maintained by Developer Experience. For markup syntax (Markdown vs. ReStructuredText formatting), see the **Markup Conventions** page (v2.5).
295	
296	## Template Copying Workflow
297	
298	When starting a new page, follow these steps:
299	
300	### Step 1: Identify Your Page Type
301	
302	Determine which template suits your content:
303	- **Procedure:** step-by-step instructions to accomplish a goal.
304	- **Reference:** lookup information in structured tables or lists.
305	- **Conceptual:** explanations of ideas, relationships, or design reasoning.
306	- **Quick Start:** brief orientation for new users or rapid task introduction.
307	
308	### Step 2: Copy the Template File
309	
310	Templates live in the `docs-style/templates/` folder. Copy the appropriate template to your working location in the `docs/` folder. For example:
311	
312	```bash
313	cp docs-style/templates/template-procedure.md docs/my-new-procedure.md
314	```
315	
316	Or in Windows PowerShell:
317	```powershell
318	Copy the template procedure file from docs-style/templates/template-procedure.md to docs/my-new-procedure.md
319	```
320	
321	The template file is a starting skeleton; it includes all required sections marked with `[CUSTOMIZABLE TEXT]` that you replace with your own content.
322	
323	### Step 3: Customize the Header Block
324	
325	Open your new file in a text editor and replace the header block:
326	- Change the title to your page's title.
327	- Set the version to `v1.0.0` (or align with your team's versioning).
328	- Assign the owner (your team name and your name, or the primary owner).
329	- Set the last-updated date to today in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD).
330	- Write a clear summary (one to two sentences).
331	
332	### Step 4: Replace Customizable Sections
333	
334	Work through each `[CUSTOMIZABLE]` marker and write your own content. For a Procedure page, you would replace `[OVERVIEW PARAGRAPH]` with your introduction, `[PREREQUISITES SECTION]` with the requirements, `[STEP 1]`, `[STEP 2]`, etc., with your numbered steps, and so on.
335	
336	### Step 5: Add Terminology
337	
338	Before you finish, review your page for terms that need definition. Add at least eight terms to the Terminology section in alphabetical order.
339	
340	### Step 6: Run the Validation Script
341	
342	From the repository root, run the validation script to check that your page has all required sections:
343	
344	```bash
345	python scripts/validate-doc-page.py docs/my-new-procedure.md
346	```
347	
348	The validation script checks for:
349	- Complete header block (title, version, owner, date, summary)
350	- At least eight terminology entries
351	- A file references table
352	- A tools and versions table
353	- A changelog with at least six entries
354	- A related pages section
355	- All headings in title case
356	- No `[CUSTOMIZABLE]` markers left behind
357	- Correct Markdown syntax (if applicable)
358	
359	If validation fails, the script prints a summary of missing or incorrect sections. Fix them and run validation again.
360	
361	### Step 7: Request Review
362	
363	Once the page passes validation, assign reviewers according to the documentation review cadence (see the Related Pages section). The review cadence schedule assigns which teams review which pages and sets expected turnaround times. Most pages are reviewed within one to two weeks.
364	
365	### Worked Example
366	
367	Suppose you are writing a new page titled "Updating Page Headers" (a Procedure page for contributors). You would:
368	
369	1. **Copy the template:** `cp docs-style/templates/template-procedure.md docs/updating-page-headers.md`
370	2. **Edit the header:**
371	   ```
372	   # Updating Page Headers
373	   
374	   **Version:** v1.0.0  
375	   **Owner:** Docs Guild (Jordan Park)  
376	   **Last updated:** 2026-09-27  
377	   
378	   **Summary:** How to modify a page header block when updating version, owner, or last-updated date.
379	   ```
380	3. **Replace the Overview:** Write why someone would update a header (when ownership changes, when the page is revised, etc.).
381	4. **Replace Prerequisites:** List what the reader needs (text editor, familiarity with your page's current format, etc.).
382	5. **Replace the Steps:** Write numbered steps like "1. Open the page file in your text editor," "2. Locate the header block at the top," "3. Change the version number from v1.0.0 to v1.0.1," etc.
383	6. **Add a Worked Example:** Show before-and-after header blocks so readers see exactly what they are changing.
384	7. **Add Validation:** Explain how to verify the change (commit and see if the page passes validation, etc.).
385	8. **Write Terminology:** Define "header block," "version number," "owner attribution," "last-updated date," "ISO format," "title case," "patch version," "minor version," and so on.
386	9. **Add File References:** List `docs-style/page-templates.md`, `docs-style/writing-style-guide.md`, etc.
387	10. **Add Tools and Versions:** List the text editor (e.g., "VS Code 1.75+"), Git, Python, and any other tools relevant to the task.
388	11. **Add Related Pages:** Link to "Writing Style Guide," "Page Templates Overview," etc.
389	12. **Add Changelog:** Write "v1.0.0 (2026-09-27) — Jordan Park: Original page."
390	13. **Run validation:** `python scripts/validate-doc-page.py docs/updating-page-headers.md`
391	14. **Request review:** Assign reviewers based on the review cadence schedule.
392	
393	## Glossary Maintenance and Master Glossary Integration
394	
395	The master glossary (`docs-style/glossary.md`, v3.0.1) is maintained by Developer Experience (Sam Whitfield). It serves as the central reference for terms used across all oauthsvc documentation.
396	
397	When you add a term to your page's Terminology section that you believe belongs in the master glossary—because it is widely used, central to understanding oauthsvc documentation practices, or needed by multiple pages—log it in the `docs-style/glossary-upkeep.md` file by adding a row to the "Candidate Terms" table.
398	
399	The glossary maintainer reviews candidate terms monthly (see the **Glossary Upkeep Process**, v1.3) and either:
400	- Adds the term to the master glossary,
401	- Explains why it is too page-specific for the master glossary, or
402	- Suggests a rephrasing or consolidation with an existing term.
403	
404	This workflow keeps the glossary from accumulating duplicate or overly narrow definitions and ensures consistency across all pages.
405	
406	## Review Process and Publishing
407	
408	Once your page is complete and passes validation:
409	
410	1. **Assign reviewers** according to the documentation review cadence (v2.4). Pages are reviewed on a monthly basis by team leads. The review cadence page lists which teams review which pages.
411	2. **Wait for verification** — reviewers will add comments (via pull request or your team's standard review tool) or mark the page verified.
412	3. **Incorporate feedback** — handle reviewer comments and update your page.
413	4. **Update the version number** — if you made changes based on feedback, increment the patch version (e.g., from v1.0.0 to v1.0.1 for small fixes, or to v1.1.0 for larger updates).
414	5. **Add a changelog entry** for the new version.
415	6. **Submit for publishing** — use the **Pre-Publish Checklist** (v1.0) to confirm you have:
416	   - Fixed all reviewer comments
417	   - Updated the header block with the new version and date
418	   - Ensured all links are current
419	   - Verified all code examples and file paths are correct
420	   - Checked for typos and formatting issues
421	7. **Monitor published pages** — after publication, watch for reader feedback or discovered errors. If readers report issues, file a fix request through your team's issue tracker, update the page, and publish a new version.
422	
423	The **Docs Publishing Workflow** document (v2.2.0) covers the full pipeline in detail, including how pages transition from draft to verified to published. Most pages move from initial draft to published within two to three weeks of first review.
424	
425	## File References
426	
427	| Path / File | Purpose | Notes |
428	|---|---|---|
429	| `docs-style/page-templates.md` | This page | Template catalog and standards |
430	| `docs-style/templates/` | Template directory | Copy templates from here for new pages |
431	| `docs-style/writing-style-guide.md` | Style conventions | v3.2, updated 2026-04-03 |
432	| `docs-style/voice-and-tone.md` | Tone guidelines | v2.0, maintained by Theo Banks |
433	| `docs-style/glossary.md` | Master glossary | v3.0.1, updated 2026-02-14 |
434	| `docs-style/glossary-upkeep.md` | Glossary maintenance process | v1.3, updated 2025-09-30 |
435	| `docs-style/review-cadence.md` | Review schedule | v2.4, updated 2026-03-01 |
436	| `docs-style/publishing-workflow.md` | Publishing process | v2.2, updated 2026-06-10 |
437	| `docs-style/markup-conventions.rst` | Markup syntax rules | v2.5, ReStructuredText conventions |
438	| `docs-style/metadata-fields.yaml` | Page metadata fields | v1.2.0, YAML format for automation |
439	| `scripts/validate-doc-page.py` | Validation utility | Checks page completeness before review |
440	| `docs/` | Published documentation folder | Pages move here after verification |
441	
442	## Terminology
443	
444	- **Changelog:** A dated list of changes to a page, ordered from newest to oldest, showing version numbers, dates, authors, and descriptions of what changed.
445	- **Conceptual page:** Documentation that explains ideas, relationships, and design reasoning rather than step-by-step procedures or reference data.
446	- **Definition list:** A markup format pairing terms with their definitions, typically using a dash or colon; commonly used for glossaries and terminology sections.
447	- **Header block:** The structured section at the very top of a page containing title, version number, owner team and point person, last-updated date, and a one-to-two-sentence summary.
448	- **Page template:** A standardized starting document that contributors copy and customize when writing new documentation pages.
449	- **Preconditions:** Requirements (software versions, prior knowledge, completed setup steps, access to files) that readers must satisfy before they can follow a procedure.
450	- **Publishing pipeline:** The staged workflow (draft → review → verified → published) that documentation pages follow before appearing in the live documentation folder.
451	- **Validation script:** A utility (typically written in Python) that programmatically checks a page for required sections, correct formatting, and the presence of all mandatory elements.
452	
453	## Tools and Versions
454	
455	| Tool / Library | Version | Purpose | Notes |
456	|---|---|---|---|
457	| Python | 3.9+ | Validation script language | For running page validation and checks |
458	| Markdown | — | Page markup format | All docs-style pages use Markdown unless otherwise specified |
459	| ReStructuredText | — | Alternate markup format | Some reference pages use RST (see markup-conventions.rst for syntax) |
460	| Git | 2.30+ | Version control | For cloning, editing, and submitting documentation |
461	| Bash | 5.1+ | Shell for running scripts | PowerShell also supported on Windows |
462	| PowerShell | 7.0+ | Shell for Windows | Bash scripts have PowerShell equivalents |
463	| SQLite3 CLI | 3.35+ | Database queries | For examples in documentation |
464	
465	## Related Pages
466	
467	- **Docs Publishing Workflow** (v2.2.0) — the complete stages documentation pages pass through from draft to published, including review verifications and the pre-publish checklist
468	- **Documentation Review Cadence** (v2.4) — schedules for when pages are reviewed, which teams review which pages, and expected turnaround times for feedback
469	- **Glossary Upkeep Process** (v1.3) — how to propose new terminology to the master glossary and how the glossary is maintained and updated over time
470	- **New Contributor Onboarding** (v1.9) — the first steps and essential orientation for people joining the documentation team
471	- **Voice and Tone Guidelines** (v2.0) — guidance on how to write accessibly and maintain consistent tone across all documentation pages
472	- **Writing Style Guide** (v3.2) — grammar, capitalization, formatting, punctuation, and voice standards for all oauthsvc documentation
473	
474	## Changelog
475	
476	- **v1.6.0** (2026-01-08) — Mara Olsen: Added Quick Start template category; expanded Template Copying Workflow section with worked example; clarified file references table format and content guidance.
477	- **v1.5.3** (2025-11-22) — Jordan Park: Updated Voice and Tone Guidelines reference to v2.0; reorganized template categories for improved clarity and scanability.
478	- **v1.5.2** (2025-10-14) — Priya Chandran: Corrected glossary reference to point to v3.0.1; expanded Glossary Maintenance section; added details to Terminology guidelines.
479	- **v1.5.1** (2025-09-30) — Jordan Park: Minor grammar fixes and improved readability in the overview section.
480	- **v1.5.0** (2025-08-15) — Mara Olsen: Restructured template categories with detailed descriptions; added Validation section; renamed Required Elements section to Required Page Elements.
481	- **v1.4.2** (2025-07-03) — Jordan Park: Fixed typos in Related Pages list; updated Publishing Workflow reference to v2.2.0; clarified changelog entry format.
