# Page Templates Overview

**Version:** v1.6.0  
**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)  
**Last updated:** 2026-01-08  

**Summary:** Catalogs the standard page layouts contributors copy when starting a new oauthsvc documentation page. Covers writing style conventions, page structure requirements, terminology maintenance, and the publication process that all documentation in this folder must follow.

## Overview

The oauthsvc documentation project maintains consistency through reusable page templates and a shared set of style conventions. Whether you are writing a procedural guide, a reference page, or a conceptual overview, this document points you to the standard starting templates and walks you through the common elements every page must contain.

All pages in this documentation folder must follow the structure outlined here. Starting with a template ensures that:

- readers can navigate documentation pages without relearning layouts;
- the glossary and terminology stay current with real usage;
- pages flow smoothly into one another through consistent cross-references;
- the publishing workflow runs cleanly without formatting surprises;
- new contributors onboard faster by following familiar patterns.

This page itself serves as a worked example of the standards it describes. When you finish reading, you should be able to copy a template, customize it with your content, pass validation, and submit to review within a single working day.

## Page Template Categories

The documentation program defines four primary template categories. Choose one as your starting point based on your content type. Each template includes customizable sections marked with `[SECTION NAME]` that you replace with your own writing.

### Procedure Template

Use the Procedure template for pages that walk readers through a sequence of steps: running a command, configuring the service, diagnosing a problem, or deploying documentation. Procedures are goal-oriented and linear; readers follow them in order to accomplish a specific task.

**When to use Procedure template:**
- Instructions for setting up the documentation environment
- Troubleshooting workflows
- Steps for validating page changes
- Processes for updating the master glossary
- Publishing or reviewing pages

The Procedure template structure:

1. Header block (title, version, owner, date, summary)
2. Overview paragraph (why someone would follow this procedure)
3. Prerequisites / Preconditions (software versions, prior knowledge, required files)
4. Main procedure steps (numbered list with clear verb phrases)
5. Worked example (actual command input and output)
6. Validation section (how to verify the procedure succeeded)
7. Troubleshooting subsection (common errors and fixes, if relevant)
8. Terminology section (terms used in the procedure)
9. File references table
10. Tools and versions table
11. Related pages section
12. Changelog

A well-structured Procedure page lets readers skim the prerequisites, jump to the step they need, and validate success without reading the entire document sequentially.

### Reference Template

Use the Reference template for pages that document options, settings, configuration formats, or information readers look up rather than read straight through. Reference pages lean on tables and structured lists. A Reference page serves as lookup documentation; readers should be able to scan it quickly and find the answer they need within thirty seconds.

**When to use Reference template:**
- Documentation page metadata fields and their valid values
- Page header block specifications and formatting rules
- Markup conventions for Markdown and ReStructuredText
- Page review checklist items and criteria
- Glossary term format and submission guidelines

The Reference template structure:

1. Header block
2. Overview paragraph (breadth of what the reference covers)
3. Options, settings, or configuration in tabular form with columns for Name, Type/Range, Required, and Description
4. Detailed descriptions for complex options (reference to a detailed section if the option is intricate)
5. Examples showing typical configurations or complete entries
6. Limitations, caveats, or deprecation warnings
7. Terminology section
8. File references table
9. Tools and versions table
10. Related pages section
11. Changelog

Reference pages often have more tables than prose. A reader should be able to screenshot or print the page and use it as a standalone reference without consulting other documents.

### Conceptual Template

Use the Conceptual template for pages that explain ideas, architecture, relationships between concepts, or the reasoning behind design choices. Conceptual pages often synthesize information from multiple reference or procedural pages into a unified explanation.

**When to use Conceptual template:**
- How the documentation program is organized
- Design principles for page structure and style
- The relationship between glossary upkeep and style consistency
- Overview of the documentation publishing workflow
- Explanation of why certain markup conventions exist

The Conceptual template structure:

1. Header block
2. Overview and coverage (what ideas the page unifies)
3. Core concepts (multiple sections, each with its own owner attribution where appropriate)
4. Relationships between concepts (how they interact)
5. Common workflows or use patterns (how these concepts apply in practice)
6. Terminology section
7. File references table
8. Tools and versions table
9. Related pages section
10. Changelog

Conceptual pages benefit from diagrams, but text descriptions and relationships tables work well too. A reader finishing a Conceptual page should understand the "why" behind related procedures and reference pages.

### Quick Start Template

Use the Quick Start template for brief orientation pages aimed at new contributors or for condensed guides to common tasks. These pages compress the essential setup steps, point to deeper documentation, and introduce key terminology without lengthy explanation. Quick Start pages are short—aim for 800–1200 words total.

**When to use Quick Start template:**
- New contributor orientation to the documentation folder
- First-time setup for page authoring
- Quick reference for the most common documentation tasks
- Brief introductions to specific tools (Git, Markdown, the validation script)

The Quick Start template structure:

1. Header block
2. What this template covers (brief coverage statement)
3. Five to seven core steps in checklist format
4. One worked example
5. Where to go next (links to deeper documentation)
6. Terminology section (abbreviated, 4–6 terms)
7. File references table (abbreviated, only the essential files)
8. Related pages section
9. Changelog

Quick Start pages trade comprehensiveness for rapid orientation. A new contributor should finish a Quick Start page and immediately begin a first task.

## Required Page Elements

Every page in this documentation folder, regardless of template type, must contain the following elements. Pages that do not include all required sections will fail the validation script and the pre-publish checklist and must be revised before entering the pipeline. The publishing team will not review incomplete pages.

### Header Block

Place a header block at the very top of your page file, before any other content:

```
# Page Title Here

**Version:** v1.2.3  
**Owner:** Team Name (Person Name)  
**Last updated:** YYYY-MM-DD  

**Summary:** One or two sentences describing what readers will learn or accomplish from this page.
```

- **Title** (heading level 1): should match the page name in index listings; use title case.
- **Version**: use format `vX.Y.Z` (e.g., `v1.6.0`) unless your team uses a different convention. Check your team's other pages to see the standard. Increment the patch version (the third number) for small fixes and adjustments. Increment the minor version (the second number) for substantial content additions or reorganizations.
- **Owner**: name the team and one point person responsible for this page. When the owner changes (e.g., due to team reorganization), update this field and note the change in the changelog.
- **Last updated**: use ISO format YYYY-MM-DD. Update this date whenever you make substantive changes; minor fixes (typos, broken links, small clarifications) do not require a date bump. The date helps readers assess freshness and determines which pages need periodic reviews on the documentation review cadence schedule.
- **Summary**: one to two sentences, readable in page listings and indexes. Avoid jargon; assume the reader is scanning many page summaries quickly.

### Section Headings and Ownership

Use heading level 2 (`##`) for top-level sections and level 3 (`###`) for subsections. Capitalize headings in title case (capitalize the first letter of the main words). Keep heading text concise; if you need to say more, use the first paragraph of the section.

For sections that deal with large topics the team actively maintains, name the section owner in parentheses after the heading. This attribution helps readers know who to contact with clarifications or questions:

```markdown
## Configuration Reference (Owner: Platform Tools — Nadia Reyes)

## Review Process and Publishing (Owner: Docs Guild — Ilse Vogel)
```

Not every section needs an owner attribution. Procedural steps, worked examples, introductory sections, and standard navigational sections (Terminology, Related Pages, Changelog) typically do not carry ownership. Use ownership attribution sparingly to avoid visual clutter.

### Terminology / Glossary Section

Every page must include a terminology section (titled "Terminology," "Glossary," or "Key Concepts") that defines at least eight terms used on the page. The glossary serves two purposes: it helps readers unfamiliar with the term find its definition without leaving the page, and it identifies candidates for the master glossary.

Terms should be:

- **specific to oauthsvc and its documentation practice** — avoid generic dictionary definitions;
- **in alphabetical order** — use a definition list format (term followed by its definition) or a two-column table;
- **linked to the master glossary** where the term is defined more broadly.

Example terminology section using definition list format:

```markdown
## Terminology

- **Changelog:** A dated list of changes to a page, ordered from newest to oldest, with version numbers, dates, authors, and descriptions of what changed.
- **Header block:** The structured section at the top of a page containing title, version, owner, date, and summary.
- **Preconditions:** Requirements (software versions, prior knowledge, completed setup steps) that readers must satisfy before following a procedure.
- ...
```

You may add a note like "See also the master glossary" at the bottom of your Terminology section to direct readers to the broader reference. For terms already well-defined in the master glossary, you may write a brief contextual definition on your page and cross-reference the broader definition.

When you encounter a term that you believe belongs in the master glossary but is not yet there, add it to your page's Terminology section and log it in the `glossary-upkeep.md` file (see the Glossary Maintenance section below).

### File and Path References

List the repository files, host paths, configuration locations, and directories your page refers to. Format this as a table with columns for **Path / File**, **Purpose**, and **Notes**. Include only files that are relevant to the page's content:

| Path / File | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `docs-style/page-templates.md` | This page | Started v1.5.0; see changelog |
| `docs-style/writing-style-guide.md` | Style conventions for all text | Updated quarterly |
| `docs-style/glossary.md` | Master term definitions | Owned by Developer Experience |
| `docs/` | Published documentation folder | Pages move here after verification |
| `scripts/validate-doc-page.py` | Validation utility | Checks page completeness before review |

Do not include system paths (like `/tmp` or `C:\Windows\System32`) unless your page discusses them directly. Do not list the documentation files themselves unless relevant to your topic (e.g., a page about the publishing workflow would list the publishing checklist, but a page about writing procedures would not).

### Tools and Versions Table

If your page mentions tools, libraries, or versions readers need to install or have available, create a table listing them. Tools might include the shell, version control systems, editors, database utilities, or any external dependency:

| Tool / Library | Version | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.9+ | Validation script language | For running page validation checks |
| Markdown | — | Page markup format | All docs-style pages use Markdown |
| Git | 2.30+ | Version control | For cloning and editing documentation repository |
| Bash | 5.1+ | Shell for examples | PowerShell also supported on Windows |
| SQLite3 CLI | 3.35+ | Example queries | Standard library, no separate install |

Use `—` in the Version column if the tool does not have a version number (e.g., Markdown markup language) or if version is not relevant to the page. This table helps readers understand prerequisites and compatibility constraints.

### Related Pages Section

At the end of your page, before the Changelog, link to sibling pages in the `docs-style/` folder and other relevant documentation. These are pages readers of your page will likely need to consult:

```markdown
## Related Pages

- **Writing Style Guide** (v3.2) — conventions for grammar, tone, and voice across all pages
- **Glossary Upkeep Process** (v1.3) — how to add and maintain terminology in the master glossary
- **Documentation Review Cadence** (v2.4) — review schedule and verification steps
- **Docs Publishing Workflow** (v2.2) — moving pages from draft to published
```

List related pages alphabetically by title. Include the page version and a one-sentence description of what it covers. Do not cross-link every page to every other page; link only pages that readers of your page will likely need to consult next.

### Changelog

Every page must have a changelog section with at least six dated entries. The changelog documents the page's changes over time and helps readers assess freshness and understand what has changed since they last read the page. Each entry names the version, date, and author, and describes what changed. Order entries from newest to oldest (reverse chronological order).

Format the changelog as a definition list:

```markdown
## Changelog

- **v1.6.0** (2026-01-08) — Mara Olsen: Added quick-start template category; revised examples in template elements section.
- **v1.5.3** (2025-11-22) — Jordan Park: Corrected file path references in the tools and versions table.
- **v1.5.2** (2025-10-14) — Priya Chandran: Updated related pages section to point to review-cadence v2.4.
- **v1.5.1** (2025-09-30) — Jordan Park: Minor grammar fixes in the overview section.
- **v1.5.0** (2025-08-15) — Mara Olsen: Restructured template categories; added detailed section for reference templates.
- **v1.4.2** (2025-07-03) — Priya Chandran: Improved worked example in the Procedure template section.
```

When you update a page:
1. Add a new changelog entry at the top of the list.
2. Increment the version number: patch for minor fixes, minor for feature/content additions, major if restructuring the page significantly.
3. Use today's date in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD).
4. Name the author (usually you).
5. Write a clear, concise description of the change (one to three lines).

If a change is truly minor—a typo, a broken link, a single clarifying word—you may group several minor fixes into a single changelog entry and note "Various edits" or "Typo fixes."

## Typical Page Structure

The following order works well for most pages in the oauthsvc documentation:

1. Header block (title, version, owner, date, summary)
2. Overview or introduction (what readers will learn, why they need to read this)
3. Main content sections (procedures, reference tables, conceptual explanations — varies by template)
4. Worked example or illustration (for procedure and quick-start templates; conceptual pages may use subsections instead)
5. Troubleshooting or common issues (where relevant; omit if not needed)
6. Terminology / Glossary section
7. File and path references table
8. Tools and versions table
9. Related pages section
10. Changelog

Some pages reorder sections if content demands it. For instance, a reference page might place Examples before Terminology if the examples are essential for understanding the topic. However, the header block must always come first, and Terminology must come before the File References table. The Changelog must always be last.

## Writing Style Consistency

All pages in this folder must conform to the conventions in the **Writing Style Guide** (v3.2). Key standards include:

- **Second person** ("you," "your") in procedures and guides aimed at readers performing actions. Use first person only when writing changelog entries or when referring to the authoring team.
- **Consistent verb tense:** use imperative mood for instructions ("Run the validation script"), present tense for descriptions ("The script checks page completeness"), and past tense for changelog entries and prior notes.
- **Standard terminology:** use the terms defined in the master glossary; do not introduce synonyms without explicit reason. If you coin a new term, define it in your Terminology section and propose it to the master glossary.
- **Oxford comma** in lists of three or more items (e.g., "title, version, and owner").
- **Code and file names in backticks** (e.g., `` `validate-doc-page.py` `` or `` `docs-style/` ``).
- **Headings in title case** (capitalize the first letter of main words; do not capitalize articles, conjunctions, or prepositions unless they are the first word).
- **Active voice preferred** over passive; write "The validation script checks your page" rather than "Your page is checked by the validation script."
- **Concise language:** use short sentences and paragraphs; avoid jargon unless defined.

For guidance on voice and tone, consult the **Voice and Tone Guidelines** page (v2.0), maintained by Developer Experience. For markup syntax (Markdown vs. ReStructuredText formatting), see the **Markup Conventions** page (v2.5).

## Template Copying Workflow

When starting a new page, follow these steps:

### Step 1: Identify Your Page Type

Determine which template suits your content:
- **Procedure:** step-by-step instructions to accomplish a goal.
- **Reference:** lookup information in structured tables or lists.
- **Conceptual:** explanations of ideas, relationships, or design reasoning.
- **Quick Start:** brief orientation for new users or rapid task introduction.

### Step 2: Copy the Template File

Templates live in the `docs-style/templates/` folder. Copy the appropriate template to your working location in the `docs/` folder. For example:

```bash
cp docs-style/templates/template-procedure.md docs/my-new-procedure.md
```

Or in Windows PowerShell:
```powershell
Copy the template procedure file from docs-style/templates/template-procedure.md to docs/my-new-procedure.md
```

The template file is a starting skeleton; it includes all required sections marked with `[CUSTOMIZABLE TEXT]` that you replace with your own content.

### Step 3: Customize the Header Block

Open your new file in a text editor and replace the header block:
- Change the title to your page's title.
- Set the version to `v1.0.0` (or align with your team's versioning).
- Assign the owner (your team name and your name, or the primary owner).
- Set the last-updated date to today in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD).
- Write a clear summary (one to two sentences).

### Step 4: Replace Customizable Sections

Work through each `[CUSTOMIZABLE]` marker and write your own content. For a Procedure page, you would replace `[OVERVIEW PARAGRAPH]` with your introduction, `[PREREQUISITES SECTION]` with the requirements, `[STEP 1]`, `[STEP 2]`, etc., with your numbered steps, and so on.

### Step 5: Add Terminology

Before you finish, review your page for terms that need definition. Add at least eight terms to the Terminology section in alphabetical order.

### Step 6: Run the Validation Script

From the repository root, run the validation script to check that your page has all required sections:

```bash
python scripts/validate-doc-page.py docs/my-new-procedure.md
```

The validation script checks for:
- Complete header block (title, version, owner, date, summary)
- At least eight terminology entries
- A file references table
- A tools and versions table
- A changelog with at least six entries
- A related pages section
- All headings in title case
- No `[CUSTOMIZABLE]` markers left behind
- Correct Markdown syntax (if applicable)

If validation fails, the script prints a summary of missing or incorrect sections. Fix them and run validation again.

### Step 7: Request Review

Once the page passes validation, assign reviewers according to the documentation review cadence (see the Related Pages section). The review cadence schedule assigns which teams review which pages and sets expected turnaround times. Most pages are reviewed within one to two weeks.

### Worked Example

Suppose you are writing a new page titled "Updating Page Headers" (a Procedure page for contributors). You would:

1. **Copy the template:** `cp docs-style/templates/template-procedure.md docs/updating-page-headers.md`
2. **Edit the header:**
   ```
   # Updating Page Headers
   
   **Version:** v1.0.0  
   **Owner:** Docs Guild (Jordan Park)  
   **Last updated:** 2026-09-27  
   
   **Summary:** How to modify a page header block when updating version, owner, or last-updated date.
   ```
3. **Replace the Overview:** Write why someone would update a header (when ownership changes, when the page is revised, etc.).
4. **Replace Prerequisites:** List what the reader needs (text editor, familiarity with your page's current format, etc.).
5. **Replace the Steps:** Write numbered steps like "1. Open the page file in your text editor," "2. Locate the header block at the top," "3. Change the version number from v1.0.0 to v1.0.1," etc.
6. **Add a Worked Example:** Show before-and-after header blocks so readers see exactly what they are changing.
7. **Add Validation:** Explain how to verify the change (commit and see if the page passes validation, etc.).
8. **Write Terminology:** Define "header block," "version number," "owner attribution," "last-updated date," "ISO format," "title case," "patch version," "minor version," and so on.
9. **Add File References:** List `docs-style/page-templates.md`, `docs-style/writing-style-guide.md`, etc.
10. **Add Tools and Versions:** List the text editor (e.g., "VS Code 1.75+"), Git, Python, and any other tools relevant to the task.
11. **Add Related Pages:** Link to "Writing Style Guide," "Page Templates Overview," etc.
12. **Add Changelog:** Write "v1.0.0 (2026-09-27) — Jordan Park: Original page."
13. **Run validation:** `python scripts/validate-doc-page.py docs/updating-page-headers.md`
14. **Request review:** Assign reviewers based on the review cadence schedule.

## Glossary Maintenance and Master Glossary Integration

The master glossary (`docs-style/glossary.md`, v3.0.1) is maintained by Developer Experience (Sam Whitfield). It serves as the central reference for terms used across all oauthsvc documentation.

When you add a term to your page's Terminology section that you believe belongs in the master glossary—because it is widely used, central to understanding oauthsvc documentation practices, or needed by multiple pages—log it in the `docs-style/glossary-upkeep.md` file by adding a row to the "Candidate Terms" table.

The glossary maintainer reviews candidate terms monthly (see the **Glossary Upkeep Process**, v1.3) and either:
- Adds the term to the master glossary,
- Explains why it is too page-specific for the master glossary, or
- Suggests a rephrasing or consolidation with an existing term.

This workflow keeps the glossary from accumulating duplicate or overly narrow definitions and ensures consistency across all pages.

## Review Process and Publishing

Once your page is complete and passes validation:

1. **Assign reviewers** according to the documentation review cadence (v2.4). Pages are reviewed on a monthly basis by team leads. The review cadence page lists which teams review which pages.
2. **Wait for verification** — reviewers will add comments (via pull request or your team's standard review tool) or mark the page verified.
3. **Incorporate feedback** — handle reviewer comments and update your page.
4. **Update the version number** — if you made changes based on feedback, increment the patch version (e.g., from v1.0.0 to v1.0.1 for small fixes, or to v1.1.0 for larger updates).
5. **Add a changelog entry** for the new version.
6. **Submit for publishing** — use the **Pre-Publish Checklist** (v1.0) to confirm you have:
   - Fixed all reviewer comments
   - Updated the header block with the new version and date
   - Ensured all links are current
   - Verified all code examples and file paths are correct
   - Checked for typos and formatting issues
7. **Monitor published pages** — after publication, watch for reader feedback or discovered errors. If readers report issues, file a fix request through your team's issue tracker, update the page, and publish a new version.

The **Docs Publishing Workflow** document (v2.2.0) covers the full pipeline in detail, including how pages transition from draft to verified to published. Most pages move from initial draft to published within two to three weeks of first review.

## File References

| Path / File | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `docs-style/page-templates.md` | This page | Template catalog and standards |
| `docs-style/templates/` | Template directory | Copy templates from here for new pages |
| `docs-style/writing-style-guide.md` | Style conventions | v3.2, updated 2026-04-03 |
| `docs-style/voice-and-tone.md` | Tone guidelines | v2.0, maintained by Theo Banks |
| `docs-style/glossary.md` | Master glossary | v3.0.1, updated 2026-02-14 |
| `docs-style/glossary-upkeep.md` | Glossary maintenance process | v1.3, updated 2025-09-30 |
| `docs-style/review-cadence.md` | Review schedule | v2.4, updated 2026-03-01 |
| `docs-style/publishing-workflow.md` | Publishing process | v2.2, updated 2026-06-10 |
| `docs-style/markup-conventions.rst` | Markup syntax rules | v2.5, ReStructuredText conventions |
| `docs-style/metadata-fields.yaml` | Page metadata fields | v1.2.0, YAML format for automation |
| `scripts/validate-doc-page.py` | Validation utility | Checks page completeness before review |
| `docs/` | Published documentation folder | Pages move here after verification |

## Terminology

- **Changelog:** A dated list of changes to a page, ordered from newest to oldest, showing version numbers, dates, authors, and descriptions of what changed.
- **Conceptual page:** Documentation that explains ideas, relationships, and design reasoning rather than step-by-step procedures or reference data.
- **Definition list:** A markup format pairing terms with their definitions, typically using a dash or colon; commonly used for glossaries and terminology sections.
- **Header block:** The structured section at the very top of a page containing title, version number, owner team and point person, last-updated date, and a one-to-two-sentence summary.
- **Page template:** A standardized starting document that contributors copy and customize when writing new documentation pages.
- **Preconditions:** Requirements (software versions, prior knowledge, completed setup steps, access to files) that readers must satisfy before they can follow a procedure.
- **Publishing pipeline:** The staged workflow (draft → review → verified → published) that documentation pages follow before appearing in the live documentation folder.
- **Validation script:** A utility (typically written in Python) that programmatically checks a page for required sections, correct formatting, and the presence of all mandatory elements.

## Tools and Versions

| Tool / Library | Version | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.9+ | Validation script language | For running page validation and checks |
| Markdown | — | Page markup format | All docs-style pages use Markdown unless otherwise specified |
| ReStructuredText | — | Alternate markup format | Some reference pages use RST (see markup-conventions.rst for syntax) |
| Git | 2.30+ | Version control | For cloning, editing, and submitting documentation |
| Bash | 5.1+ | Shell for running scripts | PowerShell also supported on Windows |
| PowerShell | 7.0+ | Shell for Windows | Bash scripts have PowerShell equivalents |
| SQLite3 CLI | 3.35+ | Database queries | For examples in documentation |

## Related Pages

- **Docs Publishing Workflow** (v2.2.0) — the complete stages documentation pages pass through from draft to published, including review verifications and the pre-publish checklist
- **Documentation Review Cadence** (v2.4) — schedules for when pages are reviewed, which teams review which pages, and expected turnaround times for feedback
- **Glossary Upkeep Process** (v1.3) — how to propose new terminology to the master glossary and how the glossary is maintained and updated over time
- **New Contributor Onboarding** (v1.9) — the first steps and essential orientation for people joining the documentation team
- **Voice and Tone Guidelines** (v2.0) — guidance on how to write accessibly and maintain consistent tone across all documentation pages
- **Writing Style Guide** (v3.2) — grammar, capitalization, formatting, punctuation, and voice standards for all oauthsvc documentation

## Changelog

- **v1.6.0** (2026-01-08) — Mara Olsen: Added Quick Start template category; expanded Template Copying Workflow section with worked example; clarified file references table format and content guidance.
- **v1.5.3** (2025-11-22) — Jordan Park: Updated Voice and Tone Guidelines reference to v2.0; reorganized template categories for improved clarity and scanability.
- **v1.5.2** (2025-10-14) — Priya Chandran: Corrected glossary reference to point to v3.0.1; expanded Glossary Maintenance section; added details to Terminology guidelines.
- **v1.5.1** (2025-09-30) — Jordan Park: Minor grammar fixes and improved readability in the overview section.
- **v1.5.0** (2025-08-15) — Mara Olsen: Restructured template categories with detailed descriptions; added Validation section; renamed Required Elements section to Required Page Elements.
- **v1.4.2** (2025-07-03) — Jordan Park: Fixed typos in Related Pages list; updated Publishing Workflow reference to v2.2.0; clarified changelog entry format.

1	# Voice and Tone Guidelines
2	
3	**Title:** Voice and Tone Guidelines  
4	**Version:** 2.0  
5	**Owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Banks)  
6	**Last Updated:** 2025-11-19  
7	**Summary:** Describes the conversational register and level of formality expected across the oauthsvc wiki.
8	
9	## Overview
10	
11	This documentation serves two primary audiences: developers integrating the package into their own services, and the small team maintaining the package itself. This guide establishes the conversational voice and tone that should appear across all wiki pages, from quick-reference guides to design documentation and operational procedures.
12	
13	Consistent voice doesn't mean repetitive language or a rigid style. Instead, it means that every page reflects the same baseline assumptions about who is reading, why they're reading, and what they need to accomplish. The voice of the oauthsvc documentation is practical, direct, and grounded in implementation details—not marketing, not academic formality, and not overcautious disclaimer language.
14	
15	## Core Voice Principles
16	
17	The oauthsvc documentation voice rests on four pillars:
18	
19	**Specificity over generality.** Names matter. Use the actual configuration file names, paths, variable names, and command-line flags that appear in your environment. "Edit the config file" is less useful than "Edit `service.ini` in the `scripts/` folder." Readers scanning quickly should be able to grab the exact string they need without having to trace through abstract descriptions.
20	
21	**Assumption of competence.** Readers of these pages understand Python, SQL concepts, HTTP basics, and the local file system. You don't need to explain what SQLite is or apologize for the command-line interface. You do need to explain why a particular design choice was made, what happens when something fails, and how one component depends on another.
22	
23	**Active voice and present tense as default.** The service reads from the database. State files are checked at startup. The loopback server listens on port 8080 by default. Use passive voice only when the actor is genuinely unknown or unimportant ("the configuration was corrupted"); even then, prefer "the configuration became corrupted" or "something corrupted the configuration."
24	
25	**Readable but frank.** Avoid cute framing, marketese, or over-explanation. If something is confusing or has sharp edges, say so. If a workaround exists, document it plainly. If a feature has limitations, list them. This builds trust and prevents readers from wasting hours on incorrect assumptions.
26	
27	## Register and Formality Levels
28	
29	The oauthsvc wiki uses a conversational register somewhere between technical journal and team chat. The following examples illustrate the acceptable range:
30	
31	**Too formal (avoid):** "It is incumbent upon the reader to verify that all prerequisites have been satisfied prior to executing the initialization sequence."
32	
33	**Correct register:** "Before you start the service, make sure the configuration file exists, the database is initialized, and you have write access to the scripts folder."
34	
35	**Too informal (avoid):** "Just config it and if you mess up it totally breaks lol"
36	
37	**Correct register:** "If you misconfigure the state file path, the service will fail to start with a file-not-found error."
38	
39	The tone remains professional and clear, but uses shorter sentences, active structures, and the occasional parenthetical aside (like this one). Second person ("you") is acceptable and often preferred over passive constructions or impersonal phrasings.
40	
41	Within this register, formality may shift slightly depending on the page type:
42	
43	- **Architecture and design pages** (owned by Platform Tools): Expect careful explanation of tradeoffs, reasoning, and constraints. Still direct, but with more depth and less conversational flavor.
44	- **Quick-reference pages** (owned by Docs Guild): Shorter lines, more lists, fewer full paragraphs. Scan-friendly above all.
45	- **Operational guides** (owned by Developer Experience): Emphasize what to do, what to expect, what to avoid. Write directly to the reader and keep procedures concrete.
46	
47	See "Page Templates Overview" (version v1.6.0, owned by Platform Tools, last updated 2026-01-08) for templates that enforce register consistency across similar page types.
48	
49	## Writing Style Application
50	
51	The "Writing Style Guide" (version 3.2, owned by Docs Guild, last updated 2026-04-03) covers punctuation, capitalization, code formatting, and other mechanics. This guide focuses on voice and register; the style guide handles the surface layer.
52	
53	When both documents apply, follow this priority:
54	
55	1. Consistency with existing pages in the same section of the wiki (e.g., all operational guides should sound alike).
56	2. The Writing Style Guide for conventions not discussed here.
57	3. Your best judgment about clarity for the reader.
58	
59	**Capitalization example:** Configuration option names are lowercase in the actual service, so write them lowercase even when they appear at the start of a sentence or in a heading. # Voice and Tone Guidelines

**Title:** Voice and Tone Guidelines  
**Version:** 2.0  
**Owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Banks)  
**Last Updated:** 2025-11-19  
**Summary:** Describes the conversational register and level of formality expected across the oauthsvc wiki.

## Overview

This documentation serves two primary audiences: developers integrating the package into their own services, and the small team maintaining the package itself. This guide establishes the conversational voice and tone that should appear across all wiki pages, from quick-reference guides to design documentation and operational procedures.

Consistent voice doesn't mean repetitive language or a rigid style. Instead, it means that every page reflects the same baseline assumptions about who is reading, why they're reading, and what they need to accomplish. The voice of the oauthsvc documentation is practical, direct, and grounded in implementation details—not marketing, not academic formality, and not overcautious disclaimer language.

## Core Voice Principles

The oauthsvc documentation voice rests on four pillars:

**Specificity over generality.** Names matter. Use the actual configuration file names, paths, variable names, and command-line flags that appear in your environment. "Edit the config file" is less useful than "Edit `service.ini` in the `scripts/` folder." Readers scanning quickly should be able to grab the exact string they need without having to trace through abstract descriptions.

**Assumption of competence.** Readers of these pages understand Python, SQL concepts, HTTP basics, and the local file system. You don't need to explain what SQLite is or apologize for the command-line interface. You do need to explain why a particular design choice was made, what happens when something fails, and how one component depends on another.

**Active voice and present tense as default.** The service reads from the database. State files are checked at startup. The loopback server listens on port 8080 by default. Use passive voice only when the actor is genuinely unknown or unimportant ("the configuration was corrupted"); even then, prefer "the configuration became corrupted" or "something corrupted the configuration."

**Readable but frank.** Avoid cute framing, marketese, or over-explanation. If something is confusing or has sharp edges, say so. If a workaround exists, document it plainly. If a feature has limitations, list them. This builds trust and prevents readers from wasting hours on incorrect assumptions.

## Register and Formality Levels

The oauthsvc wiki uses a conversational register somewhere between technical journal and team chat. The following examples illustrate the acceptable range:

**Too formal (avoid):** "It is incumbent upon the reader to verify that all prerequisites have been satisfied prior to executing the initialization sequence."

**Correct register:** "Before you start the service, make sure the configuration file exists, the database is initialized, and you have write access to the scripts folder."

**Too informal (avoid):** "Just config it and if you mess up it totally breaks lol"

**Correct register:** "If you misconfigure the state file path, the service will fail to start with a file-not-found error."

The tone remains professional and clear, but uses shorter sentences, active structures, and the occasional parenthetical aside (like this one). Second person ("you") is acceptable and often preferred over passive constructions or impersonal phrasings.

Within this register, formality may shift slightly depending on the page type:

- **Architecture and design pages** (owned by Platform Tools): Expect careful explanation of tradeoffs, reasoning, and constraints. Still direct, but with more depth and less conversational flavor.
- **Quick-reference pages** (owned by Docs Guild): Shorter lines, more lists, fewer full paragraphs. Scan-friendly above all.
- **Operational guides** (owned by Developer Experience): Emphasize what to do, what to expect, what to avoid. Write directly to the reader and keep procedures concrete.

See "Page Templates Overview" (version v1.6.0, owned by Platform Tools, last updated 2026-01-08) for templates that enforce register consistency across similar page types.

## Writing Style Application

The "Writing Style Guide" (version 3.2, owned by Docs Guild, last updated 2026-04-03) covers punctuation, capitalization, code formatting, and other mechanics. This guide focuses on voice and register; the style guide handles the surface layer.

When both documents apply, follow this priority:

1. Consistency with existing pages in the same section of the wiki (e.g., all operational guides should sound alike).
2. The Writing Style Guide for conventions not discussed here.
3. Your best judgment about clarity for the reader.

**Capitalization example:** Configuration option names are lowercase in the actual service, so write them lowercase even when they appear at the start of a sentence or in a heading. "the state_file option controls where data lives" is correct. Recapitalizing to "State_file" for grammar would create a false name that readers might mistype in their actual configuration. The "Writing Style Guide" covers this in depth in its "Code Formatting" section.

Code and file references stay in monospace: `service.ini`, `logs/` folder, the `loopback_server` module (though module names should not be named at all—use "the package" instead). When a monospace name falls inside a link, keep the monospace: [`service.ini`](path/to/docs).

## Glossary Voice Standards

The oauthsvc wiki maintains a shared glossary ("oauthsvc Glossary", version v3.0.1, owned by Developer Experience, last updated 2026-02-14) and a process for keeping it current ("Glossary Upkeep Process", version 1.3, last updated 2025-09-30). Both are owned by Developer Experience.

Every glossary entry should:

- **Define the term as it is used in the oauthsvc codebase and wiki**, not as it appears in abstract documentation or standards documents. If the glossary and the actual code diverge, update the glossary.
- **Use simple language.** Assume the reader knows their way around Python and SQL but may not be familiar with oauthsvc conventions yet.
- **Include at least one example or context sentence** showing how the term appears in actual use.
- **Note related terms** when they exist (e.g., "See also: state file, configuration").

The glossary is not a place for marketing or conceptual overview. It is a place for precision. If a term has two meanings in the codebase (which happens), document both and explain the difference clearly.

Glossary upkeep happens on a rolling basis, not on a fixed schedule. When you write a page that introduces or redefines a term, update the glossary in the same pull request. The Developer Experience owner reviews glossary PRs for consistency and flags any terms that conflict with recent entries or lack sufficient clarity.

## Integration with Page Templates

The "Page Templates Overview" (version v1.6.0, owned by Platform Tools, last updated 2026-01-08) and "Template Field Reference" (version 2.1, last updated 2025-08-22) define the structure and metadata fields for pages in the docs-style folder and the broader wiki.

Template structure shapes voice naturally. A template that forces a particular section order will promote certain kinds of voice: quick-reference templates encourage brevity and list-based organization, while design-document templates encourage context and tradeoff discussion. Don't fight the template. If the template includes an "Assumptions" or "Audience" section, use that section to set expectations about formality and depth. This prevents readers from being blindsided by a page that's either too shallow or too jargon-heavy for their needs.

When writing a page, choose the template that fits your content, then shape the voice to match the template's natural register.

## Review and Publishing Workflow

Two related documents govern how pages move from draft to published:

- "Documentation Review Cadence" (version 2.4, owned by Platform Tools, last updated 2026-03-01) sets the timing and coverage of reviews.
- "Page Review Checklist" (version 1.1, owned by Platform Tools, last updated 2025-06-17) lists specific items to verify, including voice consistency.

The review checklist includes a "Voice and Register" section. Reviewers check whether:

- The page matches the register for its template type.
- Formality doesn't drift wildly from sentence to sentence.
- Specific names and paths are used instead of vague references ("the folder" vs. "the scripts/ folder").
- The page assumes an appropriate level of reader competence (not too high, not too low).

A reviewer may request changes to voice and tone, not just mechanics. If your page reads like a sales pitch or a textbook, expect feedback. If it's too terse or assumes expertise the audience doesn't have, the reviewer will flag it.

The "Docs Publishing Workflow" (version v2.2.0, owned by Docs Guild, last updated 2026-06-10) handles the final steps: sign-off, staging, and deployment to the live wiki. Voice review happens before that stage, during the pull request discussion.

## Worked Examples

### Example One: An operational startup guide

**Draft (voice issues):**  
"The service requires that all prerequisites are met. The configuration file must be present. The database must be initialized. It is recommended that these conditions be verified before starting."

**Revised (correct voice):**  
"Before you start the service, make sure the configuration file exists, the database is initialized, and you have write access to both. Run the status check command first if you're unsure."

The rewrite is more specific (mentions a status check command), assumes competence (doesn't explain why these things matter), uses active voice and present tense, and speaks to the reader directly.

### Example Two: A glossary entry

**Draft (too vague):**  
"State: Information that the system maintains."

**Revised (specific and useful):**  
"State file: The SQLite database on disk that holds configuration and runtime data. The service reads state at startup and writes changes after each operation. The state file path is configured in the config file via the state_file option. See also: database, configuration."

The rewrite names the specific format (SQLite), explains its function, shows how to configure it, and links to related terms.

### Example Three: A quick-reference section heading

**Draft (too formal):**  
"Configuration Initialization Procedures"

**Revised:**  
"Starting the service"

Shorter, more direct. The opening paragraph can then explain the specific procedures without an elaborate title.

## Terminology and Glossary

**Audience:** The people reading a particular page or section of the wiki. Audience varies: some pages target developers using the package; others target maintainers. Pages should state their assumed audience upfront when the coverage is specific. Related: Coverage.

**Changelog:** A dated list of updates to a document, typically in reverse chronological order (newest first). Every page in the docs-style folder includes a changelog so readers can see when and how the page has been revised. Related: Version.

**Configuration:** Settings that control how the service behaves, typically read from a file at startup. Configuration is separate from state (which the service modifies during operation) and from code. Related: State file, initialization.

**Docs Guild:** The team responsible for documentation structure, publishing workflow, style consistency, and contributor onboarding. Members include Priya Chandran and Nadia Reyes.

**Developer Experience:** The team responsible for developer-facing documentation, internal guides, glossary standards, and voice/tone guidance. Members include Theo Banks and Sam Whitfield.

**Platform Tools:** The team responsible for documentation templates, markup conventions, documentation infrastructure, and review processes. Members include Mara Olsen and Ilse Vogel.

**Pull request:** A version-control mechanism for proposing changes to the wiki before they go live. Pages are reviewed via pull request before being merged and published.

**Register:** The level of formality and the assumptions about the audience embedded in a piece of writing. The oauthsvc wiki uses a conversational-technical register, not academic register or marketing tone.

**Section owner:** The person or team responsible for maintaining a subsection of the wiki or documentation topic. Named at the top of each page. Different from "Owner" (the document owner).

**State file:** The SQLite database on disk that stores configuration and runtime data. The service reads the state file at startup and writes to it during operation. Path is set via configuration option.

6	## Summary
7	
8	Defines sentence structure, word choice, and formatting rules that all oauthsvc documentation pages must follow. This guide ensures consistency across all documentation in the docs-style folder and related documentation trees. All contributors must apply these rules before pages enter the review phase.
9	
10	## Coverage and Application
11	
12	These rules apply to every page written for the oauthsvc documentation set, regardless of format (Markdown, reStructuredText, or YAML). Pages in the following locations must follow these guidelines:
13	
14	- docs-style/ folder and all subfolders
15	- docs/guides/ (operational documentation)
16	- docs/reference/ (API and database schema reference)
17	- docs/tutorials/ (step-by-step walkthroughs)
18	- scripts/documentation/ (generated doc scripts)
19	
20	The only exception is generated documentation that comes from tools like Sphinx or other builders; those use their own formatting rules. However, any manually written content in those folders must comply with this guide.
21	
22	## Sentence Structure and Grammar
23	
24	### Paragraph Length and Flow
25	
26	Keep paragraphs short. Three to four sentences is the target; anything longer than six sentences should be split. Readers scan oauthsvc documentation quickly, often while configuring the service in a nearby terminal.
27	
28	Use the active voice unless passive voice is necessary for clarity. Say "The database file stores the state" rather than "The state is stored by the database file." Passive voice is acceptable when the actor is unknown or irrelevant:
29	
30	- "Configuration values are read from the config file at startup."
31	- "SQLite is used for local persistence."
32	
33	Begin sentences with the subject whenever possible. Starting a sentence with a dependent clause slows comprehension:
34	
35	**Preferred:** "The loopback HTTP service listens on port 8080 by default. You can override this in the configuration."
36	
37	**Less preferred:** "By default, the loopback HTTP service listens on port 8080, which you can override in the configuration."
38	
39	Avoid stringing together more than two clauses with conjunctions. If you find yourself writing "and" or "or" three times in one sentence, restructure it into separate sentences or a list. Use semicolons sparingly; they are acceptable but work well for breaking up shorter sentences.
40	
41	### Headings and Capitalization
42	
43	Section headings use title case. Each major word is capitalized, including the first word:
44	
45	- Getting Started with the Command Line
46	- Understanding the SQLite Database Schema
47	- Configuring User Identity Behavior
48	- Working with the Local Service
49	
50	Subsection headings (level 3 and below) also use title case:
51	
52	- Running the Service Locally
53	- Reading Configuration from Files
54	- Troubleshooting Connection Errors
55	
56	Body text uses standard sentence capitalization. Only proper nouns and the first word are capitalized. Team names are capitalized as listed in the org chart: Developer Experience, Platform Tools, Docs Guild.
57	
58	Do NOT use ALL CAPS for emphasis. Use **bold** for key terms or UI labels instead. Italics (*word*) may be used for introducing new terms on their first occurrence.
59	
60	### Sentence Types and Variety
61	
62	Use imperative sentences when providing instructions: "Set the configuration file path before starting the service." This is clearer than "The configuration file path should be set before starting the service."
63	
64	Use indicative sentences for explanations and descriptions: "The loopback service binds to localhost by design." Use interrogative sentences sparingly, only when posing genuine questions to the reader that the next section answers.
65	
66	Mix sentence types naturally within paragraphs. A section might open with an imperative ("Configure the service using the steps below"), transition to a description ("The service reads configuration at startup"), and end with another imperative ("Verify your changes by checking the log output").
67	
68	## Word Choice and Vocabulary
69	
70	### Common Terms in oauthsvc Documentation
71	
72	These terms have specific, consistent meanings in our documentation:
73	
74	- **the service:** refers to the HTTP loopback server component
75	- **the package:** refers to the oauthsvc Python package as a whole
76	- **the database file:** refers to the SQLite database containing stored state
77	- **configuration:** settings stored in files or passed as arguments (not "config" in formal prose, though "config" is acceptable in code examples and file names)
78	- **the command line:** the command-line interface to the package
79	- **state:** the current configuration, data, and status of the service and database
80	
81	Do not use "the application," "the tool," "the system," or "the program" to refer to these components. Use the precise term defined above. This consistency helps readers quickly recognize what is being discussed.
82	
83	### Word Choices to Avoid
84	
85	Avoid jargon-heavy language. If you must use specialized terminology, define it in the glossary section of your page or in the shared glossary (glossary.md). Do not assume readers understand service architecture, HTTP semantics, SQLite internals, or network programming.
86	
87	- Instead of "orchestrate," say "manage" or "coordinate"
88	- Instead of "leverage," say "use" or "take advantage of"
89	- Instead of "granular," say "fine-grained" or just describe the capability
90	- Instead of "surface," say "expose" or "show"
91	- Instead of "instantiate," say "create" or "start"
92	
93	Do not use contractions in formal documentation. Write "do not" instead of "don't," "it is" instead of "it's," and "cannot" instead of "can't." Contractions are informal and inconsistent with the tone of reference documentation.
94	
95	Use "we" when referring to the team or our documentation: "We recommend checking the logs." Avoid "the team" or "the docs team" when "we" is clearer. However, in procedures and examples, "you" is appropriate: "You can configure the service by editing your configuration file."
96	
97	Prefer "the user" or "a team member" to singular "they" when the antecedent might be ambiguous:
98	
99	**Acceptable:** "Team members can configure the service by editing their configuration file."
100	
101	**Better:** "A team member can configure the service by editing the configuration file."
102	
103	### Measurements and Quantities
104	
105	Always include units when discussing time or size:
106	
107	- "Configure a timeout of 30 seconds" (not just "30")
108	- "The SQLite database file is approximately 2 megabytes" (not just "2")
109	- "The service was running for 4 hours before the restart"
110	
111	Use words for small numbers (one through nine) and numerals for ten and above, unless the number appears in code examples or structured data where exact formatting matters. Dates always use numerals: "2026-04-03" (ISO format in documentation).
112	
113	Use "approximately," "roughly," or "around" for estimates; avoid "about" in technical writing, as it can create ambiguity.
114	
115	## Formatting and Lists
116	
117	### Bullet Lists vs. Numbered Lists
118	
119	Use unordered (bullet) lists for items with no implied sequence:
120	
121	- Items that are equally important
122	- Options the user may choose in any order
123	- Features of a system or component
124	- Related concepts that do not depend on sequence
125	
126	Use ordered (numbered) lists for procedures with steps that must be followed in order:
127	
128	1. Start the service using the command line
129	2. Open your configuration file in an editor
130	3. Update the necessary settings
131	4. Restart the service to load the new configuration
132	
133	If your procedure involves waiting for confirmation or conditional steps (like "If you see error X, do Y"), consider a more structured format like a table or a step-by-step walkthrough with prose explanations.
134	
135	Mixed lists are appropriate in complex explanations. Here is an example from a real configuration page:
136	
137	There are three ways to provide configuration values:
138	
139	1. **Configuration file at the standard location**
140	   - Automatically loaded on startup
141	   - Can be edited at any time
142	   - Requires a service restart to take effect
143	
144	2. **Command-line arguments during startup**
145	   - Overrides file-based configuration values
146	   - Does not persist between restarts
147	   - Useful for temporary changes or verification
148	
149	3. **Environment variables** (supported in version 2.1 and later)
150	   - Useful for containerized deployments
151	   - Merged with file-based and command-line configuration
152	   - See glossary-upkeep.md for precedence rules
153	
154	### Code and Configuration Snippets
155	
156	Inline code uses backticks: `configuration_file`, `service.db`, `port_number`.
157	
158	Blocks of commands, configuration, or output use triple backticks with a language tag. For shell commands, use `bash` or `shell`:
159	
160	
161	Configuration file snippets use the format of the configuration language (YAML, INI, JSON, etc.):
162	
163	```yaml
164	service:
165	  host: 127.0.0.1
166	  port: 8080
167	  startup_timeout: 10
168	
169	database:
170	  file_path: ./service.db
171	  connection_timeout: 5
172	  enable_wal: true
173	```
174	
175	Shell output and examples may include prompts (`$` for user shell, `#` for root, `sqlite>` for interactive tools) to clarify where the command runs. Do not include prompts in pure configuration blocks.
176	
177	Configuration examples should be realistic. Use actual field names and plausible values. If the example is simplified for illustration, note that with a comment: `# Simplified example; see template-reference.rst for full schema`.
178	
179	### Tables
180	
181	Tables are useful for comparing options, showing versions, listing related files, or displaying structured information. Use Markdown table syntax with pipes and dashes:
182	
183	```
184	| Component | Purpose | File |
185	|-----------|---------|------|
186	| Configuration | Service settings | config.yaml |
187	| Log file | Service activity | ./logs/service.log |
188	```
189	
190	Align columns for readability. Avoid tables with more than five columns; break the information into multiple tables or prose instead.

192	## Headers and Organization

207	**Version:** 3.2
208	**Owner:** Docs Guild (Priya Chandran)

210	```

214	The main content should be organized into sections. Start with broad concepts and move toward specific procedures. Use consistent heading levels:
215

217	- Level 3 (`###`) for subsections

224	
225	**Section owner:** Developer Experience (Sam Whitfield)

230	## Terminology and Glossary
231	
232	All pages must include a dedicated terminology section that defines key terms used in the page content. A shared glossary exists in glossary.md, but each page may also include terms specific to its topic. Pages should cross-reference the shared glossary when appropriate: "See the oauthsvc Glossary for definitions of other terms."
233	
234	The terminology section should define at least eight terms relevant to the page content. Format as a definition list (bold term, followed by definition):
235	
236	**Configuration file:** A file that stores the settings used by the service at startup. Configuration files are read once when the service starts and are not re-read unless the service restarts.
237	
238	**Loopback interface:** The localhost location (127.0.0.1 for IPv4 or ::1 for IPv6) used for communication between processes on the same machine. All HTTP requests to this service use the loopback interface.
239	
240	**SQLite database:** A file-based relational database included in Python's standard library. The service uses SQLite for persisting state between restarts.
241	
242	**Standard library:** The set of modules and utilities included with Python without requiring additional installation. The oauthsvc package uses only standard-library modules to minimize dependencies.
243	
244	**Command-line interface (CLI):** The method of interacting with the package by running commands in a shell or terminal. The package provides a CLI for starting the service, stopping it, and managing configuration.
245	
246	**HTTP service:** A network service that communicates using HTTP over the network. The package includes a small HTTP service that listens on localhost for incoming requests.
247	
248	**State:** The current configuration, data, and status of the service and database at any given moment. State is persisted to the SQLite database file between restarts.
249	
250	**Startup:** The process of beginning service execution. At startup, the service loads configuration, initializes the database connection, and begins listening for requests.
251	
252	## Documentation Files and Folders
253	
254	This page and its sibling pages reference the following files and folders. Each entry shows the file path, its function in the documentation set, and the team that maintains it.

272	| docs/ | Main documentation folder containing guides, references, and tutorials | Multiple teams |
273	| docs/guides/ | Operational guides and how-to documentation | Docs Guild |
274	| docs/reference/ | API reference and database schema documentation | Developer Experience |
275	| scripts/documentation/ | Scripts that generate or build documentation | Platform Tools |

279	Documentation contributors and build processes use the following tools. The versions listed reflect the current standard; older versions may work but are not officially supported.

284	| Markdown | commonmark 0.9 | Primary format for documentation pages and guides |

286	| YAML | 1.2 | Format for metadata files and configuration documentation examples |

292	The build process uses a custom Makefile in the docs/ folder. The most common command is `make docs`, which builds all documentation into the build/ folder. Use `make clean` before rebuilding to ensure no stale files remain from previous builds.
293	
294	## Review and Publishing Workflow
295	
296	Pages follow a consistent workflow from creation through publication. This workflow ensures quality and consistency across all documentation.
297	
298	**Draft creation:** New pages or major updates are created in feature branches following this naming convention: `docs/page-name` or `docs/update-page-name`. This makes it easy to find documentation work in Git logs.
299	
300	**Self-review:** Before submitting for peer review, the author must review the page against this style guide and the page review checklist (review-checklist.txt). This self-review catches obvious formatting issues and missing sections.
301	
302	**Peer review:** One or more reviewers from relevant teams review the page for accuracy, consistency, and adherence to this guide. The review lead is named in review-cadence.md.

304	**Changes:** The author responds to review feedback, makes requested changes, and may request re-review of specific sections if substantial changes were made.

306	**Clearance:** The review lead confirms the page is ready for publication after verifying that all feedback has been resolved.

308	**Publication:** The page is merged to the main branch and published to the live documentation site using the publishing workflow (see publishing-workflow.md).
309	
310	Pages enter the review phase when they are substantively complete. Do not submit pages for review if sections are missing, marked as "to be filled in," or are unfinished. Incomplete sections delay review cycles unnecessarily and waste reviewer time.
311	
312	The review cadence (frequency and timeline) is documented in review-cadence.md. Standard review takes five to seven business days from submission through completion. Urgent documentation may use an expedited process.

327	- [ ] Headings use consistent capitalization (title case for H2 and H3)
328	- [ ] No prohibited words appear (see glossary-upkeep.md for the list)
329	- [ ] Cross-references to sibling pages use correct titles and file names
330	- [ ] Code snippets have appropriate syntax highlighting tags
331	- [ ] Tables are readable and have no more than five columns
332	
333	A more comprehensive review checklist suitable for copy-paste into pull request templates is available in review-checklist.txt.

335	## Related Pages
