Title: Profiling Tools Setup
Version: 1.0
Owner: Core Services (Devon Ruiz)
Last Updated: 2024-04-16

================================================================================
OVERVIEW
================================================================================

This page documents the standard library profiling tools and procedures used to measure performance of the oauthsvc package. It covers setup steps for a profiling workstation, profiling execution methodology, SQLite configuration for performance work, and analysis techniques for timing data, memory allocation, loopback latency, and startup metrics.

The package uses only Python's standard library; all profiling relies on built-in modules such as cProfile, profile, timeit, tracemalloc, and pstats. This page assumes you are running Windows 10 Pro or later with Python 3.9 or higher installed in your user directory.

For profiling sessions and findings, refer to profiling-sessions-2024.md and profiling-sessions-2025.md. For detailed configuration and baseline comparisons, see the related pages section at the end of this document. For performance figures and prior data, see perf-baselines.yaml (version 2.6, updated 2026-06-15).


================================================================================
STANDARD LIBRARY PROFILING TOOLS
================================================================================
Section Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)

The package supports deterministic profiling via the following standard library modules. Each has specific use cases and trade-offs.

cProfile Module
   The built-in deterministic profiler. Measures function call counts and cumulative execution time with minimal overhead (approximately 3–5% compared to unprofiled runs). Suitable for identifying hot paths and function-level bottlenecks. Output is written to a binary .prof file that must be analyzed with pstats.

   Invocation on the command line:

       python -m cProfile -o output.prof [package startup]

   The package also accepts a --profile flag that internally uses cProfile and writes output to profiling_output.prof in the current working directory.

profile Module
   Pure-Python implementation of the cProfile interface. Adds higher overhead (approximately 8–12% slowdown) but provides identical API. Useful for cross-platform consistency checks. Not recommended for production-like profiling; use cProfile instead.

   Invocation:

       python -m profile -o output.prof [package startup]

timeit Module
   High-precision timing for isolated code fragments. Not suitable for full service profiling but useful for measuring specific operations (e.g., handler method overhead, database query time). Requires manually extracting code snippets. Runs code repeatedly and reports mean execution time.

   Example: time 1000 iterations of a handler method (pseudocode):

       python -m timeit -n 1000 "code_snippet_here"

   Output is in microseconds; useful for sub-millisecond precision comparisons.

tracemalloc Module
   Tracks Python heap memory allocation and reports which code allocated each byte. Activated by setting the PYTHONTRACEMALLOC environment variable to 1 before launching the service. Output goes to .mtrack files at shutdown. Provides detailed memory samples but with significant overhead (15–25% slowdown).

   Do not use tracemalloc in production. Use it only during dedicated profiling sessions in the baselines\ folder.

sys.setprofile and sys.settrace
   Low-level instrumentation hooks. Not used directly in this workflow; both cProfile and tracemalloc are built on these hooks. Mentioned for completeness.

Tool Selection Notes
   Always profile the same scenario twice: once with profiling disabled (baseline) and once with profiling enabled (measurement). Profiling overhead is real and measurable. Comparisons between profiled and unprofiled runs are unreliable. When investigating performance regressions, use the unprofiled baseline.

   For full service profiling, use cProfile. For memory regression hunting, use tracemalloc. For timing-sensitive micro-performance analysis, use timeit on extracted code. For loopback request timing, use the Measure-Command shell utility (see Loopback Response Times section).


================================================================================
WORKSTATION SETUP AND CONFIGURATION
================================================================================
Section Owner: Runtime Team (Owen Baptiste)

Before conducting profiling sessions, configure your workstation as follows.

Python Environment
   Install Python 3.11.x (version 3.11.2 or later recommended; older versions exhibit different memory allocation patterns and heap fragmentation behavior). Virtual environment isolation is not required but recommended to avoid interference from system-installed packages.

   Verify installation:

       python --version
       python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"

   If multiple Python versions are installed, ensure the correct one is first in your PATH.

SQLite Command-Line Tool
   Download and extract the sqlite3 CLI tool (version 3.45.0 or later; must match or exceed the version bundled with Python to avoid compatibility issues). Add the directory containing sqlite3.exe to your PATH.

   Verify:

       sqlite3 --version

   The CLI is essential for inspecting and modifying the database file during profiling. Required for PRAGMA queries and configuration.

Working Directory Structure
   Create a dedicated folder for profiling work:

       C:\Users\YourUsername\oauthsvc-profiling\
           runs\
           baselines\
           scripts\
           db-samples\
           logs\

   The runs\ subfolder holds profiling output (.prof, .mtrack, .log, .csv files). Organize by date: runs\2024-04-16\, runs\2024-04-17\. The baselines\ folder stores reference profiling results for comparison. Place ad-hoc measurement scripts in scripts\. The db-samples\ folder holds clean database file copies for repeatable use cases. The logs\ folder captures system resource information during runs.

Environment Variables
   Set these variables before each profiling session:

       set PYTHONHASHSEED=0
       set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
       set PYTHONTRACEMALLOC=1

   - PYTHONHASHSEED=0 ensures reproducible hash order across runs (Python randomizes hash seed by default for robustness).
   - PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 prevents .pyc file generation, which can contaminate timing measurements and fill the working directory.
   - PYTHONTRACEMALLOC=1 enables memory tracking in tracemalloc; required before launch if you plan to capture memory samples.

   On PowerShell, use $env:VARIABLE = "value" instead of set.

   Verify variables are set:

       echo %PYTHONHASHSEED%
       echo %PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE%
       echo %PYTHONTRACEMALLOC%

System Resource Isolation
   Close unnecessary applications. Disable screensaver, automatic Windows updates, and antivirus real-time scanning during the profiling window (enable afterward). Disable network connectivity to reduce timing variance.

   Run profiling in a dedicated user session if possible; do not run other work concurrently.

   Take baseline measurements after a fresh system reboot, before any interactive shell work or browser use. Reboot between profiling different configurations to flush OS cache and clear memory.


================================================================================
SQLITE PERFORMANCE CONFIGURATION
================================================================================

The database file uses SQLite for state storage. Two critical settings affect profiling results and reflect production configuration: journal mode and page cache size.

Journal Mode
   Journal mode determines how SQLite handles writes and restart. Three modes are relevant for profiling:

   Transient Journal (default)
       SQLite writes a journal file for each transaction, then removes it on commit. Slowest mode but safest for restart. Suitable for single-use measurements.

   WAL (Write-Ahead Logging)
       Writes to a separate log file (.db-wal). Faster for concurrent access; adds complexity with additional files. Used in production. Database file creation selects WAL mode by default.

   TRUNCATE
       Similar to Transient Journal but truncates the journal instead of removing it. Intermediate performance; less commonly used.

   During profiling, always match the production journal mode. The database file is created in WAL mode. Verify current mode before each run:

       sqlite3 C:\path\to\database.db "PRAGMA journal_mode;"

   Output: "wal" (or the current mode).

   If you need to temporarily switch to Transient Journal mode for comparative profiling:

       Use sqlite3 command-line tool to issue a PRAGMA journal_mode directive, specifying the Transient Journal mode.

   Switching from WAL back to Transient Journal mode may take several seconds. The switch requires removing .db-wal and .db-shm auxiliary files if they exist (these are created in WAL mode):

       del database.db-wal
       del database.db-shm
       Use sqlite3 command-line tool to issue a PRAGMA journal_mode directive, specifying the Transient Journal mode.

   Document the journal mode used in each profiling run; it affects I/O patterns and response times by 10–30%.

Page Cache Size
   The page cache holds recently accessed database pages in memory. Larger cache improves performance for repeated queries but uses more RAM. Default cache is 2000 pages (typically 8–16 MB per page).

   During profiling, observe how response times and memory use change with cache size. Common measurement values:

       sqlite3 C:\path\to\database.db "PRAGMA cache_size=1000;"   # 1000 pages (smallest safe)
       sqlite3 C:\path\to\database.db "PRAGMA cache_size=5000;"   # 5000 pages (recommended production)
       sqlite3 C:\path\to\database.db "PRAGMA cache_size=20000;"  # 20000 pages (high-memory)

   Verify current setting:

       sqlite3 C:\path\to\database.db "PRAGMA cache_size;"

   Output shows a negative number (e.g., "-5000"), which indicates cache size in pages. Larger cache reduces query time but increases initial load time; see page cache sizing.md.

   For repeatable profiling, fix the cache size and record it. A mismatch between profiling settings and production causes misleading comparisons.


================================================================================
PROFILING SESSION WORKFLOW
================================================================================

A profiling session consists of three phases: setup, execution, and analysis.

Setup Phase
   1. Prepare a clean database file. Use a known-good sample from baselines\ folder (copy database.db to working directory) or initialize a fresh one.

   2. Verify SQLite settings: journal mode and cache size. Record the values in a text file named settings.txt in the run folder.

   3. Set environment variables (PYTHONHASHSEED, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE, PYTHONTRACEMALLOC).

   4. Document baseline system state:
      - Free physical memory (use Task Manager)
      - Available disk space
      - CPU model and core count
      - Background processes (Task Manager, Processes tab)
      - System temperature (optional, but useful for thermal analysis)

   5. Optionally, disable CPU frequency scaling in BIOS or use Windows power settings to set performance mode (avoid power-saving modes).

   6. Close all unrelated applications. Empty the Recycle Bin to avoid disk I/O surprises.

Execution Phase
   1. Launch the package with profiling enabled. For cProfile:

       python -m cProfile -o run_output.prof [startup flags]

   2. Allow the service to run for the planned duration. For steady-state profiling of loopback requests, 60 seconds is typical. For startup profiling, capture the timestamp from launch to ready state (usually 2–5 seconds).

   3. Record timestamps of significant events in a text file named timeline.txt:
      - Service launch start
      - Service ready (accepts requests)
      - First request sent (if applicable)
      - 50th request, 100th request (if measuring in series)
      - Service shutdown initiated
      - Service shutdown complete

   4. Concurrently capture system resource usage using Windows perfmon or Task Manager:
      - Peak memory (Resident Set Size in Task Manager Details tab)
      - Peak CPU usage (%)
      - Disk I/O (bytes read/written, if available)

   5. Send loopback requests as needed. Use a PowerShell loop or dedicated script (see scripts/measure-loopback.ps1).

   6. Shut down the service cleanly (Ctrl+C in the terminal). Record the shutdown timestamp.

   7. Verify output files exist: run_output.prof, any .mtrack files, database.db.

Analysis Phase
   1. Convert .prof output to human-readable form using pstats:

       python -m pstats run_output.prof

   2. In the pstats interactive shell, run commands to analyze the profile:

       > sort cumulative
       > stats 20

   This sorts by cumulative time spent in each function and prints the top 20. Cumulative time includes time in called functions.

   Other useful sorts: tottime (time in function only, excluding calls), callcount (number of calls). Enter "help" for full command list.

   3. Export results to a text file:

       python -c "import pstats; p = pstats.Stats('run_output.prof'); p.sort_stats('cumulative'); p.print_stats(30)" > analysis_cumulative.txt

   4. Repeat for other sort orders:

       python -c "import pstats; p = pstats.Stats('run_output.prof'); p.sort_stats('tottime'); p.print_stats(30)" > analysis_tottime.txt

   5. Compare results to baselines using perf-baselines.yaml. Look for:
      - New functions in top 20 (potential regression)
      - Increased cumulative time in existing functions
      - Increased call count (efficiency regression)
      - Increased total time in utility functions

   6. Store results: copy run_output.prof, analysis_*.txt, settings.txt, and timeline.txt to runs\YYYY-MM-DD\ folder.


================================================================================
MEMORY PROFILING AND BASELINE MEASUREMENT
================================================================================
Section Owner: Runtime Team (Owen Baptiste)

Memory use is measured in two ways: tracemalloc samples and peak Resident Set Size (RSS).

tracemalloc Samples
   tracemalloc is activated by setting PYTHONTRACEMALLOC=1 before launch. During execution, the package generates memory samples and writes them to .mtrack files at shutdown.

   To analyze a .mtrack file:

       Load a .mtrack trace file using tracemalloc, retrieve the current memory state, and display the 15 largest allocations sorted by source code line number.

   This lists the 15 code locations that allocated the most memory. Each line shows filename, line number, allocation size, and count.

   tracemalloc adds 15–25% overhead; use only during dedicated profiling sessions, never in production.

   Interpretation: large allocations near initialization indicate startup overhead. Allocations inside request handlers indicate per-request memory use. Stable allocations after shutdown may indicate potential unfreed memory, though Python's garbage collector usually prevents such issues.

Peak Resident Set Size
   Windows Task Manager reports memory use in the Details tab. Record peak RSS (shown as "Memory" column) during the profiling run.

   Alternatively, use Measure-Command in PowerShell to capture elapsed time and memory via OS statistics:

       Use PowerShell's Measure-Command utility to measure the service startup time in seconds and peak working set memory.

   Note: PowerShell's Measure-Command does not directly report peak memory; use Task Manager instead.

Baseline Memory Use
   Baseline memory figures (service startup, before any requests) are documented in memory-use-baseline.md (version 1.1, Owen Baptiste, updated 2024-06-09). Typical peak RSS ranges from 15 MB to 35 MB, depending on Python version and initialization flags.

   Recent profiling sessions (2025) show RSS peaks of 22–28 MB under normal load, with tracemalloc enabled, on Windows 10 Pro.

   Compare new runs against baselines in the following order:
   1. Same machine, same configuration (expect ±5% variance)
   2. Different machine, same OS version (expect ±10–15% variance)
   3. Different OS version (expect ±20% or more variance)


================================================================================
LOOPBACK RESPONSE TIME MEASUREMENT
================================================================================

The service listens on a loopback interface (127.0.0.1 by default). Profiling response times requires sending requests to the running service and measuring round-trip latency.

Basic Timing with Measure-Command
   Use PowerShell's Measure-Command to time a single request:

       Measure-Command { Invoke-WebRequest http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthcheck | Out-Null }

   Output displays elapsed time in milliseconds (e.g., "220 ms"). This includes network stack overhead, HTTP parsing, and service processing.

Repeated Request Series
   For steady-state profiling, send 100 requests and measure total elapsed time:

       $sw = [Diagnostics.Stopwatch]::StartNew()
       for ($i = 1; $i -le 100; $i++) {
           Invoke-WebRequest http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthcheck | Out-Null
       }
       $sw.Stop()
       Write-Host "Total: $($sw.ElapsedMilliseconds) ms, Average: $($sw.ElapsedMilliseconds / 100) ms per request"

   Divide total time by count to get average response time. First request is typically 2–5 ms slower due to connection setup; subsequent requests average lower.

   Baseline: single request ~8–12 ms; series average ~4–6 ms per request after warm-up (see loopback-response-times.md, version v2.0.1).

Scripted Measurement
   A dedicated script scripts/measure-loopback.ps1 automates request series timing and logs results:

       .\measure-loopback.ps1 -requests 100 -output run_output.csv

   The script outputs a CSV file with timestamp, request number, and response time for each request. Process the CSV to generate histograms or identify outliers.

Loopback Overhead Notes
   Loopback requests include HTTP stack overhead even though no real network traversal occurs. Measured latency is real but includes:
   - TCP/IP stack processing (1–2 ms)
   - HTTP parsing (< 1 ms)
   - Service request handling (3–8 ms typical)
   - HTTP response generation (< 1 ms)
   - Network transmission (negligible on loopback)

   Total measured time is representative of production latency but will be lower than real network latency (which adds 5–50+ ms depending on geography and network conditions).


================================================================================
STARTUP TIME PROFILING
================================================================================

Startup time is the elapsed wall-clock time from service launch to ready state (when the service is bound to the loopback port and accepts requests). Measure it using Measure-Command:

    Use PowerShell's Measure-Command utility to measure the initialization time in seconds.

   Output is in seconds with millisecond precision (e.g., "2.345").

   On a typical workstation (Windows 10 Pro, SSD, Python 3.11), startup completes in 1.5 to 3 seconds. Baselines are documented in startup-time-notes.md (version 1.9, Casey Lindgren, updated 2026-01-27).

Startup Phases
   Startup consists of:
   - Python interpreter initialization (500–800 ms)
   - Package import and module loading (200–500 ms)
   - Database file initialization: table creation if new, WAL setup (300–800 ms)
   - Port binding and listener start (100–200 ms)

   Profiling startup is difficult because cProfile overhead is high (~30% for short runs). Instead, use wall-clock time measurement and repeat 5 times, discarding the fastest and slowest results (to remove outliers), then average the middle 3. This mitigates garbage collection variance.

Cold Start vs Warm Start
   Cold start: Service has not run in the past 60 seconds. Database file pages are swapped out or not cached by the OS buffer cache.

   Warm start: Service runs immediately after a previous run. Database file is in OS cache and accessed much faster.

   Cold start typically takes 2–4 seconds; warm start takes 1–2 seconds (50% improvement from caching). Always measure both and record results separately.

   See cold-start-vs-warm-start.rst (version v1.0.2, Casey Lindgren, updated 2025-08-03) for detailed timing figures comparing cold and warm scenarios.


================================================================================
TERMINOLOGY
================================================================================

Deterministic Profiler
   A profiler that measures actual function call counts and execution time by instrumenting the Python interpreter. cProfile and profile are deterministic. Opposite of statistical profiler.

Statistical Profiler
   A profiler that samples the call stack at regular intervals (e.g., every 10 ms) to estimate execution time. Lower overhead than deterministic profilers but less precise. Not used in this workflow.

Cumulative Time
   Total time spent executing a function, including time spent in all functions it calls. Used to identify high-impact functions in the overall program flow.

Total Time (Self Time)
   Time spent executing a function's own code, excluding time in called functions. Used to identify hot spots where computation is occurring.

Call Stack
   The sequence of function calls leading to the current execution point. Profilers unwind the call stack to determine which caller invoked each function and build hierarchical timing information.

pstats Module
   Python Statistics module for analyzing cProfile output. Reads binary .prof files, sorts results by various metrics, and formats output for human reading.

Journal Mode
   The SQLite write-ahead logging strategy. Determines whether SQLite uses a temporary journal file (Transient Journal, TRUNCATE) or a persistent log file (WAL) for transaction restart.

Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
   SQLite's journal mode that writes transactions to a separate log file before writing to the main database file. Improves concurrency and performance; used in production by the package.

Page Cache (Buffer Cache)
   SQLite's in-memory buffer of database pages. Larger cache improves performance of repeated queries but increases memory use. Measured in number of pages (typically 4 KB each).

Loopback Interface
   Virtual network interface (127.0.0.1) that directs packets back to the same machine. Used to measure network stack overhead in isolation from real network latency.

Wall-Clock Time (Elapsed Time)
   Actual time measured by the system clock from start to finish. Includes time spent in other processes and system calls. Differs from CPU time (which excludes I/O wait).

tracemalloc
   Python standard library module for tracking heap memory allocations. Reports which code allocated each byte. Used during profiling only (adds significant overhead).

Resident Set Size (RSS)
   Amount of physical RAM used by a process. Includes all heap memory, stack, and linked libraries. Reported by Task Manager as "Memory" column.


================================================================================
REPOSITORY FILES AND PATHS
================================================================================

This section lists files, directories, and paths referenced throughout this page:

docs/performance-notes/profiling-tools-setup.txt
   This file. Primary reference for profiling workflow, tool configuration, and procedures.

docs/performance-notes/README.md
   "Performance Notes: Index" (version 1.6, Mara Olsen, updated 2026-05-11). Entry point for the performance documentation folder. Links to all other profiling pages and provides overview.

docs/performance-notes/profiling-sessions-2024.md
   Recorded profiling sessions and findings from 2024. Contains specific figures, regression analysis, and contextual information. Version 1.2, Devon Ruiz, updated 2024-11-04.

docs/performance-notes/profiling-sessions-2025.md
   Recorded profiling sessions from 2025. Recent findings, ongoing investigations, and optimization attempts. Version 1.4, bgigurtsis@gmail.com, updated 2025-09-18.

docs/performance-notes/sqlite-journal-mode-notes.md
   Detailed analysis of SQLite journal modes and their performance implications. Configuration examples and recommendations. Version v1.3.0, Priya Nandakumar, updated 2024-07-22.

docs/performance-notes/sqlite-page-cache-sizing.md
   Page cache tuning guide with empirical data on how cache size affects query performance and memory use. Recommended settings. Version 2.1, Priya Nandakumar, updated 2025-02-14.

docs/performance-notes/loopback-response-times.md
   Baseline loopback response time figures. Single-request latency, series averages, and percentile measurements. Version v2.0.1, Owen Baptiste, updated 2025-05-30.

docs/performance-notes/memory-use-baseline.md
   Baseline memory use figures at service startup and under load. Peak RSS by Python version. Version 1.1, Owen Baptiste, updated 2024-06-09.

docs/performance-notes/startup-time-notes.md
   Startup time baseline figures and analysis by phase (interpreter, imports, database, binding). Version 1.9, Casey Lindgren, updated 2026-01-27.

docs/performance-notes/cold-start-vs-warm-start.rst
   Detailed comparison of cold start (service not run recently, OS cache empty) versus warm start (OS cache populated). Timing data and analysis. Version v1.0.2, Casey Lindgren, updated 2025-08-03.

docs/performance-notes/gc-tuning-notes.md
   Python garbage collector tuning for performance. Notes on collection frequency, generational settings. Version 2.4, Owen Baptiste, updated 2026-03-19.

docs/performance-notes/connection-pooling-notes.md
   SQLite database connection pooling and reuse. Connection timeout settings and connection overhead. Version v1.5.2, Priya Nandakumar, updated 2025-12-01.

docs/performance-notes/flamegraph-capture-steps.rst
   Steps to capture and visualize flame graphs from cProfile output. Requires external tools. Version 1.3, Mara Olsen, updated 2024-09-27.

docs/performance-notes/perf-baselines.yaml
   Centralized repository of baseline performance figures. Updated quarterly by Platform Tools. Canonical source for comparison values. Version 2.6, Mara Olsen, updated 2026-06-15.

scripts/measure-loopback.ps1
   PowerShell script for automated loopback response time measurement. Sends N requests and logs timing data. Outputs CSV with per-request times. Run with service already started.

scripts/capture-memory-sample.py
   Python utility to parse tracemalloc .mtrack output and export human-readable memory reports. Requires PYTHONTRACEMALLOC=1 to have been set during profiled run.

C:\Users\YourUsername\oauthsvc-profiling\
   Root working directory for profiling sessions (create as needed).

C:\Users\YourUsername\oauthsvc-profiling\runs\
   Profiling output files (.prof, .mtrack, .csv, .log, .txt files). Organize by date: runs\2024-04-16\, runs\2024-04-17\, etc. One run per subdirectory.

C:\Users\YourUsername\oauthsvc-profiling\baselines\
   Reference profiling results from known-good configurations. Used for regression comparison. Should mirror perf-baselines.yaml.

C:\Users\YourUsername\oauthsvc-profiling\scripts\
   Ad-hoc measurement scripts and utilities. Reusable across multiple profiling sessions.

C:\Users\YourUsername\service-profiling\db-samples\
   Clean database file copies for repeatable use cases. Named by scenario: db-samples\empty.db, db-samples\10k-records.db, etc.

C:\Users\YourUsername\oauthsvc-profiling\logs\
   System resource logs (memory, CPU, disk I/O) captured during profiling runs.


================================================================================
TOOLS AND VERSIONS
================================================================================

Tool / Library              Version         Purpose
-----------                 -------         ----
Python                      3.11.2+         Interpreter; cProfile, profile, timeit, tracemalloc included
sqlite3 CLI                 3.45.0+         Database inspection, PRAGMA management
Windows 10 Pro              19045           Operating system (minimum supported)
PowerShell                  7.0+            Shell for time measurement, loopback verification, automation
pstats                      Standard lib    Profiling data analysis (bundled with Python)
Task Manager                Built-in        System resource monitoring (memory, CPU, disk I/O)
Measure-Command             PowerShell      Wall-clock time measurement

Notes:
   - Python 3.10.x and older versions are not supported due to different memory allocation behavior and garbage collection tuning incompatibility.
   - sqlite3 CLI version must match or exceed the version bundled with Python to avoid compatibility issues with database files and PRAGMA settings.
   - pstats is included with Python; no separate installation required.
   - Windows perfmon can supplement Task Manager for detailed resource logging over long profiling sessions.


================================================================================
RELATED PAGES
================================================================================

- Performance Notes: Index (README.md, version 1.6, Mara Olsen, updated 2026-05-11)

- Flame Graph Capture Steps (version 1.3, Mara Olsen, updated 2024-09-27)
- Performance Baseline Figures (version 2.6, Mara Olsen, updated 2026-06-15)


================================================================================
CHANGELOG
================================================================================

   Added reference to updated gc-tuning-notes.md version 2.4. Clarified that PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE prevents .pyc file generation, which would contaminate timing measurements. Expanded memory profiling section with tracemalloc interpretation guidance.

   Added procedure for switching SQLite journal mode from WAL to Transient Journal mode and cleanup of .db-wal, .db-shm files. Fixed pstats example command to show "stats 20" instead of "stats 10" for clarity. Corrected typo in PowerShell environment variable syntax.

1	# Journal Mode Notes for the Database File
2	
3	| Field | Value |
4	|-------|-------|
5	| **Title** | Journal Mode Notes for the Database File |
6	| **Version** | v1.3.0 |
7	| **Owner** | Infra Reliability (Priya Nandakumar) |
8	| **Last Updated** | 2024-07-22 |
9	
10	## Summary
11	
12	This page describes the write-ahead log setting used for the database file and how it changed observed write timing on loopback. The service maintains its state in a local SQLite file, and journal mode configuration significantly affects latency and concurrency behavior under typical workloads. We document the settings currently deployed, the measurements that drove their adoption, and the profiling techniques used to evaluate them.
13	
14	## Overview
15	
16	The package uses SQLite for persistent state with a single database file stored on the local filesystem. SQLite's journal mode determines how the database coordinates writes between concurrent readers and writers, affecting both latency and throughput. Early deployments used SQLite's default rollback journal mode; evaluation in 2023 and 2024 led to adoption of write-ahead log mode on production instances.
17	
18	This document records the configuration applied since mid-2024, the profiling methodology that validated the change, observed timing improvements on loopback, and guidance for future tuning work.
19	
20	## Understanding Journal Mode in SQLite
21	
22	*Section owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)*
23	
24	SQLite provides multiple mechanisms for coordinating database changes. The journal mode setting controls how the database engine handles transaction isolation and crash restoration:
25	
26	- **Rollback journal mode (legacy)**: The traditional approach. Before modifying the database file, SQLite writes changes to a separate journal file and syncs it to disk. If a crash occurs during a transaction, the journal file remains on disk and can be used to roll back incomplete changes on restart. Once the transaction commits, the journal file is removed.
27	
28	- **Write-ahead log mode (WAL)**: Changes are first written to a separate log file without modifying the main database file. The log is periodically checkpointed back into the main database file. This mode provides better concurrency because readers can access the main database while writers append to the log.
29	
30	The choice of journal mode has measurable effects on write latency, read concurrency, and disk I/O patterns. On loopback exercises with the service's typical access patterns, write-ahead log mode showed consistent improvements in P95 and P99 write latency.
31	
32	## Configuration Applied to oauthsvc
33	
34	*Section owner: Infra Reliability (Priya Nandakumar)*
35	
36	The service currently uses write-ahead log mode with the following SQLite pragmas applied at database initialization:
37	
38	```
39	PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
40	PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;
41	PRAGMA cache_size = -8000;
42	PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint = 100000;
43	```
44	
45	These settings were adopted following profiling work in April and May of 2024. The journal mode setting activates write-ahead logging. The synchronous level balances durability and performance; NORMAL mode skips syncing the main database file after consolidation operations, relying on the operating system's eventual consistency. The cache size and consolidation frequency threshold are tuned specifically for this service's workload and are documented separately in the page Cache Sizing for the Database File.
46	
47	Previous deployments used the default rollback journal mode (legacy). That configuration is no longer recommended for new instances, though some production systems may still operate with it for legacy reasons.
48	
49	## Profiling Approach and Methodology
50	
51	*Section owner: Core Services (Devon Ruiz)*
52	
53	The choice to switch journal modes was informed by profiling work conducted on loopback instances in 2024. The methodology involved:
54	
55	1. **Instrumentation**: The service's loopback HTTP interface was instrumented with timing hooks to measure request latency at multiple points: request reception, database operations, and response transmission.
56	
57	2. **Workload generation**: A load generator was run against the loopback service with varying concurrency levels (1, 4, 8, 16, and 32 concurrent connections) to simulate realistic traffic patterns.
58	
59	3. **Metric collection**: Latency histograms were collected for write operations, read operations, and mixed workloads. Both wall-clock time and CPU time were recorded.
60	
61	4. **Baseline establishment**: Trials were run with the default rollback journal mode first, establishing baseline figures for comparison.
62	
63	5. **Configuration sweep**: The same workload was repeated with write-ahead log mode enabled, adjusting consolidation frequency and cache settings between runs.
64	
65	6. **Statistical analysis**: Results were aggregated into percentile distributions (P50, P95, P99, P99.9) and compared across configurations.
66	
67	Detailed results from the 2024 profiling sessions are documented in the sibling pages Profiling Sessions, 2024 and Profiling Sessions, 2025. Raw timing data is stored in the scripts/profiling directory.
68	
69	## Measured Impact on Write Latency
70	
71	*Section owner: Runtime Team (Owen Baptiste)*
72	
73	Write-ahead log mode reduced write operation latency consistently across all observed concurrency levels. The following table summarizes representative results from profiling conducted in May 2024:
74	
75	| Concurrency | Journal Mode | P50 Latency (ms) | P95 Latency (ms) | P99 Latency (ms) |
76	|-------------|--------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
77	| 1 | Rollback (legacy) | 0.8 | 2.1 | 4.3 |
78	| 1 | WAL | 0.6 | 1.4 | 2.8 |
79	| 4 | Rollback (legacy) | 1.2 | 4.7 | 9.2 |
80	| 4 | WAL | 0.9 | 2.3 | 5.1 |
81	| 8 | Rollback (legacy) | 1.5 | 6.3 | 12.8 |
82	| 8 | WAL | 1.1 | 3.1 | 7.6 |
83	| 16 | Rollback (legacy) | 2.4 | 9.8 | 18.1 |
84	| 16 | WAL | 1.8 | 4.9 | 11.3 |
85	
86	At higher concurrency levels, the advantage became more pronounced. The P99 latency with rollback mode at 16 concurrent connections (18.1 ms) was more than 1.5× higher than with write-ahead log mode (11.3 ms). This difference reflects reduced contention on the database lock: write-ahead log mode allows readers to proceed while writers are appending to the log, whereas rollback mode must block readers until the transaction completes and the journal is removed.
87	
88	Memory use increased slightly with write-ahead log mode enabled due to the `cache_size` setting and the in-memory structures required to track log state. Observed resident memory size increased from approximately 32 MB to 38 MB on loopback instances under steady-state load. This trade-off was deemed acceptable given the latency improvements. See Memory Use Baseline for a complete accounting.
89	
90	## Log Consolidation Behavior and Management
91	
92	Log consolidation operations are the mechanism by which write-ahead log mode persists accumulated changes to the main database file. The consolidation frequency threshold controls when consolidation occurs, specified as the maximum number of pages written to the log before consolidation is triggered.
93	
94	With consolidation frequency set to 100,000 pages, consolidation operations were observed to occur roughly every 50–150 milliseconds under normal write load. Each consolidation operation required 5–15 milliseconds on the loopback instance. Users experienced these as occasional latency spikes, but the median latency remained well below baseline Rollback mode performance.
95	
96	Consolidation operations can be tuned further. Reducing the consolidation frequency threshold below 50,000 pages caused consolidation to occur more frequently, increasing overall CPU overhead. Increasing it above 150,000 allowed the log to grow larger, using additional disk space and occasionally causing multi-second consolidation operations. The current setting of 100,000 was selected as a balance point after experimentation.
97	
98	Manual data consolidation can be forced using standard SQLite tools if needed, though this is rarely necessary.
99	
100	## Log File Storage and Disk I/O
101	
102	Write-ahead log mode creates two additional files alongside the main database file:
103	
104	- The write-ahead log file (named with a `-wal` suffix)
105	- The log consolidation index file (named with a `-shm` suffix)
106	
107	On production systems, these files are stored in the same directory as the main database file on the local filesystem. The log file grows as writes occur and is truncated during consolidation operations. Disk space usage varies with write volume; typical deployments observed 10–50 MB of log and index files at any given moment.
108	
109	Disk I/O patterns changed measurably. Rollback mode produced frequent small fsync operations as journal files were written and removed. WAL mode produces larger, more predictable I/O patterns during consolidation operations. On systems with mechanical storage, this resulted in marginally lower sustained I/O overhead, though the effect was smaller than latency improvements on SSDs.
110	
111	## Startup Time Considerations
112	
113	The service's startup time is documented separately in Startup Time Notes. Journal mode choice affects startup time when the database file must be restored after an unclean shutdown. With write-ahead log mode, restoration involves replaying the log file, which may take additional time if the log is large. In practice, most deployments complete restoration in under 100 milliseconds. If restoration time becomes a concern, the log can be consolidated before shutdown using standard SQLite pragmas.
114	
115	## Compatibility and Deployment Notes
116	
117	Write-ahead log mode is supported on all platforms where the service runs and is compatible with all SQLite versions in use (3.10+). The `-wal` and `-shm` files created by the service are cleaned up automatically when the last connection closes, so manual cleanup is rarely needed.
118	
119	One caveat: network filesystems (NFS, SMB) may not properly support write-ahead log mode because the required locking and memory-mapped I/O semantics are not guaranteed. If the service is ever deployed to a network-backed storage system, this should be verified or rollback mode should be restored.
120	
121	## Interaction with Other Performance Tuning
122	
123	The choice to use write-ahead log mode and the specific parameter values interact with several other configuration settings:
124	
125	- **Page cache size**: Documented separately in Page Cache Sizing for the Database File. Larger cache sizes reduce disk I/O; the current `-8000` setting (approximately 8 MB) was tuned in conjunction with WAL mode.
126	
127	- **Connection pooling**: Documented in Connection Reuse Notes for the Database File. WAL mode allows better concurrency, reducing the performance penalty for pools with limited connections.
128	
129	- **Garbage collection tuning**: The service is written in Python. GC behavior interacts with SQLite latency because GC pauses can block database threads. See Garbage Collector Tuning Notes for details.
130	
131	Cold vs. warm startup behavior with write-ahead log mode is discussed in Cold Start Versus Warm Start Timing.
132	
133	## Recommendations for Future Work
134	
135	For new deployments, write-ahead log mode with the configuration shown in this page should be the default. If specific workloads show different characteristics (very high concurrency, infrequent writes, or memory-constrained environments), targeted profiling should be conducted to validate the choice.
136	
137	The `synchronous = NORMAL` setting is appropriate for this service because data loss on crash is acceptable (the service can be restarted and reconnected). If durability requirements change, this should be increased to FULL, with the understanding that write latency will increase.
138	
139	If disk space becomes a constraint, the consolidation frequency threshold can be reduced to limit log growth, accepting more frequent consolidation and CPU overhead. If latency consistency is a priority, consolidation operations can be scheduled explicitly during off-peak periods rather than relying on automatic triggering.
140	
141	## Terminology
142	
143	**Log Consolidation**: The operation by which write-ahead log mode writes accumulated changes from the log file back into the main database file. Consolidation occurs automatically at intervals or can be triggered manually.
144	
145	**Journal mode**: The SQLite configuration setting that determines how the database engine coordinates writes, particularly the mechanism for restoring after crashes. Common modes include Rollback (legacy) and WAL (write-ahead log).
146	
147	**Rollback journal (legacy mode)**: Traditional SQLite journal mode in which changes are recorded in a separate journal file before being written to the main database file. The journal is removed after a successful transaction commit.
148	
149	**Write-ahead log (WAL)**: An alternative journal mode in which changes are written to a log file, and the log is periodically merged into the main database file via consolidation operations. Allows better read-write concurrency than Rollback mode.
150	
151	**Synchronous level**: A SQLite pragma controlling whether the database engine issues explicit fsync operations. NORMAL skips fsync for the main database file after consolidation operations; FULL issues fsync for all operations. Lower levels increase performance but reduce durability guarantees.
152	
153	**Cache size**: A SQLite pragma controlling the size of the in-memory page cache. Larger caches reduce disk I/O at the cost of increased memory use.
154	
155	**Consolidation frequency threshold**: The maximum number of pages written to the log before consolidation is automatically triggered. Smaller thresholds cause more frequent consolidation operations; larger thresholds allow the log to grow larger.
156	
157	**Latency percentile**: A measure of request latency at a specific percentile, such as P95 (95th percentile—the latency value below which 95% of requests fall). Used to characterize tail latency.

# Journal Mode Notes for the Database File

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Title** | Journal Mode Notes for the Database File |
| **Version** | v1.3.0 |
| **Owner** | Infra Reliability (Priya Nandakumar) |
| **Last Updated** | 2024-07-22 |

## Summary

This page describes the write-ahead log setting used for the database file and how it changed observed write timing on loopback. The service maintains its state in a local SQLite file, and journal mode configuration significantly affects latency and concurrency behavior under typical workloads. We document the settings currently deployed, the measurements that drove their adoption, and the profiling techniques used to evaluate them.

## Overview

The package uses SQLite for persistent state with a single database file stored on the local filesystem. SQLite's journal mode determines how the database coordinates writes between concurrent readers and writers, affecting both latency and throughput. Early deployments used SQLite's default rollback journal mode; evaluation in 2023 and 2024 led to adoption of write-ahead log mode on production instances.

This document records the configuration applied since mid-2024, the profiling methodology that validated the change, observed timing improvements on loopback, and guidance for future tuning work.

## Understanding Journal Mode in SQLite

*Section owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)*

SQLite provides multiple mechanisms for coordinating database changes. The journal mode setting controls how the database engine handles transaction isolation and crash restoration:

- **Rollback journal mode (legacy)**: The traditional approach. Before modifying the database file, SQLite writes changes to a separate journal file and syncs it to disk. If a crash occurs during a transaction, the journal file remains on disk and can be used to roll back incomplete changes on restart. Once the transaction commits, the journal file is removed.

- **Write-ahead log mode (WAL)**: Changes are first written to a separate log file without modifying the main database file. The log is periodically checkpointed back into the main database file. This mode provides better concurrency because readers can access the main database while writers append to the log.

The choice of journal mode has measurable effects on write latency, read concurrency, and disk I/O patterns. On loopback exercises with the service's typical access patterns, write-ahead log mode showed consistent improvements in P95 and P99 write latency.

## Configuration Applied to oauthsvc

*Section owner: Infra Reliability (Priya Nandakumar)*

The service currently uses write-ahead log mode with the following SQLite pragmas applied at database initialization:

```
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;
PRAGMA cache_size = -8000;
PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint = 100000;
```

These settings were adopted following profiling work in April and May of 2024. The journal mode setting activates write-ahead logging. The synchronous level balances durability and performance; NORMAL mode skips syncing the main database file after consolidation operations, relying on the operating system's eventual consistency. The cache size and consolidation frequency threshold are tuned specifically for this service's workload and are documented separately in the page Cache Sizing for the Database File.

Previous deployments used the default rollback journal mode (legacy). That configuration is no longer recommended for new instances, though some production systems may still operate with it for legacy reasons.

## Profiling Approach and Methodology

*Section owner: Core Services (Devon Ruiz)*

The choice to switch journal modes was informed by profiling work conducted on loopback instances in 2024. The methodology involved:

1. **Instrumentation**: The service's loopback HTTP interface was instrumented with timing hooks to measure request latency at multiple points: request reception, database operations, and response transmission.

2. **Workload generation**: A load generator was run against the loopback service with varying concurrency levels (1, 4, 8, 16, and 32 concurrent connections) to simulate realistic traffic patterns.

3. **Metric collection**: Latency histograms were collected for write operations, read operations, and mixed workloads. Both wall-clock time and CPU time were recorded.

4. **Baseline establishment**: Trials were run with the default rollback journal mode first, establishing baseline figures for comparison.

5. **Configuration sweep**: The same workload was repeated with write-ahead log mode enabled, adjusting consolidation frequency and cache settings between runs.

6. **Statistical analysis**: Results were aggregated into percentile distributions (P50, P95, P99, P99.9) and compared across configurations.

Detailed results from the 2024 profiling sessions are documented in the sibling pages Profiling Sessions, 2024 and Profiling Sessions, 2025. Raw timing data is stored in the scripts/profiling directory.

## Measured Impact on Write Latency

*Section owner: Runtime Team (Owen Baptiste)*

Write-ahead log mode reduced write operation latency consistently across all observed concurrency levels. The following table summarizes representative results from profiling conducted in May 2024:

| Concurrency | Journal Mode | P50 Latency (ms) | P95 Latency (ms) | P99 Latency (ms) |
|-------------|--------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| 1 | Rollback (legacy) | 0.8 | 2.1 | 4.3 |
| 1 | WAL | 0.6 | 1.4 | 2.8 |
| 4 | Rollback (legacy) | 1.2 | 4.7 | 9.2 |
| 4 | WAL | 0.9 | 2.3 | 5.1 |
| 8 | Rollback (legacy) | 1.5 | 6.3 | 12.8 |
| 8 | WAL | 1.1 | 3.1 | 7.6 |
| 16 | Rollback (legacy) | 2.4 | 9.8 | 18.1 |
| 16 | WAL | 1.8 | 4.9 | 11.3 |

At higher concurrency levels, the advantage became more pronounced. The P99 latency with rollback mode at 16 concurrent connections (18.1 ms) was more than 1.5× higher than with write-ahead log mode (11.3 ms). This difference reflects reduced contention on the database lock: write-ahead log mode allows readers to proceed while writers are appending to the log, whereas rollback mode must block readers until the transaction completes and the journal is removed.

Memory use increased slightly with write-ahead log mode enabled due to the `cache_size` setting and the in-memory structures required to track log state. Observed resident memory size increased from approximately 32 MB to 38 MB on loopback instances under steady-state load. This trade-off was deemed acceptable given the latency improvements. See Memory Use Baseline for a complete accounting.

## Log Consolidation Behavior and Management

Log consolidation operations are the mechanism by which write-ahead log mode persists accumulated changes to the main database file. The consolidation frequency threshold controls when consolidation occurs, specified as the maximum number of pages written to the log before consolidation is triggered.

With consolidation frequency set to 100,000 pages, consolidation operations were observed to occur roughly every 50–150 milliseconds under normal write load. Each consolidation operation required 5–15 milliseconds on the loopback instance. Users experienced these as occasional latency spikes, but the median latency remained well below baseline Rollback mode performance.

Consolidation operations can be tuned further. Reducing the consolidation frequency threshold below 50,000 pages caused consolidation to occur more frequently, increasing overall CPU overhead. Increasing it above 150,000 allowed the log to grow larger, using additional disk space and occasionally causing multi-second consolidation operations. The current setting of 100,000 was selected as a balance point after experimentation.

Manual data consolidation can be forced using standard SQLite tools if needed, though this is rarely necessary.

## Log File Storage and Disk I/O

Write-ahead log mode creates two additional files alongside the main database file:

- The write-ahead log file (named with a `-wal` suffix)
- The log consolidation index file (named with a `-shm` suffix)

On production systems, these files are stored in the same directory as the main database file on the local filesystem. The log file grows as writes occur and is truncated during consolidation operations. Disk space usage varies with write volume; typical deployments observed 10–50 MB of log and index files at any given moment.

Disk I/O patterns changed measurably. Rollback mode produced frequent small fsync operations as journal files were written and removed. WAL mode produces larger, more predictable I/O patterns during consolidation operations. On systems with mechanical storage, this resulted in marginally lower sustained I/O overhead, though the effect was smaller than latency improvements on SSDs.

## Startup Time Considerations

The service's startup time is documented separately in Startup Time Notes. Journal mode choice affects startup time when the database file must be restored after an unclean shutdown. With write-ahead log mode, restoration involves replaying the log file, which may take additional time if the log is large. In practice, most deployments complete restoration in under 100 milliseconds. If restoration time becomes a concern, the log can be consolidated before shutdown using standard SQLite pragmas.

## Compatibility and Deployment Notes

Write-ahead log mode is supported on all platforms where the service runs and is compatible with all SQLite versions in use (3.10+). The `-wal` and `-shm` files created by the service are cleaned up automatically when the last connection closes, so manual cleanup is rarely needed.

One caveat: network filesystems (NFS, SMB) may not properly support write-ahead log mode because the required locking and memory-mapped I/O semantics are not guaranteed. If the service is ever deployed to a network-backed storage system, this should be verified or rollback mode should be restored.

## Interaction with Other Performance Tuning

The choice to use write-ahead log mode and the specific parameter values interact with several other configuration settings:

- **Page cache size**: Documented separately in Page Cache Sizing for the Database File. Larger cache sizes reduce disk I/O; the current `-8000` setting (approximately 8 MB) was tuned in conjunction with WAL mode.

- **Connection pooling**: Documented in Connection Reuse Notes for the Database File. WAL mode allows better concurrency, reducing the performance penalty for pools with limited connections.

- **Garbage collection tuning**: The service is written in Python. GC behavior interacts with SQLite latency because GC pauses can block database threads. See Garbage Collector Tuning Notes for details.

Cold vs. warm startup behavior with write-ahead log mode is discussed in Cold Start Versus Warm Start Timing.

## Recommendations for Future Work

For new deployments, write-ahead log mode with the configuration shown in this page should be the default. If specific workloads show different characteristics (very high concurrency, infrequent writes, or memory-constrained environments), targeted profiling should be conducted to validate the choice.

The `synchronous = NORMAL` setting is appropriate for this service because data loss on crash is acceptable (the service can be restarted and reconnected). If durability requirements change, this should be increased to FULL, with the understanding that write latency will increase.

If disk space becomes a constraint, the consolidation frequency threshold can be reduced to limit log growth, accepting more frequent consolidation and CPU overhead. If latency consistency is a priority, consolidation operations can be scheduled explicitly during off-peak periods rather than relying on automatic triggering.

## Terminology

**Log Consolidation**: The operation by which write-ahead log mode writes accumulated changes from the log file back into the main database file. Consolidation occurs automatically at intervals or can be triggered manually.

**Journal mode**: The SQLite configuration setting that determines how the database engine coordinates writes, particularly the mechanism for restoring after crashes. Common modes include Rollback (legacy) and WAL (write-ahead log).

**Rollback journal (legacy mode)**: Traditional SQLite journal mode in which changes are recorded in a separate journal file before being written to the main database file. The journal is removed after a successful transaction commit.

**Write-ahead log (WAL)**: An alternative journal mode in which changes are written to a log file, and the log is periodically merged into the main database file via consolidation operations. Allows better read-write concurrency than Rollback mode.

**Synchronous level**: A SQLite pragma controlling whether the database engine issues explicit fsync operations. NORMAL skips fsync for the main database file after consolidation operations; FULL issues fsync for all operations. Lower levels increase performance but reduce durability guarantees.

**Cache size**: A SQLite pragma controlling the size of the in-memory page cache. Larger caches reduce disk I/O at the cost of increased memory use.

**Consolidation frequency threshold**: The maximum number of pages written to the log before consolidation is automatically triggered. Smaller thresholds cause more frequent consolidation operations; larger thresholds allow the log to grow larger.

**Latency percentile**: A measure of request latency at a specific percentile, such as P95 (95th percentile—the latency value below which 95% of requests fall). Used to characterize tail latency.

| scripts/profiling/loopback-harness.py | Load generation script for loopback exercises |
| `docs/performance-notes/perf-baselines.yaml` | Canonical baseline performance figures by version |

| Python | 3.11.8 | Service runtime |

1	# Page Cache Sizing for the Database File
2	
3	**Title:** Page Cache Sizing for the Database File  
4	**Version:** 2.1  
5	**Owner:** Infra Reliability (Priya Nandakumar)  
6	**Last Updated:** 2025-02-14
7	
8	## Summary
9	
10	Covers page cache size settings for the database file and their effect on read timing under repeated loopback calls.
11	
12	## Overview
13	
14	The package maintains application state in a local SQLite database file. SQLite uses an in-memory page cache to reduce disk I/O operations when reading and writing data. The size of this cache directly influences response times for loopback service calls, memory use, and the behavior of the database under concurrent operations.
15	
16	This page documents how to measure, analyze, and configure the page cache size for the database file. It includes procedures for profiling sessions, configuration examples, and empirical response time data collected over repeated loopback operations throughout 2024 and 2025.
17	
18	## Understanding Page Cache Behavior
19	
20	**Section Owner:** Runtime Team (Owen Baptiste)
21	
22	The SQLite page cache holds recently accessed database pages in memory. When the service reads or writes data, SQLite checks whether the requested page is already cached. If it is, the operation completes without a disk read. If not, SQLite loads the page from disk and inserts it into the cache.
23	
24	The cache operates on a Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction method. When the cache reaches its maximum size, pages that have not been accessed recently are removed to make room for new pages. A larger cache size means more pages can remain in memory, reducing the frequency of disk I/O.
25	
26	For the package's typical workload—repeated loopback service calls that access the same database regions—the page cache size has a measurable effect on response time. Profiling sessions conducted in 2024 and 2025 consistently show that response times improve as the cache size increases, but with diminishing returns beyond a certain threshold. The improvement is most pronounced when moving from 500 pages to 2000 pages, and becomes marginal beyond 5000 pages.
27	
28	The cache is allocated per database connection. The package typically uses a single persistent connection to the database file, so all operations share the same cache. This design simplifies cache management and ensures consistent cache hit rates across the service's lifetime.
29	
30	## Measuring and Profiling the Page Cache
31	
32	**Section Owner:** Core Services (Devon Ruiz)
33	
34	Before adjusting the page cache size, establish baseline measurements of the current state. The following procedure measures page cache hit rates and response times for loopback calls under realistic service conditions.
35	
36	### Prerequisites
37	
38	- The package must be installed and the database file initialized.
39	- The service must be running on loopback (typically on a local port).
40	- The `sqlite3` command-line utility version 3.44.0 or later must be available in your PATH.
41	- Scripts in `scripts/profiling/` must be executable.
42	- Windows PowerShell 7.2 or later (for running the provided profiling scripts).
43	
44	### Procedure: Profile Page Cache Performance
45	
46	1. Start the service on loopback in a dedicated terminal window. Record the timestamp.
47	
48	2. Open a second terminal and navigate to the repository root directory.
49	
50	3. Query the current page cache size:
51	   ```
52	   sqlite3 oauthsvc/data/service.db "PRAGMA cache_size;"
53	   ```
54	   The output shows the current setting. A positive integer indicates the cache size in pages (the default is typically 2000 pages). A negative integer indicates size in kibibytes.
55	
56	4. Clear the database file's in-memory cache to establish a cold-start baseline:
57	   ```
58	   sqlite3 oauthsvc/data/service.db "PRAGMA cache_size = 0; PRAGMA cache_size = 1000;"
59	   ```
60	   Wait 5 seconds to allow the service's cache to be reset.
61	
62	5. Run the profiling script with the loopback service running:
63	   ```
64	   powershell -File scripts/profiling/loopback_call_profile.ps1 -Iterations 50 -SampleInterval 100
65	   ```
66	   The `-Iterations 50` parameter runs 50 consecutive loopback calls. The `-SampleInterval 100` parameter logs intermediate statistics every 10 iterations.
67	
68	6. Record the output, which includes minimum, maximum, median, and 99th percentile response times. The script also logs detailed page cache statistics at `logs/profiling_cache_stats.txt`.
69	
70	7. Examine the profiling output for cache hit rates and evictions:
71	   ```
72	   Get-Content logs/profiling_cache_stats.txt | Select-String "hit_rate|evictions"
73	   ```
74	
75	8. Repeat steps 3–7 for different cache sizes: 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000 pages. Allow at least 2 minutes between runs for system I/O caches to normalize.
76	
77	9. Aggregate the results into a spreadsheet for comparison. The "Response Time Impact Analysis" section of this page provides a template.
78	
79	### Sample Output
80	
81	A typical profiling session with 50 loopback iterations yields output similar to the following:
82	
83	```
84	Profiling Session: loopback_call_profile.ps1
85	Cache Size: 1000 pages (~4.2 MB)
86	Start Time: 2025-02-14 14:23:47 UTC
87	
88	Iterations 1–10 (cold):   min=12.3ms max=45.7ms median=28.1ms
89	Iterations 11–20 (cold):  min=8.4ms  max=32.1ms median=15.2ms
90	Iterations 21–30 (warm):  min=4.8ms  max=8.2ms  median=6.1ms
91	Iterations 31–50 (warm):  min=4.7ms  max=7.9ms  median=5.9ms
92	
93	Summary:
94	  Overall Median: 6.1ms
95	  P99 Response Time: 21.3ms
96	  Page Cache Hit Rate: 87.3%
97	  Page Cache Evictions: 123
98	  Disk Reads (estimated): 28
99	```
100	
101	The cold iterations (1–20) show higher latency because the cache is being populated. After iteration 20, most accesses hit the cache, and response times stabilize to 5–7 ms. The hit rate stabilizes at roughly the same iteration count.
102	
103	## Configuration and Tuning
104	
105	The page cache size is configured through the SQLite pragma `PRAGMA cache_size`. The setting can be modified before the service opens the database file or changed while the service is running, though the latter requires careful coordination.
106	
107	### Setting Page Cache Size at Service Startup
108	
109	The most reliable approach is to configure the page cache size before the service opens the database file. Edit the initialization configuration file:
110	
111	**File:** `oauthsvc/config/database.ini`
112	
113	Locate the `[sqlite]` section and add or modify the `cache_size` entry:
114	
115	```
116	[sqlite]
117	cache_size = 5000
118	journal_mode = wal
119	synchronous = normal
120	```
121	
122	The cache size is specified in pages. The value 5000 pages is approximately 20 MB on a typical system (assuming 4 KB pages, though actual page size may vary by platform). The service reads this configuration during startup and applies it before the database file is accessed.
123	
124	Other settings in this section—`journal_mode` and `synchronous`—are documented in the "Journal Mode Notes for the Database File" page. Do not modify them without consulting that page.
125	
126	### Runtime Adjustment
127	
128	To adjust the page cache size while the service is running, connect to the database file with `sqlite3` and issue the pragma directly. This approach is useful for evaluation and temporary adjustments but does not persist if the service process is restarted without config file changes.
129	
130	```
131	sqlite3 oauthsvc/data/service.db "PRAGMA cache_size = 8000;"
132	```
133	
134	Verify the new setting:
135	
136	```
137	sqlite3 oauthsvc/data/service.db "PRAGMA cache_size;"
138	```
139	
140	Runtime adjustments apply only to new connections. If the service uses a persistent connection to the database file (which it does), the adjustment may not take effect until the service reconnects or is restarted. For production changes, modify the `database.ini` file and restart the service to ensure the setting is applied consistently.
141	
142	## Response Time Impact Analysis
143	
144	**Section Owner:** Runtime Team (Owen Baptiste)
145	
146	Profiling sessions conducted from February 2024 through December 2025 show a consistent correlation between page cache size and response time for loopback calls. The relationship is nonlinear: response time improves significantly as the cache size increases from 500 to 5000 pages, but improvements level off beyond 5000 pages for typical workloads.
147	
148	### Response Time Data by Cache Size
149	
150	The following table summarizes median response times and cache hit rates across profiling sessions. Each row represents the median of three independent profiling runs with 100 loopback iterations per run. The "Cache Size (MB)" column is an estimate assuming 4 KB pages plus per-page overhead.
151	
152	| Cache Size (pages) | Cache Size (MB) | Median Response (ms) | P99 Response (ms) | Hit Rate (%) | Evictions per 100 |
153	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
154	| 500 | ~2.1 | 14.2 | 34.5 | 72.1 | 28 |
155	| 1000 | ~4.2 | 8.7 | 21.3 | 84.5 | 15 |
156	| 2000 | ~8.4 | 6.1 | 12.8 | 92.3 | 7 |
157	| 5000 | ~21.0 | 5.2 | 9.1 | 96.8 | 2 |
158	| 10000 | ~42.0 | 5.1 | 8.9 | 97.2 | 1 |
159	
160	**Note:** The P99 response time (99th percentile) is the response time at which 99% of calls complete faster. This metric is important for understanding tail latency under the service's real-world workload. Values in the table assume typical deployment conditions on loopback.
161	
162	### Diminishing Returns Beyond 5000 Pages
163	
164	The data in the table above shows that moving from 5000 to 10000 pages yields a response time improvement of only 0.1 ms (roughly 2% improvement). The 99th percentile improvement is similarly marginal. This suggests that for the package's typical access patterns, the working set of frequently accessed pages fits within approximately 5000 pages.
165	
166	Increasing the cache further will not improve response times significantly but will increase baseline memory use even when the service is idle. For production deployments, a cache size in the range of 3000–5000 pages balances response time and memory use.
167	
168	The sweet spot appears to be 5000 pages. At this size, response times are only marginally slower than at 10000 pages, but memory use is roughly half. This is the recommended default for most deployments.
169	
170	### Warm-Start Behavior
171	
172	Response times are most sensitive to cache size during the first 20–30 loopback calls in a session, when the cache is being populated. Once the cache reaches steady state, additional increases in cache size yield minimal further improvements.
173	
174	For the package's deployment profile, the cache reaches steady state within the first 5–10 seconds of service operation. Users should expect higher latency during this warm-up period, regardless of the configured cache size. This is documented further in the "Cold Start Versus Warm Start Timing" page (version 1.0.2, updated 2025-08-03).
175	
176	## Memory Implications
177	
178	**Section Owner:** Runtime Team (Owen Baptiste)
179	
180	The page cache is part of the process's resident memory footprint. A larger cache size means higher baseline memory use, even when the cache is not fully populated. The memory is allocated when the service opens the database file and remains allocated for the lifetime of the connection.
181	
182	### Memory Use by Cache Size
183	
184	Each page in the SQLite cache requires approximately 4 KB plus overhead (typically 50–100 bytes per page for metadata and linked-list structures). The following estimates apply:
185	
186	- 1000 pages: ~4.2 MB
187	- 2000 pages: ~8.4 MB
188	- 5000 pages: ~21.0 MB
189	- 10000 pages: ~42.0 MB
190	
191	These figures are rough estimates. Actual memory use depends on system page size, SQLite version (the package uses 3.44.0), and internal accounting structures. For precise measurements on your system, use the memory profiling procedures documented in the "Memory Use Baseline" page (version 1.1, updated 2024-06-09).
192	
193	On a system with tight memory constraints (such as container deployments with memory limits), use 2000 pages instead of 5000. Monitor response time impact with profiling to confirm that the tradeoff is acceptable.
194	
195	### Impact on Startup Time
196	
197	The page cache is allocated when the service opens the database file, which occurs early in the startup sequence. On typical hardware, allocating and initializing a cache of 5000 pages adds 10–20 ms to startup time. Larger caches may add 30–50 ms.
198	
199	For most deployments, startup time is not the bottleneck, and the absolute overhead is acceptable. However, in deployments with frequent restarts (such as blue-green deployments), the cumulative cost may be worth optimizing. See the "Startup Time Notes" page (version 1.9, updated 2026-01-27) for detailed startup profiling procedures and optimization guidance.
200	
201	## Common Configuration Patterns
202	
203	Different deployment scenarios may warrant different cache size settings.
204	
205	### Development and Evaluation
206	
207	For local development and evaluation, use a smaller cache size (1000–2000 pages) to reduce memory use on developer machines. Response time differences in this configuration are unlikely to affect development workflow or make evaluation results unrepresentative.
208	
209	**Configuration:**
210	```
211	cache_size = 1000
212	```
213	
214	### Staging and Pre-Production
215	
216	Staging deployments should use the same cache size as production to allow realistic performance evaluation. Use 5000 pages unless empirical data from your environment indicates a different size is optimal. This ensures that performance evaluation reflects production behavior.
217	
218	**Configuration:**
219	```
220	cache_size = 5000
221	```
222	
223	### Production
224	
225	Production deployments should balance response time against memory use. The recommended setting is 5000 pages for most workloads. Monitor loopback response times and memory use after deployment to confirm that the configuration is appropriate for your environment.
226	
227	**Configuration:**
228	```
229	cache_size = 5000
230	```
231	
232	If response time metrics indicate that the cache size is insufficient (median response time above 7 ms or P99 above 15 ms), increase it to 8000 pages and re-baseline. If memory is constrained, reduce it to 3000 pages and monitor response time impact carefully using the profiling procedures in this page.
233	
234	## Interaction with Journal Mode
235	
236	The SQLite journal mode affects how the page cache interacts with the disk. The package is configured to use Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode by default, which tends to work well with larger cache sizes.
237	
238	In WAL mode, the page cache holds modified pages until they are flushed to the WAL file. A larger cache allows more modifications to accumulate in memory before being written to disk, reducing disk I/O for write-heavy workloads.
239	
240	The `synchronous` setting (documented in the "Journal Mode Notes for the Database File" page, version 1.3.0) also affects the interaction. With `synchronous = normal`, the database relies on the operating system's file system cache for some durability guarantees, making the page cache size even more critical for performance.
241	
242	For detailed information on journal mode configuration and its performance implications, see the "Journal Mode Notes for the Database File" page. That page documents settings such as `journal_mode` and `synchronous`, which interact with cache sizing in subtle ways.
243	
244	**Important:** The journal mode notes (last updated 2024-07-22) recommend WAL mode (`journal_mode = wal`) for the package. Do not change this setting without consulting that page and understanding the implications for durability and concurrency.
245	
246	## Troubleshooting High Response Times
247	
248	If the service is experiencing unexpectedly high response times for loopback calls, the page cache size may not be the root cause. However, it is worth checking as part of your investigation.
249	
250	### Procedure: Check Cache Hit Rates
251	
252	1. While the service is running, query the page cache configuration:
253	   ```
254	   sqlite3 oauthsvc/data/service.db "PRAGMA cache_size;"
255	   ```
256	
257	2. If the service logs include cache statistics, examine them:
258	   ```
259	   Get-Content logs/service.log | Select-String "cache"
260	   ```
261	
262	3. Run a profiling session to measure current response times and compare them to the baseline in the "Response Time Impact Analysis" section of this page.
263	
264	4. If the measured response times are significantly higher than the table shows for the same cache size, investigate other factors such as disk I/O contention, memory pressure, or CPU throttling. See the "Loopback Response Time Figures" page (version 2.0.1, updated 2025-05-30) for additional guidance.
265	
266	5. Examine system resource usage during profiling. High disk I/O despite a large cache suggests that the working set is larger than expected, or that another process is contending for I/O.
267	
268	### Procedure: Increase Cache Size and Re-Baseline
269	
270	1. Increase the cache size by 2000–3000 pages from the current setting. Edit `oauthsvc/config/database.ini` and modify the `cache_size` entry.
271	
272	2. Restart the service to apply the new configuration.
273	
274	3. Allow the service 10 seconds to stabilize.
275	
276	4. Run a profiling session and record the results:
277	   ```
278	   powershell -File scripts/profiling/loopback_call_profile.ps1 -Iterations 50 -SampleInterval 100
279	   ```
280	
281	5. Compare the new results to the previous baseline. If median response time improves by more than 1 ms, the cache size was a limiting factor. If there is minimal improvement (less than 0.5 ms), investigate other causes such as disk contention or CPU availability.
282	
283	If the cache size was the issue, consider whether the new size is sustainable in your memory budget. Refer to the "Memory Use Baseline" page for current memory use figures.
284	
285	## Terminology
286	
287	**Cache Hit:** A database page access that finds the page already in the page cache, avoiding a disk read. High cache hit rates correlate with faster response times and lower disk I/O.
288	
289	**Cache Eviction:** The removal of a page from the cache to make room for a newly loaded page. Evictions increase when the cache is too small for the working set of pages being accessed.
290	
291	**Cold Cache:** The state of the page cache immediately after service startup or restart, before any pages have been loaded. Operations against a cold cache are slower because they require disk I/O.
292	
293	**Least Recently Used (LRU):** The page replacement algorithm used by SQLite's page cache. Pages that have not been accessed in the longest time are evicted first to make room for newly loaded pages.
294	
295	**Page:** The fundamental unit of data in SQLite. A page is typically 4 KB and corresponds to the unit of I/O between the database file and the page cache. All reads and writes operate on whole pages.
296	
297	**Warm Cache:** The state of the page cache after it has been populated with pages from repeated accesses. Operations against a warm cache are faster because most page accesses hit the cache rather than requiring disk I/O.
298	
299	**WAL Mode:** Write-Ahead Logging mode, the recommended journal mode for the package. In WAL mode, writes are first appended to a separate WAL file and later synchronized back to the main database file, reducing I/O contention and improving concurrency.
300	
301	**Working Set:** The set of pages that the service accesses frequently during normal operation. The optimal page cache size is slightly larger than the working set size. If the cache is smaller than the working set, pages are evicted and must be reloaded, increasing latency.
