# Guide to the sample listing files

`examples/` holds fictional sample data for a planned developer portal page
that lists applications built on this service. Each `.jsonl` file is one
product group, in [JSON Lines](https://jsonlines.org/) format: one JSON
object per line, no wrapping array. None of this data is loaded into the
service, and none of it should be treated as real applications, teams, or
support channels — see `examples/README.md` for the full field reference.

Every file follows the same shape: 12 categories specific to its product
group, 5 sample listings per category, 60 listings per file. The counts
below come straight from `tools/summarize_examples.py`, run against the
files as they exist today (`python tools/summarize_examples.py --json`).
If you add or edit a sample file, re-run the script — the numbers in this
guide will drift out of date otherwise.

## Files

### `education.jsonl` — Education

School and campus tooling: Learning Management, Student Assessment,
Classroom Collaboration, Enrollment & Admissions, Financial Aid, Course
Catalog, Attendance Tracking, Tutoring & Support, Curriculum Planning,
Accessibility Tools, Alumni Engagement, and Campus Operations.

- 48 general / 12 beta.
- Launch years 2021–2026 (13, 12, 12, 11, 9, 3) — one of only three files
  with any 2026 listings weighted this early in the year.
- 12 distinct owning teams, one per category (5 listings each); the
  top-10 team list cuts off 2 of them.

### `energy.jsonl` — Energy

Utility and grid tooling: Smart Meter Analytics, Outage Management, Grid
Monitoring, Solar Asset Management, Demand Response, Billing & Rate Plans,
Field Technician Tools, Energy Trading, Sustainability Reporting, EV
Charging Management, Load Forecasting, and Customer Usage Portal.

- 48 general / 12 beta.
- Launch years 2021–2026 (12, 12, 12, 12, 11, 1) — only a single 2026
  listing, the lightest 2026 showing of any file.
- 12 distinct owning teams, one per category; the top-10 list cuts off 2.

### `finance.jsonl` — Finance

Corporate finance tooling: Expense Management, Invoicing & Billing,
Payments Processing, Fraud Detection, Ledger & Reconciliation, Budgeting &
Forecasting, Tax Compliance, Payroll, Risk Scoring, Treasury Management,
Financial Reporting, and Vendor Payments.

- 48 general / 12 beta.
- Launch years 2021–2026 (12, 12, 12, 12, 8, 4).
- 12 distinct owning teams, one per category; the top-10 list cuts off 2.

### `healthcare.jsonl` — Healthcare

Clinical and patient-facing tooling: Patient Scheduling, Telehealth,
Electronic Health Records, Billing & Claims, Care Coordination, Medication
Management, Remote Monitoring, Clinical Decision Support, Patient
Messaging, Lab Results, Provider Directory, and Insurance Eligibility.

- 47 general / 13 beta.
- Launch years 2021–2026 (12, 12, 12, 12, 9, 3).
- 12 distinct owning teams, one per category; the top-10 list cuts off 2.

### `logistics.jsonl` — Logistics

Freight and delivery tooling: Route Optimization, Fleet Tracking,
Warehouse Management, Last-Mile Delivery, Freight Booking, Driver Mobile
Tools, Load Planning, Customs & Compliance, Yard Management, Carrier
Management, Shipment Visibility, and Dock Scheduling.

- 48 general / 12 beta.
- Launch years 2021–2026 (12, 12, 12, 12, 8, 4).
- Only 11 distinct owning teams: Network Planning Team owns both Route
  Optimization and Load Planning (10 listings), every other category has
  its own team (5 listings each). Because of that, the top-10 team list
  cuts off only the Dock Scheduling team, not two teams like the other
  12-category files.

### `manufacturing.jsonl` — Manufacturing

Plant and production tooling: Production Scheduling, Quality Inspection,
Equipment Maintenance, Supply Chain Planning, Inventory & Materials, Shop
Floor Monitoring, Safety Compliance, Worker Training, Supplier
Collaboration, Predictive Maintenance, Packaging & Labeling, and Plant
Analytics.

- 48 general / 12 beta.
- Launch years 2021–2025 only (12, 12, 12, 12, 12) — a perfectly even
  spread, and one of only two files with no 2026 listings at all.
- 12 distinct owning teams, one per category; the top-10 list cuts off 2.

### `media.jsonl` — Media

Streaming and publishing tooling: Video Streaming, Content Management, Ad
Serving, Audience Analytics, Recommendation Engine, Live Broadcast Tools,
Subscription Management, Content Moderation, Podcast Hosting, Rights &
Licensing, Creator Tools, and Metadata & Cataloging.

- 47 general / 13 beta.
- Launch years 2021–2026 (13, 12, 12, 11, 9, 3).
- 12 distinct owning teams, one per category; the top-10 list cuts off 2.

### `realestate.jsonl` — Real Estate

Property and leasing tooling: Listing Management, Property Search,
Mortgage Tools, Lease Management, Maintenance Requests, Virtual Tours,
Tenant Screening, Rent Payments, Market Analytics, Agent CRM, Document
Signing, and Property Inspections.

- 48 general / 12 beta.
- Launch years 2021–2025 only (12, 12, 12, 12, 12) — the other file, along
  with manufacturing.jsonl, with no 2026 listings.
- 12 distinct owning teams, one per category; the top-10 list cuts off 2.

### `retail.jsonl` — Retail

Store and e-commerce tooling: Inventory Management, Point of Sale,
Customer Loyalty, Merchandising, Store Operations, E-Commerce Storefront,
Order Fulfillment, Returns Management, Pricing & Promotions, Supply Chain
Visibility, Customer Analytics, and Product Discovery & Search.

- 46 general / 14 beta — the highest beta share of any file.
- Launch years 2021–2026 (11, 13, 12, 12, 8, 4).
- Only 7 distinct owning teams, the fewest of any file: Checkout
  Experience Team (Point of Sale, Returns Management), Loyalty & CRM Team
  (Customer Loyalty, Supply Chain Visibility), Commerce Platform Team
  (Merchandising, Order Fulfillment), Store Operations Team (Customer
  Analytics, Store Operations), and Fulfillment Engineering (E-Commerce
  Storefront, Product Discovery & Search) each own two categories (10
  listings apiece); Merchandising Engineering and Retail Data Team own one
  category each (5). All 7 teams fit in the script's top-10 list, unlike
  every other file.

### `travel.jsonl` — Travel

Booking and trip-support tooling: Flight Booking, Hotel Reservations,
Itinerary Planning, Loyalty & Rewards, Trip Disruption Alerts, Car Rental,
Travel Expense, Check-In & Boarding, Baggage Tracking, Customer Support
Tools, Group Travel, and Destination Discovery.

- 48 general / 12 beta.
- Launch years 2021–2026 (12, 12, 12, 12, 10, 2).
- 12 distinct owning teams, one per category; the top-10 list cuts off 2.

## All files combined

Across all 600 listings: 476 general / 124 beta. Launch years run
2021–2026 (121, 121, 120, 118, 96, 24) — a steady decline that's just the
2026 files being cut off partway through the year, not a real slowdown.
Every `support_channel` in every file is a Slack channel (`#...`); none of
the current sample data uses the email form the schema also allows.

## Running `tools/summarize_examples.py`

The script is standard-library-only and reads only the `.jsonl` files
under `examples/` — it never imports the application package or opens a
database.

```
python tools/summarize_examples.py
```

Prints a `== <filename> ==` section per file (total listings, then counts
by category, by status, and by launch year, then the ten owning teams
with the most listings), followed by an `== all files combined ==`
section with the same breakdown merged across every file.

```
python tools/summarize_examples.py --file retail.jsonl
```

Restricts the run to one file — pass either the bare filename (as above)
or a path; only the filename is used to look the file up under
`examples/`. With a single file selected there's nothing to combine, so
the combined section is omitted.

```
python tools/summarize_examples.py --json
```

Same data, printed as one JSON object instead of formatted text: a
`files` object keyed by filename, each holding `total_listings`,
`by_category`, `by_status`, `by_launch_year`, and `top_owning_teams`; plus
a top-level `combined` key (present only when more than one file was
summarized) with the same shape. `--json` and `--file` combine normally.

Reading the output: `by_category`, `by_status`, and `top_owning_teams`
are sorted by count descending (ties broken alphabetically for
categories and statuses, by first appearance in the file for teams);
`by_launch_year` is sorted chronologically instead, since ordering by
count would scramble the timeline. `top_owning_teams` is always capped at
10 entries — as the `logistics.jsonl` and `retail.jsonl` sections above
show, a file with fewer than 10 distinct teams will show all of them, and
a file with more will have some cut off.

## Checklist for adding a new sample file

1. Pick a product group not already covered, and choose exactly 12
   categories specific to it (the format all the existing files use).
2. Write exactly 5 listings per category (60 listings total), each with
   every field from the table in `examples/README.md`:
   `listing_id`, `display_name`, `owning_team`, `category`, `summary`,
   `launch_date`, `status`, `support_channel`.
3. Keep `listing_id` unique within the file and give it a short prefix
   tied to the product group (e.g. `retail-014`), matching the pattern
   the other files use.
4. Set `status` to either `"beta"` or `"general"` — no other values are
   recognized by the summary script's category/status grouping (anything
   else falls into an `"unknown"` bucket instead of a real one).
5. Use `YYYY-MM-DD` for `launch_date`; the script derives the launch year
   by splitting on `-`, so any other format will misgroup or land in
   `"unknown"`.
6. Decide whether each category gets its own `owning_team` (the pattern
   most files use) or whether some teams intentionally own more than one
   category (as in `retail.jsonl` and `logistics.jsonl`) — either is
   fine, but be deliberate about it since it changes how the top-10 team
   list reads.
7. Use a real-looking `support_channel` — a `#slack-channel` or an email
   address, per the README.
8. Save the file as `examples/<name>.jsonl`, one JSON object per line, no
   wrapping array and no trailing commas.
9. Run `python tools/summarize_examples.py --file <name>.jsonl` to sanity
   check the new file alone, then `python tools/summarize_examples.py` to
   confirm it folds cleanly into the combined summary.
10. Update this guide's per-file section and the combined totals to match
    the new counts.

# Release Notes Folder Index

**Title:** Release Notes Folder Index  
**Version:** 3.4  
**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)

---

## Overview

The `release-notes/` folder contains all documentation governing how this package is versioned, released, and documented. This index centralizes links to process documents, technical guides, documentation standards, and previous release notes covering documentation, packaging, command help text, console output format, and performance changes across versions. Use this page to navigate the folder, understand release workflows, and locate version-specific notes.

This package follows structured release practices maintained by Platform Tools, Release Engineering, and Documentation Guild. All releases require adherence to the version numbering scheme, changelog conventions, and release checklists before package distribution. Most changes documented here affect users of the package rather than the package internals.

**Section Owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools)**

---

## Process & Guidelines Documents

These documents define how releases are planned, versioned, and validated before distribution.

- **[Version Numbering Scheme](./version-numbering.md)** — version v1.2.0, updated 2024-06-03, owner Release Engineering (Priya Chandran). Describes the semantic versioning approach used for all oauthsvc releases, including major, minor, and patch semantics. Also documents version identifier format in package metadata and file naming conventions.

- **[Changelog Conventions](./changelog-conventions.md)** — version 2.1, updated 2025-01-20, owner Documentation Guild (Sana Iqbal). Specifies how changelog entries are written, categorized, and ordered within the CHANGELOG file. Covers entry templates, required fields, and examples for common change types.

- **[Release Checklist](./release-checklist.md)** — version v1.0.3, updated 2026-02-14, owner Release Engineering (Priya Chandran). A sequential task list for release managers, including validation steps, file updates, building artifacts, and final verification before publication.

## Technical Guides

Implementation and workflow documents for package distribution and build processes.

Complete step-by-step walkthrough of building the source distribution, including validation of contents and verification of packaging completeness before release.

## Documentation Standards

Normative documents for consistency across user-facing documentation and console output.

- **[Console Log Format Notes](./console-log-format-notes.md)** — version 1.1, updated 2026-03-22, owner Developer Experience (Theo Banks). Documents the standard format for messages printed to the console during service startup, runtime, and shutdown. Covers log levels, timestamp formats, and guidance on structured output.

- **[Command Help Text Style Guide](./command-help-text-style.md)** — version v1.3.0, updated 2024-11-05, owner Documentation Guild (Sana Iqbal). Standardizes the language and format of help text displayed by command-line options. Includes terminology preferences and examples of well-formatted help output.

- **[Release Notes: v2.0.0](./release-notes-v2.0.0.md)** — version v2.0.0, updated 2025-12-09, owner Documentation Guild (Sana Iqbal). Major release with significant documentation restructuring. Help text reformatted according to new style guide. Console logging interface redesigned for clarity and consistency across all output channels.

Additional older releases may be located in the legacy folder; consult Mara Olsen for access to pre-release documentation.

## Terminology & Glossary

**Section Owner: Sana Iqbal (Documentation Guild)**

- **Release candidate**: A version of the package prepared and verified according to the release checklist, awaiting final validation before marking as released.

- **Release manager**: A member of Release Engineering responsible for executing the release checklist, validating the release, and publishing the package.

- **Package user**: Any person or system that downloads, installs, or uses this package.

1	================================================================================
2	Building the Source Distribution
3	================================================================================
4	
5	:Title:        Building the Source Distribution
6	:Version:      v2.0.1
7	:Owner:        Core Services (Liam Fitzgerald)
8	:Last Updated: 2025-07-01
9	
10	Overview
11	========
12	
13	This page documents the complete workflow for building a source distribution package of oauthsvc, from preparing the repository to creating the final distributable package. The process integrates version numbering, changelog management, documentation updates, and packaging validation.
14	
15	The oauthsvc package is a lightweight, dependency-free service with both a command-line interface and a loopback HTTP component. All state is stored in a local SQLite database file. This guide assumes you are working from a local clone of the repository and have completed the pre-release checklist.
16	
17	Quick Start Workflow
18	====================
19	
20	The release workflow follows these high-level steps:
21	
22	1. Update version information in version markers
23	2. Verify and finalize the changelog
24	3. Run the pre-release validation checklist
25	4. Build the source distribution package
26	5. Create release notes documentation
27	6. Tag the repository and mark as released
28	
29	For most releases, the process takes 30–45 minutes from start to finish. Allow extra time if updating console output formatting or regenerating command help text.
30	
31	Version Numbering Overview
32	==========================
33	
34	*Owner: Release Engineering (Priya Chandran)*
35	
36	oauthsvc follows semantic versioning as described in the Version Numbering Scheme documentation. The short form:
37	
38	- **Major.Minor.Patch** format: for example, v2.0.1
39	- Increment Major for backward-incompatible changes to behavior or storage
40	- Increment Minor for new features or enhancements
41	- Increment Patch for bug fixes, documentation updates, and performance improvements
42	
43	When you prepare a release, first check the Version Numbering Scheme page to confirm the version bump category. The classification flow on that page guides you based on the changes in the current development cycle.
44	
45	Version markers live in two locations:
46	
47	- The main version constant in the package initialization file (look for the version string)
48	- The version field in the package metadata file (usually `setup.py` or `pyproject.toml`)
49	- Documentation version headers in the `docs/` folder may also reference the release version
50	
51	Consistency is critical. Before building, grep for the old version across the entire repository to catch any markers you may have missed:
52	
53	.. code-block:: bash
54	
55	  grep -r "v1\.4\.2" .
56	
57	Replace all occurrences with the new version before proceeding.
58	
59	Changelog Conventions
60	====================
61	
62	*Owner: Documentation Guild (Sana Iqbal)*
63	
64	The changelog lives in `CHANGELOG.md` at the repository root. Each release gets its own section with a heading that includes the version and the date, formatted as follows:
65	
66	.. code-block:: text
67	
68	  ## v2.0.1 – 2025-07-01
69	
70	Under the version heading, organize changes into these categories:
71	
72	- **Documentation** – Help text, README updates, internal wiki pages, console output formatting
73	- **Packaging** – Build configuration, source distribution layout, setup automation
74	- **Performance** – Speed improvements, query optimization, memory usage
75	- **Maintenance** – Dependency updates, code cleanup, code reorganization (no functional change)
76	- **Bug Fixes** – Changes to existing behavior
77	- **Features** – New capabilities
78	
79	Each category is optional; include only those with changes. List each item as a bullet point with a brief, imperative statement:
80	
81	.. code-block:: text
82	
83	  - Update help text for the loopback server startup message
84	  - Optimize SQLite connection pooling in the service layer
85	  - Refactor configuration loading for clarity (no behavior change)
86	
87	Do not include items about system safeguards, validation procedures, or performance analysis. Refer to the Changelog Conventions page for detailed style rules, including capitalization and item format.
88	
89	The Changelog Entry Format configuration file (`changelog-entry-format.yaml`) documents the YAML format for structured entries if your team uses that workflow. As of this writing, that file specifies format version 1.0 and was last updated 2026-06-01.
90	
91	Pre-release Checklist
92	=====================
93	
94	Before you build the source distribution, run through the Release Checklist page (v1.0.3, updated 2026-02-14). That page is maintained by Release Engineering and covers:
95	
96	- Verifying all code changes are committed
97	- Checking that the changelog is complete and accurate
98	- Confirming version numbers are updated everywhere
99	- Running smoke validation on the package
100	- Reviewing documentation for any outdated references
101	
102	Do not skip this step. The checklist prevents most shipping errors.
103	
104	Building the Source Distribution
105	=================================
106	
107	*Owner: Core Services (Liam Fitzgerald)*
108	
109	Once you have completed the pre-release checklist and verified all version markers, you are ready to build the package.
110	
111	Preparation Steps
112	-----------------
113	
114	1. Ensure your working directory is clean (no uncommitted changes):
115	
116	   .. code-block:: bash
117	
118	     git status
119	
120	2. If using a virtual environment, activate it:
121	
122	   .. code-block:: bash
123	
124	     # On Windows
125	     venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
126	     
127	     # On macOS/Linux
128	     source venv/bin/activate
129	
130	3. Install or upgrade build tools. The package uses standard library only, but the build process itself requires packaging tools:
131	
132	   .. code-block:: bash
133	
134	     pip install --upgrade build wheel
135	
136	Building the Package
137	--------------------
138	
139	The standard method uses the `build` module:
140	
141	.. code-block:: bash
142	
143	  python -m build --sdist
144	
145	This command:
146	
147	- Reads the version and metadata from the package configuration
148	- Compiles any non-Python data files (documentation, configuration templates)
149	- Creates a `.tar.gz` file (source distribution) in the `dist/` directory
150	
151	The resulting file is named `oauthsvc-<version>.tar.gz`. For version 2.0.1, the filename is `oauthsvc-2.0.1.tar.gz`.
152	
153	Validation
154	----------
155	
156	After building, validate the package:
157	
158	1. Check the file exists and has reasonable size (typically 15–35 KB for oauthsvc):
159	
160	   .. code-block:: bash
161	
162	     ls -lh dist/oauthsvc-*.tar.gz
163	
164	2. Extract and inspect the contents in a temporary location:
165	
166	   .. code-block:: bash
167	
168	     mkdir -p /tmp/oauthsvc-verify
169	     tar -xzf dist/oauthsvc-2.0.1.tar.gz -C /tmp/oauthsvc-verify
170	     ls -la /tmp/oauthsvc-verify/oauthsvc-2.0.1/
171	
172	   Verify the directory contains:
173	
174	   - The `oauthsvc/` package directory with all modules
175	   - The `docs/` folder with README and other documentation
176	   - The `setup.py` or `pyproject.toml` configuration file
177	   - A `PKG-INFO` file with metadata
178	
179	3. Attempt an installation from the package:
180	
181	   .. code-block:: bash
182	
183	     pip install dist/oauthsvc-2.0.1.tar.gz
184	
185	   This confirms the package can be unpacked and dependencies (if any) are available.
186	
187	4. Verify the installed version matches your target:
188	
189	   The command-line tool should report the correct version when invoked with the version flag.
190	
191	Common Issues
192	~~~~~~~~~~~~~
193	
194	- **Package is empty or missing files**: Check that `MANIFEST.in` lists all non-Python data files. See the Source Distribution Packaging Guide (v1.4, updated 2024-09-10) for details.
195	- **setup.py reports wrong version**: Ensure version markers in the package directory match the version in `setup.py`.

================================================================================
Building the Source Distribution
================================================================================

:Title:        Building the Source Distribution
:Version:      v2.0.1
:Owner:        Core Services (Liam Fitzgerald)
:Last Updated: 2025-07-01

Overview
========

This page documents the complete workflow for building a source distribution package of oauthsvc, from preparing the repository to creating the final distributable package. The process integrates version numbering, changelog management, documentation updates, and packaging validation.

The oauthsvc package is a lightweight, dependency-free service with both a command-line interface and a loopback HTTP component. All state is stored in a local SQLite database file. This guide assumes you are working from a local clone of the repository and have completed the pre-release checklist.

Quick Start Workflow
====================

The release workflow follows these high-level steps:

1. Update version information in version markers
2. Verify and finalize the changelog
3. Run the pre-release validation checklist
4. Build the source distribution package
5. Create release notes documentation
6. Tag the repository and mark as released

For most releases, the process takes 30–45 minutes from start to finish. Allow extra time if updating console output formatting or regenerating command help text.

Version Numbering Overview
==========================

*Owner: Release Engineering (Priya Chandran)*

oauthsvc follows semantic versioning as described in the Version Numbering Scheme documentation. The short form:

- **Major.Minor.Patch** format: for example, v2.0.1
- Increment Major for backward-incompatible changes to behavior or storage
- Increment Minor for new features or enhancements
- Increment Patch for bug fixes, documentation updates, and performance improvements

When you prepare a release, first check the Version Numbering Scheme page to confirm the version bump category. The classification flow on that page guides you based on the changes in the current development cycle.

Version markers live in two locations:

- The main version constant in the package initialization file (look for the version string)
- The version field in the package metadata file (usually `setup.py` or `pyproject.toml`)
- Documentation version headers in the `docs/` folder may also reference the release version

Consistency is critical. Before building, grep for the old version across the entire repository to catch any markers you may have missed:

.. code-block:: bash

  grep -r "v1\.4\.2" .

Replace all occurrences with the new version before proceeding.

Changelog Conventions
====================

*Owner: Documentation Guild (Sana Iqbal)*

The changelog lives in `CHANGELOG.md` at the repository root. Each release gets its own section with a heading that includes the version and the date, formatted as follows:

.. code-block:: text

  ## v2.0.1 – 2025-07-01

Under the version heading, organize changes into these categories:

- **Documentation** – Help text, README updates, internal wiki pages, console output formatting
- **Packaging** – Build configuration, source distribution layout, setup automation
- **Performance** – Speed improvements, query optimization, memory usage
- **Maintenance** – Dependency updates, code cleanup, code reorganization (no functional change)
- **Bug Fixes** – Changes to existing behavior
- **Features** – New capabilities

Each category is optional; include only those with changes. List each item as a bullet point with a brief, imperative statement:

.. code-block:: text

  - Update help text for the loopback server startup message
  - Optimize SQLite connection pooling in the service layer
  - Refactor configuration loading for clarity (no behavior change)

Do not include items about system safeguards, validation procedures, or performance analysis. Refer to the Changelog Conventions page for detailed style rules, including capitalization and item format.

The Changelog Entry Format configuration file (`changelog-entry-format.yaml`) documents the YAML format for structured entries if your team uses that workflow. As of this writing, that file specifies format version 1.0 and was last updated 2026-06-01.

Pre-release Checklist
=====================

Before you build the source distribution, run through the Release Checklist page (v1.0.3, updated 2026-02-14). That page is maintained by Release Engineering and covers:

- Verifying all code changes are committed
- Checking that the changelog is complete and accurate
- Confirming version numbers are updated everywhere
- Running smoke validation on the package
- Reviewing documentation for any outdated references

Do not skip this step. The checklist prevents most shipping errors.

Building the Source Distribution
=================================

*Owner: Core Services (Liam Fitzgerald)*

Once you have completed the pre-release checklist and verified all version markers, you are ready to build the package.

Preparation Steps
-----------------

1. Ensure your working directory is clean (no uncommitted changes):

   .. code-block:: bash

     git status

2. If using a virtual environment, activate it:

   .. code-block:: bash

     # On Windows
     venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
     
     # On macOS/Linux
     source venv/bin/activate

3. Install or upgrade build tools. The package uses standard library only, but the build process itself requires packaging tools:

   .. code-block:: bash

     pip install --upgrade build wheel

Building the Package
--------------------

The standard method uses the `build` module:

.. code-block:: bash

  python -m build --sdist

This command:

- Reads the version and metadata from the package configuration
- Compiles any non-Python data files (documentation, configuration templates)
- Creates a `.tar.gz` file (source distribution) in the `dist/` directory

The resulting file is named `oauthsvc-<version>.tar.gz`. For version 2.0.1, the filename is `oauthsvc-2.0.1.tar.gz`.

Validation
----------

After building, validate the package:

1. Check the file exists and has reasonable size (typically 15–35 KB for oauthsvc):

   .. code-block:: bash

     ls -lh dist/oauthsvc-*.tar.gz

2. Extract and inspect the contents in a temporary location:

   .. code-block:: bash

     mkdir -p /tmp/oauthsvc-verify
     tar -xzf dist/oauthsvc-2.0.1.tar.gz -C /tmp/oauthsvc-verify
     ls -la /tmp/oauthsvc-verify/oauthsvc-2.0.1/

   Verify the directory contains:

   - The `oauthsvc/` package directory with all modules
   - The `docs/` folder with README and other documentation
   - The `setup.py` or `pyproject.toml` configuration file
   - A `PKG-INFO` file with metadata

3. Attempt an installation from the package:

   .. code-block:: bash

     pip install dist/oauthsvc-2.0.1.tar.gz

   This confirms the package can be unpacked and dependencies (if any) are available.

4. Verify the installed version matches your target:

   The command-line tool should report the correct version when invoked with the version flag.

Common Issues
~~~~~~~~~~~~~

- **Package is empty or missing files**: Check that `MANIFEST.in` lists all non-Python data files. See the Source Distribution Packaging Guide (v1.4, updated 2024-09-10) for details.
- **setup.py reports wrong version**: Ensure version markers in the package directory match the version in `setup.py`.
- **Install fails with missing file**: Confirm that any custom data or documentation files are included in the source distribution layout.

Release Notes Documentation
============================

*Owner: Documentation Guild (Sana Iqbal)*

After a successful build, create or update the release notes. The release notes live in the same folder as this page and follow the naming convention `release-notes-v<version>.<ext>`.

Release notes cover:

- **Documentation** updates: changes to help text, README additions, internal wiki pages, console log format improvements
- **Packaging** changes: build process improvements, distribution layout changes, setup automation enhancements
- **Console Output** improvements: changes to command help text, log message format, startup messages
- **Performance** improvements: speed gains, memory optimization, I/O reduction
- **Maintenance** updates: code reorganization, dependency updates, no functional changes

Do NOT include release notes items for system safeguards, validation procedures, performance metrics, stored access information, or internal module details.

Example release notes structure:

.. code-block:: text

  # Release Notes: v2.0.1

  **Release Date:** 2025-07-01

  ## Documentation
  - Updated command help text to clarify startup options
  - Expanded README section on database initialization
  - Internal wiki updated with build instructions

  ## Packaging
  - Simplified build configuration for maintainability
  - Added MANIFEST.in to ensure docs are included in distribution

  ## Console Output
  - Standardized log message prefixes across startup and shutdown sequences
  - Improved error output formatting for clarity

  ## Performance
  - Reduced SQLite connection overhead by 15% in typical scenarios
  - Optimized loopback server request handling

The past release notes files in this folder include:

- Release Notes: v1.0.0 (v1.0.0, owner Mara Olsen, updated 2024-04-02)
- Release Notes: v1.1.0 (v1.1.0, owner Mara Olsen, updated 2024-08-15)
- Release Notes: v1.2.0 (v1.2.0, owner Priya Chandran, updated 2025-02-27)
- Release Notes: v2.0.0 (v2.0.0, owner Sana Iqbal, updated 2025-12-09)

Refer to these for style consistency and usage examples.

Tagging and Distribution
========================

After the package is created and validated:

1. Tag the repository with the release version:

   .. code-block:: bash

     git tag -a v2.0.1 -m "Release v2.0.1"
     git push origin v2.0.1

2. The source distribution package (`oauthsvc-2.0.1.tar.gz`) is now ready for distribution. It is typically uploaded to a package repository or released through your internal distribution system.

3. Store the build artifacts (optional but recommended):

   .. code-block:: bash

     cp dist/oauthsvc-2.0.1.tar.gz /mnt/releases/oauthsvc/

   Store the package in a location accessible to deployment teams.

Terminology
===========

.. glossary::

  Source Distribution
    A compressed file (usually `.tar.gz` on Unix-like systems or `.zip` on Windows) containing the complete source code, documentation, and configuration files needed to build and install the package from scratch.

  Version Marker
    A string or variable in the source code that declares the current release version, typically found in package metadata files or a special version file read at import time.

  Semantic Versioning
    A versioning scheme using the format Major.Minor.Patch, where each component increments based on the type of change: Major for breaking changes, Minor for new features, and Patch for fixes.

  Changelog
    A structured document listing changes made in each release, organized by category (Features, Bug Fixes, Documentation, etc.) to help users understand what changed between versions.

  Pre-release Checklist
    A verification procedure run before packaging a release to confirm all code, documentation, and metadata are consistent and ready for distribution.

  Build Artifact
    Any file generated during the build process, including compiled code, package files, metadata files, and package distributions.

  Package Metadata
    Configuration and version information stored in `setup.py`, `pyproject.toml`, or similar files, including version number, author, dependencies, and description.

  MANIFEST.in
    A configuration file that specifies which non-Python files (documentation, data, configuration) should be included in the source distribution package.

  Release Tag
    A named marker in version control that points to a specific commit and is associated with a release version, used to identify and retrieve release versions from the repository record.

Repository Files and Paths
===========================

The following files and directories are referenced in this workflow:

- `oauthsvc/` – Main package directory; contains the package implementation
- The package initialization file contains the version marker
- `setup.py` – Package metadata and build configuration; includes version field
- `pyproject.toml` – Alternative or supplemental build configuration (if used)
- `MANIFEST.in` – Specifies non-Python files to include in source distribution
- `CHANGELOG.md` – Changelog file at repository root; updated for each release
- `docs/` – Documentation directory; may contain README files and wiki pages
- `dist/` – Build output directory; contains generated `.tar.gz` files
- `README.md` – Primary README at repository root
- Release notes folder (`release-notes/`) – Contains release notes and build process documentation

Tools and Package Versions
==========================

The following tools are used in the build and release process:

==================  ===========  =============================================
Tool                Version      Purpose
==================  ===========  =============================================
build               0.10.0       Build backend; creates source distributions
wheel               0.40.0       Wheel format support; optional for wheels
Python              3.9+         Standard library utilities; git, tar, grep
git                 2.35+        Repository tagging and commit verification
tar / gzip          GNU          File compression and decompression
setuptools          65.5.0       Package metadata handling; used by build
==================  ===========  =============================================

These are minimum recommended versions. Newer point releases are generally safe.

Changelog
=========

The following entries document changes to this page and the release process:

1	# Changelog Conventions
2	
3	**Title:** Changelog Conventions  
4	**Version:** 2.1  
5	**Owner:** Documentation Guild (Sana Iqbal)  
6	**Last updated:** 2025-01-20
7	
8	## Overview
9	
10	This page describes the conventions used when writing changelog entries for oauthsvc releases. It covers the structure of changelog entries, the relationship to version numbering, how to organize entries for a release, and reference material about what has shipped in past releases.
11	
12	## Changelog Entry Structure
13	
14	Each changelog entry should follow a consistent format to keep our release timeline clear and scannable. Entries are organized chronologically within a release section, newest changes first.
15	
16	### Format and Style
17	
18	A changelog entry consists of:
19	
20	- **Category**: One of the following (use bullets or numbers consistently within a release):
21	  - **Documentation** — updates to the markdown files in `docs/`, parameter documentation, or README files
22	  - **Packaging** — changes to the setup scripts, distribution metadata, or how the package is built
23	  - **Command help** — changes to output produced by command-line flags like `--help`
24	  - **Console output** — changes to log messages, status output, or formatted text written to stdout or stderr
25	  - **Performance** — speed improvements, reduced memory use, or other efficiency gains
26	  - **Bug fixes** — fixes to the loopback HTTP service behavior, SQLite database interactions, or command-line parsing
27	  - **Other** — miscellaneous items that don't fit above
28	
29	- **Area**: Where the change applies (optional, but recommended). Examples: "service startup", "configuration parsing", "database initialization"
30	
31	- **Summary**: A brief, past-tense description (50–100 characters, no period)
32	
33	Examples of well-formed entries:
34	
35	```
36	- Documentation: Clarified payload schema in HTTP API reference
37	- Packaging: Updated setup script to require Python 3.9+
38	- Command help: Improved descriptions in --help output for loopback flags
39	- Console output: Changed log timestamp format to ISO 8601
40	- Performance: Reduced startup latency by deferring SQLite file creation
41	- Bug fixes: Fixed database file creation when run in read-only directory
42	```
43	
44	### Grouping by Category
45	
46	Within each release section, group entries by category using a second-level heading for each category present:
47	
48	```markdown
49	### Bug Fixes
50	- Fixed issue with service shutdown on Windows
51	- Resolved incorrect path handling for relative SQLite file locations
52	
53	### Documentation
54	- Added quickstart guide to docs/
55	- Updated all internal references from /tmp to %TEMP%
56	
57	### Packaging
58	- Bumped minimum Python version from 3.8 to 3.9
59	```
60	
61	This grouping makes it easy for maintainers and users to scan for the type of change they care about.
62	
63	## Version Numbering Integration
64	
65	See [Version Numbering Scheme](version-numbering.md) for the semantic versioning scheme used by oauthsvc. Changelog entries map logically to commits or cohesive changes, but releases are tagged only at certain version milestones.
66	
67	When preparing a release:

# Changelog Conventions

**Title:** Changelog Conventions  
**Version:** 2.1  
**Owner:** Documentation Guild (Sana Iqbal)  
**Last updated:** 2025-01-20

## Overview

This page describes the conventions used when writing changelog entries for oauthsvc releases. It covers the structure of changelog entries, the relationship to version numbering, how to organize entries for a release, and reference material about what has shipped in past releases.

## Changelog Entry Structure

Each changelog entry should follow a consistent format to keep our release timeline clear and scannable. Entries are organized chronologically within a release section, newest changes first.

### Format and Style

A changelog entry consists of:

- **Category**: One of the following (use bullets or numbers consistently within a release):
  - **Documentation** — updates to the markdown files in `docs/`, parameter documentation, or README files
  - **Packaging** — changes to the setup scripts, distribution metadata, or how the package is built
  - **Command help** — changes to output produced by command-line flags like `--help`
  - **Console output** — changes to log messages, status output, or formatted text written to stdout or stderr
  - **Performance** — speed improvements, reduced memory use, or other efficiency gains
  - **Bug fixes** — fixes to the loopback HTTP service behavior, SQLite database interactions, or command-line parsing
  - **Other** — miscellaneous items that don't fit above

- **Area**: Where the change applies (optional, but recommended). Examples: "service startup", "configuration parsing", "database initialization"

- **Summary**: A brief, past-tense description (50–100 characters, no period)

Examples of well-formed entries:

```
- Documentation: Clarified payload schema in HTTP API reference
- Packaging: Updated setup script to require Python 3.9+
- Command help: Improved descriptions in --help output for loopback flags
- Console output: Changed log timestamp format to ISO 8601
- Performance: Reduced startup latency by deferring SQLite file creation
- Bug fixes: Fixed database file creation when run in read-only directory
```

### Grouping by Category

Within each release section, group entries by category using a second-level heading for each category present:

```markdown
### Bug Fixes
- Fixed issue with service shutdown on Windows
- Resolved incorrect path handling for relative SQLite file locations

### Documentation
- Added quickstart guide to docs/
- Updated all internal references from /tmp to %TEMP%

### Packaging
- Bumped minimum Python version from 3.8 to 3.9
```

This grouping makes it easy for maintainers and users to scan for the type of change they care about.

## Version Numbering Integration

See [Version Numbering Scheme](version-numbering.md) for the semantic versioning scheme used by oauthsvc. Changelog entries map logically to commits or cohesive changes, but releases are tagged only at certain version milestones.

When preparing a release:

1. Identify the new version number using the scheme in version-numbering.md
2. Create or update a new release section in CHANGELOG.md (or CHANGES.txt, depending on which the team is currently maintaining)
3. Move all unreleased entries into the dated release section
4. Add the release date in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD)

## Release Notes vs. Changelog

- **Changelog** (maintained in the repository at `CHANGELOG.md` or `CHANGES.txt`): A detailed, technical log of every change per release, grouped by category. Intended for developers and maintainers following development closely.
  
- **Release notes** (stored in `release-notes/release-notes-v*.md` or `.txt`): A curated summary aimed at end users and integrators, highlighting major changes, improvements, and migration guidance. May combine multiple changelog entries or reword them for clarity.

The release notes folder contains:
- `release-notes/README.md` — index of all release note documents  
- `release-notes/release-notes-v1.0.0.txt` — original release (plaintext format)
- `release-notes/release-notes-v1.1.0.txt` — minor update
- `release-notes/release-notes-v1.2.0.md` — first switch to markdown format
- `release-notes/release-notes-v2.0.0.md` — major version release

## Past Release Coverage

### v1.0.0 (2024-04-02)

First stable release. Details in `release-notes-v1.0.0.txt`.

- Initial documentation suite in `docs/`
- Command-line help text for core flags and main entry points
- Console output standardized on newline-delimited format
- Service startup on localhost with configurable port
- SQLite file initialization on first run

### v1.1.0 (2024-08-15)

Incremental improvements. See `release-notes-v1.1.0.txt`.

- Documentation expanded for config file format and schema interpretation
- Help text improved for multi-word flags, making descriptions clearer
- Console log output now includes millisecond precision in timestamps
- Packaging simplified; dropped support for Python versions below 3.8
- Improved error messages when SQLite file is corrupted or unreadable

### v1.2.0 (2025-02-27)

Refinements to startup and documentation. Documented in `release-notes-v1.2.0.md`.

- Docs reorganized under major headings; new operational guide added
- Help text made consistent across all entry points and flags
- Log format updated to use ISO 8601 timestamps throughout
- Build process simplified; setup script made more portable across Windows and POSIX
- Performance improvement: reduced time to open and attach SQLite file on startup

### v2.0.0 (2025-12-09)

Major version with significant internal restructuring. Refer to `release-notes-v2.0.0.md`.

- Documentation completely rewritten for new architecture
- Help text updated for clarity and consistency
- Console output redesigned for both machine and human readability
- Packaging overhauled; now produces wheel distributions in addition to source tarball
- Speed improvements in service startup and steady-state operation; see [Speed Notes Across Releases](speed-notes.md)

## Files and Paths

| File or Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `CHANGELOG.md` | Master record of all changes per release; maintained during development |
| `CHANGES.txt` | Alternate name used in early releases before switching to markdown |
| `README.md` | Project overview; includes link to release notes folder |
| `docs/` | User-facing documentation; changes logged under "Documentation" category |
| `docs/config.md` | Configuration file format reference; updates tracked in changelog |
| `docs/http-api.md` | HTTP service API reference; all changes documented |
| `release-notes/README.md` | Index and guide for all release note documents |
| `release-notes/release-notes-v*.md` or `.txt` | Per-release user-facing summary and highlights |
| `release-notes/changelog-conventions.md` | This file; conventions for writing changelog entries |
| `release-notes/version-numbering.md` | Version scheme and semantic versioning rules |
| `release-notes/release-checklist.md` | Procedural checklist for executing a release |
| `release-notes/packaging-guide.rst` | How to prepare and validate the source distribution |
| `release-notes/building-source-distribution.rst` | Detailed build commands and process flow |
| `release-notes/console-log-format-notes.md` | Standards for console and log output formatting |
| `release-notes/command-help-text-style.md` | Writing and formatting conventions for help text |
| `release-notes/speed-notes.md` | Performance tracking and improvements across releases |
| `.git/tags/` | Git tags mark release points (e.g., `v2.0.0`) |
| `scripts/` | Release automation and build helper scripts |

## Tools and Versions

| Tool or Library | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.9+ (as of v1.1.0) | Runtime environment for service and CLI |
| SQLite | bundled in stdlib | Local state storage and database engine |
| Standard Library modules | N/A | HTTP, argument parsing, file I/O, JSON |
| git | any recent | Repository management and release tagging |
| Markdown or reStructuredText | N/A | Documentation authoring format |

**Note:** The packaging-guide.rst file mentions Python 3.8, but support was dropped in v1.1.0. Current minimum is 3.9; see version-numbering.md for the absolute latest requirements.

## Terminology and Glossary

**Changelog**: The detailed, versioned list of all changes made in each release, grouped by category (documentation, packaging, command help, console output, performance, bug fixes, other). Stored in the repository and maintained throughout development.

**Release**: A tagged, numbered version of oauthsvc made available for installation and use. Identified by a semantic version string (e.g., v2.0.0, v1.2.0).

**Release notes**: A curated, user-focused summary of what changed in a release, written for end users and integrators. Stored as individual files in `release-notes/` and typically less technical and more concise than the changelog.

**Semantic versioning**: A versioning scheme using the format MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where MAJOR changes signal breaking changes, MINOR indicates new features or improvements, and PATCH covers bug fixes and minor updates. Defined in version-numbering.md.

**Entry**: A single line or bullet point in a changelog, describing one logical change or fix.

**Category**: The type or domain of a change: documentation, packaging, command help, console output, performance, bug fixes, or other.

**Unreleased**: Changes merged into the main development branch that have not yet been assigned to a release version number.

**Source distribution** (sdist): A compressed package (typically `.tar.gz`) containing the source code, setup files, and packaging metadata, suitable for building and installation.

**Console output**: Text written by the service or command-line tools to stdout or stderr, including log messages, status information, and diagnostic output.

## Worked Example: Preparing a Release

Suppose we are preparing to release v1.3.0. The CHANGELOG.md currently contains:

```markdown
# Changelog

## Unreleased

- Documentation: Rewrote quickstart guide for better clarity
- Packaging: Added Python 3.11 and 3.12 to CI matrix
- Command help: Expanded flag descriptions for edge cases
- Console output: Added timestamps to service connection events
- Performance: Reduced service startup time by 12%

## v1.2.0 (2025-02-27)

- Documentation: ...
```

To release v1.3.0:

1. Refer to [Release Checklist](release-checklist.md) to confirm all prerequisites are met.
2. Update CHANGELOG.md, converting "Unreleased" into a dated v1.3.0 section with categories:

```markdown
# Changelog

## v1.3.0 (2025-09-27)

### Documentation
- Rewrote quickstart guide for better clarity

### Packaging
- Added Python 3.11 and 3.12 to CI matrix

### Command Help
- Expanded flag descriptions for edge cases

### Console Output
- Added timestamps to service connection events

### Performance
- Reduced service startup time by 12%

## v1.2.0 (2025-02-27)
```

3. Create a new file `release-notes/release-notes-v1.3.0.md` with a user-focused summary (fewer entries, more context for readers).
4. Commit the changes and tag the commit with `git tag v1.3.0`.
5. Build the source distribution following the steps in [Building the Source Distribution](building-source-distribution.rst).
6. Upload or publish according to your deployment process.

## Page Change Log

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-01-20 | 2.1 | v2.1 | Sana Iqbal | Clarified the distinction between changelog and release notes; expanded worked example |
| 2024-12-15 | 2.0 | v2.0 | Sana Iqbal | Restructured sections for consistency; updated v1.2.0 and v2.0.0 release descriptions |
| 2024-10-01 | 1.2 | v1.2 | Sana Iqbal | Added "Tools and Versions" table; expanded glossary with eight terms |
| 2024-08-20 | 1.1 | v1.1 | Sana Iqbal | Fixed formatting issues; clarified category grouping rules |
| 2024-07-05 | 1.0 | v1.0 | Documentation Guild | Initial publication and adoption |
| 2024-06-15 | 0.9 | (unreleased) | Theo Banks | Proposed structure and format for changelog conventions |

## Related Pages

- [Release Notes Folder Index](README.md) — overview and navigation guide to all release documentation

7	summary: This page shows the field layout used for individual changelog entries in the release notes for oauthsvc.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Overview
12	
13	Each release of oauthsvc maintains a corresponding release notes file that documents changes made since the previous version. This page specifies the canonical structure for individual changelog entries within those release notes. All entries follow a consistent format to ensure clarity during release planning and for users reviewing what changed between versions.
14	
15	Changelog entries are the primary mechanism by which the team communicates modifications to the package. Unlike the release checklist, which guides the mechanics of packaging and deployment, these entries form the user-facing record of what was actually changed.
16	
17	**Coverage:** This page covers entry structure only. For broader conventions about tone, categorization, and writing style, see *Changelog Conventions*. For version numbering that drives when entries are created, see *Version Numbering Scheme*.
18	
19	---
20	
21	## Changelog Entry Fields
22	
23	### Standard Field Set
24	
25	Every changelog entry must include the following fields:
26	
27	- **version**: The semantic version identifier applied at release time.
28	- **release_date**: The date the version was tagged and released (YYYY-MM-DD format).
29	- **category**: One of `Documentation`, `Packaging`, `Command Help`, `Console Logging`, or `Performance`.
30	- **summary**: A one-line description of what changed, written in past tense.
31	- **description**: Expanded details, typically 2–4 sentences, explaining the impact and context.
32	- **related_files**: A list of files modified by this change (internal reference only; not shown in user-facing release notes).
33	- **authors**: Names of team members who contributed to this entry's changes. Use first name and last initial (e.g., "Theo B.").
34	
35	### Optional Fields
36	
37	- **breaking_change**: Boolean flag. Set to `true` only if this entry documents a backward-incompatible change affecting users of the command line or service API.
38	- **deprecation_notice**: Text describing a feature or behavior that will be removed in a future release.
39	- **migration_notes**: Instructions for users to adapt to this change.
40	
41	---
42	
43	## Entry Field Definitions
44	
45	**version**
46	The semantic version tag (e.g., `1.2.0`, `2.0.0`) assigned at release. Must match the version string recorded in the source tree and Git tag. See *Version Numbering Scheme* for the versioning convention.
47	
48	**release_date**
49	The calendar date when the Git tag was created and the package was released. Format: `YYYY-MM-DD`. This date should match the commit timestamp of the release commit, allowing readers to correlate release notes with Git records. Dates should be in UTC.
50	
51	**category**
52	The type of change being documented. Accepted values are:
53	- `Documentation`: Changes to README files, internal wiki pages, or user-facing documentation that do not affect package behavior.
54	- `Packaging`: Modifications to the source distribution, wheel contents, or package metadata (setup configuration, manifest, etc.).
55	- `Command Help`: Updates to command-line help text, flag descriptions, or usage messages shown in console output.
56	- `Console Logging`: Changes to the format, verbosity, or content of messages written to stdout or stderr by the service or CLI.
57	- `Performance`: Improvements to speed, memory usage, or startup time; reductions in file size or network bandwidth.
58	
59	No entry should document changes that fall outside these categories. If a change feels like it belongs elsewhere, it is out of bounds for this release notes series.
60	
61	**summary**
62	A single sentence (under 80 characters) describing what changed, written in past tense. Examples:
63	- "Updated help text for the session command to clarify required arguments."
64	- "Reduced package tarball size by 15% through dependency optimization."
65	- "Standardized console log timestamps to ISO 8601 format."
66	
67	Avoid jargon; assume the reader is not a developer on the oauthsvc team.
68	
69	**description**
70	A paragraph expanding on the summary, providing context about why the change was made, how it affects users, and any relevant implementation details. Keep to 2–4 sentences. If migration steps are needed, mention that migration notes are provided separately (in the optional field).
71	
72	Example:
73	```
74	The command help text for the status operation has been rewritten to clarify which arguments are required and which are optional. Previously, users often omitted required flags, leading to confusing error messages. The new help output uses bold formatting and bullet lists to improve readability on terminals that support ANSI text styling.
75	```
76	
77	**related_files**
78	A YAML list of file paths relative to the repository root that were modified to implement this change. Example:
79	
80	This field is for internal tracking and is not included in user-facing release notes files. It helps the release engineer verify that all changes have been captured and aids in backport determinations.
81	
82	**authors**
83	A YAML list of first name and last initial for each contributor. Example:
84	```yaml
85	authors:
86	  - Theo B.
87	  - Sana I.
88	```

---
title: Changelog Entry Format
version: "1.0"
owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks)
last_updated: "2026-06-01"

summary: This page shows the field layout used for individual changelog entries in the release notes for oauthsvc.

---

## Overview

Each release of oauthsvc maintains a corresponding release notes file that documents changes made since the previous version. This page specifies the canonical structure for individual changelog entries within those release notes. All entries follow a consistent format to ensure clarity during release planning and for users reviewing what changed between versions.

Changelog entries are the primary mechanism by which the team communicates modifications to the package. Unlike the release checklist, which guides the mechanics of packaging and deployment, these entries form the user-facing record of what was actually changed.

**Coverage:** This page covers entry structure only. For broader conventions about tone, categorization, and writing style, see *Changelog Conventions*. For version numbering that drives when entries are created, see *Version Numbering Scheme*.

---

## Changelog Entry Fields

### Standard Field Set

Every changelog entry must include the following fields:

- **version**: The semantic version identifier applied at release time.
- **release_date**: The date the version was tagged and released (YYYY-MM-DD format).
- **category**: One of `Documentation`, `Packaging`, `Command Help`, `Console Logging`, or `Performance`.
- **summary**: A one-line description of what changed, written in past tense.
- **description**: Expanded details, typically 2–4 sentences, explaining the impact and context.
- **related_files**: A list of files modified by this change (internal reference only; not shown in user-facing release notes).
- **authors**: Names of team members who contributed to this entry's changes. Use first name and last initial (e.g., "Theo B.").

### Optional Fields

- **breaking_change**: Boolean flag. Set to `true` only if this entry documents a backward-incompatible change affecting users of the command line or service API.
- **deprecation_notice**: Text describing a feature or behavior that will be removed in a future release.
- **migration_notes**: Instructions for users to adapt to this change.

---

## Entry Field Definitions

**version**
The semantic version tag (e.g., `1.2.0`, `2.0.0`) assigned at release. Must match the version string recorded in the source tree and Git tag. See *Version Numbering Scheme* for the versioning convention.

**release_date**
The calendar date when the Git tag was created and the package was released. Format: `YYYY-MM-DD`. This date should match the commit timestamp of the release commit, allowing readers to correlate release notes with Git records. Dates should be in UTC.

**category**
The type of change being documented. Accepted values are:
- `Documentation`: Changes to README files, internal wiki pages, or user-facing documentation that do not affect package behavior.
- `Packaging`: Modifications to the source distribution, wheel contents, or package metadata (setup configuration, manifest, etc.).
- `Command Help`: Updates to command-line help text, flag descriptions, or usage messages shown in console output.
- `Console Logging`: Changes to the format, verbosity, or content of messages written to stdout or stderr by the service or CLI.
- `Performance`: Improvements to speed, memory usage, or startup time; reductions in file size or network bandwidth.

No entry should document changes that fall outside these categories. If a change feels like it belongs elsewhere, it is out of bounds for this release notes series.

**summary**
A single sentence (under 80 characters) describing what changed, written in past tense. Examples:
- "Updated help text for the session command to clarify required arguments."
- "Reduced package tarball size by 15% through dependency optimization."
- "Standardized console log timestamps to ISO 8601 format."

Avoid jargon; assume the reader is not a developer on the oauthsvc team.

**description**
A paragraph expanding on the summary, providing context about why the change was made, how it affects users, and any relevant implementation details. Keep to 2–4 sentences. If migration steps are needed, mention that migration notes are provided separately (in the optional field).

Example:
```
The command help text for the status operation has been rewritten to clarify which arguments are required and which are optional. Previously, users often omitted required flags, leading to confusing error messages. The new help output uses bold formatting and bullet lists to improve readability on terminals that support ANSI text styling.
```

**related_files**
A YAML list of file paths relative to the repository root that were modified to implement this change. Example:

This field is for internal tracking and is not included in user-facing release notes files. It helps the release engineer verify that all changes have been captured and aids in backport determinations.

**authors**
A YAML list of first name and last initial for each contributor. Example:
```yaml
authors:
  - Theo B.
  - Sana I.
```

**breaking_change**
Set to `true` if this entry documents a change that breaks backward compatibility. For example, if a command-line flag is renamed or removed, set this to `true`. If `true`, you must provide migration notes explaining how users should update their workflows.

**deprecation_notice**
A sentence or short paragraph indicating that a feature or behavior is being phased out. This should be included if you are warning users that something will be removed in a future release but is still supported now. Example:
```
The --legacy-format flag is deprecated and will be removed in oauthsvc 3.0. Please migrate to --modern-format before then.
```

**migration_notes**
Step-by-step guidance for users to adapt to this change. Use this when a change requires action on the user's part. Example:
```
If you have scripts that rely on the old console log format, update your log parsing logic to handle timestamps in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS) instead of the previous Unix timestamp format. Validate parsing against a staging instance before deploying to production.
```

---

## Example Entries

### Documentation Change

```yaml
- version: "1.2.0"
  release_date: "2025-02-27"
  category: Documentation
  summary: "Clarified database initialization steps in README."
  description: >
    The README.md file was updated to provide clearer instructions for setting up the local SQLite database on first run. The new instructions include sample shell commands and expected output, reducing confusion for new users deploying the service locally.
  related_files:
    - README.md
  authors:
    - Mara O.
  breaking_change: false
```

8	
9	## Overview
10	
11	The command-line help text interface is the primary documentation surface for users of the oauthsvc package. This style guide establishes consistency across all command-line help output, ensuring that the tool remains discoverable, predictable, and accessible to users at all experience levels. Help text appears when users invoke the service with the `--help` flag and serves as real-time reference material for command syntax and behavior.
12	
13	This guide coordinates with the package's broader release process to ensure that help text changes are tracked in version numbers, documented in changelogs, and validated before release. It defines the standards developers and documentarians must apply before any release is cut, and it serves as the reference authority for adding new commands or modifying existing help text.
14	
15	## Coverage and Application
16	
17	This guide applies to all help text generated by the command-line interface of oauthsvc, including:
18	
19	- Summary descriptions of available commands
20	- Usage lines showing required and optional parameters
21	- Detailed explanations of command behavior and side effects
22	- Examples of typical invocation patterns
23	- Guidance on argument and option syntax
24	- Error messages and feedback from input validation
25	
26	The guide explicitly does not cover:
27	
28	- The package's HTTP service interface or request formatting
29	- Logging output sent to console or files (see console-log-format-notes.md instead)
30	- Internal documentation of modules or functions
31	- Database schema or field-level documentation
32	- Installation or configuration instructions beyond what appears in help text itself
33	
34	## Help Text Format Standards
35	
36	**Owner: Documentation Guild (Sana Iqbal)**
37	
38	### Line Length and Wrapping
39	
40	Help text must not exceed 88 characters per line when displayed in a standard terminal window. This limit accommodates users working in constrained display environments while maintaining readability in wider windows. Wrap longer descriptions at word boundaries; avoid breaking words or using hyphenation.
41	
42	For multi-line descriptions, align continuation lines consistently. The most common pattern is to indent continuation lines to column 4, or to column 24 when aligning with the start of preceding text:
43	
44	```
45	--verbose, -v           Enable verbose output to the console when the
46	                        service is running or when processing state
47	```
48	
49	### Verb and Tone
50	
51	Use imperative mood for action-oriented commands directed at the user. Examples:
52	
53	- "Start the service"
54	- "Configure the host location"
55	- "Initialize the database"
56	- "Display current state"
57	
58	For descriptive help text explaining what a command or option does, use present tense in the third person:
59	
60	- "Shows the current status"
61	- "Enables automatic reconnection"
62	- "Sets the output format"
63	- "Reads from the database file"
64	
65	Tone should be direct, professional, and unambiguous. Avoid colloquialisms, exclamation points (except within code examples), rhetorical questions, and overly casual phrasing. Help text is read quickly and under pressure; clarity takes precedence over personality.
66	
67	### Argument and Option Naming
68	
69	Maintain consistent naming patterns throughout help text:
70	
71	- **Command names:** lowercase, hyphenated (e.g., `run-service`, `show-config`, `init-db`)
72	- **Argument placeholders:** UPPERCASE with underscores (e.g., `HOST_ADDRESS`, `PORT_NUMBER`, `DATABASE_FILE`)
73	- **Boolean flags:** long form with `--` prefix, single-letter shortcuts with single `-` (e.g., `--verbose, -v`)
74	- **Options requiring values:** indicate with `=VALUE` syntax or space-separated notation (e.g., `--host=HOST_ADDRESS` or `--host HOST_ADDRESS`)
75	
76	Single-letter shortcuts should appear on the same line as their long form, separated by a comma and space.
77	
78	### Organization of Help Text
79	
80	Structure help output in this consistent order:
81	
82	1. **Usage line(s)** — Show the command name, required arguments, and optional elements in square brackets
83	2. **Brief description** — One sentence, 50–80 characters, capturing the primary purpose
84	3. **Detailed description** — Explain behavior, preconditions, and side effects (if non-obvious)
85	4. **Arguments section** — List positional arguments with descriptions (if any)
86	5. **Options section** — List all flags and named options with descriptions
87	6. **Examples section** — Provide 1–3 typical invocation patterns
88	
89	Separate each section with a blank line. Use consistent indentation: typically 2 spaces for section headers and 4 spaces for content within sections.
90	
91	## Changelog and Version Integration
92	
93	**Owner: Release Engineering (Priya Chandran)**
94	
95	All modifications to help text must be documented in the changelog before a release is cut. Our version numbering scheme uses semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Changes to help text typically affect only the patch component, unless the changes represent new commands (minor version increment) or breaking changes to command syntax (major version increment).
96	
97	For detailed version numbering rules, see version-numbering.md. In brief:
98	
99	- **Major version** increments indicate removal of commands or breaking changes to command syntax
100	- **Minor version** increments indicate new commands or significant new options added to existing commands
101	- **Patch version** increments cover improvements to help text, reordering of options, formatting fixes, and clarifications
102	
103	Each changelog entry must name the version being released and specify which commands are affected. When multiple changes affect the same command, they should be consolidated into a single entry per version. Changelog entries follow the format defined in changelog-conventions.md and changelog-entry-format.yaml.
104	
105	Before a release, verify that:
106	
107	- All help text changes since the previous release have changelog entries
108	- Each entry is assigned to the correct version number
109	- Entries are organized chronologically (newest first)
110	- No entries are marked as incomplete or under review
111	
112	## Release Checklist Integration
113	
114	**Owner: Release Engineering (Priya Chandran)**
115	
116	Help text consistency is part of the pre-release verification process. The checklist in release-checklist.md includes these help text–specific items:
117	
118	- [ ] All command help text conforms to this style guide
119	- [ ] No help text exceeds the 88-character line length limit
120	- [ ] Verb tense and tone are consistent across all commands
121	- [ ] Argument names are lowercase and hyphenated; placeholders are uppercase
122	- [ ] All options and arguments appear in the help text
123	- [ ] Examples (if present) are valid and representative
124	- [ ] Changelog entries describe all help text changes
125	- [ ] Version number has been incremented according to the versioning scheme
126	- [ ] Release notes have been generated and include help text updates
127	- [ ] At least one reviewer has signed off on help text changes
128	
129	These items must be checked before the source distribution is built and released. Failing to verify help text consistency can lead to confusion among users and may delay release finalization.
130	
131	## Integration with Source Distribution
132	
133	Help text is embedded directly in the package binary and does not depend on external files or configuration. When building the source distribution:
134	
135	- All help text strings are compiled into the package during build
136	- No external help text files, man pages, or documentation files are required
137	- The package depends only on the Python standard library (no external documentation libraries)
138	- Help text is immediately available upon installation, with no additional setup steps
139	
140	The source distribution build process is detailed in building-source-distribution.rst. The packaging guide (packaging-guide.rst) specifies which files are included in distributions and how help text is validated as part of the build. After a source distribution is built, verify the help text by running the command-line interface with the `--help` flag and confirming that output matches the documented format.
141	
142	## Worked Examples
143	
144	### Example 1: Simple Command with Options
145	
146	```
147	Usage: run-service [OPTIONS]
148	
149	Start the loopback HTTP service. The service listens on the configured
150	host and port and maintains state in the local database file.
151	
152	Options:
153	  --host HOST_LOCATION     Listen on this host location (default: 127.0.0.1)
154	  --port PORT_NUMBER      Listen on this port (default: 8080)
155	  --verbose, -v           Enable verbose logging to the console
156	  --help                  Show this help message and exit
157	```
158	
159	### Example 2: Command with Positional Arguments
160	
161	```
162	Usage: read-state DATABASE_FILE [OPTIONS]
163	
164	Display the current state stored in the database file. Output is
165	formatted according to the selected format option.
166	
167	Arguments:
168	  DATABASE_FILE           Path to the SQLite database file
169	
170	Options:
171	  --format {json,text}    Output format (default: text)
172	  --limit ROW_COUNT       Limit output to this many rows
173	  --help                  Show this help message and exit
174	```
175	
176	### Example 3: Multi-line Description with Examples
177	
178	```
179	Usage: init-db [OPTIONS] DATABASE_FILE
180	
181	Initialize a new database file for use with the service. If the
182	specified file already exists, it will not be modified. The database
183	schema is created with default settings suitable for most deployments.
184	
185	Arguments:
186	  DATABASE_FILE           Path where the new database file will be
187	                          created
188	
189	Options:
190	  --schema-version VERSION Use this schema version (default: current)
191	  --help                  Show this help message and exit
192	
193	Examples:
194	  init-db /var/lib/oauthsvc/state.db
195	  init-db --schema-version=2.0 ./state.db
196	```
197	
198	## Terminology and Glossary
199	
200	**Argument notation:** A UPPERCASE identifier in help text representing a value the user must supply. Examples: `DATABASE_FILE`, `HOST_LOCATION`, `PORT_NUMBER`. Distinguishes user-supplied values from literal command names.
201	
202	**Brief description:** The single-sentence summary appearing after the usage line in help text. Must be 50–80 characters and capture the command's primary purpose without qualification or examples.
203	
204	**Changelog entry:** A line or paragraph in the changelog documenting a change to help text, the command affected, and the version in which the change appears. See changelog-conventions.md for format details.
205	
206	**Command name:** The primary identifier used to invoke a command from the command line. Always lowercase and hyphenated in this package. Examples: `run-service`, `show-config`, `init-db`.
207	
208	**Continuation line:** A line of help text that continues from a previous line, typically indented to align with the start of the previous line's descriptive text, usually at column 4 or column 24.
209	
210	**Detailed description:** The longer explanation of what a command does, including preconditions, side effects, or unusual behavior. Appears in help text after the brief description and before argument/option sections.
211	
212	**Option:** A flag or named parameter that modifies command behavior or supplies data. Prefixed with `--` (long form) or `-` (single-letter shortcut). Examples: `--verbose`, `--host=HOST_ADDRESS`, `-v`.
213	
214	**Positional argument:** A parameter identified by its position on the command line rather than by a flag name. Typically required for most commands; optional arguments appear in square brackets in the usage line.
215	
216	**Semantic versioning:** A version numbering scheme using the format MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH where changes to help text typically affect only the PATCH component, new commands affect MINOR, and breaking syntax changes affect MAJOR.
217	
218	**Style guide:** This document, establishing standards for formatting, tone, and organization of all help text in the package.
219	
220	**Usage line:** The first line of help text showing the command name, required positional arguments, and optional elements (in square brackets). Sets expectations for how the user should invoke the command.

**Version:** v1.3.0  
**Owner:** Documentation Guild (Sana Iqbal)

**Summary:** This page sets the style guide for command help text shown by the package.

## Overview
