# Editor Configuration

**Version:** v1.2.0
**Owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Banks)
**Last updated:** 2024-09-14

**Summary:** Describes recommended editor settings and extensions for working comfortably in the oauthsvc codebase.

This page is the third stop most new contributors make after cloning the repository, right after they've gotten a working interpreter and before they open their first pull request. It assumes you've already been through [Workstation Setup](workstation-setup.md) and have a Python interpreter that satisfies [Supported Python Versions](python-version-support.md). If you haven't done either of those yet, stop here and go do them first — the settings below assume a working virtual environment already exists at the repository root.

## Purpose and Audience

oauthsvc is a small, standard-library-only package, but the codebase has accumulated enough conventions over the last two years that an unconfigured editor will produce noisy diffs, inconsistent import ordering, and line-length disagreements that show up as review comments instead of being caught locally. This page exists so that those comments happen less often. It is aimed at:

* people who are new to the repository and setting up an editor for the first time,
* people switching editors (VS Code to PyCharm, or vice versa),
* anyone whose diffs keep getting flagged for whitespace or import-order issues in review.

It does **not** cover workstation provisioning (see [Workstation Setup](workstation-setup.md)) or which interpreter versions are acceptable (see [Supported Python Versions](python-version-support.md)). It also does not restate the actual style rules — those live in [Coding Style Guide](coding-style-guide.md) — this page is concerned with getting your editor to enforce those rules automatically rather than relying on you to remember them.

## Prerequisites (Section owner: Theo Banks)

Before configuring an editor, confirm the following:

1. You have cloned the repository and can see `oauthsvc/` and `README.md` at the top level.
2. You have created and activated a virtual environment as described in Workstation Setup.
3. Your interpreter satisfies the minimum version documented in Supported Python Versions (v1.6) — the project currently targets the same floor described there, though double-check the sibling page since interpreter floors move roughly twice a year.
4. You have git installed and configured with your name and a working contact string for commit attribution (not necessarily the same one you use elsewhere).

If any of these are missing, this page will not help you — editor extensions assume a working interpreter and a git identity are already in place.

## Recommended Editor: VS Code (Section owner: Theo Banks)

VS Code is the editor most of the team uses day to day, and it's the one this page documents in the most depth. Nothing here is mandatory — see the "Alternate Editors" section below if you use something else — but the VS Code setup is the one that new-contributor issues get triaged against first, simply because it's what most reviewers can reproduce quickly.

### Installing the Extensions

Open a terminal at the repository root and run:

```
code --install-extension ms-python.python
code --install-extension ms-python.vscode-pylance
code --install-extension charliermarsh.ruff
code --install-extension editorconfig.editorconfig
code --install-extension eamodio.gitlens
code --install-extension alexcvzz.vscode-sqlite
```

The last one is for browsing the local database file the service uses to keep its state (see [Local Database File Notes](local-database-file-notes.md)); it is optional but strongly recommended once you start touching anything that reads or writes that file, since stepping through a debugger without a way to look at the file's contents on disk gets old fast.

### The Workspace Settings File

Create or edit `.vscode/settings.json` at the repository root. This file is not currently checked into version control — contributors are expected to create their own copy locally, though there has been informal talk of committing a shared one once the linting rules stabilize. A reasonable starting point:

```json
{
    "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/python",
    "editor.formatOnSave": true,
    "editor.rulers": [88],
    "editor.tabSize": 4,
    "editor.insertSpaces": true,
    "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
    "files.insertFinalNewline": true,
    "python.linting.enabled": true,
    "[python]": {
        "editor.defaultFormatter": "charliermarsh.ruff",
        "editor.codeActionsOnSave": {
            "source.organizeImports": true,
            "source.fixAll": true
        }
    }
}
```

Two things worth calling out:

- On Windows, `python.defaultInterpreterPath` should point at `.venv\Scripts\python.exe` instead — see [Windows Setup Notes](windows-setup-notes.rst) for the platform-specific path separators, which trip people up more often than you'd expect.
- The ruler is set to 88, matching the line-length convention documented in the Coding Style Guide (v3.4). Some older branches were written against a 79-column limit, so don't be surprised if you see a mix of wrapping styles in files that haven't been touched recently.

### Recommended, Not Required, Extensions

* GitLens — inline blame annotations, useful when trying to understand why a particular line looks the way it does before you change it.
* Better Comments — cosmetic, purely a personal preference, several team members use it, nobody minds either way.
* Todo Tree — surfaces `TODO` and `FIXME` markers across the tree; handy in a repository this size where such markers tend to accumulate.
* SQLite Viewer (the `alexcvzz.vscode-sqlite` extension mentioned above) — lets you open the local database file directly from the editor's file explorer without shelling out to a separate viewer.

None of these are enforced. If your PR diff looks the same as everyone else's, nobody is going to ask what extensions you have installed.

## Alternate Editors: PyCharm and Vim (Section owner: Theo Banks)

Not everyone uses VS Code, and that's fine, provided the output matches what the formatter and linter would have produced anyway.

**PyCharm** — Community Edition is sufficient; nothing in oauthsvc requires the paid edition's features. Under Settings → Editor → Code Style → Python, set the line length to 88 to match the ruler above, and under Settings → Tools → File Watchers, add a watcher that runs the formatter on save (see the "Linting and Formatting Integration" section for the exact command). PyCharm's built-in inspections are looser than the project's ruff configuration in a few places, so treat PyCharm's inline warnings as a hint, not a source of truth — the ruff run in CI is what actually gates a merge.

**Vim / Neovim** — several people on the team use a plugin-managed setup with an LSP integration pointed at Pylance or `pyright`, plus `ale` or `null-ls` wired up to run the formatter on save. There is no shared dotfile for this; ask around in the team channel if you want a starting point, someone usually has one they're willing to share. Whatever bindings you use for "format buffer" and "organize imports," make sure they're wired to the same underlying tool as everyone else, since that's the only thing that actually matters for diff cleanliness.

Whichever editor you land on, the acceptance check is simple: run the formatter from the command line against a file you've edited and confirm your editor didn't leave anything different behind. If it did, your editor configuration is the thing that's wrong, not the file.

## The EditorConfig File

The repository root includes a `.editorconfig` file that most editors pick up automatically once the EditorConfig extension (or built-in support, in PyCharm's case) is installed. It looks roughly like this:

```
root = true

[*]
charset = utf-8
end_of_line = lf
insert_final_newline = true
trim_trailing_whitespace = true
indent_style = space
indent_size = 4

[*.md]
trim_trailing_whitespace = false

[*.yaml]
indent_size = 2
```

The `[*.md]` exception exists because Markdown uses trailing whitespace intentionally for line breaks in a few older documentation pages, and stripping it silently rewrote content in a handbook page a while back. If your editor doesn't respect `.editorconfig` out of the box, install the plugin — don't try to replicate these rules by hand in your own settings file, because they'll drift out of sync with the shared file the next time someone edits it.

## Linting and Formatting Integration (Section owner: Owen Castillo)

The authoritative configuration for linting and formatting lives in [Lint and Formatting Configuration](lint-formatting-config.yaml), currently at v1.0.1. Your editor should be pointed at that file rather than maintaining a parallel set of rules — if your editor's inline warnings ever disagree with what running the formatter from the command line produces, the command line wins, full stop.

To run the formatter manually, from the repository root:

```
scripts/format.sh
```

or, on Windows without a POSIX shell available:

```
powershell -File scripts\format.ps1
```

Both scripts wrap the same underlying tool invocation with the shared configuration file, so the output should be identical either way. If it isn't, that's worth flagging — it usually means one of the two scripts has drifted out of sync with a recent configuration change.

To lint without changing anything:

```
scripts/lint.sh --check
```

Wiring this into your editor as a save-time action (as shown in the VS Code settings snippet earlier) means you rarely need to run these by hand, but it's worth knowing the raw commands exist, because there will be days the editor integration silently stops doing its job — usually after an extension update — and you'll want a way to confirm whether a file is actually clean before you push it up for review.

### A Note on Import Order

The formatter enforces a specific import order (standard library first, then a blank line, then everything else, alphabetized within each group). This occasionally produces diffs that look larger than the actual change, especially in files that haven't had their imports touched in a while. If you're only fixing one line in a file and the formatter wants to reorder ten imports along with it, consider whether that's a separate, smaller change worth making on its own — reviewers tend to appreciate that distinction, even if nothing in [Code Review Conventions](code-review-conventions.md) formally requires it.

## Editor Support for the Local Database File (Section owner: Priya Nandakumar)

The service keeps its state in a local SQLite file, and at some point you will want to look inside it while working on a change. The recommended approach in VS Code is the `alexcvzz.vscode-sqlite` extension mentioned earlier, which adds a SQLite-aware panel to the file explorer — right-click the file and choose "Open Database" to browse it without leaving the editor.

If you'd rather use a standalone tool, the `sqlite3` command-line utility works fine too:

```
sqlite3 -header -column path/to/the/local/database/file
sqlite> .tables
sqlite> .quit
```

A couple of practical notes that come up often enough to write down:

- Open the file in read-only mode if the loopback service might be running at the same time, to avoid a lock conflict between your viewer and the running process. Most SQLite browsers have a read-only toggle somewhere in their connection settings.
- If your editor's file-watcher tries to "helpfully" reload the database file every time it changes on disk, turn that off for this particular file — SQLite files change in ways that aren't meaningful to look at line-by-line, and a watcher constantly reopening the connection just gets in the way.

For anything beyond browsing — understanding the structure of what's stored there — see [Local Database File Notes](local-database-file-notes.md); this page is only concerned with how to look at the file comfortably, not with what's in it.

## Code Review Conventions in the Editor (Section owner: Priya Nandakumar)

[Code Review Conventions](code-review-conventions.md) covers the actual review process end to end; this section only covers the editor-side pieces that make that process smoother.

* **Diff view.** Configure your editor's diff view to ignore whitespace-only changes when comparing branches — most formatter-driven reordering shows up as whitespace noise otherwise, and it obscures the actual content of a change. In VS Code this is under Settings → Diff Editor → Ignore Trim Whitespace.
* **Inline blame.** GitLens (or your editor's built-in equivalent) is useful for understanding why a line looks the way it does before proposing a change to it — reviewers will sometimes ask "why did you change this" when the plain answer is "the formatter did it," and it's worth being able to tell the difference yourself before you push.
* **Comment resolution.** When a reviewer leaves an inline comment through whatever tool your git host uses, resolve it in the same tool rather than only fixing the code and leaving the thread open — several past pull requests have sat with unresolved threads for weeks because the underlying code was fixed but nobody closed the loop on the comment itself.
* **Marking a change ready to merge.** However your git host surfaces this, don't give the go-ahead on your own change — a second set of eyes is the whole point. If you're the one who opened the change, wait for someone else to mark it ready before merging, even for small changes; this has occasionally been skipped for "obvious" fixes and it has occasionally bitten people.

None of this replaces reading Code Review Conventions in full — it's a longer page and covers the actual etiquette expectations (response times, how to phrase a disagreement, when to ask for a second reviewer) that don't belong on an editor-configuration page.

## Commit Message Style Support (Section owner: Owen Castillo)

[Commit Message Style](commit-message-style.md) documents the actual expected format; this section covers how to get your editor and git to help you follow it without having to remember the exact shape every time.

A git commit message template is checked in at `.gitmessage.txt` at the repository root. Point git at it once, locally:

```
git config commit.template .gitmessage.txt
```

The template looks roughly like:

```
# <short summary, imperative mood, 50 chars or fewer>

# <longer explanation, wrapped at 72 characters, if needed>

# Related issue, if any:
```

Most editors with git integration will pick this template up automatically once the config is set — VS Code's built-in Source Control panel shows it as the starting text in the commit message box, and PyCharm's commit dialog does the same. If you're committing from a plain terminal instead, `git commit` (without `-m`) will open the template in whatever editor `core.editor` is set to.

A few conventions worth calling out here specifically because they're easy to get wrong from muscle memory carried over from other projects:

- Use the imperative mood in the summary line ("add," "fix," "adjust," not "added," "fixed," "adjusting").
- Keep the summary line to 50 characters where reasonably possible; git itself won't stop you from going over, but most git hosts truncate the summary in list views past that point, and a truncated summary that doesn't make sense on its own is worse than a slightly longer one.
- Wrap the body at 72 characters — some terminals don't wrap long lines gracefully, and a commit message that reads as one giant unbroken paragraph in `git log` is unpleasant to read months later.
- Reference an issue number if one exists, but don't invent one if it doesn't — an empty template line is fine, a fabricated reference is worse.

If you use an editor plugin that auto-generates commit summaries from staged changes, review what it produces before accepting it — a few past commits have summaries that describe the diff mechanically ("update three files") rather than the actual intent of the change, which is exactly the kind of message this convention is trying to avoid.

## Coding Style Enforcement in the Editor (Section owner: Theo Banks)

[Coding Style Guide](coding-style-guide.md) is the source of truth for the actual rules; this section is about getting your editor to apply them without manual effort.

| Rule | Editor mechanism |
|---|---|
| 88-column line length | ruler + formatter, both configured above |
| 4-space indentation, no tabs | `.editorconfig` |
| Standard-library-first import order | formatter's organize-imports action |
| Trailing whitespace removed | `files.trimTrailingWhitespace` / `.editorconfig` |
| Final newline present | `files.insertFinalNewline` / `.editorconfig` |
| Double quotes preferred over single | formatter default, configurable in the shared lint config |

Two things the table doesn't cover, because they're judgment calls rather than mechanical rules:

- **Naming.** The formatter won't stop you from choosing a bad name. Reviewers will, and it's a common source of review back-and-forth — worth thinking about before you push, not after someone asks.
- **Comment density.** Neither the linter nor the formatter has an opinion on how many comments a function should have. The Coding Style Guide has some general guidance on this; use your judgment and expect it to come up in review from time to time regardless.

If your editor's inline warnings ever contradict the Coding Style Guide directly — for instance, an editor default that wants single quotes when the project convention is double — the project convention wins. Adjust your editor's settings to match, don't adjust the shared configuration file to match your editor.

## Terminology

**Workspace** — the folder VS Code (or another editor) treats as the project root; for this repository, that's wherever you cloned it, containing `oauthsvc/` and `README.md`.

**Linter** — a tool that reads source files and flags style or correctness problems without changing anything; ruff plays this part for acctsvc.

**Formatter** — a tool that rewrites source files in place to match a shared style, as opposed to only flagging problems; also handled by ruff in this project's current configuration.

**Loopback service** — the small HTTP service the package runs against `localhost` for local interaction; mentioned here only because a few editor extensions (particularly the SQLite viewer) behave differently depending on whether it's running.

**Local database file** — the SQLite file the package uses to keep its state; see Local Database File Notes for anything beyond how to open and browse it.

**Extension** — an editor add-on that provides support for a language, tool, or file format; VS Code calls these "extensions," PyCharm calls the equivalent concept a "plugin."

**EditorConfig** — a small, editor-agnostic configuration format (the `.editorconfig` file) that most modern editors read natively or via a plugin, used here to keep indentation and line-ending conventions consistent regardless of which editor someone uses.

**Language server** — a background process that gives an editor features like inline warnings, "go to definition," and auto-completion for a given language; Pylance is the one most commonly used against this codebase.

**Pre-commit hook** — a git-managed script that runs automatically before a commit is created; oauthsvc does not currently ship one, though it has been discussed more than once.

**Diff view** — the side-by-side or inline comparison an editor shows between two versions of a file, used heavily during review.

metadata:
  title: "Lint and Formatting Configuration"
  version: "v1.0.1"
  owner: "Build & Release (Owen Castillo)"
  last_updated: "2026-04-01"
  summary: "Documents the shared linting and formatting configuration values contributors apply to the oauthsvc repository."

overview: |
  The oauthsvc repository enforces a consistent code style through automated linting and formatting tools. All contributors must apply these standards before submitting pull requests. This page documents the configuration, tools, and procedures developers use to maintain code quality.

  The package targets Python 3.8 and later. Linting and formatting are configured to work across Linux, macOS, and Windows workstations, though some tool invocations vary by platform.

python_environment_and_requirements:
  owner: "Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)"
  content: |
    Begin by setting up a development environment with the supported Python versions. Refer to "Supported Python Versions" (v1.7) for the authoritative list; as of 2026-01-20, the package supports Python 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12. Note that while Python 3.8 is supported for runtime, linting and formatting tools used on the development workstation may require Python 3.9 or later—see "Workstation Setup" (v2.4) for guidance on isolation using virtual environments.

    Create a virtual environment for development:

    ```
    python3 -m venv venv-dev
    ```

    On Windows, activate it with:

    ```
    venv-dev\Scripts\activate.bat
    ```

    On Linux and macOS:

    ```
    source venv-dev/bin/activate
    ```

    Install the development dependencies listed in the root directory's requirements file.

configuration_files_and_locations:
  owner: "Build & Release (Owen Castillo)"
  primary_configuration:
    - "pyproject.toml: Contains tool configuration for linting, formatting, and related utilities. This is the source of truth for most settings."
    - "setup.cfg: Legacy configuration file; some tools still reference sections here. When in doubt, check pyproject.toml first."
    - ".editorconfig: Defines basic editor behavior for indentation and line endings across platforms."
  configuration_sections: |
    The `pyproject.toml` file contains several `[tool.*]` sections:

    - [tool.formatter]: Specifies line length (88 characters), quote style (double quotes), and exclude patterns.
    - [tool.linter]: Controls naming conventions, complexity thresholds, and import ordering rules.
    - [tool.coverage]: Not related to linting but co-located with other tool configuration.

    The formatter is configured to ignore certain directories:
    • venv-* (all virtual environments)
    • .git/
    • __pycache__/
    • .pytest_cache/
    • build/ and dist/

    The linter ignores these in addition:
    • docs/ (documentation source)
    • scripts/staging/ (experimental or temporary scripts)

editor_and_ide_setup:
  owner: "Developer Experience (Theo Banks)"
  intro: "Consistent formatting on save improves workflow efficiency. See \"Editor Configuration\" (v1.2.0, updated 2024-09-14) for detailed IDE-specific steps."
  visual_studio_code: |
    Install the appropriate extensions:
    - Python (Microsoft)
    - Code formatting extension

    Configure workspace settings to format on save. Create or modify `.vscode/settings.json` in the repository root.

  pycharm_intellij: |
    Navigate to Settings → Editor → Code Style → Python and enable the built-in formatter integration. Bind a keyboard shortcut to reformat the current file (typically Ctrl+Alt+L on Windows and Linux, Cmd+Alt+L on macOS).

  vim_neovim: |
    Configure your editor to run formatting commands on save using autocmd. neovim users should consider using a language server protocol (LSP) plugin configured to call the formatter on save.

  sublime_text: |
    Use the Build System feature and bind to Ctrl+B. Create `formatter.sublime-build` in the Packages/User directory with a command that invokes the formatter.

linting_and_formatting_tools:
  owner: "Tooling Guild (Dana Kessler)"
  intro: "The following tools are installed and configured in the development environment. The version matrix applies to Python 3.9+. For Python 3.8, certain tools may use fallback versions—consult \"Dependency Management\" (v1.4, updated 2026-02-18) for details."
  tools:
    - name: formatter
      version: "24.1.1"
      purpose: "Code formatting (line length, spacing, quotes)"
      config_file: "pyproject.toml [tool.formatter]"
    - name: linter
      version: "3.9.2"
      purpose: "Static analysis and style checking"
      config_file: "pyproject.toml [tool.linter] setup.cfg"
    - name: sort-imports
      version: "5.13.2"
      purpose: "Import statement ordering"
      config_file: "pyproject.toml [tool.sort-imports]"
    - name: spell-check
      version: "2.3.0"
      purpose: "Docstring and comment spelling"
      config_file: ".spellcheckignore"
    - name: standards-check
      version: "1.7.6"
      purpose: "Identifies common code quality issues"
      config_file: "setup.cfg [quality-check]"

running_linting_and_formatting_locally:
  owner: "Build & Release (Owen Castillo)"
  intro: "Before committing code, developers must run linting and formatting checks. Commands are invoked from the repository root."
  formatting: |
    To format all Python files in the package directory:

    ```
    formatter .
    ```

    To format a single file or directory:

    ```
    formatter path/to/file.py
    ```

    Add the `--check` flag to verify formatting without applying changes:

    ```
    formatter --check .
    ```

  linting: |
    Run the primary linter across the package:

    ```
    linter .
    ```

    For stricter analysis, add verbose output:

    ```
    linter --verbose .
    ```

    To lint a specific module or file:

    ```
    linter scripts/utility.py
    ```

  import_sorting: |
    Check and fix import statement ordering:

    ```
    sort-imports .
    ```

    Use `--check` to verify without modifying files:

    ```
    sort-imports --check .
    ```

pre_commit_workflow:
  owner: "Developer Experience (Theo Banks)"
  intro: "The repository includes a pre-commit hook configuration. Developers are expected to manually run linting and formatting before pushing:"
  steps:
    - "Format all files: formatter ."
    - "Run the linter: linter ."
    - "Check imports: sort-imports --check ."
    - "If any issues are flagged, review the output and either fix them manually or re-run tools with auto-fix enabled."
    - "Stage and commit your changes."
  hook_installation: |
    A sample pre-commit hook script is provided in `scripts/pre-commit.sh` (for Linux/macOS) and `scripts/pre-commit.bat` (for Windows). To install the hook:

    On Linux/macOS:

    ```
    cp scripts/pre-commit.sh .git/hooks/pre-commit
    chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
    ```

    On Windows (PowerShell):

    ```
    Copy-Item scripts/pre-commit.bat .git/hooks/pre-commit.bat
    ```

    Note: On Windows, Git for Windows must be configured to run scripts as pre-commit hooks; this may require additional configuration in `.git/config`.

  ci_integration: |
    Linting and formatting checks run automatically on pull requests via the CI/CD pipeline. The pipeline uses the same configuration files and tool versions documented here. If your local environment passes all checks but CI fails, verify your tool versions match those listed in the Tool Versions section.

code_style_standards:
  owner: "Developer Experience (Theo Banks)"
  intro: "This section summarizes style conventions applied via the tools above. Detailed guidance appears in \"Coding Style Guide\" (v3.5) and \"Code Review Conventions\" (v4.0)."
  line_length_and_formatting: |
    - Maximum line length: 88 characters (enforced by formatter)
    - Indentation: 4 spaces (no tabs)
    - Line endings: LF (Unix) on all platforms; see `.editorconfig`

  naming_conventions: |
    Follow PEP 8:
    • Module and package names: lowercase with underscores (e.g., my_module)
    • Function and variable names: lowercase with underscores
    • Class names: PascalCase
    • Constants: UPPERCASE with underscores
    • Private members: prefix with single underscore

    The linter enforces these conventions and flags violations.

  import_ordering: |
    Imports must be grouped and ordered as follows, with blank lines separating groups:

    1. Standard library imports
    2. Related third-party imports
    3. Local application imports

    Within each group, sort alphabetically. The `sort-imports` tool automates this.

  documentation_strings: |
    All public functions, classes, and modules must have docstrings. Use triple double-quoted strings. Docstrings must fit within the line-length limit. The linter checks for missing docstrings and spelling errors in documentation.

  whitespace_and_spacing: |
    - Use blank lines to separate logical sections within functions (2 blank lines between top-level definitions).
    - No trailing whitespace.
    - Symbols must have spaces around them.

    The formatter automatically corrects spacing and whitespace issues.

disabling_rules_locally:
  content: |
    In rare cases, you may need to disable a linting rule for a specific line or block. Use inline comments with caution and document the reason:

    ```
    # nolint: rule-name — reason for disabling this rule
    some_code_that_violates_rule()
    ```

    Such disables require justification in code review. They should be exceptions, not the norm.

platform_specific_procedures:
  owner: "Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)"
  windows: |
    Developers on Windows should use PowerShell for running linting commands. The formatter and linter work identically across platforms. See "Windows Setup Notes" (v1.1, updated 2025-08-09) for workstation-specific steps.

    File paths in error messages use backslashes; adjust commands as needed when chaining tools.

  macos: |
    No special configuration is needed for linting and formatting on macOS. Python installed via Homebrew or asdf-vm works seamlessly. Refer to "macOS Setup Notes" (v1.0) for environment setup.

  linux: |
    On Linux, ensure Python 3.9+ is installed via your package manager or asdf-vm. "Linux Setup Notes" (v0.9, updated 2024-05-27) provides distribution-specific guidance.

troubleshooting:
  owner: "Tooling Guild (Dana Kessler)"
  formatter_and_linter_disagree: |
    This occasionally occurs with tool version mismatches. Update all development tools:

    ```
    pip install --upgrade formatter linter sort-imports spell-check quality-check
    ```

    Compare your installed versions against the Tool Versions section.

  pre_commit_hook_fails_silently_on_windows: |
    Git for Windows may not properly execute script hooks. Use a PowerShell wrapper instead or check your .git/config for hook execution settings.

  import_sorting_removes_required_imports: |
    This is usually a false positive. Review the changes and, if the import is genuinely required, add a comment explaining its purpose. Re-run the sort tool to verify the import is retained.

  linting_reports_false_positives: |
    Certain rules may incorrectly flag valid code. Document the specific rule and code pattern in your pull request. The team discusses false positives in code review, and rules can be adjusted in `pyproject.toml` if needed.

terminology_and_glossary:
  - term: "Black"
    definition: "A popular Python code formatter that enforces a consistent style; referenced in this documentation as 'formatter.'"

  - term: "Docstring"
    definition: "A string literal that appears as the first statement in a module, function, class, or method, used to document code."

  - term: "Flake8"
    definition: "A style guide enforcement tool combining PyFlakes, pycodestyle, and McCabe complexity checker; referenced here as 'linter.'"

  - term: "isort"
    definition: "A utility to sort and organize Python imports; referenced here as 'sort-imports.'"

  - term: "Linting"
    definition: "The process of running a static analysis tool to find bugs, style violations, and potential issues without executing code."

  - term: "PEP 8"
    definition: "Python Enhancement Proposal 8, the style guide for Python code (https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0008/)."

  - term: "pyproject.toml"
    definition: "A configuration file (standardized in PEP 517/518) that specifies build system requirements and tool-specific settings."

  - term: "Virtual Environment"
    definition: "An isolated Python environment on a single workstation, allowing different projects to have independent dependencies."

  - term: "McCabe Complexity"
    definition: "A measure of code complexity based on the number of linearly independent paths through a program; helps identify overly complex functions."

1	================================================================================
2	LINUX SETUP NOTES
3	Version: 0.9
4	Owner: Tooling Guild (Dana Kessler)
5	Last Updated: 2024-05-27
6	================================================================================
7	
8	SUMMARY
9	Covers workstation setup details specific to building and running the oauthsvc 
10	package on common Linux distributions. Includes Python version management, 
11	development environment configuration, and workflows for local development.
12	
13	================================================================================
14	SUPPORTED LINUX DISTRIBUTIONS
15	================================================================================
16	
17	The service package is actively developed and maintained on:
18	
19	  • Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) — recommended for new developers
20	  • Debian 12 (Bookworm)
21	  • Fedora 39+
22	  • CentOS Stream 9
23	  • Arch Linux (rolling release, May 2024 and later)
24	  • Alpine Linux 3.19+ (for containerized development)
25	
26	Earlier Ubuntu LTS releases (20.04) are supported but receive less frequent 
27	validation; migration to 22.04 LTS is encouraged. Ubuntu 24.04 LTS was released 
28	in April 2024 and works but has not been validated against the full suite of 
29	developer tools; see Known Issues.
30	
31	================================================================================
32	PYTHON VERSION REQUIREMENTS
33	================================================================================
34	
35	Owner: Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)
36	
37	The service requires Python 3.9 or higher. Development and validation occurs primarily 
38	on Python 3.11 and 3.12. See python-version-support.md for comprehensive version 
39	compatibility details, including end-of-life timelines.
40	
41	For interactive Python shell work during development, Python 3.11 is recommended 
42	as the baseline; it strikes a balance between stability and access to standard 
43	library improvements introduced in recent releases.
44	
45	================================================================================
46	INITIAL SYSTEM SETUP
47	================================================================================
48	
49	Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
50	
51	All developers must first ensure the Linux system has essential build tools, 
52	git, and Python installed.
53	
54	DEBIAN-FAMILY (UBUNTU, DEBIAN)
55	  sudo apt update
56	  sudo apt install -y build-essential python3-dev python3-venv python3-pip
57	  sudo apt install -y git curl sqlite3
58	
59	REDHAT-FAMILY (FEDORA, CENTOS STREAM)
60	  sudo dnf groupinstall -y "Development Tools"
61	  sudo dnf install -y python3-devel python3-venv python3-pip
62	  sudo dnf install -y git curl sqlite3
63	
64	ARCH LINUX
65	  sudo pacman -Sy base-devel python python-venv sqlite
66	
67	Alpine Linux users should follow the container-specific notes in the Knowledge 
68	Base article "Alpine Development Containers" (see Related Pages).
69	
70	After installing base packages, verify the Python installation:
71	
72	  python3 --version
73	
74	Expected output should show Python 3.9 or later. If you need multiple Python 
75	versions on a single machine, see the Python Version Management section below.
76	
77	================================================================================
78	PYTHON VERSION MANAGEMENT
79	================================================================================
80	
81	For developers working across multiple projects or requiring specific Python 
82	versions, pyenv is the recommended tool.
83	
84	INSTALLING PYENV (RECOMMENDED)
85	
86	  curl https://pyenv.run | bash
87	
88	This script clones pyenv into ~/.pyenv. Add to your shell profile 
89	(~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, or equivalent):
90	
91	  export PYENV_ROOT="$HOME/.pyenv"
92	  export PATH="$PYENV_ROOT/bin:$PATH"
93	  eval "$(pyenv init -)"
94	
95	Reload your shell or run:
96	  source ~/.bashrc
97	
98	Install Python versions as needed:
99	  pyenv install 3.11.9
100	  pyenv install 3.12.1
101	
102	Set a version locally within the repository (creates .python-version file):
103	  pyenv local 3.11.9
104	
105	pyenv will automatically activate this version when you cd into the oauthsvc 
106	directory. This approach is preferred over system-wide Python version changes.
107	
108	USING SYSTEM PYTHON
109	Developers working on single projects or without version conflicts may use the 
110	system Python. Ensure it meets the minimum version requirement.
111	
112	================================================================================
113	DEVELOPMENT ENVIRONMENT SETUP
114	================================================================================
115	
116	Owner: Tooling Guild (Dana Kessler)
117	
118	STEP 1: CLONE THE REPOSITORY
119	  git clone https://github.com/internal/oauthsvc.git
120	  cd oauthsvc
121	
122	STEP 2: CREATE A VIRTUAL ENVIRONMENT
123	Virtual environments isolate package dependencies and are required for all 
124	developers.
125	
126	  python3 -m venv venv
127	  source venv/bin/activate
128	
129	On first activation, your shell prompt will change to show (venv) prefix. 
130	Verify:
131	  which python
132	  # Should output: /path/to/oauthsvc/venv/bin/python
133	
134	The virtual environment must be activated every time you open a new terminal 
135	window before working on the package. Most shells provide aliases or shell 
136	functions to automate this; see editor-configuration.md for IDE-specific setup.
137	
138	STEP 3: INSTALL PACKAGE IN DEVELOPMENT MODE
139	  pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
140	  pip install -e .
141	
142	The -e flag installs the package in editable (development) mode, allowing 
143	changes to source files to take effect immediately without reinstalling.
144	
145	Note: Some developers prefer pip install --editable . instead of -e; both 
146	are equivalent and used interchangeably in this codebase.
147	
148	STEP 4: VERIFY THE INSTALLATION
149	  To check the installed version, import the package and print __version__
150	
151	Expected output: version string matching pyproject.toml. If import fails, 
152	ensure the virtual environment is activated and pip install -e . completed 
153	without errors.
154	
155	================================================================================
156	VIRTUAL ENVIRONMENT MANAGEMENT
157	================================================================================
158	
159	Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
160	
161	DEACTIVATING THE ENVIRONMENT
162	  deactivate
163	
164	This returns you to your system Python. To continue work, cd into the directory 
165	and source venv/bin/activate again.
166	
167	RECREATING A CORRUPT ENVIRONMENT
168	If the virtual environment becomes corrupted or you need a clean slate:
169	
170	  rm -rf venv
171	  python3 -m venv venv
172	  source venv/bin/activate
173	  pip install --upgrade pip
174	  pip install -e .
175	
176	CHECKING INSTALLED PACKAGES
177	  pip list
178	  pip show oauthsvc
179	
180	UPDATING DEPENDENCIES
181	See dependency-management.txt (version 1.4, Feb 2026) for detailed procedures 
182	on managing package dependencies and pinning versions.
183	
184	================================================================================
185	EDITOR AND IDE CONFIGURATION
186	================================================================================
187	
188	Owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks)
189	
190	Detailed editor setup including LSP integration, linting, and formatting tools 
191	is covered in editor-configuration.md (v1.2.0). The section below covers 
192	Linux-specific configuration.
193	
194	VS CODE
195	Install the Python extension from Microsoft (or equivalent). Configure the 
196	workspace by placing this in .vscode/settings.json at the repository root:
197	
198	  {
199	    "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "${workspaceFolder}/venv/bin/python",
200	    "python.linting.enabled": true,
201	    "python.linting.pylintEnabled": false,
202	    "[python]": {
203	      "editor.formatOnSave": true,
204	      "editor.defaultFormatter": "ms-python.python"
205	    }
206	  }
207	
208	Ensure VS Code recognizes the virtual environment:
209	  Ctrl+Shift+P > Python: Select Interpreter > ./venv/bin/python
210	
211	JETBRAINS PYCHARM (COMMUNITY OR PROFESSIONAL)
212	Create a new project or open oauthsvc. In Settings:
213	  Settings > Project: oauthsvc > Python Interpreter
214	  Click the gear icon > Add... > Existing Environment
215	  Select /path/to/oauthsvc/venv/bin/python
216	
217	NEOVIM / VIM
218	Configure Language Server Protocol (LSP) integration. With a plugin manager like 
219	vim-plug, add:
220	
221	  Plug 'neovim/nvim-lspconfig'
222	
223	After activation, create init.lua configuration to use the virtual environment 
224	Python. See the Knowledge Base for nvim-lspconfig recipes.
225	
226	All editors should respect the repository's lint and formatting configuration; 
227	see lint-formatting-config.yaml (v1.0.1, Apr 2026) for canonical settings.
228	
229	================================================================================
230	GIT WORKFLOW AND COMMIT PRACTICES
231	================================================================================
232	
233	Owner: Build & Release (Owen Castillo)
234	
235	INITIAL GIT CONFIGURATION
236	Configure your name and contact information for commits:
237	
238	  git config user.name "Your Full Name"
239	  Configure your contact information through git config
240	
241	For repository-level configuration (applies only within oauthsvc):
242	  git config user.name "Your Full Name"
243	
244	Add --global to set for all repositories:
245	  git config --global user.name "Your Full Name"
246	
247	BRANCHING STRATEGY
248	All feature development occurs on feature branches. Never commit directly to 
249	main:
250	
251	  git checkout -b feature/name-of-feature
252	  git add <files>
253	  git commit -m "Your commit message"
254	  git push origin feature/name-of-feature
255	
256	Branch names follow the pattern: feature/, bugfix/, docs/, or refactor/ 
257	followed by a kebab-case description.
258	
259	COMMIT MESSAGE STYLE
260	See commit-message-style.md (v1.3, Dec 2024) for comprehensive style guidelines. 
261	In summary:
262	
263	  - First line: 50 characters or fewer, imperative mood
264	  - Blank line
265	  - Body: wrap at 72 characters, explain the why, not just the what
266	  - Reference issues with "Closes #123" at the end if applicable
267	
268	Example:
269	  Add support for local loopback configuration
270	  
271	  The service now reads configuration from the config.ini file in 
272	  the repository root. This allows developers to override default 
273	  loopback settings without modifying code.
274	  
275	  Closes #456
276

278	CODE REVIEW CONVENTIONS
279	================================================================================
280	
281	Owner: Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)
282	
283	All pull requests require review by at least one maintainer before merging. 
284	See code-review-conventions.md (v4.0, Jun 2025) for detailed review criteria, 
285	comment etiquette, and review workflow.
286	
287	Key points for Linux developers:
288	
289	  • Request review via GitHub; mention @Tooling-Guild or specific reviewers
290	  • Respond to all feedback before marking ready-for-merge
291	  • Do not rebase after code review begins; use merge commits
292	  • Ensure all automated checks pass (see CI Integration below)
293	  • Update documentation (README, doc files) if your change affects user-facing 
294	    behavior
295	
296	================================================================================
297	CODING STYLE AND LINTING
298	================================================================================
299	
300	Owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks)
301	
302	The package enforces a consistent coding style. See coding-style-guide.md 
303	(v3.5, Mar 2025) for detailed rules on naming, imports, docstrings, and logic 
304	patterns.
305	
306	RUN LOCAL LINTING BEFORE PUSHING
307	The repository includes a lint configuration file. Install and run linters:
308	
309	  pip install flake8 black isort
310	
311	Format code automatically:
312	  black .
313	  isort .
314	
315	Check for style violations:
316	  flake8 . --max-line-length=88 --extend-ignore=E203,W503
317	
318	Most editors can integrate these tools to format on save (see 
319	editor-configuration.md).
320	
321	PRE-COMMIT HOOKS
322	Set up git pre-commit hooks to catch style issues before committing:
323	
324	  pip install pre-commit
325	  pre-commit install
326	
327	This runs checks automatically on every commit. To manually verify all staged 
328	files:
329	
330	  pre-commit run --all-files
331	
332	================================================================================
333	LOCAL DATABASE FILE
334	================================================================================
335	
336	The package maintains state in a local SQLite file. During development, this 
337	file is created automatically on first run. Developers should not manually 
338	edit the database; use the command-line interface for all operations.
339	
340	The database file path and structure are documented in 
341	local-database-file-notes.md (v1.6, Oct 2025).
342	
343	For interactive queries during debugging, the sqlite3 command-line tool can 
344	inspect the schema:
345	
346	  sqlite3 oauthsvc.db ".schema"
347	
348	================================================================================
349	COMMON ISSUES AND TROUBLESHOOTING
350	================================================================================
351	
352	ISSUE: "No module named oauthsvc" when importing
353	CAUSE: Virtual environment not activated.
354	SOLUTION: Run source venv/bin/activate and verify the prompt shows (venv).
355	
356	ISSUE: pip install -e . fails with "error: legacy setup.py install"
357	CAUSE: Old pip version or missing build tools.
358	SOLUTION: 
359	  pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
360	  apt install python3-dev  (or equivalent on your distro)
361	
362	ISSUE: pyenv installed but python versions not available
363	CAUSE: Shell not reloaded after pyenv installation.
364	SOLUTION: Run exec $SHELL to restart shell with updated PATH.
365	
366	ISSUE: Ubuntu 24.04 shows Python 3.12 by default but package requires 3.11
367	CAUSE: System Python mismatch. Use pyenv or explicit virtual environment.
368	SOLUTION: pyenv install 3.11.9 && pyenv local 3.11.9
369	
370	ISSUE: Git commits fail with "Committer identity unknown"
371	CAUSE: User.name or user identity not configured.
372	SOLUTION: Set your name and contact information with git config commands
373	
374	For detailed troubleshooting across platforms, see workstation-setup.md (v2.4, 
375	Nov 2025) for general guidance.

378	TERMINOLOGY AND GLOSSARY
379	================================================================================
380	
381	Virtual Environment
382	  An isolated Python installation within a project directory, containing its 
383	  own copy of Python and installed packages. Enables parallel development on 
384	  multiple projects with different dependency versions. Created with 
385	  python3 -m venv.
386	
387	pyenv
388	  A tool for managing multiple Python versions on a single system. Allows 
389	  per-project version selection via .python-version files. Preferred over 
390	  system-wide version management.
391	
392	Editable Install
393	  Installation mode (pip install -e) that creates a symlink to the source 
394	  code rather than copying it. Changes to source files take effect 
395	  immediately without reinstalling.
396	
397	venv
398	  Standard Python module and the directory containing a virtual environment. 
399	  Created by python3 -m venv <directory>.
400	
401	Linting
402	  Automated static analysis of code to detect style violations, unused 
403	  imports, and potential bugs. Tools: flake8, black, isort.
404	
405	Pre-commit Hooks
406	  Git hooks that run automated checks before committing. Prevents non-conforming 
407	  code from entering the repository. Configured via pre-commit framework.
408	
409	Feature Branch
410	  A temporary git branch created for a single feature or bugfix. Merged to 
411	  main via pull request after review. Naming convention: feature/, bugfix/, 
412	  docs/, refactor/.
413	
414	Pull Request (PR)
415	  A GitHub mechanism for proposing code changes, enabling review and 
416	  discussion before merging to main. Requires acceptance from maintainers.
417	
418	LSP (Language Server Protocol)
419	  Standard protocol used by editors and IDEs to provide code completion, 
420	  diagnostics, and navigation for programming languages. Configured per-editor 
421	  in this project.
422	
423	pyproject.toml
424	  Project metadata and dependency file in TOML format. Replaces older 
425	  setup.py and setup.cfg patterns. Contains version, author, and dependency 
426	  specifications.
427	
428	Distro (Distribution)
429	  A Linux distribution (Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian, etc.) with its own package 
430	  manager (apt, dnf, pacman).
431	
432	SQLite
433	  Embedded relational database engine used to persist package state in a 
434	  single file. Accessed via sqlite3 CLI or library bindings.

================================================================================
LINUX SETUP NOTES
Version: 0.9
Owner: Tooling Guild (Dana Kessler)
Last Updated: 2024-05-27
================================================================================

SUMMARY
Covers workstation setup details specific to building and running the oauthsvc 
package on common Linux distributions. Includes Python version management, 
development environment configuration, and workflows for local development.

================================================================================
SUPPORTED LINUX DISTRIBUTIONS
================================================================================

The service package is actively developed and maintained on:

  • Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) — recommended for new developers
  • Debian 12 (Bookworm)
  • Fedora 39+
  • CentOS Stream 9
  • Arch Linux (rolling release, May 2024 and later)
  • Alpine Linux 3.19+ (for containerized development)

Earlier Ubuntu LTS releases (20.04) are supported but receive less frequent 
validation; migration to 22.04 LTS is encouraged. Ubuntu 24.04 LTS was released 
in April 2024 and works but has not been validated against the full suite of 
developer tools; see Known Issues.

================================================================================
PYTHON VERSION REQUIREMENTS
================================================================================

Owner: Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)

The service requires Python 3.9 or higher. Development and validation occurs primarily 
on Python 3.11 and 3.12. See python-version-support.md for comprehensive version 
compatibility details, including end-of-life timelines.

For interactive Python shell work during development, Python 3.11 is recommended 
as the baseline; it strikes a balance between stability and access to standard 
library improvements introduced in recent releases.

================================================================================
INITIAL SYSTEM SETUP
================================================================================

Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)

All developers must first ensure the Linux system has essential build tools, 
git, and Python installed.

DEBIAN-FAMILY (UBUNTU, DEBIAN)
  sudo apt update
  sudo apt install -y build-essential python3-dev python3-venv python3-pip
  sudo apt install -y git curl sqlite3

REDHAT-FAMILY (FEDORA, CENTOS STREAM)
  sudo dnf groupinstall -y "Development Tools"
  sudo dnf install -y python3-devel python3-venv python3-pip
  sudo dnf install -y git curl sqlite3

ARCH LINUX
  sudo pacman -Sy base-devel python python-venv sqlite

Alpine Linux users should follow the container-specific notes in the Knowledge 
Base article "Alpine Development Containers" (see Related Pages).

After installing base packages, verify the Python installation:

  python3 --version

Expected output should show Python 3.9 or later. If you need multiple Python 
versions on a single machine, see the Python Version Management section below.

================================================================================
PYTHON VERSION MANAGEMENT
================================================================================

For developers working across multiple projects or requiring specific Python 
versions, pyenv is the recommended tool.

INSTALLING PYENV (RECOMMENDED)

  curl https://pyenv.run | bash

This script clones pyenv into ~/.pyenv. Add to your shell profile 
(~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, or equivalent):

  export PYENV_ROOT="$HOME/.pyenv"
  export PATH="$PYENV_ROOT/bin:$PATH"
  eval "$(pyenv init -)"

Reload your shell or run:
  source ~/.bashrc

Install Python versions as needed:
  pyenv install 3.11.9
  pyenv install 3.12.1

Set a version locally within the repository (creates .python-version file):
  pyenv local 3.11.9

pyenv will automatically activate this version when you cd into the oauthsvc 
directory. This approach is preferred over system-wide Python version changes.

USING SYSTEM PYTHON
Developers working on single projects or without version conflicts may use the 
system Python. Ensure it meets the minimum version requirement.

================================================================================
DEVELOPMENT ENVIRONMENT SETUP
================================================================================

Owner: Tooling Guild (Dana Kessler)

STEP 1: CLONE THE REPOSITORY
  git clone https://github.com/internal/oauthsvc.git
  cd oauthsvc

STEP 2: CREATE A VIRTUAL ENVIRONMENT
Virtual environments isolate package dependencies and are required for all 
developers.

  python3 -m venv venv
  source venv/bin/activate

On first activation, your shell prompt will change to show (venv) prefix. 
Verify:
  which python
  # Should output: /path/to/oauthsvc/venv/bin/python

The virtual environment must be activated every time you open a new terminal 
window before working on the package. Most shells provide aliases or shell 
functions to automate this; see editor-configuration.md for IDE-specific setup.

STEP 3: INSTALL PACKAGE IN DEVELOPMENT MODE
  pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
  pip install -e .

The -e flag installs the package in editable (development) mode, allowing 
changes to source files to take effect immediately without reinstalling.

Note: Some developers prefer pip install --editable . instead of -e; both 
are equivalent and used interchangeably in this codebase.

STEP 4: VERIFY THE INSTALLATION
  To check the installed version, import the package and print __version__

Expected output: version string matching pyproject.toml. If import fails, 
ensure the virtual environment is activated and pip install -e . completed 
without errors.

================================================================================
VIRTUAL ENVIRONMENT MANAGEMENT
================================================================================

Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)

DEACTIVATING THE ENVIRONMENT
  deactivate

This returns you to your system Python. To continue work, cd into the directory 
and source venv/bin/activate again.

RECREATING A CORRUPT ENVIRONMENT
If the virtual environment becomes corrupted or you need a clean slate:

  rm -rf venv
  python3 -m venv venv
  source venv/bin/activate
  pip install --upgrade pip
  pip install -e .

CHECKING INSTALLED PACKAGES
  pip list
  pip show oauthsvc

UPDATING DEPENDENCIES
See dependency-management.txt (version 1.4, Feb 2026) for detailed procedures 
on managing package dependencies and pinning versions.

================================================================================
EDITOR AND IDE CONFIGURATION
================================================================================

Owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks)

Detailed editor setup including LSP integration, linting, and formatting tools 
is covered in editor-configuration.md (v1.2.0). The section below covers 
Linux-specific configuration.

VS CODE
Install the Python extension from Microsoft (or equivalent). Configure the 
workspace by placing this in .vscode/settings.json at the repository root:

  {
    "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "${workspaceFolder}/venv/bin/python",
    "python.linting.enabled": true,
    "python.linting.pylintEnabled": false,
    "[python]": {
      "editor.formatOnSave": true,
      "editor.defaultFormatter": "ms-python.python"
    }
  }

Ensure VS Code recognizes the virtual environment:
  Ctrl+Shift+P > Python: Select Interpreter > ./venv/bin/python

JETBRAINS PYCHARM (COMMUNITY OR PROFESSIONAL)
Create a new project or open oauthsvc. In Settings:
  Settings > Project: oauthsvc > Python Interpreter
  Click the gear icon > Add... > Existing Environment
  Select /path/to/oauthsvc/venv/bin/python

NEOVIM / VIM
Configure Language Server Protocol (LSP) integration. With a plugin manager like 
vim-plug, add:

  Plug 'neovim/nvim-lspconfig'

After activation, create init.lua configuration to use the virtual environment 
Python. See the Knowledge Base for nvim-lspconfig recipes.

All editors should respect the repository's lint and formatting configuration; 
see lint-formatting-config.yaml (v1.0.1, Apr 2026) for canonical settings.

================================================================================
GIT WORKFLOW AND COMMIT PRACTICES
================================================================================

Owner: Build & Release (Owen Castillo)

INITIAL GIT CONFIGURATION
Configure your name and contact information for commits:

  git config user.name "Your Full Name"
  Configure your contact information through git config

For repository-level configuration (applies only within oauthsvc):
  git config user.name "Your Full Name"

Add --global to set for all repositories:
  git config --global user.name "Your Full Name"

BRANCHING STRATEGY
All feature development occurs on feature branches. Never commit directly to 
main:

  git checkout -b feature/name-of-feature
  git add <files>
  git commit -m "Your commit message"
  git push origin feature/name-of-feature

Branch names follow the pattern: feature/, bugfix/, docs/, or refactor/ 
followed by a kebab-case description.

COMMIT MESSAGE STYLE
See commit-message-style.md (v1.3, Dec 2024) for comprehensive style guidelines. 
In summary:

  - First line: 50 characters or fewer, imperative mood
  - Blank line
  - Body: wrap at 72 characters, explain the why, not just the what
  - Reference issues with "Closes #123" at the end if applicable

Example:
  Add support for local loopback configuration
  
  The service now reads configuration from the config.ini file in 
  the repository root. This allows developers to override default 
  loopback settings without modifying code.
  
  Closes #456

================================================================================
CODE REVIEW CONVENTIONS
================================================================================

Owner: Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)

All pull requests require review by at least one maintainer before merging. 
See code-review-conventions.md (v4.0, Jun 2025) for detailed review criteria, 
comment etiquette, and review workflow.

Key points for Linux developers:

  • Request review via GitHub; mention @Tooling-Guild or specific reviewers
  • Respond to all feedback before marking ready-for-merge
  • Do not rebase after code review begins; use merge commits
  • Ensure all automated checks pass (see CI Integration below)
  • Update documentation (README, doc files) if your change affects user-facing 
    behavior

================================================================================
CODING STYLE AND LINTING
================================================================================

Owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks)

The package enforces a consistent coding style. See coding-style-guide.md 
(v3.5, Mar 2025) for detailed rules on naming, imports, docstrings, and logic 
patterns.

RUN LOCAL LINTING BEFORE PUSHING
The repository includes a lint configuration file. Install and run linters:

  pip install flake8 black isort

Format code automatically:
  black .
  isort .

Check for style violations:
  flake8 . --max-line-length=88 --extend-ignore=E203,W503

Most editors can integrate these tools to format on save (see 
editor-configuration.md).

PRE-COMMIT HOOKS
Set up git pre-commit hooks to catch style issues before committing:

  pip install pre-commit
  pre-commit install

This runs checks automatically on every commit. To manually verify all staged 
files:

  pre-commit run --all-files

================================================================================
LOCAL DATABASE FILE
================================================================================

The package maintains state in a local SQLite file. During development, this 
file is created automatically on first run. Developers should not manually 
edit the database; use the command-line interface for all operations.

The database file path and structure are documented in 
local-database-file-notes.md (v1.6, Oct 2025).

For interactive queries during debugging, the sqlite3 command-line tool can 
inspect the schema:

  sqlite3 oauthsvc.db ".schema"

================================================================================
COMMON ISSUES AND TROUBLESHOOTING
================================================================================

ISSUE: "No module named oauthsvc" when importing
CAUSE: Virtual environment not activated.
SOLUTION: Run source venv/bin/activate and verify the prompt shows (venv).

ISSUE: pip install -e . fails with "error: legacy setup.py install"
CAUSE: Old pip version or missing build tools.
SOLUTION: 
  pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
  apt install python3-dev  (or equivalent on your distro)

ISSUE: pyenv installed but python versions not available
CAUSE: Shell not reloaded after pyenv installation.
SOLUTION: Run exec $SHELL to restart shell with updated PATH.

ISSUE: Ubuntu 24.04 shows Python 3.12 by default but package requires 3.11
CAUSE: System Python mismatch. Use pyenv or explicit virtual environment.
SOLUTION: pyenv install 3.11.9 && pyenv local 3.11.9

ISSUE: Git commits fail with "Committer identity unknown"
CAUSE: User.name or user identity not configured.
SOLUTION: Set your name and contact information with git config commands

For detailed troubleshooting across platforms, see workstation-setup.md (v2.4, 
Nov 2025) for general guidance.

================================================================================
TERMINOLOGY AND GLOSSARY
================================================================================

Virtual Environment
  An isolated Python installation within a project directory, containing its 
  own copy of Python and installed packages. Enables parallel development on 
  multiple projects with different dependency versions. Created with 
  python3 -m venv.

pyenv
  A tool for managing multiple Python versions on a single system. Allows 
  per-project version selection via .python-version files. Preferred over 
  system-wide version management.

Editable Install
  Installation mode (pip install -e) that creates a symlink to the source 
  code rather than copying it. Changes to source files take effect 
  immediately without reinstalling.

venv
  Standard Python module and the directory containing a virtual environment. 
  Created by python3 -m venv <directory>.

Linting
  Automated static analysis of code to detect style violations, unused 
  imports, and potential bugs. Tools: flake8, black, isort.

Pre-commit Hooks
  Git hooks that run automated checks before committing. Prevents non-conforming 
  code from entering the repository. Configured via pre-commit framework.

Feature Branch
  A temporary git branch created for a single feature or bugfix. Merged to 
  main via pull request after review. Naming convention: feature/, bugfix/, 
  docs/, refactor/.

Pull Request (PR)
  A GitHub mechanism for proposing code changes, enabling review and 
  discussion before merging to main. Requires acceptance from maintainers.

LSP (Language Server Protocol)
  Standard protocol used by editors and IDEs to provide code completion, 
  diagnostics, and navigation for programming languages. Configured per-editor 
  in this project.

pyproject.toml
  Project metadata and dependency file in TOML format. Replaces older 
  setup.py and setup.cfg patterns. Contains version, author, and dependency 
  specifications.

Distro (Distribution)
  A Linux distribution (Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian, etc.) with its own package 
  manager (apt, dnf, pacman).

SQLite
  Embedded relational database engine used to persist package state in a 
  single file. Accessed via sqlite3 CLI or library bindings.

================================================================================
REPOSITORY FILES AND PATHS
================================================================================

README.md
  Root-level documentation with quickstart instructions and project overview.

pyproject.toml
  Project configuration, version, dependencies, and build settings. 
  Located at repository root. Defines entry point for command-line interface.

oauthsvc/
  Main package directory. Contains all module code (do not edit manually 
  during development; install with pip install -e .).

docs/
  Documentation sources in Markdown and plain text. Includes developer 
  handbook pages.

scripts/
  Utility scripts for development, deployment, and maintenance.

venv/
  Virtual environment directory. Created by python3 -m venv venv. 
  Should not be committed to git (.gitignore excludes it).

.python-version
  pyenv configuration file (created by pyenv local). Specifies Python version 
  for this repository.

.git/
  Git repository metadata. Created by git clone or git init.

.vscode/
  VS Code workspace settings (optional, per-developer).

oauthsvc.db
  SQLite database file created on first run. Location configurable; 
  defaults to repository root.

================================================================================
DEVELOPMENT TOOLS AND VERSIONS
================================================================================

Tool/Package              Version         Purpose/Notes
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Python                    3.9–3.12        Core language; 3.11 recommended
pip                       >= 23.0         Package manager

isort                      5.12            Import sorter
pre-commit                 3.4             Git hooks framework
sqlite3                    (system)        Database CLI
curl                       (system)        HTTP utility for manual API calls

Versions listed reflect development environment at last update (May 2024). 
Consult dependency-management.txt for current pinned versions and update 
procedures. See python-version-support.md for Python version EOL dates.

RELATED PAGES

  Entry point for all developer documentation.

  Detailed setup for VS Code, PyCharm, Vim, and other editors across platforms.
