1	# Supported Python Versions
2	
3	| | |
4	|---|---|
5	| **Title** | Supported Python Versions |
6	| **Version** | 1.7 |
7	| **Owner** | Core Services (Priya Nandakumar) |
8	| **Last updated** | 2026-01-20 |
9	
10	**Summary:** This page lists the Python interpreter versions the `oauthsvc` package is expected to run under, explains how the supported range is chosen and reviewed, and describes the local steps a developer takes to install, pin, and check an interpreter before working on the repository. It also covers how the standard-library-only nature of the package interacts with interpreter version differences, and how the bundled SQLite library that backs the local database file varies across Python builds.
11	
12	## Purpose and Coverage
13	
14	Owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services
15	
16	`oauthsvc` ships as a small standard-library package with a command line front end and a loopback HTTP service, and it keeps its working state in a local SQLite file. Because it has no third-party runtime dependencies, the single biggest source of behavioral drift between developer machines is the interpreter itself — differences in the standard library, in the bundled SQLite library, and in default settings for things like hash seeding or byte-compiled cache placement.
17	
18	This page exists so that every contributor, whether on a laptop running Windows, a Linux workstation, or a Mac, is working against an interpreter that Core Services has actually exercised. It is the page to check before you install anything, before you open an editor, and before you file a pull request that touches interpreter-sensitive code such as anything that reads or writes the local database file.
19	
20	## Supported Version Matrix
21	
22	The table below is the current picture of what Core Services builds against, checks against, and will accept pull requests against. "Primary" means the interpreter used for day-to-day development and for the reference builds published from the release branch. "Secondary" means we check against it but do not develop on it by default. "Sunset" means support is winding down on the stated date.
23	
24	| Python version | Status | Windows | macOS | Linux | Notes |
25	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
26	| 3.9 | Sunset (2026-03-31) | Allowed on older laptops only | Not checked | Allowed | Kept alive mainly for one long-lived internal host; do not develop new work against it |
27	| 3.10 | Secondary | Supported | Supported | Supported | Floor for any new machine setup |
28	| 3.11 | Secondary | Supported | Supported | Supported | Good middle ground; some contributors still prefer it for the faster startup time |
29	| 3.12 | Primary | Supported | Supported | Supported | The interpreter Core Services develops and packages against |
30	| 3.13 | Secondary, promoting to Primary in Q2 2026 | Supported | Supported | Supported | Watch this page for the promotion date |
31	| 3.14 | Not yet supported | — | — | — | Tracked but not installed on any shared machine as of this writing |
32	
33	If you are setting up a new machine today, install 3.12 as your working interpreter and keep 3.10 available for a quick local check, since 3.10 remains the floor for the supported range.
34	
35	## How Supported Versions Are Chosen
36	
37	Owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services
38	
39	Core Services reviews the supported range roughly once a quarter, timed loosely to align with upstream Python's own release calendar. The inputs to that review are:
40	
41	- the oldest interpreter still installed on any machine that runs the loopback service outside of a developer's own laptop;
42	- any standard-library change that affects the package's behavior, most often in argument parsing, the `sqlite3` module, or `http.server`;
43	- the interpreter versions available through the operating-system package managers used across the team (Homebrew, apt, and the Windows installer from python.org); and
44	- capacity on the Tooling Guild's side to keep additional interpreters installed on the shared build machine.
45	
46	The outcome of each review is recorded as an update to the version matrix above and to the `requires-python` line in the root `pyproject.toml`. A short note goes out on the team channel; there is no separate sign-off step, though Build & Release is looped in whenever the change affects the packaging metadata.
47	
48	A typical `requires-python` line, after a review that dropped 3.9 from Secondary to Sunset, looks like this:
49	
50	```
51	requires-python = ">=3.10,<3.14"
52	```
53	
54	## Minimum, Target, and Upcoming Versions
55	
56	| Category | Version | Notes |
57	|---|---|---|
58	| Minimum supported | 3.10 | Anything older is Sunset or unsupported |
59	| Target / Primary | 3.12 | What new contributors should install first |
60	| Next Primary | 3.13 | Promotion planned for Q2 2026 |
61	| Under evaluation | 3.14 | No installed reference build yet |
62	
63	## Checking Your Interpreter Version
64	
65	Owner: Dana Kessler, Tooling Guild
66	
67	Before doing anything else, confirm which interpreter is first on your shell's search path and what version it reports.
68	
69	On Linux or macOS:
70	
71	```
72	python3 --version
73	which -a python3
74	```
75	
76	On Windows, using the `py` launcher that ships with the python.org installer:
77	
78	```
79	py -0p
80	py -3.12 --version
81	```
82	
83	If `python3 --version` (or `py -3.12 --version`) reports anything outside the Supported Version Matrix above, stop and install a supported interpreter before continuing with the rest of workstation setup.
84	
85	Dana's team also keeps a small helper script at `scripts/check-python-version.sh` (and a PowerShell equivalent at `scripts/verify-interpreter-matrix.ps1`) that reads the current `requires-python` line out of `pyproject.toml` and compares it against whatever interpreter is first on the path, printing a plain warning line if they disagree. Neither script installs anything for you; they only report what is already on the machine.
86	
87	## Installing and Pinning Interpreters Locally
88	
89	Owner: Dana Kessler, Tooling Guild
90	
91	Most contributors keep more than one interpreter installed and use one of the following to pin the version for this repository specifically.
92	
93	**pyenv (Linux and macOS)**
94	
95	```
96	pyenv install 3.12.6
97	pyenv install 3.10.14
98	pyenv local 3.12.6
99	```
100	
101	Running `pyenv local` writes a `.python-version` file at the repository root. That file is checked in, so everyone who clones the repository and has `pyenv` on their path gets the same primary interpreter automatically. If you need to check the repository against the floor version instead, run `pyenv shell 3.10.14` for a single terminal session rather than changing the checked-in pin.
102	
103	**py launcher (Windows)**
104	
105	Windows contributors generally do not use a per-repository pin file; instead they select the interpreter explicitly with the `py` launcher:
106	
107	```
108	py -3.12 -m venv .venv
109	.venv\Scripts\activate
110	```
111	
112	**Virtual environments (all platforms)**
113	
114	Regardless of how the interpreter itself is selected, create a virtual environment scoped to the repository rather than installing anything into a shared or system interpreter:
115	
116	```
117	python3 -m venv .venv
118	source .venv/bin/activate
119	python -m pip install --upgrade pip
120	```
121	
122	Because the package has no runtime dependencies outside the standard library, the virtual environment mainly exists to isolate the developer-side tooling (type checker, formatter, and linter) named later on this page, not to hold the package's own runtime requirements.
123	
124	## Standard Library Considerations for a Stdlib-Only Package
125	
126	Owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services
127	
128	Since `oauthsvc` has no third-party runtime dependencies, standard-library differences between interpreter versions are the main source of cross-version surprises. A few areas Core Services watches closely:
129	
130	- **Argument parsing.** Minor formatting changes to the built-in argument parser's help and error output have shown up between minor Python releases. If you are changing how the command line reports errors, check the rendered output on both the Primary interpreter (3.12) and the floor interpreter (3.10) before opening a pull request.
131	- **The local HTTP handling in the standard library.** The loopback HTTP service relies on the standard library's own HTTP server support. Timeout and connection-close behavior for that support has shifted slightly across versions; if you touch anything in that area, run a manual check on at least two interpreters from the matrix.
132	- **`sqlite3` module updates.** The standard library's `sqlite3` module tracks a bundled build of the SQLite library, and that build is not the same across Python versions. See the next section for specifics.
133	- **`tomllib`.** Added to the standard library in Python 3.11. Any packaging-adjacent code that reads TOML must not assume its presence on the floor interpreter (3.10), which does not have it.
134	- **Hash seeding.** Python's default hash randomization affects the iteration order of unordered structures. This has occasionally caused a false sense of a version-specific bug when the underlying cause was just an assumption about ordering that happened to hold on one machine and not another.
135	
136	None of the above requires special code paths for each interpreter version in most cases, but it does mean a change should be spot-checked on more than one interpreter, particularly the floor version, before a pull request goes up for review.
137	
138	## The Bundled SQLite Library and the Local Database File
139	
140	Owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services
141	
142	The service keeps its working state in a local SQLite file, and the version of the underlying SQLite library that ships inside a given Python build matters more than most contributors expect. The table below reflects what Core Services has observed on the interpreters in the matrix, using the python.org installers and the platform package managers current as of this update.
143	
144	| Python version | Bundled SQLite library (typical) |
145	|---|---|
146	| 3.10 | 3.37.x |
147	| 3.11 | 3.39.x |
148	| 3.12 | 3.43.x |
149	| 3.13 | 3.45.x |
150	
151	Because the floor and the Primary interpreter can be several SQLite minor versions apart, always confirm the bundled library's version and the installed command-line shell's version separately, rather than assuming they match. The command-line shell is a separate binary from whatever the interpreter links against:
152	
153	```
154	sqlite3 -version
155	```
156	
157	If you need to inspect the settings SQLite is using for the local database file directly, the command-line shell also accepts `PRAGMA` statements interactively:
158	
159	```
160	sqlite3 path\to\the.db
161	sqlite> PRAGMA journal_mode;
162	sqlite> PRAGMA compile_options;
163	```
164	
165	Further detail on the local database file itself — its location on disk and how it is opened by the service — lives on the sibling page **Local Database File Notes**, not here; this page is only concerned with how the interpreter's bundled SQLite library varies.
166	
167	## Type-Checking Across Multiple Interpreter Versions
168	
169	Owner: Theo Banks, Developer Experience
170	
171	The team's type checker needs to be told which interpreter version it is checking against, since it otherwise defaults to whatever interpreter it was itself installed under. Set this explicitly rather than relying on the default:
172	
173	For `mypy`, in `pyproject.toml`:
174	
175	```
176	[tool.mypy]
177	python_version = "3.10"
178	```
179	
180	Setting this to the floor version (3.10) rather than the Primary version (3.12) is deliberate — it catches uses of standard-library features that are newer than what the floor interpreter provides, such as an accidental reliance on `tomllib`.
181	
182	For editors using Pyright (see the sibling page **Editor Configuration** for the rest of the editor setup), the equivalent setting lives in `pyrightconfig.json`:
183	
184	```
185	{
186	  "pythonVersion": "3.10"
187	}
188	```
189	
190	## Local Verification Before Opening a Pull Request
191	
192	Owner: Owen Castillo, Build & Release
193	
194	Before a pull request goes up, run a local verification pass against at least the floor interpreter and the Primary interpreter. There is no shared verification runner beyond what each contributor runs locally, so this step is on you rather than something that happens automatically later.
195	
196	```
197	pyenv shell 3.10.14
198	python -m compileall oauthsvc/
199	pyenv shell 3.12.6
200	python -m compileall oauthsvc/
201	```
202	
203	Running `compileall` is a fast way to surface anything that fails to byte-compile on one interpreter but not the other, which usually means a syntax feature newer than the floor version has crept in. It does not substitute for a manual check of the command line and the loopback HTTP service on both interpreters, but it catches the cheapest class of mistake early.
204	
205	Byte-compiled caches are written under `__pycache__/` directories throughout `oauthsvc/`. These are local artifacts; do not check them in, and clear them if you switch interpreters and see stale-looking behavior:
206	
207	```
208	find oauthsvc -name "__pycache__" -type d -exec rm -rf {} +
209	```
210	
211	On Windows PowerShell:
212	
213	```
214	Get-ChildItem -Path oauthsvc -Recurse -Directory -Filter "__pycache__" | Remove-Item -Recurse -Force
215	```
216	
217	## Platform-Specific Notes
218	
219	Owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools
220	
221	Interpreter installation and pinning differ enough by platform that Platform Tools maintains separate pages rather than folding everything into this one:
222	
223	- **Windows Setup Notes** covers the `py` launcher, the python.org installer, and a note about older laptops still running 3.9 that this page treats as Sunset.
224	- **macOS Setup Notes** covers Homebrew-installed interpreters and a known conflict between the system-provided Python and a Homebrew-installed one on the search path.
225	- **Linux Setup Notes**, maintained by the Tooling Guild rather than Platform Tools, covers `apt`- and `pyenv`-based installs and is the oldest of the three, having last been reviewed well before the current version matrix took shape.
226	
227	If a platform-specific page and this page disagree on a minimum version, treat this page's matrix as current, since the platform pages are reviewed on their own slower rhythm.
228	
229	## Sunset Timeline for Older Interpreters
230	
231	| Version | Status | Sunset date | Notes |
232	|---|---|---|---|
233	| 3.8 | Unsupported | 2025-04-01 | Removed from the matrix in version 1.4 of this page |
234	| 3.9 | Sunset | 2026-03-31 | One remaining long-lived host still runs this; do not start new work against it |
235	| 3.10 | Secondary, becomes floor going forward | — | No sunset date currently set |

240	## Requesting an Exception
241	
242	If a piece of work genuinely needs to target an interpreter outside the current Supported Version Matrix — most often an older interpreter still running on a single long-lived host — open an issue tagged `python-version` and loop in Priya Nandakumar directly rather than assuming silence means agreement. Exceptions are tracked informally on the team channel rather than in a separate page, and they are reviewed at the same quarterly cadence as the rest of the matrix. As of this update, the only standing exception is the 3.9 host referenced in the Sunset Timeline above, and it is expected to close out once that host is replaced, currently planned for sometime around March of 2026.
243	
244	## Terminology
245	
246	- **Interpreter** — the specific Python binary a machine runs the package under, identified by its version number (for example, 3.12.6).
247	- **Primary interpreter** — the version the team develops and packages against day to day.
248	- **Secondary interpreter** — a version Core Services checks against but does not use as the default working interpreter.
249	- **Sunset** — the state of a version that is still allowed but is being wound down, with a stated end date after which it drops off the matrix entirely.
250	- **Floor version** — the oldest interpreter version the package is still required to run correctly under.
251	- **`requires-python`** — the packaging metadata field, set in `pyproject.toml`, that declares the allowed interpreter range.
252	- **Virtual environment** — an isolated installation of developer-side tooling created with the standard library's `venv` module, kept separate from any system interpreter.
253	- **Byte-compiled cache** — the `__pycache__` directories an interpreter writes alongside source files; these are local artifacts and are never checked in.
254	- **Bundled SQLite library** — the specific build of SQLite linked into a given Python interpreter's `sqlite3` module, which varies by interpreter version.
255	- **Version matrix** — the table on this page listing each interpreter version, its status, and the platforms it is supported on.

# Supported Python Versions

| | |
|---|---|
| **Title** | Supported Python Versions |
| **Version** | 1.7 |
| **Owner** | Core Services (Priya Nandakumar) |
| **Last updated** | 2026-01-20 |

**Summary:** This page lists the Python interpreter versions the `oauthsvc` package is expected to run under, explains how the supported range is chosen and reviewed, and describes the local steps a developer takes to install, pin, and check an interpreter before working on the repository. It also covers how the standard-library-only nature of the package interacts with interpreter version differences, and how the bundled SQLite library that backs the local database file varies across Python builds.

## Purpose and Coverage

Owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services

`oauthsvc` ships as a small standard-library package with a command line front end and a loopback HTTP service, and it keeps its working state in a local SQLite file. Because it has no third-party runtime dependencies, the single biggest source of behavioral drift between developer machines is the interpreter itself — differences in the standard library, in the bundled SQLite library, and in default settings for things like hash seeding or byte-compiled cache placement.

This page exists so that every contributor, whether on a laptop running Windows, a Linux workstation, or a Mac, is working against an interpreter that Core Services has actually exercised. It is the page to check before you install anything, before you open an editor, and before you file a pull request that touches interpreter-sensitive code such as anything that reads or writes the local database file.

## Supported Version Matrix

The table below is the current picture of what Core Services builds against, checks against, and will accept pull requests against. "Primary" means the interpreter used for day-to-day development and for the reference builds published from the release branch. "Secondary" means we check against it but do not develop on it by default. "Sunset" means support is winding down on the stated date.

| Python version | Status | Windows | macOS | Linux | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3.9 | Sunset (2026-03-31) | Allowed on older laptops only | Not checked | Allowed | Kept alive mainly for one long-lived internal host; do not develop new work against it |
| 3.10 | Secondary | Supported | Supported | Supported | Floor for any new machine setup |
| 3.11 | Secondary | Supported | Supported | Supported | Good middle ground; some contributors still prefer it for the faster startup time |
| 3.12 | Primary | Supported | Supported | Supported | The interpreter Core Services develops and packages against |
| 3.13 | Secondary, promoting to Primary in Q2 2026 | Supported | Supported | Supported | Watch this page for the promotion date |
| 3.14 | Not yet supported | — | — | — | Tracked but not installed on any shared machine as of this writing |

If you are setting up a new machine today, install 3.12 as your working interpreter and keep 3.10 available for a quick local check, since 3.10 remains the floor for the supported range.

## How Supported Versions Are Chosen

Owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services

Core Services reviews the supported range roughly once a quarter, timed loosely to align with upstream Python's own release calendar. The inputs to that review are:

- the oldest interpreter still installed on any machine that runs the loopback service outside of a developer's own laptop;
- any standard-library change that affects the package's behavior, most often in argument parsing, the `sqlite3` module, or `http.server`;
- the interpreter versions available through the operating-system package managers used across the team (Homebrew, apt, and the Windows installer from python.org); and
- capacity on the Tooling Guild's side to keep additional interpreters installed on the shared build machine.

The outcome of each review is recorded as an update to the version matrix above and to the `requires-python` line in the root `pyproject.toml`. A short note goes out on the team channel; there is no separate sign-off step, though Build & Release is looped in whenever the change affects the packaging metadata.

A typical `requires-python` line, after a review that dropped 3.9 from Secondary to Sunset, looks like this:

```
requires-python = ">=3.10,<3.14"
```

## Minimum, Target, and Upcoming Versions

| Category | Version | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum supported | 3.10 | Anything older is Sunset or unsupported |
| Target / Primary | 3.12 | What new contributors should install first |
| Next Primary | 3.13 | Promotion planned for Q2 2026 |
| Under evaluation | 3.14 | No installed reference build yet |

## Checking Your Interpreter Version

Owner: Dana Kessler, Tooling Guild

Before doing anything else, confirm which interpreter is first on your shell's search path and what version it reports.

On Linux or macOS:

```
python3 --version
which -a python3
```

On Windows, using the `py` launcher that ships with the python.org installer:

```
py -0p
py -3.12 --version
```

If `python3 --version` (or `py -3.12 --version`) reports anything outside the Supported Version Matrix above, stop and install a supported interpreter before continuing with the rest of workstation setup.

Dana's team also keeps a small helper script at `scripts/check-python-version.sh` (and a PowerShell equivalent at `scripts/verify-interpreter-matrix.ps1`) that reads the current `requires-python` line out of `pyproject.toml` and compares it against whatever interpreter is first on the path, printing a plain warning line if they disagree. Neither script installs anything for you; they only report what is already on the machine.

## Installing and Pinning Interpreters Locally

Owner: Dana Kessler, Tooling Guild

Most contributors keep more than one interpreter installed and use one of the following to pin the version for this repository specifically.

**pyenv (Linux and macOS)**

```
pyenv install 3.12.6
pyenv install 3.10.14
pyenv local 3.12.6
```

Running `pyenv local` writes a `.python-version` file at the repository root. That file is checked in, so everyone who clones the repository and has `pyenv` on their path gets the same primary interpreter automatically. If you need to check the repository against the floor version instead, run `pyenv shell 3.10.14` for a single terminal session rather than changing the checked-in pin.

**py launcher (Windows)**

Windows contributors generally do not use a per-repository pin file; instead they select the interpreter explicitly with the `py` launcher:

```
py -3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
```

**Virtual environments (all platforms)**

Regardless of how the interpreter itself is selected, create a virtual environment scoped to the repository rather than installing anything into a shared or system interpreter:

```
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
```

Because the package has no runtime dependencies outside the standard library, the virtual environment mainly exists to isolate the developer-side tooling (type checker, formatter, and linter) named later on this page, not to hold the package's own runtime requirements.

## Standard Library Considerations for a Stdlib-Only Package

Owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services

Since `oauthsvc` has no third-party runtime dependencies, standard-library differences between interpreter versions are the main source of cross-version surprises. A few areas Core Services watches closely:

- **Argument parsing.** Minor formatting changes to the built-in argument parser's help and error output have shown up between minor Python releases. If you are changing how the command line reports errors, check the rendered output on both the Primary interpreter (3.12) and the floor interpreter (3.10) before opening a pull request.
- **The local HTTP handling in the standard library.** The loopback HTTP service relies on the standard library's own HTTP server support. Timeout and connection-close behavior for that support has shifted slightly across versions; if you touch anything in that area, run a manual check on at least two interpreters from the matrix.
- **`sqlite3` module updates.** The standard library's `sqlite3` module tracks a bundled build of the SQLite library, and that build is not the same across Python versions. See the next section for specifics.
- **`tomllib`.** Added to the standard library in Python 3.11. Any packaging-adjacent code that reads TOML must not assume its presence on the floor interpreter (3.10), which does not have it.
- **Hash seeding.** Python's default hash randomization affects the iteration order of unordered structures. This has occasionally caused a false sense of a version-specific bug when the underlying cause was just an assumption about ordering that happened to hold on one machine and not another.

None of the above requires special code paths for each interpreter version in most cases, but it does mean a change should be spot-checked on more than one interpreter, particularly the floor version, before a pull request goes up for review.

## The Bundled SQLite Library and the Local Database File

Owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services

The service keeps its working state in a local SQLite file, and the version of the underlying SQLite library that ships inside a given Python build matters more than most contributors expect. The table below reflects what Core Services has observed on the interpreters in the matrix, using the python.org installers and the platform package managers current as of this update.

| Python version | Bundled SQLite library (typical) |
|---|---|
| 3.10 | 3.37.x |
| 3.11 | 3.39.x |
| 3.12 | 3.43.x |
| 3.13 | 3.45.x |

Because the floor and the Primary interpreter can be several SQLite minor versions apart, always confirm the bundled library's version and the installed command-line shell's version separately, rather than assuming they match. The command-line shell is a separate binary from whatever the interpreter links against:

```
sqlite3 -version
```

If you need to inspect the settings SQLite is using for the local database file directly, the command-line shell also accepts `PRAGMA` statements interactively:

```
sqlite3 path\to\the.db
sqlite> PRAGMA journal_mode;
sqlite> PRAGMA compile_options;
```

Further detail on the local database file itself — its location on disk and how it is opened by the service — lives on the sibling page **Local Database File Notes**, not here; this page is only concerned with how the interpreter's bundled SQLite library varies.

## Type-Checking Across Multiple Interpreter Versions

Owner: Theo Banks, Developer Experience

The team's type checker needs to be told which interpreter version it is checking against, since it otherwise defaults to whatever interpreter it was itself installed under. Set this explicitly rather than relying on the default:

For `mypy`, in `pyproject.toml`:

```
[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.10"
```

Setting this to the floor version (3.10) rather than the Primary version (3.12) is deliberate — it catches uses of standard-library features that are newer than what the floor interpreter provides, such as an accidental reliance on `tomllib`.

For editors using Pyright (see the sibling page **Editor Configuration** for the rest of the editor setup), the equivalent setting lives in `pyrightconfig.json`:

```
{
  "pythonVersion": "3.10"
}
```

## Local Verification Before Opening a Pull Request

Owner: Owen Castillo, Build & Release

Before a pull request goes up, run a local verification pass against at least the floor interpreter and the Primary interpreter. There is no shared verification runner beyond what each contributor runs locally, so this step is on you rather than something that happens automatically later.

```
pyenv shell 3.10.14
python -m compileall oauthsvc/
pyenv shell 3.12.6
python -m compileall oauthsvc/
```

Running `compileall` is a fast way to surface anything that fails to byte-compile on one interpreter but not the other, which usually means a syntax feature newer than the floor version has crept in. It does not substitute for a manual check of the command line and the loopback HTTP service on both interpreters, but it catches the cheapest class of mistake early.

Byte-compiled caches are written under `__pycache__/` directories throughout `oauthsvc/`. These are local artifacts; do not check them in, and clear them if you switch interpreters and see stale-looking behavior:

```
find oauthsvc -name "__pycache__" -type d -exec rm -rf {} +
```

On Windows PowerShell:

```
Get-ChildItem -Path oauthsvc -Recurse -Directory -Filter "__pycache__" | Remove-Item -Recurse -Force
```

## Platform-Specific Notes

Owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools

Interpreter installation and pinning differ enough by platform that Platform Tools maintains separate pages rather than folding everything into this one:

- **Windows Setup Notes** covers the `py` launcher, the python.org installer, and a note about older laptops still running 3.9 that this page treats as Sunset.
- **macOS Setup Notes** covers Homebrew-installed interpreters and a known conflict between the system-provided Python and a Homebrew-installed one on the search path.
- **Linux Setup Notes**, maintained by the Tooling Guild rather than Platform Tools, covers `apt`- and `pyenv`-based installs and is the oldest of the three, having last been reviewed well before the current version matrix took shape.

If a platform-specific page and this page disagree on a minimum version, treat this page's matrix as current, since the platform pages are reviewed on their own slower rhythm.

## Sunset Timeline for Older Interpreters

| Version | Status | Sunset date | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.8 | Unsupported | 2025-04-01 | Removed from the matrix in version 1.4 of this page |
| 3.9 | Sunset | 2026-03-31 | One remaining long-lived host still runs this; do not start new work against it |
| 3.10 | Secondary, becomes floor going forward | — | No sunset date currently set |
| 3.11 | Secondary | — | No sunset date currently set |
| 3.12 | Primary | — | No sunset date currently set |
| 3.13 | Secondary, promotes to Primary | 2026-04 (promotion, not sunset) | Watch the Q2 2026 review |

## Requesting an Exception

If a piece of work genuinely needs to target an interpreter outside the current Supported Version Matrix — most often an older interpreter still running on a single long-lived host — open an issue tagged `python-version` and loop in Priya Nandakumar directly rather than assuming silence means agreement. Exceptions are tracked informally on the team channel rather than in a separate page, and they are reviewed at the same quarterly cadence as the rest of the matrix. As of this update, the only standing exception is the 3.9 host referenced in the Sunset Timeline above, and it is expected to close out once that host is replaced, currently planned for sometime around March of 2026.

## Terminology

- **Interpreter** — the specific Python binary a machine runs the package under, identified by its version number (for example, 3.12.6).
- **Primary interpreter** — the version the team develops and packages against day to day.
- **Secondary interpreter** — a version Core Services checks against but does not use as the default working interpreter.
- **Sunset** — the state of a version that is still allowed but is being wound down, with a stated end date after which it drops off the matrix entirely.
- **Floor version** — the oldest interpreter version the package is still required to run correctly under.
- **`requires-python`** — the packaging metadata field, set in `pyproject.toml`, that declares the allowed interpreter range.
- **Virtual environment** — an isolated installation of developer-side tooling created with the standard library's `venv` module, kept separate from any system interpreter.
- **Byte-compiled cache** — the `__pycache__` directories an interpreter writes alongside source files; these are local artifacts and are never checked in.
- **Bundled SQLite library** — the specific build of SQLite linked into a given Python interpreter's `sqlite3` module, which varies by interpreter version.
- **Version matrix** — the table on this page listing each interpreter version, its status, and the platforms it is supported on.

## Files and Paths Referenced

| Path | Component |
|---|---|
| `pyproject.toml` | Root packaging file; carries the `requires-python` range and the `mypy` interpreter setting |
| `.python-version` | Repository-root file written by `pyenv local`, pinning the default interpreter for anyone with `pyenv` on their path |
| `pyrightconfig.json` | Editor-side type-checker configuration; carries the `pythonVersion` setting |
| `oauthsvc/` | The package directory itself; the target of local byte-compile checks across interpreters |
| `scripts/check-python-version.sh` | Helper script comparing the active interpreter against the `requires-python` line, for Linux and macOS |
| `scripts/verify-interpreter-matrix.ps1` | PowerShell equivalent of the above, for Windows |
| `README.md` | Repository-root readme; points newcomers toward the developer handbook |
| `docs/developer-handbook/python-version-support.md` | This page |
| `docs/developer-handbook/workstation-setup.md` | General workstation setup, referenced for install order |
| `docs/developer-handbook/editor-configuration.md` | Editor setup, including where the type-checker's interpreter version is configured |
| `docs/developer-handbook/local-database-file-notes.md` | Detail on the local database file's location and handling, separate from interpreter concerns covered here |
| `docs/developer-handbook/windows-setup-notes.rst` | Platform-specific interpreter installation for Windows |
| `docs/developer-handbook/macos-setup-notes.rst` | Platform-specific interpreter installation for macOS |
| `docs/developer-handbook/linux-setup-notes.txt` | Platform-specific interpreter installation for Linux |
| `docs/developer-handbook/dependency-management.txt` | Covers developer-side tooling versions distinct from the package's own (nonexistent) runtime dependencies |
| `docs/developer-handbook/lint-formatting-config.yaml` | Lint and formatting tool configuration, including any per-interpreter settings for those tools |

## Tools and Libraries

| Tool | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| pyenv | 2.4.10 | Local interpreter installation and pinning on Linux and macOS |
| py launcher | ships with python.org 3.12 installer | Interpreter selection on Windows |
| venv (standard library) | matches host interpreter | Isolated developer-side tooling environment |
| pip | 24.0 | Installing developer-side tooling into the virtual environment |
| mypy | 1.10.0 | Type-checking against the floor interpreter version |
| Pyright | 1.1.370 | Editor-integrated type-checking |
| SQLite command-line shell | 3.45.1 | Inspecting the local database file's settings independently of the interpreter's bundled library |
| git | 2.45 | Version control |

## Change Log

- **2026-01-20 — v1.7.** Promoted 3.12 from Secondary to Primary; set a Q2 2026 target for promoting 3.13; updated the bundled-SQLite-library table after Priya's March 2026 stdlib survey confirmed the 3.13 figures.
- **2025-11-02 — v1.6.** Moved 3.9 from Secondary to Sunset with an end date of 2026-03-31; added the Requesting an Exception section after two informal requests came in over the same quarter.
- **2025-07-14 — v1.5.** Added the Standard Library Considerations section following a round of reports about argument-parsing help text differing between 3.10 and 3.11.

## Related Pages

1	# Workstation Setup
2	
3	**Version:** 2.4
4	**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-11-03
6	
7	This page walks a new contributor through building a working local development environment for the `oauthsvc` repository on a personal workstation, from a bare checkout to a virtual environment that can run the package's command line and loopback service and open its local SQLite state file. It also covers the conventions contributors are expected to follow once the environment is running: supported Python versions, editor configuration, code review conventions, commit message style, and coding style. Several of these topics have their own, more detailed sibling pages in this folder; this page gives the version a new contributor needs on day one and points to the deeper page where useful.
8	
9	If you are setting up a shared or managed workstation image rather than a personal laptop, read the Windows, macOS, or Linux setup notes for platform-specific detail before you start — this page assumes you have shell access and can install software yourself.
10	
11	## Coverage and Audience
12	
13	This page is aimed at engineers joining the team that maintains `oauthsvc`, whether they are full-time contributors or visiting from another team for a short-lived piece of work. It does not cover how to deploy the service, how the command line or loopback service behave once running, or what the local database file stores — those are out of coverage for a workstation setup guide and are described, where they are described at all, in other parts of the handbook.
14	
15	By the end of this page you should have:
16	
17	- A cloned copy of the repository on your workstation.
18	- A Python virtual environment with the package installed in editable mode along with the developer tooling used by the team.
19	- An editor configured to pick up the repository's formatting and lint settings automatically.
20	- A working understanding of how the team reviews changes, writes commit messages, and formats code, so your first pull request doesn't come back covered in comments about style.
21	
22	## Prerequisites
23	
24	Before you start, confirm the following are true for your workstation. Section owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen).
25	
26	1. You have a supported Python interpreter installed (see "Supported Python Versions" below).
27	2. You have `git` installed and can reach the internal git remote from your network.
28	3. You have a terminal and an editor you're comfortable in — VS Code is the team default, but nothing here requires it.
29	4. You have at least 500 MB of free disk space for the virtual environment and any local database files you create while working.
30	
31	A minimal prerequisites checklist, for people who like checklists:
32	
33	- [ ] Python interpreter installed and on your `PATH`
34	- [ ] `git` installed, version 2.34 or newer
35	- [ ] Terminal access (PowerShell, bash, or zsh)
36	- [ ] Editor installed and, ideally, the recommended extensions from the Editor Configuration page
37	
38	## Cloning the Repository
39	
40	Clone the repository the way you would any other internal project:
41	
42	```
43	git clone git@git.internal.example.com:platform/oauthsvc.git
44	cd oauthsvc
45	```
46	
47	The repository root holds the `oauthsvc/` package directory and a top-level `README.md`. There is no `src/` layout — the package directory sits directly under the repository root. You'll also find a `docs/` folder (this handbook lives under `docs/developer-handbook/`) and a `scripts/` folder with a couple of small setup helpers described later on this page.
48	
49	## Creating a Virtual Environment
50	
51	The package uses only the standard library at runtime, but the developer tooling around it (formatter, linter, and a couple of editor helpers) is installed from a small `pyproject.toml` in the repository root. Create an isolated environment before installing anything:
52	
53	**macOS / Linux**
54	
55	```
56	python3 -m venv .venv
57	source .venv/bin/activate
58	python -m pip install --upgrade pip
59	python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
60	```
61	
62	**Windows (PowerShell)**
63	
64	```
65	py -3.11 -m venv .venv
66	.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
67	python -m pip install --upgrade pip
68	python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
69	```
70	
71	The `-e` install links the package directory into the environment so that changes you make on disk are picked up immediately, without reinstalling. The `[dev]` extra pulls in the formatter, linter, and a couple of small helper packages the team uses; it does not include anything the service needs to run.
72	
73	If you'd rather not type this out every time you set up a new workstation, the repository ships two small wrapper scripts:
74	
75	- `scripts/setup-workstation.sh` — bash wrapper for macOS and Linux that creates `.venv`, upgrades `pip`, and installs the `dev` extras.
76	- `scripts/setup-workstation.ps1` — PowerShell equivalent for Windows.
77	
78	Both scripts are thin; read them before running them if you're unsure what they do on your machine. Neither script starts the service or the command line — they only prepare the environment.
79	
80	## Verifying the Install
81	
82	Once the virtual environment is active, confirm the interpreter and the installed package resolve the way you expect:
83	
84	```
85	python --version
86	python -m pip show oauthsvc
87	```
88	
89	You should see a version string matching the current `pyproject.toml` and an install location under your `.venv`. If `pip show` reports the package as missing, re-run the editable install step above — this is the most common setup mistake and almost always means the virtual environment wasn't active when you ran `pip install`.
90	
91	## Supported Python Versions
92	
93	Section owner: Core Services (Priya Nandakumar). See the "Supported Python Versions" page (v1.5, last updated 2025-11-20) for the full compatibility table and the reasoning behind dropped versions; the short version, for workstation setup purposes, is in the table below.
94	
95	| Python version | Status | Notes |
96	|---|---|---|
97	| 3.9 | Not supported | Dropped after the last long-term workstation image update |
98	| 3.10 | Supported, minimum | Baseline for local development and CI |
99	| 3.11 | Supported, recommended | Default on team-issued workstation images since December 2025 |
100	| 3.12 | Supported | Used in a couple of contributors' personal setups; no known issues |
101	| 3.13 | Not yet validated | Avoid for now unless you're specifically asked to try it |
102	
103	Use whichever supported interpreter is already on your workstation image. If you're setting up from scratch, install 3.11 — it's the version Platform Tools currently images new laptops with, and it's the version most contributors are running.
104	
105	A quick way to confirm which interpreters are on your `PATH`:
106	
107	```
108	py -0            # Windows: lists installed interpreters
109	which -a python3 # macOS/Linux: lists python3 on PATH
110	```
111	
112	If you manage multiple Python versions with `pyenv` or a similar tool, make sure the version you activate inside `.venv` matches one of the supported versions above before you install anything.
113	
114	## Editor Configuration
115	
116	Section owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks). This section gives you enough to be productive on day one; the "Editor Configuration" page (v1.1) has the full set of recommended extensions and keybindings for several editors.
117	
118	The repository ships a root `.editorconfig` that most editors pick up automatically:
119	
120	```
121	root = true
122	
123	[*]
124	indent_style = space
125	indent_size = 4
126	end_of_line = lf
127	charset = utf-8
128	trim_trailing_whitespace = true
129	insert_final_newline = true
130	
131	[*.md]
132	trim_trailing_whitespace = false
133	```
134	
135	If you use VS Code, add the following to your workspace settings (`.vscode/settings.json`, not checked into the repository) so the built-in formatter and linter integrations behave:
136	
137	```
138	{
139	  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
140	  "editor.rulers": [100],
141	  "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
142	  "python.analysis.typeCheckingMode": "basic"
143	}
144	```
145	
146	Recommended settings by editor, for reference:
147	
148	| Editor | Line length ruler | Format on save | Notes |
149	|---|---|---|---|
150	| VS Code | 100 | Yes | Team default; extensions listed on the Editor Configuration page |
151	| PyCharm | 100 | Yes | Set under Editor > Code Style |
152	| Vim / Neovim | 100 | Depends on plugin | `.editorconfig` support via a plugin is required |
153	| Sublime Text | 100 | Yes | Less common on this team; ask in the team channel if you need help |
154	
155	Whatever editor you use, make sure it respects `.editorconfig` and doesn't silently reformat whitespace on files it opens — that's the single most common source of noisy, unreviewable diffs on this project.
156	
157	## Code Review Conventions
158	
159	Section owner: Core Services (Priya Nandakumar). Full detail lives on the "Code Review Conventions" page; the working conventions below are what you need to open your first pull request.
160	
161	General expectations:
162	
163	- Keep pull requests small. A change that touches more than roughly 400 lines (excluding generated or vendored files) should usually be split.
164	- Every pull request needs at least one other contributor to sign off before it merges into the main branch. Two sign-offs are expected for changes that touch the package's core behavior rather than tooling or docs.
165	- Draft pull requests are fine, and encouraged, for work you want early feedback on before it's ready to merge.
166	- Don't merge your own change, even if you have the technical ability to do so, unless the change is a documentation typo fix or similarly trivial and a second reviewer isn't reasonably available.
167	
168	A rough checklist reviewers use, and one you should run through yourself before requesting review:
169	
170	1. Does the change do one thing, and does the description say what that thing is?
171	2. Are commit messages readable on their own, without the pull request description open? (See "Commit Message Style" below.)
172	3. Does the diff match the description — no unrelated formatting-only changes mixed in?
173	4. Is anything left commented out, or any leftover debugging output, that shouldn't ship?
174	
175	The reviewer's job is to read the change carefully enough to explain it back, not just to click through and sign off. If a reviewer can't summarize what a change does, that's a signal the pull request needs a better description or needs splitting.
176	
177	| Pull request size (lines changed) | Expected reviewers | Typical turnaround |
178	|---|---|---|
179	| Under 50 | 1 | Same day |
180	| 50–200 | 1 | Within one working day |
181	| 200–400 | 2 | Within two working days |
182	| Over 400 | 2, plus a short design note | Split if at all possible |

184	## Commit Message Style
185	
186	Section owner: Build & Release (Owen Castillo). Full convention lives on the "Commit Message Style" page; the short version:
187	
188	- Subject line: imperative mood, no trailing period, under 72 characters. "Fix loopback service shutdown on Windows," not "Fixed loopback service shutdown on Windows."
189	- Leave a blank line between the subject and the body.
190	- Body: wrap at roughly 72 characters, explain *why* the change was made, not just *what* changed — the diff already shows what changed.
191	- Reference an issue number in the body when one exists, on its own line, e.g. `Refs: PLAT-214`.
192	
193	A worked example:
194	
195	```
196	Guard virtual environment activation script for spaces in paths
197	
198	Contributors on shared workstations sometimes have a workstation
199	username containing a space, which broke the PowerShell activation
200	script's path handling. Quote the path before passing it to
201	Set-Location so activation works regardless of username.
202	
203	Refs: PLAT-238
204	```
205	
206	Squash small, exploratory commits before opening a pull request so the git log on the main branch stays readable — nobody six months from now wants to page through eleven "fix typo" commits to understand a single change. `git rebase -i` against the branch point is the usual tool for this:
207	
208	```
209	git rebase -i main
210	```
211	
212	Mark the commits you want folded together as `squash` (or `s`) in the editor that opens, keep the first commit as `pick`, and write a combined message that follows the format above.

214	## Coding Style
215	
216	Section owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks). Full detail, including the automated lint and formatter configuration, lives on the "Coding Style Guide" page and in `lint-formatting-config.yaml` at the repository root.
217	
218	Naming and layout conventions:
219	
220	- Modules, functions, and local names: `snake_case`.
221	- Classes and exceptions: `PascalCase`.
222	- Constants: `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`.
223	- Line length: 100 characters, matching the editor ruler configured above.
224	- Prefer double quotes for strings unless the string itself contains a double quote, in which case use single quotes rather than escaping.
225	- Group imports in three blocks — standard library, third-party, local — separated by a single blank line, each block sorted alphabetically.
226	- Type hints are expected on any function whose parameters or return value aren't obvious from the name alone; they're not required everywhere, but reviewers will ask for them where they'd help.
227	
228	Docstrings follow a short, one-line summary followed by an optional blank line and further detail; the team doesn't require a particular docstring format (no strict adherence to a specific style guide's field syntax) but does expect every public function and class to have one.
229	
230	Formatting and lint checks run automatically through the tooling installed with the `dev` extras above; run them yourself before opening a pull request rather than waiting for a reviewer to point out a formatting issue:
231	
232	```
233	ruff format .
234	ruff check .
235	```
236	
237	Fix anything the linter flags before you push, or leave a short note in the pull request description explaining why a particular flagged line is intentional — reviewers will otherwise assume it was missed.

239	## Local Database File on a Workstation
240	
241	Section owner: Tooling Guild (Dana Kessler). The package keeps its state in a single local SQLite file. For workstation setup purposes, all you need is where that file lives by default and how to point it somewhere else while developing:
242	
243	| Platform | Default location |
244	|---|---|
245	| Linux | `~/.local/share/oauthsvc/state.db` |
246	| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/oauthsvc/state.db` |
247	| Windows | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\oauthsvc\state.db` |
248	
249	You can override the directory with an environment variable (`PLATSVC_STATE_DIR`) if you want to keep a separate copy of the file per checkout, which is useful if you're working on more than one branch's worth of local state at a time and don't want them mixing:

253	```

286	- **Formatter** — a tool that automatically rewrites code to a consistent layout, run before or as part of committing.
287	- **Main branch** — the primary long-lived branch that pull requests target; called `main` in this repository.
288	- **Feature branch** — a short-lived branch created for a single piece of work, removed once it merges.

# Workstation Setup

**Version:** 2.4
**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
**Last updated:** 2025-11-03

This page walks a new contributor through building a working local development environment for the `oauthsvc` repository on a personal workstation, from a bare checkout to a virtual environment that can run the package's command line and loopback service and open its local SQLite state file. It also covers the conventions contributors are expected to follow once the environment is running: supported Python versions, editor configuration, code review conventions, commit message style, and coding style. Several of these topics have their own, more detailed sibling pages in this folder; this page gives the version a new contributor needs on day one and points to the deeper page where useful.

If you are setting up a shared or managed workstation image rather than a personal laptop, read the Windows, macOS, or Linux setup notes for platform-specific detail before you start — this page assumes you have shell access and can install software yourself.

## Coverage and Audience

This page is aimed at engineers joining the team that maintains `oauthsvc`, whether they are full-time contributors or visiting from another team for a short-lived piece of work. It does not cover how to deploy the service, how the command line or loopback service behave once running, or what the local database file stores — those are out of coverage for a workstation setup guide and are described, where they are described at all, in other parts of the handbook.

By the end of this page you should have:

- A cloned copy of the repository on your workstation.
- A Python virtual environment with the package installed in editable mode along with the developer tooling used by the team.
- An editor configured to pick up the repository's formatting and lint settings automatically.
- A working understanding of how the team reviews changes, writes commit messages, and formats code, so your first pull request doesn't come back covered in comments about style.

## Prerequisites

Before you start, confirm the following are true for your workstation. Section owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen).

1. You have a supported Python interpreter installed (see "Supported Python Versions" below).
2. You have `git` installed and can reach the internal git remote from your network.
3. You have a terminal and an editor you're comfortable in — VS Code is the team default, but nothing here requires it.
4. You have at least 500 MB of free disk space for the virtual environment and any local database files you create while working.

A minimal prerequisites checklist, for people who like checklists:

- [ ] Python interpreter installed and on your `PATH`
- [ ] `git` installed, version 2.34 or newer
- [ ] Terminal access (PowerShell, bash, or zsh)
- [ ] Editor installed and, ideally, the recommended extensions from the Editor Configuration page

## Cloning the Repository

Clone the repository the way you would any other internal project:

```
git clone git@git.internal.example.com:platform/oauthsvc.git
cd oauthsvc
```

The repository root holds the `oauthsvc/` package directory and a top-level `README.md`. There is no `src/` layout — the package directory sits directly under the repository root. You'll also find a `docs/` folder (this handbook lives under `docs/developer-handbook/`) and a `scripts/` folder with a couple of small setup helpers described later on this page.

## Creating a Virtual Environment

The package uses only the standard library at runtime, but the developer tooling around it (formatter, linter, and a couple of editor helpers) is installed from a small `pyproject.toml` in the repository root. Create an isolated environment before installing anything:

**macOS / Linux**

```
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

**Windows (PowerShell)**

```
py -3.11 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

The `-e` install links the package directory into the environment so that changes you make on disk are picked up immediately, without reinstalling. The `[dev]` extra pulls in the formatter, linter, and a couple of small helper packages the team uses; it does not include anything the service needs to run.

If you'd rather not type this out every time you set up a new workstation, the repository ships two small wrapper scripts:

- `scripts/setup-workstation.sh` — bash wrapper for macOS and Linux that creates `.venv`, upgrades `pip`, and installs the `dev` extras.
- `scripts/setup-workstation.ps1` — PowerShell equivalent for Windows.

Both scripts are thin; read them before running them if you're unsure what they do on your machine. Neither script starts the service or the command line — they only prepare the environment.

## Verifying the Install

Once the virtual environment is active, confirm the interpreter and the installed package resolve the way you expect:

```
python --version
python -m pip show oauthsvc
```

You should see a version string matching the current `pyproject.toml` and an install location under your `.venv`. If `pip show` reports the package as missing, re-run the editable install step above — this is the most common setup mistake and almost always means the virtual environment wasn't active when you ran `pip install`.

## Supported Python Versions

Section owner: Core Services (Priya Nandakumar). See the "Supported Python Versions" page (v1.5, last updated 2025-11-20) for the full compatibility table and the reasoning behind dropped versions; the short version, for workstation setup purposes, is in the table below.

| Python version | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 3.9 | Not supported | Dropped after the last long-term workstation image update |
| 3.10 | Supported, minimum | Baseline for local development and CI |
| 3.11 | Supported, recommended | Default on team-issued workstation images since December 2025 |
| 3.12 | Supported | Used in a couple of contributors' personal setups; no known issues |
| 3.13 | Not yet validated | Avoid for now unless you're specifically asked to try it |

Use whichever supported interpreter is already on your workstation image. If you're setting up from scratch, install 3.11 — it's the version Platform Tools currently images new laptops with, and it's the version most contributors are running.

A quick way to confirm which interpreters are on your `PATH`:

```
py -0            # Windows: lists installed interpreters
which -a python3 # macOS/Linux: lists python3 on PATH
```

If you manage multiple Python versions with `pyenv` or a similar tool, make sure the version you activate inside `.venv` matches one of the supported versions above before you install anything.

Section owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks). This section gives you enough to be productive on day one; the "Editor Configuration" page (v1.1) has the full set of recommended extensions and keybindings for several editors.

The repository ships a root `.editorconfig` that most editors pick up automatically:

```
root = true

[*]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 4
end_of_line = lf
charset = utf-8
trim_trailing_whitespace = true
insert_final_newline = true

[*.md]
trim_trailing_whitespace = false
```

{

  "editor.rulers": [100],
  "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
  "python.analysis.typeCheckingMode": "basic"
}

|---|---|---|---|

| Vim / Neovim | 100 | Depends on plugin | `.editorconfig` support via a plugin is required |
| Sublime Text | 100 | Yes | Less common on this team; ask in the team channel if you need help |

## Terminology

- **Workstation** — the personal or team-issued machine a contributor develops on, as distinct from any shared build or CI machine.
- **Virtual environment** — an isolated Python installation, created with the standard library `venv` module, that keeps a project's installed packages separate from the system interpreter.
- **Loopback service** — the HTTP service the package can run locally, listening only on the loopback interface rather than being reachable from other machines on the network.
- **Local database file** — the single SQLite file the package uses to keep its state on disk, as opposed to any remote database.
- **Editor configuration profile** — the set of editor settings (indentation, line length, format-on-save, and similar) a contributor's editor uses for this repository, ideally derived from `.editorconfig` and the lint and formatter configuration rather than set by hand.
- **Working tree** — the checked-out files on disk for a git repository, as opposed to the git object store or the remote.
- **Pull request** — a proposed change submitted for review before it merges into the main branch; used interchangeably with "review request" on this team.
- **Lint** — automated static checking of code for style and common mistakes, run through the tooling installed with the `dev` extras.
- **Formatter** — a tool that automatically rewrites code to a consistent layout, run before or as part of committing.
- **Main branch** — the primary long-lived branch that pull requests target; called `main` in this repository.

- `local-database-file-notes.md` names the file `oauthsvc.db`, located at

Two documents that each formally define the same glossary term point to a different

is supposed to be the one local database file the service uses.

Beyond point 7's factual conflict, the six documents that define this concept don't even

"Database file" (`coding-style-guide.md`, `local-database-file-notes.md`), and "Local
database file" (`code-review-conventions.md`, `editor-configuration.md`,
`workstation-setup.md`). Notably, `dependency-management.txt` discusses the database file at
length in its body text but does not define any of these headwords in its own glossary at
all.

## Minor, single-document terms (no cross-document conflict found)

A number of terms are defined in only one glossary, with no other document's glossary using
or contradicting them: "Ambient dependency," "External dependency," "Stdlib," "Module," and
"CI/CD" (all `dependency-management.txt`); "Handler function," "Naming case," and "Draft pull
request" (all `coding-style-guide.md`); "Floor version," "Sunset," and "Bundled SQLite
library" (all `python-version-support.md`); "Console filter" and "File filter" (both
`logging-conventions.md`); "WAL mode" and "Read-only mode" (both `local-database-file-notes.md`).
These are internally consistent simply because nothing elsewhere in the folder engages with
them.

- `workstation-setup.md`'s Tools table lists "pre-commit | 3.7.1 | Optional local hook runner
  for lint checks before commit" — optional, but present as a real, usable tool.
- `lint-formatting-config.yaml` complicates this further on its own: its
  `pre_commit_workflow` section states "The repository includes a pre-commit hook
  configuration," but its own `repository_file_manifest` lists `.pre-commit-config.yaml` as
  "Configuration for pre-commit hooks **(in-progress integration)**" — an internal hedge
  between "included" and "in progress."

### 3. The line length budget: 88 vs. 100

`coding-style-guide.md`'s own glossary fixes this term precisely: "Line length budget — the
maximum number of characters allowed on a single line before the formatter wraps it; **88**
for this package." This is corroborated by `lint-formatting-config.yaml` ("[tool.formatter]:
Specifies line length (88 characters)..." and "Maximum line length: 88 characters"),
`editor-configuration.md` (`"editor.rulers": [88]`), and `linux-setup-notes.txt`'s flake8
invocation (`--max-line-length=88`).

`workstation-setup.md` disagrees with all of them: its VS Code snippet sets
`"editor.rulers": [100]`, its "Recommended settings by editor" table lists "100" as the line
length ruler for every editor, and its own Coding Style section states "Line length: 100
characters, matching the editor ruler configured above." Nothing in `workstation-setup.md`
acknowledges the other pages' 88-character figure.

Separately, `editor-configuration.md` cites the ruler as "matching the line-length convention
documented in the Coding Style Guide (**v3.4**)" — but `coding-style-guide.md`'s own header
identifies itself as version **3.5**, so the citation points at a version one behind the
document's own stated current version.

### 4. The quoted `.editorconfig` contents don't match across documents

Three documents quote what each presents as the repository-root `.editorconfig` file:
`coding-style-guide.md`, `editor-configuration.md`, and `workstation-setup.md`. All three
agree on the `[*]` block (4-space indent, LF line endings, UTF-8, trim trailing whitespace,
insert final newline) and the `[*.md]` exception (trailing whitespace not trimmed). Only
`editor-configuration.md`'s copy includes an additional section:

```
[*.yaml]
indent_size = 2
```

This section is absent from the otherwise-matching copies quoted in `coding-style-guide.md`
and `workstation-setup.md`.

### 5. Inconsistent granularity for "venv" vs. "Virtual environment"

`dependency-management.txt` defines "venv (virtual environment)" as one entry and then
separately lists "Virtual environment: See venv" — treating the two spellings as pure
synonyms of a single concept. `linux-setup-notes.txt` instead defines them as two distinct
things: "Virtual Environment" is the isolated installation concept, while "venv" is
specifically "Standard Python module and the directory containing a virtual environment."
`python-version-support.md`'s definition additionally narrows the purpose of a virtual
environment to isolating "developer-side tooling" specifically (consistent with that page's
framing that the package itself has no runtime dependencies), whereas `README.md` and
`workstation-setup.md` describe it more broadly as isolating "project dependencies" or "a
project's installed packages" in general.

### 6. Pull request: inconsistent branch terminology, and an uncorroborated synonym

The four glossaries that define "Pull request" each name the target branch differently:
`README.md` says "the main development branch," `code-review-conventions.md` says "the
default branch," `linux-setup-notes.txt` says "main," and `workstation-setup.md` says "the
main branch."

`workstation-setup.md`'s entry also adds a claim no other document supports: "used
interchangeably with 'review request' on this team." `code-review-conventions.md` — the page
whose entire subject is the pull request review process, at roughly 8,000 words — never uses
the phrase "review request" anywhere.

### 7. The local database file's identity conflicts across the two documents most focused on it

Both `local-database-file-notes.md` and `workstation-setup.md` define "Local database
file"/"Database file" in their glossaries as the single SQLite file holding the service's
state, and both agree on the concept. But the concrete details their surrounding pages give
for that same term conflict:

- `local-database-file-notes.md` names the file `oauthsvc.db`, located at
  `~/.oauthsvc/oauthsvc.db` (macOS/Linux) or `%USERPROFILE%\.oauthsvc\oauthsvc.db` (Windows),
  overridable via an unnamed "database path environment variable."
- `workstation-setup.md` gives entirely different per-platform paths — `~/.local/share/oauthsvc/state.db`
  (Linux), `~/Library/Application Support/oauthsvc/state.db` (macOS), and
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\oauthsvc\state.db` (Windows) — naming the file `state.db`, not `oauthsvc.db`,
  and overridable via a specifically-named variable, `PLATSVC_STATE_DIR`.

Two documents that each formally define the same glossary term point to a different
filename, a different directory layout, and a differently-named override variable for what
is supposed to be the one local database file the service uses.

### 8. Naming headword inconsistency for the same database-file concept

Beyond point 7's factual conflict, the six documents that define this concept don't even
agree on what to call the glossary headword itself: "SQLite database file" (`README.md`),
"Database file" (`coding-style-guide.md`, `local-database-file-notes.md`), and "Local
database file" (`code-review-conventions.md`, `editor-configuration.md`,
`workstation-setup.md`). Notably, `dependency-management.txt` discusses the database file at
length in its body text but does not define any of these headwords in its own glossary at
all.

## Minor, single-document terms (no cross-document conflict found)

A number of terms are defined in only one glossary, with no other document's glossary using
or contradicting them: "Ambient dependency," "External dependency," "Stdlib," "Module," and
"CI/CD" (all `dependency-management.txt`); "Handler function," "Naming case," and "Draft pull
request" (all `coding-style-guide.md`); "Floor version," "Sunset," and "Bundled SQLite
library" (all `python-version-support.md`); "Console filter" and "File filter" (both
`logging-conventions.md`); "WAL mode" and "Read-only mode" (both `local-database-file-notes.md`).
These are internally consistent simply because nothing elsewhere in the folder engages with
them.

"""Helpers for reasoning about refresh grant decision state."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any, Mapping, Optional


def effective_decision(grant: Mapping[str, Any]) -> Optional[Any]:
    """Return a refresh grant's effective decision record.

    A grant's `current_decision` field is authoritative when present. Grants
    created before that field existed leave it empty, so the effective
    decision falls back to the most recent entry in the append-only
    `decision_history` list.
    """
    current = grant.get("current_decision")
    if current:
        return current

    history = grant.get("decision_history") or []
    return history[-1] if history else None

1	"""SQLite-backed durable storage for accounts, clients, and login state."""
2	
3	from __future__ import annotations
4	
5	import json
6	import sqlite3
7	import time
8	from typing import Optional
9	
10	_SCHEMA = """
11	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS accounts (
12	    account_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
13	    email TEXT NOT NULL,
14	    salt TEXT NOT NULL,
15	    password_hash TEXT NOT NULL
16	);
17	
18	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS clients (
19	    client_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
20	    redirect_uri TEXT NOT NULL
21	);
22	
23	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS pending_logins (
24	    login_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
25	    client_id TEXT NOT NULL,
26	    redirect_uri TEXT NOT NULL,
27	    state TEXT NOT NULL,
28	    kind TEXT NOT NULL,
29	    status TEXT NOT NULL,
30	    created_at REAL NOT NULL
31	);
32	
33	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS legacy_logins (
34	    client_id TEXT NOT NULL,
35	    legacy_handle TEXT NOT NULL,
36	    login_id TEXT NOT NULL,
37	    recovery_locator TEXT NOT NULL,
38	    PRIMARY KEY (client_id, legacy_handle)
39	);
40	
41	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS auth_codes (
42	    code TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
43	    client_id TEXT NOT NULL,
44	    account_id TEXT NOT NULL,
45	    created_at REAL NOT NULL,
46	    used INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
47	);
48	
49	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS refresh_tokens (
50	    token TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
51	    client_id TEXT NOT NULL,
52	    account_id TEXT NOT NULL,
53	    created_at REAL NOT NULL,
54	    revoked INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
55	);
56	
57	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS refresh_grants (
58	    token TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
59	    client_id TEXT NOT NULL,
60	    account_id TEXT NOT NULL,
61	    current_decision TEXT NOT NULL,
62	    decision_history TEXT NOT NULL,
63	    created_at REAL NOT NULL
64	);
65	"""
66	
67	
68	class Database:
69	    def __init__(self, path: str):
70	        self._conn = sqlite3.connect(path, check_same_thread=False)
71	        self._conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
72	        self._conn.executescript(_SCHEMA)
73	        self._conn.commit()
74	
75	    def close(self) -> None:
76	        self._conn.close()
77	
78	    # -- accounts ---------------------------------------------------
79	
80	    def create_account(self, account_id: str, email: str, salt_hex: str, hash_hex: str) -> None:
81	        try:
82	            self._conn.execute(
83	                "INSERT INTO accounts (account_id, email, salt, password_hash) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
84	                (account_id, email, salt_hex, hash_hex),
85	            )
86	            self._conn.commit()
87	        except sqlite3.IntegrityError as exc:
88	            raise ValueError(f"account already exists: {account_id}") from exc
89	
90	    def get_account(self, account_id: str) -> Optional[sqlite3.Row]:
91	        return self._conn.execute(
92	            "SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE account_id = ?", (account_id,)
93	        ).fetchone()
94	
95	    # -- clients ------------------------------------------------------
96	
97	    def register_client(self, client_id: str, redirect_uri: str) -> None:
98	        try:
99	            self._conn.execute(
100	                "INSERT INTO clients (client_id, redirect_uri) VALUES (?, ?)",
101	                (client_id, redirect_uri),
102	            )
103	            self._conn.commit()
104	        except sqlite3.IntegrityError as exc:
105	            raise ValueError(f"client already exists: {client_id}") from exc
106	
107	    def get_client(self, client_id: str) -> Optional[sqlite3.Row]:
108	        return self._conn.execute(
109	            "SELECT * FROM clients WHERE client_id = ?", (client_id,)
110	        ).fetchone()
111	
112	    # -- pending logins -------------------------------------------------
113	
114	    def create_pending_login(
115	        self, login_id: str, client_id: str, redirect_uri: str, state: str, kind: str
116	    ) -> None:
117	        self._conn.execute(
118	            "INSERT INTO pending_logins "
119	            "(login_id, client_id, redirect_uri, state, kind, status, created_at) "
120	            "VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 'pending', ?)",
121	            (login_id, client_id, redirect_uri, state, kind, time.time()),
122	        )
123	        self._conn.commit()
124	
125	    def get_pending_login(self, login_id: str) -> Optional[sqlite3.Row]:
126	        return self._conn.execute(
127	            "SELECT * FROM pending_logins WHERE login_id = ?", (login_id,)
128	        ).fetchone()
129	
130	    def mark_login_completed(self, login_id: str) -> None:
131	        self._conn.execute(
132	            "UPDATE pending_logins SET status = 'completed' WHERE login_id = ?", (login_id,)
133	        )
134	        self._conn.commit()
135	
136	    # -- legacy import ----------------------------------------------------
137	
138	    def import_legacy_login(
139	        self,
140	        client_id: str,
141	        legacy_handle: str,
142	        login_id: str,
143	        recovery_locator: str,
144	    ) -> None:
145	        try:
146	            self._conn.execute(
147	                "INSERT INTO legacy_logins (client_id, legacy_handle, login_id, recovery_locator) "
148	                "VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
149	                (client_id, legacy_handle, login_id, recovery_locator),
150	            )
151	            self._conn.commit()
152	        except sqlite3.IntegrityError as exc:
153	            raise ValueError(
154	                f"legacy handle already imported for client: {client_id}/{legacy_handle}"
155	            ) from exc
156	
157	    # -- authorization codes ------------------------------------------
158	
159	    def create_auth_code(self, code: str, client_id: str, account_id: str) -> None:
160	        self._conn.execute(
161	            "INSERT INTO auth_codes (code, client_id, account_id, created_at, used) "
162	            "VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, 0)",
163	            (code, client_id, account_id, time.time()),
164	        )
165	        self._conn.commit()
166	
167	    def get_auth_code(self, code: str) -> Optional[sqlite3.Row]:
168	        return self._conn.execute("SELECT * FROM auth_codes WHERE code = ?", (code,)).fetchone()
169	
170	    def mark_auth_code_used(self, code: str) -> None:
171	        self._conn.execute("UPDATE auth_codes SET used = 1 WHERE code = ?", (code,))
172	        self._conn.commit()
173	
174	    # -- refresh tokens -------------------------------------------------
175	
176	    def create_refresh_token(self, token: str, client_id: str, account_id: str) -> None:
177	        self._conn.execute(
178	            "INSERT INTO refresh_tokens (token, client_id, account_id, created_at, revoked) "
179	            "VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, 0)",
180	            (token, client_id, account_id, time.time()),
181	        )
182	        self._conn.commit()
183	
184	    def get_refresh_token(self, token: str) -> Optional[sqlite3.Row]:
185	        return self._conn.execute(
186	            "SELECT * FROM refresh_tokens WHERE token = ?", (token,)
187	        ).fetchone()
188	
189	    def revoke_refresh_token(self, token: str) -> None:
190	        self._conn.execute("UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked = 1 WHERE token = ?", (token,))
191	        self._conn.commit()
192	
193	    # -- refresh grants ---------------------------------------------------
194	
195	    def create_refresh_grant(
196	        self, token: str, client_id: str, account_id: str, decision: dict
197	    ) -> None:
198	        """Create a grant with `decision` as both its current decision and the sole entry of its append-only decision history."""
199	        self._conn.execute(
200	            "INSERT INTO refresh_grants "
201	            "(token, client_id, account_id, current_decision, decision_history, created_at) "
202	            "VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
203	            (
204	                token,
205	                client_id,
206	                account_id,
207	                json.dumps(decision),
208	                json.dumps([decision]),
209	                time.time(),
210	            ),
211	        )
212	        self._conn.commit()
213	
214	    def get_refresh_grant(self, token: str) -> Optional[sqlite3.Row]:
215	        return self._conn.execute(
216	            "SELECT * FROM refresh_grants WHERE token = ?", (token,)
217	        ).fetchone()
218	
219	    def append_grant_decision(self, token: str, decision: dict) -> None:
220	        """Append `decision` to the grant's history and make it the current decision."""
221	        record = self.get_refresh_grant(token)
222	        history = json.loads(record["decision_history"])
223	        history.append(decision)
224	        self._conn.execute(
225	            "UPDATE refresh_grants SET current_decision = ?, decision_history = ? WHERE token = ?",
226	            (json.dumps(decision), json.dumps(history), token),
227	        )
228	        self._conn.commit()
